# FOUNDATIONS OF PHYSICS I: MECHANICS

## 1. Physical quantities, units, and mathematical models

Physics describes observations using measurable quantities and mathematical relations. A physical quantity needs both a numerical value and a unit. In the International System of Units, length is measured in metres (m), time in seconds (s), and mass in kilograms (kg). Velocity therefore has units m/s, acceleration m/s^2, force kg m/s^2 or newtons (N), and energy kg m^2/s^2 or joules (J). Every equation must be dimensionally consistent: quantities added or equated must have compatible dimensions. Dimensional analysis can detect an error but cannot determine dimensionless numerical factors.

A model deliberately retains some features of a system while neglecting others. A point particle has position and mass but no resolved shape; a rigid body keeps distances between its parts fixed; a frictionless surface ignores tangential contact forces. A good explanation states which model is used, the physical regime in which it is reasonable, and the meaning of any approximation. Numerical agreement with one example does not prove that an approximation remains valid for other regimes.

Scalars, such as mass, temperature, and energy, have magnitude but no spatial direction. Vectors, such as displacement, velocity, acceleration, and force, have both magnitude and direction. In Cartesian coordinates, a vector may be decomposed into components along orthogonal axes. The magnitude of a two-dimensional vector A = (Ax, Ay) is sqrt(Ax^2 + Ay^2), and its direction is fixed by the signs and ratio of its components. Equations involving vectors must respect directions and signs, not just magnitudes.

## 2. Position, displacement, velocity, and acceleration

Position x(t) specifies where a particle is relative to a chosen origin. Displacement Delta x = x_final - x_initial is a signed change of position, while distance travelled is the total path length. Over a time interval Delta t, average velocity is Delta x/Delta t. Instantaneous velocity is the derivative v(t) = dx/dt. In one dimension, speed equals |v|, but average speed (distance/time) is generally different from the magnitude of average velocity.

Acceleration measures the change in velocity: a(t) = dv/dt = d^2x/dt^2. Negative acceleration does not necessarily mean slowing down. A body moving in the negative x direction speeds up when acceleration is also negative. A velocity-time graph has slope equal to acceleration, while the signed area under the velocity-time graph gives displacement. The signed area under an acceleration-time curve gives the change in velocity.

When acceleration a is constant, integration gives v(t) = v0 + a t and x(t) = x0 + v0 t + (1/2) a t^2. Eliminating time yields v^2 = v0^2 + 2 a (x - x0). These relations are exact only for constant acceleration. If acceleration depends on time, velocity, or position, one must integrate the appropriate differential equation instead.

## 3. Motion in two and three dimensions

Velocity in two dimensions is v = (vx, vy), and acceleration is a = (ax, ay). Cartesian components can be treated independently as long as the chosen coordinate axes are fixed. For a projectile in uniform gravity without air resistance, ax = 0 and ay = -g if the positive y axis points upward. The trajectory obeys x(t) = x0 + v0 cos(theta) t and y(t) = y0 + v0 sin(theta) t - (1/2) g t^2. The acceleration is downward at every point, including at the maximum height where vertical velocity momentarily vanishes.

For launch and landing at the same height, the flight time is T = 2 v0 sin(theta)/g and the range is R = v0^2 sin(2 theta)/g. The maximum rise above launch is H = v0^2 sin^2(theta)/(2g). These compact formulas fail if the launch and landing heights differ, drag matters, or gravity varies appreciably. The general parametric trajectory should be used instead of applying a special-case range expression blindly.

Relative velocity depends on the reference frame. In Galilean mechanics, v_A relative to B = v_A - v_B. A passenger moving inside a train may have a small speed relative to the train and a much larger speed relative to the ground. Distinguishing the frame prevents confusion when combining velocities and interpreting motion.

## 4. Newton's laws and free-body diagrams

Newton's first law states that a body with zero net external force maintains constant velocity in an inertial frame. The second law connects net external force and momentum: F_net = dp/dt; for constant mass this reduces to F_net = m a. The third law states that forces between two interacting bodies occur in equal and opposite pairs acting on different bodies. The pair does not cancel in the force balance for either body taken individually.

A free-body diagram isolates one chosen body and shows only forces acting on that body. After assigning axes, write the signed component equations sum(Fx) = m ax and sum(Fy) = m ay. Weight near Earth's surface is mg downward. The normal force is perpendicular to a contact surface, and its magnitude must be determined from the dynamics; it is not automatically equal to mg. Tension is directed along a taut ideal string away from the body being pulled.

Consider a block resting on a level floor. With no vertical acceleration and no other vertical forces, N = mg. On a slope of angle theta, the weight components relative to the surface are mg sin(theta) along the slope and mg cos(theta) perpendicular to it. If there is no acceleration perpendicular to the slope and no other perpendicular force, N = mg cos(theta). Resolving forces before substituting numbers is more reliable than memorizing a force diagram without its assumptions.

## 5. Friction, elasticity, and resistance

Static friction adjusts to oppose relative slipping up to a maximum magnitude |fs| <= mu_s N. Its actual value is not always mu_s N. Once sliding occurs, an approximate kinetic-friction model is |fk| = mu_k N, directed opposite the relative motion of the surfaces. The coefficients depend on the materials and conditions, so they are not universal constants.

Hooke's law describes a linear restoring force F = -k x for displacement x from an equilibrium position. The negative sign means that the force points toward equilibrium. An ideal spring stores elastic potential energy U = (1/2) k x^2. The relation becomes inaccurate for sufficiently large deformation, plastic deformation, or strongly nonlinear materials. Springs in parallel add stiffness; ideal springs in series add reciprocal stiffnesses.

Fluid drag often depends on speed and can change direction with motion. At sufficiently low Reynolds number, linear drag models may be appropriate; in other regimes a force proportional to speed squared may provide a better approximation. Terminal speed occurs when total force becomes zero, not because gravity ceases to act. Acceleration approaches zero even though the body may continue to move.

## 6. Work, kinetic energy, and power

The work done by a force during displacement is the line integral W = integral(F dot dr). A constant force F over straight displacement d makes W = F d cos(theta). Work can be positive, negative, or zero depending on the angle between force and displacement. A centripetal force perpendicular to velocity does no instantaneous work on uniform circular motion.

Kinetic energy is K = (1/2) m v^2 for nonrelativistic motion. The net-work theorem W_net = K_final - K_initial follows from the equation of motion and applies even when individual forces vary. Power is the rate of doing work: P = dW/dt = F dot v for an instantaneous force acting on a moving particle. Power has SI units J/s or watts (W).

Energy methods can eliminate the time dependence when the final speed or position is sought. They do not by themselves reveal how long a trajectory takes. If friction removes mechanical energy, the lost mechanical energy normally appears as thermal energy or other nonmechanical forms, rather than disappearing.

## 7. Potential energy and energy conservation

A conservative force can be represented by a potential-energy function U with F = -grad(U). In one dimension F(x) = -dU/dx. Work by a conservative force is W = -Delta U, so mechanical energy E = K + U remains constant if only conservative forces do work and the system has no relevant time-dependent driving. A convenient choice of zero potential energy does not change any measurable force or energy difference.

For approximately uniform gravity, U(y) = m g y. A mass dropped from height h gains kinetic energy mgh by the time it reaches the lower reference level if drag is negligible and its initial speed is zero. Its impact speed is sqrt(2gh), independent of mass, under those assumptions. The formula does not incorporate aerodynamic resistance, internal deformation, or variable g.

At a stable equilibrium, potential energy has a local minimum. Expanding a smooth potential around such a minimum gives U(x) approximately U(x_eq) + (1/2) k (x-x_eq)^2, which explains why harmonic oscillations arise across many different physical systems. A local maximum corresponds to an unstable equilibrium for small perturbations.

## 8. Momentum, impulse, and collisions

Momentum is the vector p = m v for a particle of constant mass. External impulse J = integral(F_ext dt) changes a system's total momentum: J = Delta p. Internal action-reaction forces cancel in the total momentum balance for a suitable isolated system. Therefore total momentum is conserved when the net external impulse is zero, even if the forces during a collision are very large.

In a one-dimensional perfectly inelastic collision, two objects stick together and share a final velocity v_final = (m1 v1 + m2 v2)/(m1 + m2). Momentum is conserved but kinetic energy usually decreases. For an elastic collision of an isolated system, both total momentum and total kinetic energy are conserved. Mechanical energy can also be temporarily stored elastically during impact; total energy is always conserved when all relevant forms are counted.

The centre-of-mass position is R = sum(mi ri)/sum(mi), and its acceleration obeys M a_cm = F_external. This provides a powerful separation between overall motion of a system and motion of its parts. It is essential to state which bodies belong to the system before claiming that momentum is conserved.

## 9. Circular motion and gravitation

Uniform circular motion has constant speed but changing velocity direction. The inward radial acceleration has magnitude a_c = v^2/r = omega^2 r, where v = omega r. The net radial force must have magnitude m v^2/r. 'Centripetal force' is not an additional fundamental interaction: the necessary inward force might be tension, gravity, friction, or some combination of actual forces.

Newton's gravitational law for two point masses is F = G m1 m2/r^2, with attraction along their separation. For a spherically symmetric body, the exterior field acts as if its mass were concentrated at its centre. Circular orbital speed about a much heavier central mass M is v = sqrt(GM/r); orbital period is T = 2 pi sqrt(r^3/(GM)). At the same radius, Newtonian escape speed is sqrt(2GM/r), provided other forces and energy losses can be neglected.

The common near-Earth approximation g = GM/R^2 treats g as almost constant over modest height changes. At large altitudes one must work with U(r) = -GMm/r instead of extending the linear expression mgh indefinitely. A satellite in circular orbit is continually accelerating inward while its speed stays constant in the ideal two-body model.

## 10. Rotational kinematics and dynamics

For rotation about a fixed axis, angular position theta, angular velocity omega = dtheta/dt, and angular acceleration alpha = domega/dt parallel position, velocity, and acceleration in linear motion. The tangential acceleration at radius r is a_t = r alpha, while radial acceleration is a_r = r omega^2. The full acceleration combines these perpendicular components.

Torque about an origin is the vector tau = r cross F. Its magnitude is r F sin(phi), where phi is the angle between the lever arm and force. The rotational analogue of mass is moment of inertia I = integral(r_perp^2 dm), which depends on the selected axis. For a rigid body rotating about a fixed principal axis, tau_net = I alpha. Rotational kinetic energy is K_rot = (1/2) I omega^2, and angular momentum for fixed-axis rotation is L = I omega.

For a uniform disk about its symmetry axis, I = (1/2) M R^2; for a thin hoop, I = M R^2. The parallel-axis theorem relates the moment of inertia about a shifted parallel axis to the centre-of-mass moment via I = I_cm + M d^2. If external torque vanishes, angular momentum is conserved; a skater who reduces I increases omega when angular momentum along the axis is maintained.

## 11. Oscillations and simple harmonic motion

Simple harmonic motion results from a restoring force proportional to displacement: m x'' + k x = 0. The solution is x(t) = A cos(omega t + phi), where omega = sqrt(k/m), period T = 2 pi/omega, and frequency f = 1/T. The velocity and acceleration follow by differentiation. Acceleration points toward equilibrium and has magnitude omega^2 |x|.

Total oscillator energy in the ideal spring model is E = (1/2) k A^2, partitioned between kinetic and elastic potential energy during motion. Frequency is independent of amplitude only while the oscillator stays in the linear regime. Damping introduces energy loss; a simple viscously damped oscillator satisfies m x'' + b x' + k x = 0. Depending on the damping strength, the system can oscillate with decaying amplitude or return to equilibrium without oscillating.

A simple pendulum of length L satisfies theta'' + (g/L) sin(theta) = 0 in an ideal plane without drag. For small angles measured in radians, sin(theta) approximately theta and the equation becomes harmonic. Its period is T approximately 2 pi sqrt(L/g). At larger amplitudes, the period depends on amplitude, so applying the small-angle relation without checking theta can introduce systematic error.

## 12. Fluid statics and buoyancy

Pressure is force per unit area acting normally on a surface. In a static fluid with uniform density rho under uniform gravity, the pressure difference between depths is Delta p = rho g Delta h, with deeper points at higher pressure. Absolute pressure is surface pressure plus the hydrostatic increment; gauge pressure is measured relative to a chosen ambient reference.

Archimedes' principle states that the buoyant force on a submerged object is equal to the weight of displaced fluid: Fb = rho_fluid g V_displaced. For a fully submerged object with uniform density rho_object, weight is rho_object g V_object. If the upward buoyant force exceeds weight and no other vertical forces counteract it, the initial net force is upward. A floating object displaces just enough liquid to support its weight in equilibrium.

Hydrostatic formulas assume the liquid is at rest and that variations in fluid density can be neglected. Compressibility, acceleration of the container, or substantial density gradients modify the pressure profile. Buoyancy results from the integrated pressure on the object's surface rather than a mysterious force independent of pressure.

## 13. Fluid motion and continuity

Conservation of mass for steady, incompressible flow in a pipe gives A1 v1 = A2 v2, where A is cross-sectional area and v is the average speed normal to the section. Narrowing a pipe increases speed if the volume flow rate remains constant. For compressible fluids, the more general mass-flow relation rho A v must be considered.

An ideal Bernoulli relation along a streamline is p + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant. It represents mechanical energy per unit volume when flow is steady, inviscid, and incompressible, and no shaft work or other complications occur. It should not be applied blindly across viscous losses, pumps, turbulent mixing, or unrelated streamlines.

The Reynolds number compares inertial and viscous scales: Re = rho v L/mu for a chosen characteristic length L and dynamic viscosity mu. It helps identify regimes where laminar-flow approximations may be reasonable, but the onset of turbulence depends on geometry and perturbations as well as Re.

# FOUNDATIONS OF PHYSICS I: THERMODYNAMICS

## 14. Thermal equilibrium and temperature

Temperature is an intensive property that characterizes thermal equilibrium. The zeroth law states that if system A is in thermal equilibrium with system C, and B is independently in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B share a common equilibrium temperature. Heat is energy transferred because of temperature difference; it is not a substance stored inside the body. Internal energy is instead a property of the system's microscopic state.

The absolute temperature scale uses kelvin, with T(K) = T(degrees C) + 273.15. Differences in Celsius degrees and kelvin have the same numerical size, but ratios and ideal-gas relations must use absolute temperature. Thermal expansion can be approximated for small changes by Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T, where alpha is the linear expansion coefficient. Constraints can produce thermal stress even when an object cannot freely expand.

## 15. Gases and the kinetic model

The ideal-gas equation is P V = n R T = N k_B T. Here P is absolute pressure, V is volume, n is number of moles, N is the number of particles, R is the universal gas constant, and k_B is Boltzmann's constant. This equation is approximate for dilute gases at temperatures and densities where microscopic interactions and particle volumes may be neglected. It is not generally accurate near condensation or at very high density.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas in equilibrium, the average translational kinetic energy per particle is (3/2) k_B T. The internal energy is U = (3/2) n R T, so Delta U depends only on the temperature change in this model. At fixed n and V, pressure increases in direct proportion to absolute temperature; at fixed n and T, pressure is inversely proportional to volume. The microscopic assumptions matter when interpreting these macroscopic trends.

## 16. The first law of thermodynamics

With W_by defined as work done by the system on its surroundings, the first law is Delta U = Q - W_by. Positive Q denotes net heat transferred into the system; positive W_by denotes energy leaving the system as mechanical work. Another sign convention may use work done on the system, so the convention must always be declared explicitly.

In a quasistatic expansion of a gas against an external pressure, W_by = integral(P dV) when the gas pressure agrees with the relevant boundary pressure. For an ideal gas undergoing a reversible isothermal process, Delta U = 0 and W_by = n R T ln(V_final/V_initial). Expansion gives positive work, compression negative work by the gas. In an ideal isochoric process volume is fixed, hence boundary work vanishes. In a reversible adiabatic process, Q = 0, and energy changes through work alone.

## 17. Heat capacities and calorimetry

Heat capacity C relates a small heat input to a corresponding temperature rise under specified conditions. Specific heat c is heat capacity per unit mass. When c is approximately constant and no phase change occurs, Q = m c Delta T. Heat lost by one isolated component equals heat gained by others if there are no unaccounted energy transfers. This forms the basis for idealized calorimetry.

For an ideal monatomic gas, the molar constant-volume heat capacity is Cv = (3/2) R and the constant-pressure value is Cp = (5/2) R, so Cp - Cv = R. The extra heat at constant pressure partly supplies expansion work. Heat capacity varies with accessible molecular degrees of freedom, and real materials may have temperature-dependent heat capacities.

During melting or vaporization, energy can be absorbed or released while temperature remains approximately constant for a pure substance undergoing a phase transition at fixed pressure. This energy is often modelled by Q = m L, where L is the latent heat per unit mass, and it is distinct from sensible heating proportional to Delta T.

## 18. Heat transfer mechanisms

Heat can flow by conduction, convection, and radiation. Conduction arises from microscopic energy transfer within material. For a uniform plane slab with steady one-dimensional temperature gradient, heat-transfer power approximately equals k A Delta T/L, where k is thermal conductivity, A is cross-sectional area, and L is thickness. This simple result assumes constant k, no internal heat generation, and a steady state.

Convection involves heat transported by the motion of fluid together with conduction across boundary layers. It depends strongly on geometry, flow regime, fluid properties, and boundary conditions. Thermal radiation can transfer energy through vacuum. An ideal blackbody emits a total power per surface area proportional to the fourth power of absolute temperature: M = sigma T^4. A real surface has emissivity that may depend on wavelength, temperature, and angle.

## 19. Heat engines and the second law

A cyclic heat engine absorbs heat Qh from a hot reservoir, rejects some heat Qc to a colder reservoir, and produces work W = Qh - Qc when magnitudes are used. Its efficiency eta = W/Qh is less than one for a conventional engine operating between finite-temperature reservoirs. For reversible operation between reservoirs at Th and Tc, Carnot efficiency is eta_C = 1 - Tc/Th, with all temperatures in kelvin.

The second law constrains which energy transformations are possible. A process can conserve energy yet be impossible because of the direction of spontaneous change. Clausius' statement rules out spontaneous heat flow from colder to hotter body without other effects. Kelvin-Planck's statement rules out converting all heat absorbed from one reservoir into net work in a purely cyclic device without other changes.

## 20. Entropy and reversible processes

For a reversible transfer of an infinitesimal amount of heat at temperature T, the system entropy change obeys dS = dQ_rev/T. Entropy is a state function; the entropy change between two equilibrium states does not depend on the chosen reversible reference path. For an isolated system the total entropy does not decrease. An actual irreversible process may generate entropy even though the energy budget satisfies the first law exactly.

A reversible Carnot cycle has zero net change in entropy of the working substance over one cycle and balances reservoir entropy transfers. A real engine generates entropy because of dissipation and finite temperature differences. Entropy is not simply a synonym for everyday 'disorder'; quantitative statements require identifying the macrostate, relevant microscopic configurations, or an operational thermodynamic definition.

## 21. Model checking, uncertainty, and extrapolation

Every calculation should state the chosen system, the sign convention, the known parameters, and the predicted quantity. After deriving an expression, check dimensions, units, extreme limits, and whether the result is physically plausible. For example, the period of an ideal simple pendulum should increase with length and decrease with gravitational acceleration. An energy expression with dimensions of force is inconsistent before any numerical substitution is performed.

Measurements include random scatter and possible systematic errors. Repeating the same biased measurement reduces some random uncertainty but does not eliminate calibration bias. When fitting a model, report what parameters were estimated, what error model was assumed, and how goodness of fit was checked. A fit that describes a narrow range of measurements does not necessarily justify extrapolation to larger forces, temperatures, speeds, or different materials.

## Dimensional analysis

[force] = M L T^-2; [energy] = M L^2 T^-2. A dimensionless coefficient cannot be fixed from units alone, and additive terms must share dimensions. A physically meaningful equation must balance dimensions on both sides. Unit checks can reject a proposed law without proving that it is correct. This reasoning underlies similarity laws and nondimensional modeling.

## Fluid statics

## Hamiltonian mechanics

qdot = partial H/partial p; pdot = -partial H/partial q. The Hamiltonian equals the energy only under suitable assumptions. The Hamiltonian formulation turns dynamics into first-order equations in generalized positions and momenta. Phase-space flow offers a natural setting for symplectic numerical integration.

## Lagrangian mechanics

## Measurement uncertainty

Every reported measurement combines a numerical estimate with assumptions about resolution, noise, calibration, and bias. Careful error budgets connect laboratory procedures to quantitative inference. For uncorrelated errors, var(x+y) = var(x) + var(y). Systematic uncertainty is not reduced merely by repeating identical observations.

## Newtonian dynamics

## Numerical integration

The choice of state variables determines how efficiently the physics can be described. Forward Euler uses x(t+dt) = x(t) + dt f(x,t). Stability and truncation error depend on the solver and the chosen step size. A differential equation can be approximated by advancing a solution across discrete time steps. Symplectic methods are valuable for long-term Hamiltonian dynamics.


## Orbital mechanics

Circular orbits balance inward gravitational acceleration with centripetal acceleration. Orbital trajectories connect conservation of energy to angular momentum. v_c = sqrt(GM/r); T = 2 pi sqrt(r^3/(GM)). A circular-orbit formula should not be substituted directly into an eccentric orbit.


## Orbital mechanics

## Potential energy

F = -grad U. Only potential-energy differences affect classical equations of motion. A conservative force can be represented by the negative gradient of a scalar potential. Stable equilibria occur near local minima of the potential energy.

## Reference frames

Galilean transformations use x' = x - ut in the nonrelativistic limit. Accelerating frames generally require apparent inertial forces. Coordinates describe measurements relative to a chosen observer, but a change of coordinates cannot alter the physical event being described. The choice of frame often converts a complicated motion into a simpler one.

## Rotational motion

Torques change angular momentum, just as forces change linear momentum. Conservation of angular momentum explains spin-up during contraction. tau = dL/dt; K_rot = I omega^2/2. The moment of inertia depends on the mass distribution about the selected axis.

## Universal gravitation

Two point masses attract with an inverse-square force directed along their separation. The same law explains terrestrial attraction and Keplerian orbital motion. F = G M m/r^2. Extended bodies require integration unless spherical symmetry applies.

## Work and kinetic energy

The work done by the net force equals the change in kinetic energy along a trajectory. Energy arguments often avoid solving the full time-dependent trajectory. W_net = Delta K = (m/2)(v_f^2 - v_i^2). Work depends on displacement along the force, not on elapsed time alone.

## Entropy

Delta S = integral(dQ_rev/T) for a reversible path. The entropy of an isolated system cannot decrease in the macroscopic second-law description. Entropy counts, in a statistical sense, how many microscopic arrangements are compatible with a macroscopic description. Entropy connects equilibrium thermodynamics to probability.

## First law of thermodynamics

Delta U = Q - W_by for the convention in which W_by is work done by the system. Sign conventions must be stated before comparing formulas from different texts. The internal energy of a system changes through heat transfer and work. This bookkeeping principle applies to engines, refrigeration, and gas cycles.

## Free energy

Thermodynamic potentials identify equilibrium under different environmental constraints. Free-energy differences determine the direction of many spontaneous processes. F = U - T S; G = H - T S. The appropriate potential depends on controlled variables such as pressure or volume.

## Partition function

The choice of state variables determines how efficiently the physics can be described. Z = sum_i exp(-E_i/(k_B T)). ## Phase transitions

The choice of state variables determines how efficiently the physics can be described. Latent heat equals T Delta S at a reversible first-order transition. Continuous transitions need not involve a latent heat. Matter can change qualitative behavior when temperature, pressure, or other control parameters cross a phase boundary. Critical phenomena link macroscopic behavior to correlations across scales.

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.075 m^3 and material density 375.88 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1192.3 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 876.9 N and the weight is 276.46 N; their signed upward difference is 600.45 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 201.64 N acts at a distance of 0.579 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 35.041 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 67.034 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 4.719 kg is released from rest at a height of 82.127 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 40.135 m/s and the kinetic energy is 3800.6 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 213.45 kg follows a circle of radius 2.883 m at constant speed 27.887 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 269.75 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 57579 N, and rotation frequency is 1.5395 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Physical setup: A simple pendulum has length 4.924 m and an initial angular displacement of 2.369 degrees.

Relevant law: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Calculated result: The estimated oscillation period is 4.4522 s and its frequency is 0.22461 Hz.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Conditions of validity: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 912.22 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 171.29 m below a surface at pressure 101.66 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

The pressure increase is 1532.3 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1634 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Worked example: Standing wave on a stretched string

Physical setup: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 2.473 m, tension 213.3 N, and linear mass density 0.042 kg/m.

Relevant law: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Calculated result: The speed of transverse waves is 71.264 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 14.408 Hz.

Interpretation: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Conditions of validity: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 6359.5 Hz and has spatial wavelength 3.1 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 0.00015724 s and the propagation speed is 19715 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 726.44 K and cold reservoir at 325.17 K, absorbing 1430 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 55.238 percent, corresponding to at most 789.89 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 39.356 m/s and elevation angle 15.808 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 2.1865 s, the horizontal range is 82.798 m, and maximum height above launch is 5.8605 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Problem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 9.724 cm^2 and 7.636 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 0.323 m/s.

Solution method: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Answer: The speed in the second section is 0.41132 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.00031409 m^3/s.

Physical check: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Idealizations: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Ideal gas equation of state

A vessel contains 1.05 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 427.34 K in volume 153.68 liters.

The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

The equilibrium pressure is 24.276 kPa.

At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Worked example: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Physical setup: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 234.45 W/(m K), thickness 0.543 m, area 2.007 m^2, and temperature difference 27.253 K.

Relevant law: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Calculated result: The conduction rate is 23616 W.

Interpretation: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Conditions of validity: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 15.595 m/s, emitting a tone of 594.69 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 623.02 Hz, a frequency increase of 28.326 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1364 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7735 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.1786 km/s and the orbital period is 112.84 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Worked example: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Physical setup: A sample of mass 9.668 kg has specific heat capacity 1716.1 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 304.13 to 363.25 K.

Relevant law: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Calculated result: The required energy is 980.81 kJ.

Interpretation: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Conditions of validity: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.

## Worked example: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Physical setup: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 2.5826e-05 W/m^2.

Relevant law: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Calculated result: The ideal intensity level is 74.121 dB.

Interpretation: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Conditions of validity: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Problem: 7.861 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 407.35 K to 957.98 K.

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Answer: The internal energy change is 53984 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 14.746 kg and radius 0.193 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 55.64 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 0.27464 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 425.11 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 833.68 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.519 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Reversible isothermal gas work

1.98 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 365.96 K, changing volume from 35.262 to 71.088 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 4224 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 3.213 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 38.279 N/m and displaced by 0.474 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 3.4516 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.54934 Hz, and turning-point energy is 4.3002 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 17.309 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 3.389 m/s^2 for 16.393 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 72.865 m/s, and the signed displacement is 739.11 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

Interpretation: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Conditions of validity: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 74.616 kg follows a circle of radius 4.978 m at constant speed 67.555 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 916.77 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 68406 N, and rotation frequency is 2.1598 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Linear thermal expansion

A rod with initial length 8.198 m has expansion coefficient 2.1232e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 88.281 K.

For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

The calculated signed change in length is 15.366 mm.

For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 15.54 kg is released from rest at a height of 78.286 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 39.185 m/s and the kinetic energy is 11930 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 36.811 m/s, emitting a tone of 576.68 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 646.01 Hz, a frequency increase of 69.33 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Small-angle pendulum

The estimated oscillation period is 5.1865 s and its frequency is 0.19281 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Problem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 12.729 cm^2 and 7.326 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 4.691 m/s.

Solution method: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Answer: The speed in the second section is 8.1507 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0059712 m^3/s.

Physical check: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Idealizations: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Standing wave on a stretched string

A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 4.738 m, tension 16.171 N, and linear mass density 0.031 kg/m.

Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

The speed of transverse waves is 22.84 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 2.4103 Hz.

The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.

## Worked example: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Answer: The required energy is 762.6 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 186.05 W/(m K), thickness 0.475 m, area 2.358 m^2, and temperature difference 68.092 K.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 62890 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A force of magnitude 282.57 N acts at a distance of 3.869 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 93.587 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 1091.1 N m.

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.106 m^3 and material density 283.98 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 866.76 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 901 N and the weight is 295.2 N; their signed upward difference is 605.8 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 23.359 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 5.51 m/s^2 for 8.209 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 68.591 m/s, and the signed displacement is 377.41 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 34.412 kg block starts at 19.483 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.433. The surface extends for 14.215 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 44.696 m. After the available distance its speed is 16.089 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 4.2463 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Thermal conduction measurement

A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

The fitted slope is 3.8583 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 3.9036 W/K.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 59.846 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 11.134 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 7.448 m/s and elevation angle 48.708 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 1.1413 s, the horizontal range is 5.6093 m, and maximum height above launch is 1.5967 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 31.402 kg and radius 1.87 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 132.33 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 54.905 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 4.8072e+05 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Worked example: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Physical setup: A fully submerged body has volume 0.062 m^3 and material density 1307.9 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 952.09 kg/m^3.

Relevant law: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Calculated result: The upward buoyancy is 578.88 N and the weight is 795.24 N; their signed upward difference is -216.35 N.

Interpretation: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Conditions of validity: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

Problem: A vessel contains 4.438 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 983.88 K in volume 146.6 liters.

Solution method: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Answer: The equilibrium pressure is 247.64 kPa.

Physical check: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 4.64 kg changes signed velocity from -5.488 to 7.267 m/s during 1.952 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 59.183 N s and the average net force is 30.319 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 21.233 kg and 17.416 kg and initial signed speeds 19.008 and 9.88 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is 14.895 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 398.61 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Answer: The speed in the second section is 1.0258 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.001122 m^3/s.

Physical check: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Idealizations: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Linear thermal expansion

The calculated signed change in length is 2.1912 mm.

For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.

## Reversible isothermal gas work

5.933 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 328.06 K, changing volume from 24.787 to 16.806 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is -6288.9 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 28.968 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 0.561 m/s^2 for 15.09 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 37.433 m/s, and the signed displacement is 501 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 2489.6 Hz and has spatial wavelength 4.482 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 0.00040168 s and the propagation speed is 11158 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Calculated result: The estimated oscillation period is 3.4115 s and its frequency is 0.29313 Hz.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 1381.2 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.141 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 24.127 m/s and elevation angle 54.294 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 3.9956 s, the horizontal range is 56.262 m, and maximum height above launch is 19.57 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 94.652 kg block starts at 20.109 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.079. The surface extends for 12.165 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 260.98 m. After the available distance its speed is 19.635 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 0.77473 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 43.766 m/s, emitting a tone of 932.82 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 1069.3 Hz, a frequency increase of 136.43 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

Problem: A stationary liquid has density 1086.1 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 97.085 m below a surface at pressure 103.26 kPa.

Solution method: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Answer: The pressure increase is 1034.1 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1137.3 kPa.

Physical check: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Idealizations: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 785.92 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.554 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 19.74 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 480.87 N/m and displaced by 0.299 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 4.9356 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.78552 Hz, and turning-point energy is 21.495 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Problem: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

Solution method: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 4.0346 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.75556 s^2.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 368.55 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 6739.5 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.6905 km/s and the orbital period is 91.771 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1047.5 K and cold reservoir at 296.48 K, absorbing 1667.6 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 71.697 percent, corresponding to at most 1195.6 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 237.87 kg follows a circle of radius 6.421 m at constant speed 67.546 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 710.55 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 1.6902e+05 N, and rotation frequency is 1.6742 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Worked example: Periodic wave propagation

Physical setup: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 12608 Hz and has spatial wavelength 0.253 m.

Relevant law: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Calculated result: The period is 7.9316e-05 s and the propagation speed is 3189.8 m/s.

Interpretation: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Conditions of validity: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 650.18 N m.

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 50.127 m/s, emitting a tone of 1213.6 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 1421.3 Hz, a frequency increase of 207.72 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 3.502 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -2.584 m/s^2 for 9.764 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is -21.728 m/s, and the signed displacement is -88.98 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

7.665 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 798.89 K to 846.18 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

The internal energy change is 4521.5 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Worked example: Ideal gas equation of state

Physical setup: A vessel contains 11.225 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 699.28 K in volume 27.309 liters.

Relevant law: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Calculated result: The equilibrium pressure is 2389.8 kPa.

Interpretation: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Conditions of validity: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 13.145 kg and 0.893 kg and initial signed speeds 19.259 and -5.288 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is 17.697 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 251.93 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 7.3277e-05 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 78.65 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 17.431 kg and radius 0.777 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 171.94 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 5.2618 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 77783 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 6.033 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 666.29 K, changing volume from 27.767 to 13.273 liters.

Calculated result: The work by the gas is -24670 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum

Answer: The estimated oscillation period is 2.9317 s and its frequency is 0.3411 Hz.

Physical check: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Idealizations: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 14.023 cm^2 and 10.24 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 1.311 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 1.7953 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0018384 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 5.256 kg is released from rest at a height of 45.949 m.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 15.181 kg changes signed velocity from 12.572 to -16.764 m/s during 1.87 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -445.35 N s and the average net force is -238.15 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

Problem: A force of magnitude 430.72 N acts at a distance of 3.311 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 9.747 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 241.44 N m.

## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 1166.1 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 152.42 m below a surface at pressure 102.3 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

The pressure increase is 1743 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1845.2 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 14.658 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -1.938 m/s^2 for 13.71 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is -11.912 m/s, and the signed displacement is 18.824 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 15.565 kg and radius 1.397 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 69.909 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 15.188 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 37115 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Spring oscillator

A mass of 4.282 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 589.01 N/m and displaced by 0.234 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 11.728 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.8666 Hz, and turning-point energy is 16.126 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 11.074 s, the horizontal range is 501 m, and maximum height above launch is 150.34 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Problem: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 150.28 W/(m K), thickness 0.23 m, area 3.332 m^2, and temperature difference 32.264 K.

Solution method: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Answer: The conduction rate is 70243 W.

Physical check: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Idealizations: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 63.313 kg block starts at 20.988 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.468. The surface extends for 21.082 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 47.989 m. After the available distance its speed is 15.716 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 4.5895 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 14.527 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 11.173 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 65.689 kg changes signed velocity from 12.155 to 8.565 m/s during 1.634 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -235.82 N s and the average net force is -144.32 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Physical setup: A fully submerged body has volume 0.013 m^3 and material density 952.36 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 790.9 kg/m^3.

Relevant law: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Calculated result: The upward buoyancy is 100.83 N and the weight is 121.41 N; their signed upward difference is -20.584 N.

Interpretation: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Conditions of validity: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 10.3 kg is released from rest at a height of 4.362 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 9.2495 m/s and the kinetic energy is 440.6 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 651.57 K and cold reservoir at 390.49 K, absorbing 8368.6 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 40.069 percent, corresponding to at most 3353.2 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 23.741 m/s, emitting a tone of 775.65 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 833.33 Hz, a frequency increase of 57.68 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 3.527 kg and 18.144 kg and initial signed speeds -6.514 and 3.014 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is 1.4633 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 134.04 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.
