## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 4.455 m and an initial angular displacement of 6.327 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 4.2349 s and its frequency is 0.23613 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Worked example: Periodic wave propagation

Physical setup: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 13221 Hz and has spatial wavelength 0.087 m.

Relevant law: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Calculated result: The period is 7.5638e-05 s and the propagation speed is 1150.2 m/s.

Interpretation: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Conditions of validity: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1653.8 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 8024.8 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 7.0478 km/s and the orbital period is 119.24 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Physical setup: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

Relevant law: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 4.0214 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.10218 s^2.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Reversible isothermal gas work

1.228 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 673.73 K, changing volume from 15.717 to 44.448 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 7151 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Worked example: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Physical setup: A sample of mass 2.717 kg has specific heat capacity 1324.7 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 279.16 to 374.27 K.

Relevant law: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Calculated result: The required energy is 342.3 kJ.

Interpretation: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Conditions of validity: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 150.89 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 11.056 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1001.8 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7372.8 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.3528 km/s and the orbital period is 105 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 13.43 kg is released from rest at a height of 37.377 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 27.076 m/s and the kinetic energy is 4922.7 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 30.941 m/s and elevation angle 71.381 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 5.9799 s, the horizontal range is 59.074 m, and maximum height above launch is 43.835 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 10.939 cm^2 and 5.748 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 3.213 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 6.1146 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0035147 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.13 m^3 and material density 1186.2 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1044.1 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 1331.1 N and the weight is 1512.2 N; their signed upward difference is -181.14 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Spring oscillator

A mass of 12.612 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 520.23 N/m and displaced by 0.366 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 6.4225 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.0222 Hz, and turning-point energy is 34.844 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Worked example: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Physical setup: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 74.589 W/(m K), thickness 0.41 m, area 2.542 m^2, and temperature difference 36.953 K.

Relevant law: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Calculated result: The conduction rate is 17089 W.

Interpretation: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Conditions of validity: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 64.556 kg block starts at 22.879 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.307. The surface extends for 19.225 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 86.933 m. After the available distance its speed is 20.191 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 3.0106 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Worked example: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Physical setup: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 20.038 kg and radius 1.676 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 133.54 rad/s.

Relevant law: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Calculated result: The moment of inertia is 28.143 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 2.5093e+05 J.

Interpretation: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Conditions of validity: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum

Problem: A simple pendulum has length 1.303 m and an initial angular displacement of 4.209 degrees.

Solution method: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Answer: The estimated oscillation period is 2.2903 s and its frequency is 0.43662 Hz.

Physical check: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Idealizations: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 18.045 kg changes signed velocity from -12.125 to 2.258 m/s during 0.321 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 259.54 N s and the average net force is 808.54 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Worked example: Hooke-law force calibration

Physical setup: A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

Relevant law: For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 556.82 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 554.96 N/m.

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.53029 N.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Problem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 2.29 m, tension 355.79 N, and linear mass density 0.017 kg/m.

Solution method: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Answer: The speed of transverse waves is 144.67 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 31.587 Hz.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 1.6894e-08 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 42.277 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 17.043 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -2.207 m/s^2 for 1.266 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 14.249 m/s, and the signed displacement is 19.808 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Solution method: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 4.0281 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.19168 s^2.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Linear thermal expansion

A rod with initial length 8.014 m has expansion coefficient 8.862e-06 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 144.16 K.

The calculated signed change in length is 10.238 mm.

For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.

## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1432.5 K and cold reservoir at 308.22 K, absorbing 1703.6 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 78.484 percent, corresponding to at most 1337 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 11.6 kg and 22.598 kg and initial signed speeds -4.804 and 12.597 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is 6.6946 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 1160.5 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Answer: The ideal intensity level is 23.237 dB.

Physical check: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Idealizations: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 184.68 kg follows a circle of radius 21.944 m at constant speed 75.524 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 259.93 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 48004 N, and rotation frequency is 0.54776 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 75.037 m/s and elevation angle 45.547 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 10.924 s, the horizontal range is 574.05 m, and maximum height above launch is 146.28 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 1.598 kg and 1.739 kg and initial signed speeds 0.875 and 13.181 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is 7.288 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 63.056 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 11.243 cm^2 and 14.332 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 1.575 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 1.2355 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0017708 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

Problem: A vessel contains 5.417 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 796.94 K in volume 122.17 liters.

Solution method: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Answer: The equilibrium pressure is 293.79 kPa.

Physical check: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 26.774 kg changes signed velocity from 7.086 to 14.508 m/s during 0.862 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 198.72 N s and the average net force is 230.53 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Hooke-law force calibration

Physical setup: A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

Relevant law: For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 422.06 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 426.55 N/m.

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 1.2546 N.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 993.81 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 155.57 m below a surface at pressure 93.754 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

The pressure increase is 1516.2 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1610 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 46.469 kg block starts at 18.76 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.187. The surface extends for 23.147 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 95.956 m. After the available distance its speed is 16.341 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.8338 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 749.13 K and cold reservoir at 229.25 K, absorbing 2295.9 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 69.398 percent, corresponding to at most 1593.3 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Steady heat conduction through a slab

The conduction rate is 37872 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 48.888 m/s, emitting a tone of 823.86 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 960.8 Hz, a frequency increase of 136.94 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 12.844 kg and radius 1.007 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 76.051 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 6.5122 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 18833 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 0.832 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 275.13 K, changing volume from 34.862 to 22.347 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is -846.41 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Worked example: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Conditions of validity: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Problem: 0.603 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 311.53 K to 727.51 K.

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 5.377 cm^2 and 14.874 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 1.856 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 0.67095 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.00099797 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 506.61 N acts at a distance of 0.041 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 22.83 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 8.0592 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 10.43 kg has specific heat capacity 2412.8 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 311.04 to 356.65 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 1147.9 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 1.585 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 2.063 m/s^2 for 15.818 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 34.218 m/s, and the signed displacement is 283.16 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 101.88 kg block starts at 9.128 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.54. The surface extends for 27.769 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 7.867 m. After the available distance its speed is 0 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 5.2956 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 950.04 K and cold reservoir at 312.11 K, absorbing 2532.1 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 67.148 percent, corresponding to at most 1700.3 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 3.457 m and an initial angular displacement of 1.476 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 3.7305 s and its frequency is 0.26806 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 75.459 m/s and elevation angle 54.811 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 12.577 s, the horizontal range is 546.91 m, and maximum height above launch is 193.9 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 207.11 kg follows a circle of radius 8.125 m at constant speed 27.573 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 93.572 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 19380 N, and rotation frequency is 0.54011 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 56.113 kg changes signed velocity from -18.801 to 0.267 m/s during 1.949 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 1070 N s and the average net force is 548.98 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Physical setup: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 25.742 kg and radius 0.914 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 164.49 rad/s.

Relevant law: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Calculated result: The moment of inertia is 10.752 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 1.4545e+05 J.

Interpretation: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Conditions of validity: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 3.262 kg and 8.515 kg and initial signed speeds -2.256 and -9.663 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is -7.6114 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 64.698 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Ideal gas equation of state

A vessel contains 3.532 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 307.43 K in volume 46.296 liters.

The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

The equilibrium pressure is 195.01 kPa.

At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.0169 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.30211 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 5807.5 Hz and has spatial wavelength 0.245 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 0.00017219 s and the propagation speed is 1422.8 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Linear thermal expansion

A rod with initial length 5.83 m has expansion coefficient 1.5642e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 26.987 K.

For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

The calculated signed change in length is 2.461 mm.

For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Worked example: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Physical setup: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 268.21 W/(m K), thickness 0.33 m, area 1.295 m^2, and temperature difference 41.493 K.

Relevant law: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Calculated result: The conduction rate is 43672 W.

Interpretation: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Conditions of validity: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Problem: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 0.00079978 W/m^2.

Solution method: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Answer: The ideal intensity level is 89.03 dB.

Physical check: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Idealizations: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.008 m^3 and material density 470.37 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 760.79 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 59.686 N and the weight is 36.902 N; their signed upward difference is 22.784 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 13.405 m/s and elevation angle 70.52 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 2.5774 s, the horizontal range is 11.522 m, and maximum height above launch is 8.143 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 44.899 kg changes signed velocity from 13.931 to -6.483 m/s during 1.942 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -916.57 N s and the average net force is -471.97 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Ideal gas equation of state

Calculated result: The equilibrium pressure is 314.65 kPa.

Conditions of validity: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 31.695 m/s, emitting a tone of 546.53 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 602.17 Hz, a frequency increase of 55.644 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 1.146 kg is released from rest at a height of 94.055 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 42.95 m/s and the kinetic energy is 1057 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Hooke-law force calibration

A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

The fitted slope is 153.15 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 153.32 N/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.12639 N.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 18860 Hz and has spatial wavelength 1.509 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 5.3024e-05 s and the propagation speed is 28459 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.0559 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.21118 s^2.

## Worked example: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Physical setup: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 8.5335e-09 W/m^2.

Relevant law: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Calculated result: The ideal intensity level is 39.311 dB.

Interpretation: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Conditions of validity: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 149.62 kg block starts at 17.618 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.601. The surface extends for 9.488 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 26.332 m. After the available distance its speed is 14.091 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 5.8938 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 524.79 K and cold reservoir at 357.28 K, absorbing 7327.9 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 31.919 percent, corresponding to at most 2339 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Worked example: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 112.03 kg follows a circle of radius 15.91 m at constant speed 51.435 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 166.28 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 18628 N, and rotation frequency is 0.51453 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1116.6 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7487.6 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.2962 km/s and the orbital period is 107.47 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.086 m^3 and material density 1185.5 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1249 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 1053.4 N and the weight is 999.8 N; their signed upward difference is 53.558 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 1314.1 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.185 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 6.9898 km/s and the orbital period is 122.23 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Problem: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 9.5274e-10 W/m^2.

Solution method: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Answer: The ideal intensity level is 29.79 dB.

Physical check: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Idealizations: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.124 m^3 and material density 558.14 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 828.97 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 1008.1 N and the weight is 678.71 N; their signed upward difference is 329.34 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Escape speed from a central mass

Physical setup: Consider a test object at altitude 315.09 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Relevant law: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Calculated result: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.919 km/s.

Interpretation: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Conditions of validity: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Problem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 13.405 cm^2 and 1.699 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 0.411 m/s.

Solution method: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Answer: The speed in the second section is 3.2428 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.00055095 m^3/s.

Physical check: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Idealizations: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 10.357 kg is released from rest at a height of 64.986 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 35.701 m/s and the kinetic energy is 6600.5 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1463.4 K and cold reservoir at 404.08 K, absorbing 5842 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 72.388 percent, corresponding to at most 4228.9 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 3893.1 Hz and has spatial wavelength 3.738 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 0.00025686 s and the propagation speed is 14553 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 16.813 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 1.707 m/s^2 for 16.106 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 44.306 m/s, and the signed displacement is 492.19 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 6.028 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 649.5 K, changing volume from 20.144 to 15.833 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is -7838.6 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A force of magnitude 84.097 N acts at a distance of 2.139 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 161.97 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 55.662 N m.

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 1224.8 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 40.194 m below a surface at pressure 94.217 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

The pressure increase is 482.78 kPa and the absolute pressure is 576.99 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 5.263 kg and 2.513 kg and initial signed speeds -9.35 and 18.837 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is -0.2407 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 675.67 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 4.738 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 85.187 N/m and displaced by 0.092 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 4.2402 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.67485 Hz, and turning-point energy is 0.36051 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 77.28 m/s and elevation angle 51.482 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 12.331 s, the horizontal range is 593.47 m, and maximum height above launch is 186.4 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 8.728 kg changes signed velocity from 0.343 to -1.94 m/s during 1.106 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is -19.926 N s and the average net force is -18.016 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 147.66 kg follows a circle of radius 23.072 m at constant speed 38.435 m/s.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 91.597 kg block starts at 29.988 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.597. The surface extends for 15.029 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 76.802 m. After the available distance its speed is 26.894 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 5.8546 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 2.294 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.00061845 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 13.412 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -0.556 m/s^2 for 1.504 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 12.576 m/s, and the signed displacement is 19.543 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1588.2 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7959.2 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.0768 km/s and the orbital period is 117.78 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Physical setup: A simple pendulum has length 5.491 m and an initial angular displacement of 3.334 degrees.

Relevant law: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Calculated result: The estimated oscillation period is 4.7016 s and its frequency is 0.21269 Hz.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Conditions of validity: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Problem: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 14.919 W/(m K), thickness 0.362 m, area 1.06 m^2, and temperature difference 28.75 K.

Solution method: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Answer: The conduction rate is 1256 W.

Physical check: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Idealizations: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Worked example: Standing wave on a stretched string

Relevant law: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Calculated result: The speed of transverse waves is 105.7 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 14.528 Hz.

Interpretation: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 4.646 kg follows a circle of radius 17.592 m at constant speed 33.861 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 65.175 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 302.81 N, and rotation frequency is 0.30634 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 4556 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

0.183 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 323.89 K to 367.26 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

The internal energy change is 98.968 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 503.89 K and cold reservoir at 448.47 K, absorbing 4263.2 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 10.998 percent, corresponding to at most 468.88 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

Solution method: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Answer: The equilibrium pressure is 54.843 kPa.

Physical check: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Problem: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

Solution method: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 4.0453 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.22094 s^2.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Lever arm and rotational effect

A force of magnitude 342.2 N acts at a distance of 2.252 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 105.28 degrees to the lever.

The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

The calculated torque magnitude is 743.38 N m.

For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 6.495 kg is released from rest at a height of 118.16 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 48.141 m/s and the kinetic energy is 7526.2 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 3.827 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 480.54 N/m and displaced by 0.471 m.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 111.92 kg block starts at 27.522 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.641. The surface extends for 7.965 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 60.249 m. After the available distance its speed is 25.638 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 6.2861 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 27.731 m/s, emitting a tone of 1394.3 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 1517 Hz, a frequency increase of 122.64 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 1.783 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 637.25 K, changing volume from 25.277 to 44.134 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is 5265.1 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 9.547 kg changes signed velocity from -11.711 to 16.561 m/s during 0.812 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 269.91 N s and the average net force is 332.4 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 8860.7 Hz and has spatial wavelength 2.932 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 0.00011286 s and the propagation speed is 25980 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 257.83 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.966 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 14.84 kg and 2.105 kg and initial signed speeds -4.61 and 18.472 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is -1.7426 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 491.09 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Ideal gas equation of state

## Worked example: Periodic wave propagation

Interpretation: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

## Quantitative physics problem: Pressure at depth

Answer: The pressure increase is 1747.5 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1839.7 kPa.

Physical check: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Idealizations: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 1009.6 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.393 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 327.55 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 6698.5 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 7.714 km/s and the orbital period is 90.935 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 23.873 kg and 0.972 kg and initial signed speeds 19.163 and 8.721 m/s. They stick together after impact.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.

## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1097.5 K and cold reservoir at 267.11 K, absorbing 2310.7 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 75.662 percent, corresponding to at most 1748.3 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Physical setup: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 64.582 kg follows a circle of radius 17.232 m at constant speed 58.59 m/s.

The centripetal acceleration is 199.21 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 12865 N, and rotation frequency is 0.54114 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Worked example: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Physical setup: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 4.691 kg and radius 0.353 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 77.863 rad/s.

## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 69.185 kg block starts at 28.235 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.369. The surface extends for 17.56 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 110.15 m. After the available distance its speed is 25.887 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 3.6187 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 15.5 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 626.11 N/m and displaced by 0.44 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 6.3556 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.0115 Hz, and turning-point energy is 60.607 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 20.746 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 0.558 m/s^2 for 5.539 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 23.837 m/s, and the signed displacement is 123.47 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Reversible isothermal gas work

4.075 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 675.06 K, changing volume from 14.013 to 37.275 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 22376 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Worked example: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Physical setup: A fully submerged body has volume 0.02 m^3 and material density 960.37 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1171.9 kg/m^3.

Relevant law: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Calculated result: The upward buoyancy is 229.85 N and the weight is 188.36 N; their signed upward difference is 41.489 N.

Interpretation: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Conditions of validity: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 17.202 kg is released from rest at a height of 65.845 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 35.937 m/s and the kinetic energy is 11108 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Spring oscillator

## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 17.663 kg and radius 1.91 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 167.77 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 32.218 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 4.5343e+05 J.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Hooke-law force calibration

A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

The fitted slope is 643.24 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 638.9 N/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 2.4295 N.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 0.595 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 646.09 K, changing volume from 17.834 to 34.812 liters.

Answer: The work by the gas is 2137.8 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Circular Earth orbit

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 40.992 kg changes signed velocity from 13.788 to 8.988 m/s during 0.073 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -196.76 N s and the average net force is -2695.4 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 2799.2 Hz and has spatial wavelength 1.361 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 0.00035725 s and the propagation speed is 3809.7 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

A sample of mass 2.854 kg has specific heat capacity 2244 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 309.96 to 476.65 K.

The required energy is 1067.5 kJ.

The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 19.836 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -0.857 m/s^2 for 15.177 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 6.8293 m/s, and the signed displacement is 202.35 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 1620.4 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 9.9879 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

## Periodic wave propagation

## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 4.33 cm^2 and 12.594 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 1.224 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 0.42083 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.00052999 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Reversible isothermal gas work

4.584 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 649.66 K, changing volume from 42.495 to 114.01 liters.

## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 11.31 kg and radius 0.935 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 48.796 rad/s.

## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1945.4 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 8316.4 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 6.9231 km/s and the orbital period is 125.79 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 31.666 m/s and elevation angle 71.684 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 6.1309 s, the horizontal range is 61.01 m, and maximum height above launch is 46.076 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.
