## Thermal conduction measurement

A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

The fitted slope is 5.1343 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 5.1343 W/K.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 53.42 W.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Hooke-law force calibration

Physical setup: A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

Relevant law: For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 645.76 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 645.88 N/m.

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 1.8967 N.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 3.703 kg has specific heat capacity 665.93 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 330.72 to 498.16 K.

Answer: The required energy is 412.91 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 324.73 W/(m K), thickness 0.572 m, area 3.261 m^2, and temperature difference 15.584 K.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 28851 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.135 m^3 and material density 1296.5 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1049.1 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 1388.9 N and the weight is 1716.5 N; their signed upward difference is -327.59 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 16.978 kg is released from rest at a height of 4.005 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 8.8629 m/s and the kinetic energy is 666.82 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 61.646 kg changes signed velocity from 5.455 to 16.339 m/s during 0.694 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is 670.96 N s and the average net force is 966.79 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 17 kg is released from rest at a height of 13.278 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 16.138 m/s and the kinetic energy is 2213.6 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 103.02 kg block starts at 18.628 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.121. The surface extends for 3.444 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 146.22 m. After the available distance its speed is 18.407 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.1866 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Problem: 7.346 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 583.51 K to 658.05 K.

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Answer: The internal energy change is 6829 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.043 m^3 and material density 1698.1 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1246 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 525.42 N and the weight is 716.05 N; their signed upward difference is -190.63 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 12.917 cm^2 and 8.976 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 1.285 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 1.8492 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0016598 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 24.146 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 4.551 m/s^2 for 13.965 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 87.701 m/s, and the signed displacement is 780.97 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 14.262 cm^2 and 7.852 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.297 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 4.1722 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.003276 m^3/s.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

Problem: A vessel contains 8.823 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 787.1 K in volume 172.74 liters.

Solution method: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Answer: The equilibrium pressure is 334.27 kPa.

Physical check: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 667.29 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7038.3 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.5255 km/s and the orbital period is 97.94 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Worked example: Uniform circular motion

Physical setup: A mass of 42.979 kg follows a circle of radius 21.798 m at constant speed 69.19 m/s.

Relevant law: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Calculated result: The centripetal acceleration is 219.62 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 9439 N, and rotation frequency is 0.50518 Hz.

Interpretation: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Conditions of validity: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 24.756 kg and 13.496 kg and initial signed speeds -4.432 and 19.653 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is 4.0656 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 2533.3 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Problem: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 0.00079147 W/m^2.

Solution method: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Answer: The ideal intensity level is 88.984 dB.

Physical check: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Idealizations: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 2.642 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 571.05 K, changing volume from 39.626 to 38.081 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is -499.02 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 6.332 kg has specific heat capacity 4081 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 301.39 to 463.42 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 4186.9 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Thermal conduction measurement

Problem: A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

Solution method: For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

Answer: The fitted slope is 4.1099 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0966 W/K.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 3.9626 W.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 227.63 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.992 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Physical setup: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

Relevant law: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 4.0349 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.26972 s^2.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 6.801 m and an initial angular displacement of 2.282 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 5.2325 s and its frequency is 0.19111 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 18943 Hz and has spatial wavelength 0.372 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 5.2789e-05 s and the propagation speed is 7046.9 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Worked example: Hooke-law force calibration

Physical setup: A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

Relevant law: For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 560.74 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 563.11 N/m.

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.25677 N.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 996.85 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 156.68 m below a surface at pressure 99.458 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

The pressure increase is 1531.6 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1631.1 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 19.161 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 68.39 N/m and displaced by 0.198 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 1.8892 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.30068 Hz, and turning-point energy is 1.3406 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Problem: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 79.282 W/(m K), thickness 0.534 m, area 0.204 m^2, and temperature difference 71.442 K.

Solution method: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Answer: The conduction rate is 2163.8 W.

Physical check: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Idealizations: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 96.218 W/(m K), thickness 0.308 m, area 0.509 m^2, and temperature difference 83.735 K.

The conduction rate is 13315 W.

## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 64.663 m/s and elevation angle 39.172 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 8.3299 s, the horizontal range is 417.58 m, and maximum height above launch is 85.058 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Worked example: Linear thermal expansion

Physical setup: A rod with initial length 26.858 m has expansion coefficient 2.1722e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 134.53 K.

Relevant law: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Calculated result: The calculated signed change in length is 78.484 mm.

Interpretation: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Conditions of validity: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A force of magnitude 84.263 N acts at a distance of 1.384 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 158.59 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 42.578 N m.

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 48.688 m/s, emitting a tone of 745.45 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 868.77 Hz, a frequency increase of 123.32 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

Physical check: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Idealizations: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 1694.6 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 9.9419 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Worked example: Periodic wave propagation

Physical setup: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 16253 Hz and has spatial wavelength 0.381 m.

Relevant law: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Calculated result: The period is 6.1528e-05 s and the propagation speed is 6192.3 m/s.

Interpretation: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Conditions of validity: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 15.945 m/s, emitting a tone of 873.33 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 915.91 Hz, a frequency increase of 42.578 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 10.559 cm^2 and 6.63 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 4.255 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 6.7766 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0044929 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1575.7 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7946.7 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 7.0823 km/s and the orbital period is 117.5 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 17.112 kg is released from rest at a height of 26.396 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 22.753 m/s and the kinetic energy is 4429.5 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 5.654 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 319.16 K, changing volume from 5.285 to 7.2299 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is 4701.5 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 7.556 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 0.433 m/s^2 for 10.666 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 12.174 m/s, and the signed displacement is 105.22 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 8.583 kg and 16.574 kg and initial signed speeds 1.144 and -8.033 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is -4.902 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 238.11 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 30.763 kg and radius 0.99 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 79.062 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 15.075 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 47117 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.007 m^3 and material density 1009.2 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 794.32 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 54.527 N and the weight is 69.281 N; their signed upward difference is -14.754 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Quantitative physics problem: Hooke-law force calibration

Problem: A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

Solution method: For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 253.52 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 253.66 N/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.52281 N.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Lever arm and rotational effect

The calculated torque magnitude is 701.42 N m.

The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 33.103 kg block starts at 27.133 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.185. The surface extends for 15.489 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 202.9 m. After the available distance its speed is 26.077 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.8142 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Quantitative physics problem: Pressure at depth

Problem: A stationary liquid has density 1086.7 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 21.79 m below a surface at pressure 105.27 kPa.

Solution method: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Answer: The pressure increase is 232.22 kPa and the absolute pressure is 337.49 kPa.

Physical check: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Idealizations: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

7.69 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 692.93 K to 739.84 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

The internal energy change is 4499.1 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Worked example: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Physical setup: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 7.34 W/(m K), thickness 0.284 m, area 2.069 m^2, and temperature difference 28.811 K.

Relevant law: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Calculated result: The conduction rate is 1540.6 W.

Interpretation: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Conditions of validity: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Quantitative physics problem: Thermal conduction measurement

Problem: A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

Solution method: For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

Answer: The fitted slope is 5.774 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 5.7505 W/K.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 42.888 W.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1432.3 K and cold reservoir at 405.85 K, absorbing 1502.3 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 71.665 percent, corresponding to at most 1076.6 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Quantitative physics problem: Spring oscillator

Problem: A mass of 11.241 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 352.11 N/m and displaced by 0.119 m.

Solution method: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Answer: The angular frequency is 5.5967 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.89075 Hz, and turning-point energy is 2.4931 J.

Physical check: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Idealizations: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 0.00055786 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 87.465 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 3.64 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 541.84 K, changing volume from 14.754 to 36.605 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is 14901 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 19.156 kg and radius 1.206 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 82.857 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 13.931 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 47819 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 1653.5 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 9.9673 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Worked example: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Physical setup: A sample of mass 12.132 kg has specific heat capacity 858.06 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 275.25 to 360.8 K.

Relevant law: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Calculated result: The required energy is 890.53 kJ.

Interpretation: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Conditions of validity: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 7.461 kg is released from rest at a height of 69.275 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 36.861 m/s and the kinetic energy is 5068.7 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 32.98 m/s and elevation angle 38.666 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 4.2023 s, the horizontal range is 108.21 m, and maximum height above launch is 21.647 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Worked example: Periodic wave propagation

Physical setup: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 4450.5 Hz and has spatial wavelength 3.755 m.

Relevant law: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Calculated result: The period is 0.00022469 s and the propagation speed is 16712 m/s.

Interpretation: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Conditions of validity: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 26.516 m/s, emitting a tone of 1636.9 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 1774.1 Hz, a frequency increase of 137.15 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 201.54 W/(m K), thickness 0.263 m, area 3.035 m^2, and temperature difference 7.613 K.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 17706 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1403 K and cold reservoir at 292.14 K, absorbing 5833.1 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 79.178 percent, corresponding to at most 4618.6 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 433.49 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 6804.5 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Spring oscillator

Problem: A mass of 10.805 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 609.45 N/m and displaced by 0.465 m.

Solution method: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.019 m^3 and material density 1512.9 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1198.8 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 223.36 N and the weight is 281.9 N; their signed upward difference is -58.535 N.

## Worked example: Pressure at depth

Interpretation: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Conditions of validity: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 5.776 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -0.88 m/s^2 for 9.336 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is -2.4397 m/s, and the signed displacement is 15.574 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 2.136 cm^2 and 5.105 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 1.246 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 0.52134 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.00026615 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 82.961 kg block starts at 31.508 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.515. The surface extends for 10.974 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 98.284 m. After the available distance its speed is 29.697 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 5.0504 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Worked example: Hooke-law force calibration

Physical setup: A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 383.4 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 382.59 N/m.

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.63559 N.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 14.261 kg changes signed velocity from -7.261 to 8.582 m/s during 0.766 s.

Physical setup: An object of mass 19.625 kg is released from rest at a height of 110.72 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 46.599 m/s and the kinetic energy is 21308 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 25.882 kg and radius 1.468 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 158.2 rad/s.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 27.888 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 3.4899e+05 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Reversible isothermal gas work

8.254 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 613.15 K, changing volume from 11.103 to 5.1518 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is -32311 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 34.621 m/s, emitting a tone of 1220.9 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 1358 Hz, a frequency increase of 137.07 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Spring oscillator

Problem: A mass of 14.772 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 313.44 N/m and displaced by 0.203 m.

Solution method: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Answer: The angular frequency is 4.6063 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.73312 Hz, and turning-point energy is 6.4583 J.

Physical check: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Idealizations: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 446.54 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.814 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 8.614 kg changes signed velocity from 16.265 to 14.591 m/s during 0.437 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -14.42 N s and the average net force is -32.997 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 133.59 kg block starts at 27.709 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.209. The surface extends for 5.216 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 187.3 m. After the available distance its speed is 27.32 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 2.0496 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 9.605 kg and 19.122 kg and initial signed speeds 11.457 and -5.663 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 0.061148 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 936.95 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

The speed of transverse waves is 43.67 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 7.5267 Hz.

The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Worked example: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Conditions of validity: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Worked example: Escape speed from a central mass

Physical setup: Consider a test object at altitude 899.92 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Relevant law: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Calculated result: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.471 km/s.

Interpretation: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Conditions of validity: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Problem: A rod with initial length 24.411 m has expansion coefficient 1.25e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 0.288 K.

Solution method: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is 0.08788 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 29.822 m/s, emitting a tone of 1646.8 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 1803.6 Hz, a frequency increase of 156.81 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A force of magnitude 281.69 N acts at a distance of 3.727 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 70.523 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 989.79 N m.

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 45.794 m/s and elevation angle 20.934 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 3.3369 s, the horizontal range is 142.72 m, and maximum height above launch is 13.649 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Worked example: Ideal gas equation of state

Conditions of validity: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 42.624 kg and radius 1.488 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 128.8 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 47.188 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 3.914e+05 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1209.6 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7580.6 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.2514 km/s and the orbital period is 109.47 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Worked example: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Physical setup: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 2.9909e-10 W/m^2.

Relevant law: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Calculated result: The ideal intensity level is 24.758 dB.

Interpretation: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Conditions of validity: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 1.69 cm^2 and 13.254 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 0.432 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 0.055084 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 7.3008e-05 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.108 m^3 and material density 324.43 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1076 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 1139.6 N and the weight is 343.61 N; their signed upward difference is 796.02 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

## Worked example: Pressure at depth

Physical setup: A stationary liquid has density 862.56 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 109.85 m below a surface at pressure 97.138 kPa.

Relevant law: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Calculated result: The pressure increase is 929.23 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1026.4 kPa.

Interpretation: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Conditions of validity: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Quantitative physics problem: Hooke-law force calibration

Problem: A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

Solution method: For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 324.19 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 322.82 N/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.70684 N.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 13214 Hz and has spatial wavelength 0.807 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 7.5679e-05 s and the propagation speed is 10663 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1175 K and cold reservoir at 422.41 K, absorbing 8872.4 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 64.052 percent, corresponding to at most 5683 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 13.044 kg block starts at 21.156 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.572. The surface extends for 15.1 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 39.895 m. After the available distance its speed is 16.678 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 5.6094 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 10.876 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 633.28 N/m and displaced by 0.451 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 7.6307 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.2145 Hz, and turning-point energy is 64.405 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Reversible isothermal gas work

7.185 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 528.64 K, changing volume from 4.645 to 4.3059 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is -2393.9 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 1780 Hz, a frequency increase of 126.04 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 0.29 kg is released from rest at a height of 36.526 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 26.766 m/s and the kinetic energy is 103.88 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 7630.4 Hz and has spatial wavelength 0.924 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 0.00013105 s and the propagation speed is 7050.5 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 9.283 kg changes signed velocity from -0.169 to -15.653 m/s during 0.512 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is -143.74 N s and the average net force is -280.74 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 96.104 kg follows a circle of radius 15.848 m at constant speed 33.183 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 69.48 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 6677.3 N, and rotation frequency is 0.33324 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Worked example: Standing wave on a stretched string

Interpretation: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1962.1 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 8333.1 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 6.9162 km/s and the orbital period is 126.17 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

5.143 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 742.9 K to 326.55 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

The internal energy change is -26705 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 2.7131 s, the horizontal range is 62.63 m, and maximum height above launch is 9.0235 m.

## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 1.4187e-08 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 41.519 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Worked example: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Physical setup: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 2.905 kg and radius 1.471 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 56.627 rad/s.

Relevant law: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Calculated result: The moment of inertia is 3.143 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 5039.2 J.

Interpretation: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Conditions of validity: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 907.11 K and cold reservoir at 364.55 K, absorbing 5580.8 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 59.812 percent, corresponding to at most 3338 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Worked example: Escape speed from a central mass

Physical setup: Consider a test object at altitude 1150 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Relevant law: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Interpretation: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Conditions of validity: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Physical setup: A simple pendulum has length 7.701 m and an initial angular displacement of 2.221 degrees.

Relevant law: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Calculated result: The estimated oscillation period is 5.5679 s and its frequency is 0.1796 Hz.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 16.052 kg and 2.297 kg and initial signed speeds 12.724 and 4.677 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is 11.717 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 65.06 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.11 m^3 and material density 397 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 789.01 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 851.13 N and the weight is 428.26 N; their signed upward difference is 422.88 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Problem: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

Solution method: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 4.0303 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.22407 s^2.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 847.14 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 23.695 m below a surface at pressure 98.53 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

The pressure increase is 196.85 kPa and the absolute pressure is 295.38 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Reversible isothermal gas work

7.74 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 401.01 K, changing volume from 31.954 to 94.36 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 27944 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 143.73 kg block starts at 15.096 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.37. The surface extends for 5.927 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 31.403 m. After the available distance its speed is 13.597 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 3.6285 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Steady heat conduction through a slab

## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 10.666 cm^2 and 8.449 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 1.598 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 2.0173 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0017044 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

Problem: A force of magnitude 238.74 N acts at a distance of 1.546 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 63.868 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 331.36 N m.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 9.791 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 3.334 m/s^2 for 1.413 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 14.502 m/s, and the signed displacement is 17.163 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

## Reversible isothermal gas work

7.18 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 638.88 K, changing volume from 48.209 to 46.377 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is -1477.6 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Linear thermal expansion

A rod with initial length 29.851 m has expansion coefficient 1.9591e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 45.191 K.

## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 8.521 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 110.7 N/m and displaced by 0.08 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 3.6044 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.57367 Hz, and turning-point energy is 0.35426 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Problem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 4.972 m, tension 616.41 N, and linear mass density 0.026 kg/m.

Solution method: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Answer: The speed of transverse waves is 153.97 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 15.484 Hz.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

A sample of mass 11.586 kg has specific heat capacity 754.12 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 291.02 to 377.61 K.

For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

The required energy is 756.52 kJ.

The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Idealizations: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 30.06 kg block starts at 20.27 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.318. The surface extends for 1.057 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 65.876 m. After the available distance its speed is 20.107 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 3.1185 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 1198.7 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.262 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Projectile trajectory above level ground

## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 1.485 cm^2 and 6.792 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 0.447 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 0.097732 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 6.638e-05 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Physical setup: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

Relevant law: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 4.0827 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.77825 s^2.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 11.383 kg changes signed velocity from 6.733 to -18.084 m/s during 0.769 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -282.49 N s and the average net force is -367.35 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 1.925 kg and 18.27 kg and initial signed speeds 17.733 and -1.405 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 0.41925 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 318.92 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Worked example: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Physical setup: A fully submerged body has volume 0.086 m^3 and material density 1123.8 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 972.38 kg/m^3.

Calculated result: The upward buoyancy is 820.08 N and the weight is 947.78 N; their signed upward difference is -127.71 N.

Interpretation: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Conditions of validity: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.
