## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 96.663 W/(m K), thickness 0.34 m, area 1.008 m^2, and temperature difference 65.764 K.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 18846 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Worked example: Uniform circular motion

Physical setup: A mass of 135.66 kg follows a circle of radius 8.605 m at constant speed 56.754 m/s.

Relevant law: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Calculated result: The centripetal acceleration is 374.32 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 50780 N, and rotation frequency is 1.0497 Hz.

Interpretation: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Conditions of validity: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

Problem: A vessel contains 10.466 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 953.38 K in volume 81.948 liters.

Solution method: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Answer: The equilibrium pressure is 1012.4 kPa.

Physical check: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 47.606 m/s, emitting a tone of 415.26 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 482.18 Hz, a frequency increase of 66.923 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.019 m^3 and material density 1448.5 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 788.77 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 146.97 N and the weight is 269.9 N; their signed upward difference is -122.93 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 4.561 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 3.117 m/s^2 for 15.448 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 52.712 m/s, and the signed displacement is 442.38 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 34.294 kg changes signed velocity from -12.008 to -4.836 m/s during 1.351 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is 245.96 N s and the average net force is 182.06 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Lever arm and rotational effect

The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 21.021 kg and 23.685 kg and initial signed speeds 10.014 and 11.685 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 10.899 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 15.548 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

Conditions of validity: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.0543 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.43922 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 17.922 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 6.32 m/s^2 for 14.2 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 107.67 m/s, and the signed displacement is 891.67 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 0.12 kg is released from rest at a height of 37.873 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 27.255 m/s and the kinetic energy is 44.569 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.126 m^3 and material density 584.24 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1370.7 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 1693.7 N and the weight is 721.9 N; their signed upward difference is 971.85 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 2.302 kg changes signed velocity from -11.005 to 1.075 m/s during 0.871 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is 27.808 N s and the average net force is 31.927 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 6.754 kg and 19.507 kg and initial signed speeds 15.073 and 2.195 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 5.5071 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 416.01 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Worked example: Escape speed from a central mass

Physical setup: Consider a test object at altitude 206.66 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Relevant law: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Calculated result: The minimum escape speed at that position is 11.009 km/s.

Interpretation: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Conditions of validity: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 619.51 K and cold reservoir at 442.58 K, absorbing 3975.7 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 28.56 percent, corresponding to at most 1135.5 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 17.699 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 409.14 N/m and displaced by 0.326 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 4.808 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.76521 Hz, and turning-point energy is 21.741 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 101.73 kg block starts at 10.241 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.291. The surface extends for 1.924 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 18.376 m. After the available distance its speed is 9.69 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 2.8537 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Problem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 10.908 cm^2 and 14.906 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 3.965 m/s.

Solution method: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Answer: The speed in the second section is 2.9015 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.004325 m^3/s.

Physical check: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Idealizations: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Problem: A rod with initial length 4.048 m has expansion coefficient 8.366e-06 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 38.891 K.

Solution method: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is 1.3171 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.

## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 0.00033141 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 85.204 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Projectile trajectory above level ground

The nonzero return time is 1.5806 s, the horizontal range is 10.871 m, and maximum height above launch is 3.0624 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

Physical check: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Idealizations: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Reversible isothermal gas work

5.281 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 433.06 K, changing volume from 2.581 to 6.77 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 18337 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1261.4 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7632.4 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 7.2267 km/s and the orbital period is 110.6 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 931.8 K and cold reservoir at 418.44 K, absorbing 3097 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 55.093 percent, corresponding to at most 1706.2 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 949.77 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 163.78 m below a surface at pressure 108.3 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

The pressure increase is 1525.5 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1633.8 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 8.798 kg and 14.159 kg and initial signed speeds -9.611 and -7.937 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is -8.5785 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 7.603 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Problem: A rod with initial length 23.893 m has expansion coefficient 1.5768e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 95.294 K.

Solution method: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is 35.902 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 56.406 m/s and elevation angle 38.854 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 7.2167 s, the horizontal range is 317 m, and maximum height above launch is 63.842 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 3.487 cm^2 and 4.829 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.303 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 1.663 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.00080306 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 19860 Hz and has spatial wavelength 4.937 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 5.0352e-05 s and the propagation speed is 98049 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 17.239 kg is released from rest at a height of 33.833 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 25.76 m/s and the kinetic energy is 5719.7 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 16.253 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -2.971 m/s^2 for 7.777 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is -6.8525 m/s, and the signed displacement is 36.554 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 1102.9 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.328 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Ideal gas equation of state

The equilibrium pressure is 484.27 kPa.

## Worked example: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Calculated result: The required energy is 9253.8 kJ.

Interpretation: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Conditions of validity: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.

## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 30.322 kg block starts at 12.396 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.155. The surface extends for 10.92 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 50.545 m. After the available distance its speed is 10.976 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.52 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 4.046 m/s, emitting a tone of 628.85 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 636.35 Hz, a frequency increase of 7.5064 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Uniform circular motion

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 31.76 kg changes signed velocity from 16.746 to 7.245 m/s during 1.947 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -301.75 N s and the average net force is -154.98 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 35.85 kg and radius 0.907 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 18.781 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 14.746 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 2600.6 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Thermal conduction measurement

## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 19.731 kg is released from rest at a height of 69.864 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 37.017 m/s and the kinetic energy is 13518 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Reversible heat engine upper bound

## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 89.85 kg block starts at 25.292 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.518. The surface extends for 2.595 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 62.963 m. After the available distance its speed is 24.765 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 5.0798 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Worked example: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Physical setup: A fully submerged body has volume 0.116 m^3 and material density 1427.7 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1376.6 kg/m^3.

Relevant law: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Calculated result: The upward buoyancy is 1566 N and the weight is 1624.1 N; their signed upward difference is -58.146 N.

Interpretation: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Conditions of validity: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Ideal gas equation of state

## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 4.2877 s, the horizontal range is 82.159 m, and maximum height above launch is 22.537 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Worked example: Spring oscillator

## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 20.193 kg and 22.504 kg and initial signed speeds -1.218 and 2.012 m/s. They stick together after impact.

## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 1178 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.276 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 9685.3 Hz and has spatial wavelength 0.435 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 0.00010325 s and the propagation speed is 4213.1 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

Relevant law: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Calculated result: The upward buoyancy is 1700.6 N and the weight is 1419.9 N; their signed upward difference is 280.78 N.

Interpretation: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Conditions of validity: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Problem: A rod with initial length 9.547 m has expansion coefficient 8.002e-06 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 70.857 K.

Solution method: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is 5.4131 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 4.448 cm^2 and 14.233 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.567 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 0.80222 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0011418 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Worked example: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Physical setup: A sample of mass 3.069 kg has specific heat capacity 2360.4 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 286.23 to 478.18 K.

Relevant law: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Calculated result: The required energy is 1390.5 kJ.

Interpretation: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Conditions of validity: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 13.933 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -1.129 m/s^2 for 5.359 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 7.8827 m/s, and the signed displacement is 58.455 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1195.6 K and cold reservoir at 273.08 K, absorbing 5246.2 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 77.16 percent, corresponding to at most 4048 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Thermal conduction measurement

Problem: A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

Solution method: For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

Answer: The fitted slope is 0.99358 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 0.99417 W/K.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.087517 W.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 41.56 kg follows a circle of radius 19.856 m at constant speed 7.014 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 2.4776 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 102.97 N, and rotation frequency is 0.05622 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 1767.4 Hz and has spatial wavelength 1.81 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 0.00056582 s and the propagation speed is 3198.9 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Worked example: Pressure at depth

Physical setup: A stationary liquid has density 892.96 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 183.08 m below a surface at pressure 98.01 kPa.

Relevant law: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Calculated result: The pressure increase is 1603.2 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1701.2 kPa.

Interpretation: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Conditions of validity: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 0.831 kg is released from rest at a height of 100.62 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 44.425 m/s and the kinetic energy is 820.03 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 185.07 W/(m K), thickness 0.1 m, area 3.34 m^2, and temperature difference 46.287 K.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 2.8612e+05 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 11.402 m/s, emitting a tone of 451.03 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 466.54 Hz, a frequency increase of 15.509 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Answer: The internal energy change is 16646 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.

## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 68.854 kg block starts at 20.342 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.068. The surface extends for 6.668 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 310.26 m. After the available distance its speed is 20.122 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 0.66685 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Standing wave on a stretched string

A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 3.466 m, tension 841.42 N, and linear mass density 0.017 kg/m.

The speed of transverse waves is 222.48 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 32.094 Hz.

The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 49.175 m/s and elevation angle 68.489 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 9.3304 s, the horizontal range is 168.24 m, and maximum height above launch is 106.72 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 2.851 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 251.87 K, changing volume from 10.29 to 12.718 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Relevant law: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Calculated result: The equilibrium pressure is 289.72 kPa.

Interpretation: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Conditions of validity: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 61.25 kg changes signed velocity from 0.581 to -0.908 m/s during 1.292 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is -91.201 N s and the average net force is -70.589 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 81.577 m/s and elevation angle 35.373 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 9.6312 s, the horizontal range is 640.64 m, and maximum height above launch is 113.71 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 62.324 kg block starts at 4.287 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.158. The surface extends for 25.294 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 5.9306 m. After the available distance its speed is 0 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.5495 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 1003.1 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.398 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 42.089 m/s, emitting a tone of 1018.8 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 1161.3 Hz, a frequency increase of 142.5 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 19.786 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 0.037 m/s^2 for 7.58 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 20.066 m/s, and the signed displacement is 151.04 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1868.9 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 8239.9 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 6.9552 km/s and the orbital period is 124.06 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 970.33 K and cold reservoir at 341.93 K, absorbing 2768.1 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 64.761 percent, corresponding to at most 1792.6 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 236.63 N acts at a distance of 2.62 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 119.9 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 537.46 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 9.568 kg is released from rest at a height of 9.073 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 13.34 m/s and the kinetic energy is 851.32 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 5.486 cm^2 and 5.006 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 4.054 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 4.4427 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.002224 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Problem: A rod with initial length 9.573 m has expansion coefficient 1.1697e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by -26.204 K.

Solution method: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is -2.9342 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.

## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 11.985 kg and 10.772 kg and initial signed speeds 1.536 and -4.344 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is -1.2473 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 98.072 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Quantitative physics problem: Spring oscillator

Problem: A mass of 4 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 132.4 N/m and displaced by 0.324 m.

Solution method: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Answer: The angular frequency is 5.7532 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.91565 Hz, and turning-point energy is 6.9493 J.

Physical check: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Idealizations: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

9.191 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 386.24 K to 745.05 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

The internal energy change is 41130 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.078 m^3 and material density 1554.1 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 865.74 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 662.22 N and the weight is 1188.8 N; their signed upward difference is -526.56 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 14.735 kg follows a circle of radius 9.111 m at constant speed 38.832 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 165.51 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 2438.7 N, and rotation frequency is 0.67833 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Worked example: Pressure at depth

Physical setup: A stationary liquid has density 1067.2 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 85.889 m below a surface at pressure 96.844 kPa.

Relevant law: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Calculated result: The pressure increase is 898.88 kPa and the absolute pressure is 995.73 kPa.

Interpretation: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Conditions of validity: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Quantitative physics problem: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Problem: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 303.81 W/(m K), thickness 0.508 m, area 3.363 m^2, and temperature difference 9.184 K.

Solution method: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Answer: The conduction rate is 18471 W.

Physical check: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Idealizations: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Worked example: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Physical setup: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 4.8344e-07 W/m^2.

Relevant law: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Calculated result: The ideal intensity level is 56.843 dB.

Interpretation: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Conditions of validity: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 3925.8 Hz and has spatial wavelength 4.806 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 0.00025473 s and the propagation speed is 18867 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Standing wave on a stretched string

A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 2.223 m, tension 736.93 N, and linear mass density 0.029 kg/m.

Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

The speed of transverse waves is 159.41 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 35.855 Hz.

The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.

## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 4.711 kg and radius 0.043 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 90.703 rad/s.

The common final velocity is 14.138 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 3.5713 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Worked example: Periodic wave propagation

Physical setup: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 8643.3 Hz and has spatial wavelength 2.66 m.

Relevant law: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Calculated result: The period is 0.0001157 s and the propagation speed is 22991 m/s.

Interpretation: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Conditions of validity: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Problem: 6.433 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 410.82 K to 759.12 K.

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Answer: The internal energy change is 27944 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 83.489 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 11.114 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 9.444 cm^2 and 5.324 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.636 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 4.6759 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0024894 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Problem: A rod with initial length 15.181 m has expansion coefficient 1.6989e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 42.202 K.

Solution method: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is 10.884 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 1070.1 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 124.34 m below a surface at pressure 91.695 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

The pressure increase is 1304.8 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1396.5 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 52.411 kg changes signed velocity from 8.331 to 5.685 m/s during 1.347 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is -138.68 N s and the average net force is -102.95 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1982.9 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 8353.9 km.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Idealizations: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Thermal conduction measurement

A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

The fitted slope is 2.756 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 2.7559 W/K.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 3.3912 W.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Worked example: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 45.287 m/s, emitting a tone of 1398.9 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 1611.7 Hz, a frequency increase of 212.8 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 7.638 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 248.22 N/m and displaced by 0.493 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 5.7007 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.9073 Hz, and turning-point energy is 30.165 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 627.93 K and cold reservoir at 387.21 K, absorbing 1087.8 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 38.336 percent, corresponding to at most 417.04 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.

## Reversible isothermal gas work

7.638 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 648.18 K, changing volume from 23.704 to 34.513 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 15465 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 1.408 kg is released from rest at a height of 18.693 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 19.148 m/s and the kinetic energy is 258.11 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 17.085 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 0.84 m/s^2 for 2.314 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 19.029 m/s, and the signed displacement is 41.784 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 1370.9 N and the weight is 528.4 N; their signed upward difference is 842.51 N.

## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 13.101 kg block starts at 11.303 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.255. The surface extends for 12.137 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 25.544 m. After the available distance its speed is 8.1888 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 2.5007 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

## Quantitative physics problem: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Problem: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 0.00025067 W/m^2.

Solution method: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Answer: The ideal intensity level is 83.991 dB.

Physical check: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Idealizations: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 512.99 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.761 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Answer: The common final velocity is 8.7754 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 127.13 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 51.808 m/s, emitting a tone of 1008.5 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 1187.9 Hz, a frequency increase of 179.43 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 12.034 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -2.245 m/s^2 for 16.379 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is -24.737 m/s, and the signed displacement is -104.03 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Standing wave on a stretched string

A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 1.43 m, tension 696.7 N, and linear mass density 0.036 kg/m.

The speed of transverse waves is 139.11 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 48.641 Hz.

The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.

## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

## Ideal gas equation of state

The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

The equilibrium pressure is 370.77 kPa.

At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Physical setup: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

Relevant law: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 4.0238 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.098137 s^2.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 18.653 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 468.82 N/m and displaced by 0.42 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 5.0134 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.7979 Hz, and turning-point energy is 41.35 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Quantitative physics problem: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Problem: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 320.04 W/(m K), thickness 0.551 m, area 0.087 m^2, and temperature difference 24.704 K.

Solution method: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Answer: The conduction rate is 1248.4 W.

Physical check: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Idealizations: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 3.184 kg and 0.99 kg and initial signed speeds -1.92 and 19.318 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 3.1173 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 170.32 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Worked example: Ideal gas equation of state

Physical setup: A vessel contains 11.381 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 778.14 K in volume 25.895 liters.

Relevant law: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Calculated result: The equilibrium pressure is 2843.5 kPa.

Interpretation: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Conditions of validity: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Reversible isothermal gas work

2.776 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 313.65 K, changing volume from 16.58 to 19.697 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 1247.1 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 21.193 m/s and elevation angle 22.908 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 1.6824 s, the horizontal range is 32.843 m, and maximum height above launch is 3.4697 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 23.508 m/s, emitting a tone of 1397.6 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 1500.4 Hz, a frequency increase of 102.84 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 582.32 K and cold reservoir at 317.07 K, absorbing 2632.6 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 45.551 percent, corresponding to at most 1199.2 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 37.425 kg and radius 0.943 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 84.007 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 16.64 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 58716 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1835 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 8206 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 6.9695 km/s and the orbital period is 123.3 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Worked example: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Physical setup: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 9.4742e-06 W/m^2.

Relevant law: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Calculated result: The ideal intensity level is 69.765 dB.

Interpretation: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Conditions of validity: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.073 m^3 and material density 1256.4 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1129.7 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 808.77 N and the weight is 899.45 N; their signed upward difference is -90.677 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 10.052 kg is released from rest at a height of 65.806 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 35.926 m/s and the kinetic energy is 6486.9 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum

Problem: A simple pendulum has length 7.606 m and an initial angular displacement of 6.116 degrees.

Solution method: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Answer: The estimated oscillation period is 5.5335 s and its frequency is 0.18072 Hz.

Physical check: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Idealizations: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 201.53 kg follows a circle of radius 2.315 m at constant speed 50.847 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 1116.8 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 2.2507e+05 N, and rotation frequency is 3.4957 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Standing wave on a stretched string

A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 1.281 m, tension 457.69 N, and linear mass density 0.054 kg/m.

Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

The speed of transverse waves is 92.064 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 35.934 Hz.

The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.

## Thermal conduction measurement

A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

The fitted slope is 1.5776 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 1.612 W/K.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 16.224 W.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Quantitative physics problem: Pressure at depth

Problem: A stationary liquid has density 808.97 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 64.037 m below a surface at pressure 90.53 kPa.

Solution method: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Answer: The pressure increase is 508.02 kPa and the absolute pressure is 598.55 kPa.

Physical check: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Idealizations: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Worked example: Periodic wave propagation

Interpretation: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Conditions of validity: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 13.467 cm^2 and 13.116 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 4.474 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 4.5937 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0060251 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 25.041 kg changes signed velocity from 18.428 to -1.832 m/s during 0.939 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -507.33 N s and the average net force is -540.29 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 15.962 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 5.959 m/s^2 for 13.119 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 94.138 m/s, and the signed displacement is 722.2 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

A sample of mass 12.359 kg has specific heat capacity 2013.8 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 329.5 to 463.48 K.

For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

The required energy is 3334.5 kJ.

The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.
