Answer: The work by the gas is -2078.1 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Standing wave on a stretched string

A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 4.584 m, tension 247.89 N, and linear mass density 0.014 kg/m.

Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

The speed of transverse waves is 133.07 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 14.514 Hz.

The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.117 m^3 and material density 589.83 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 806.58 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 925.45 N and the weight is 676.76 N; their signed upward difference is 248.69 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 13.081 m/s, emitting a tone of 258.87 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 269.13 Hz, a frequency increase of 10.264 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 1244.4 Hz and has spatial wavelength 3.957 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 0.0008036 s and the propagation speed is 4924.1 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 25.461 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 2.103 m/s^2 for 8.247 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 42.804 m/s, and the signed displacement is 281.49 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Solution method: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Physical check: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 9.547 kg changes signed velocity from -1.022 to -14.341 m/s during 1.06 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -127.16 N s and the average net force is -119.96 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Lever arm and rotational effect

The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 597.87 K and cold reservoir at 275.52 K, absorbing 5876.1 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 53.916 percent, corresponding to at most 3168.2 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 8.335 kg is released from rest at a height of 99.569 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 44.191 m/s and the kinetic energy is 8138.6 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 393.1 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 6764.1 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 7.6765 km/s and the orbital period is 92.273 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 31.629 kg and radius 1.685 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 164.27 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 44.901 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 6.0582e+05 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Worked example: Uniform circular motion

Interpretation: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 14.899 kg and 14.913 kg and initial signed speeds 4.704 and 10.212 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 7.4593 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 113.05 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 87.113 kg block starts at 10.439 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.371. The surface extends for 10.352 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 14.976 m. After the available distance its speed is 5.8005 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 3.6383 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.0209 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.27065 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

Idealizations: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 778.31 K and cold reservoir at 234.56 K, absorbing 8201.4 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 69.863 percent, corresponding to at most 5729.7 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 667.67 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.642 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 971.97 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7343 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 7.3677 km/s and the orbital period is 104.37 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Spring oscillator

Problem: A mass of 11.981 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 46.157 N/m and displaced by 0.114 m.

Solution method: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Answer: The angular frequency is 1.9628 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.31239 Hz, and turning-point energy is 0.29993 J.

Physical check: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Idealizations: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Physical setup: A simple pendulum has length 3.746 m and an initial angular displacement of 2.174 degrees.

Relevant law: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Calculated result: The estimated oscillation period is 3.8833 s and its frequency is 0.25751 Hz.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Conditions of validity: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Problem: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

Solution method: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 4.0094 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.32259 s^2.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 38.029 m/s, emitting a tone of 1788.1 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 2011.1 Hz, a frequency increase of 222.97 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 1228.4 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 72.03 m below a surface at pressure 90.515 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

The pressure increase is 867.7 kPa and the absolute pressure is 958.22 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 12.045 kg and 4.902 kg and initial signed speeds 15.953 and 9.897 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 38.246 kg changes signed velocity from 16.099 to 13.705 m/s during 1.722 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -91.561 N s and the average net force is -53.171 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 267.54 W/(m K), thickness 0.245 m, area 1.842 m^2, and temperature difference 67.89 K.

## Worked example: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Physical setup: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 28.693 kg and radius 0.576 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 124.82 rad/s.

Relevant law: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Calculated result: The moment of inertia is 4.7598 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 37077 J.

Interpretation: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Conditions of validity: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1095.6 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7466.6 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 7.3065 km/s and the orbital period is 107.02 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 13.73 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 199.72 N/m and displaced by 0.491 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 3.8139 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.607 Hz, and turning-point energy is 24.074 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Problem: A rod with initial length 9.113 m has expansion coefficient 1.3139e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 75.844 K.

Solution method: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is 9.0812 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 55.648 m/s and elevation angle 40.372 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 7.3513 s, the horizontal range is 311.66 m, and maximum height above launch is 66.246 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Worked example: Escape speed from a central mass

Physical setup: Consider a test object at altitude 155.52 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Relevant law: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Calculated result: The minimum escape speed at that position is 11.052 km/s.

Interpretation: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Conditions of validity: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 35.421 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Problem: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 1.1114e-05 W/m^2.

Solution method: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Answer: The ideal intensity level is 70.459 dB.

Physical check: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Idealizations: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 1139 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 9.5 m below a surface at pressure 94.142 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

The pressure increase is 106.11 kPa and the absolute pressure is 200.25 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 8.957 kg is released from rest at a height of 2.061 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 6.3579 m/s and the kinetic energy is 181.03 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.092 m^3 and material density 1291 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1142.8 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 1031 N and the weight is 1164.8 N; their signed upward difference is -133.77 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 53.496 kg changes signed velocity from 15.793 to 19.387 m/s during 0.208 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 192.26 N s and the average net force is 924.35 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 23.929 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -0.557 m/s^2 for 14.619 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 15.786 m/s, and the signed displacement is 290.3 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 2.71 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 510.46 K, changing volume from 30.803 to 67.674 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is 9052.9 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

9.883 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 461.51 K to 222.33 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

The internal energy change is -29480 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 7.499 m and an initial angular displacement of 5.743 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 5.4944 s and its frequency is 0.182 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 34.122 N acts at a distance of 3.333 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 6.311 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 12.502 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 20.376 kg and 0.268 kg and initial signed speeds 1.913 and 2.167 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is 1.9163 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 0.0085329 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Hooke-law force calibration

A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

The fitted slope is 425.24 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 425.35 N/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.48018 N.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Small-angle pendulum

## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 14.688 kg and 13.798 kg and initial signed speeds -2.425 and 18.271 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 7.5997 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 1523.7 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Worked example: Periodic wave propagation

Physical setup: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 2680.9 Hz and has spatial wavelength 3.234 m.

Relevant law: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Calculated result: The period is 0.00037301 s and the propagation speed is 8670 m/s.

Interpretation: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Conditions of validity: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 5.162 kg has specific heat capacity 2044.3 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 322.22 to 424.08 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 1074.9 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1277.8 K and cold reservoir at 279.86 K, absorbing 688.72 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 78.098 percent, corresponding to at most 537.88 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 6.824 kg is released from rest at a height of 63.768 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 35.365 m/s and the kinetic energy is 4267.4 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 7.037 m/s, emitting a tone of 581.39 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 593.57 Hz, a frequency increase of 12.178 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Worked example: Escape speed from a central mass

Physical setup: Consider a test object at altitude 458.51 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Relevant law: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Calculated result: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.804 km/s.

Interpretation: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Conditions of validity: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Thermal conduction measurement

A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

The fitted slope is 2.4856 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 2.4644 W/K.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 9.2514 W.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 122.18 kg block starts at 11.815 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.171. The surface extends for 20.184 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 41.622 m. After the available distance its speed is 8.4794 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.6769 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 19.671 m. After the available distance its speed is 14.495 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 5.5113 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Problem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 2.783 m, tension 451.99 N, and linear mass density 0.003 kg/m.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.

## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum

## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 45.654 kg and radius 1.569 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 10.158 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 56.195 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 2899.2 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 997.42 K and cold reservoir at 328.96 K, absorbing 1148.1 J per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 35.173 kg changes signed velocity from 16.225 to 3.475 m/s during 1.039 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -448.46 N s and the average net force is -431.62 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Pressure at depth

Physical setup: A stationary liquid has density 1273.1 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 163.86 m below a surface at pressure 92.45 kPa.

Relevant law: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Calculated result: The pressure increase is 2045.8 kPa and the absolute pressure is 2138.3 kPa.

Interpretation: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Conditions of validity: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

Solution method: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Answer: The equilibrium pressure is 33.671 kPa.

Physical check: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.0031 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.30598 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 25.442 m/s, emitting a tone of 672.04 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 725.88 Hz, a frequency increase of 53.842 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 41.162 W/(m K), thickness 0.485 m, area 2.777 m^2, and temperature difference 40.024 K.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 9433 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

## Lever arm and rotational effect

## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 28.052 kg follows a circle of radius 21.853 m at constant speed 75.743 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 262.53 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 7364.4 N, and rotation frequency is 0.55163 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 5.922 kg is released from rest at a height of 27.95 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 23.413 m/s and the kinetic energy is 1623.2 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 1.565 cm^2 and 1.156 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 1.145 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 1.5501 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.00017919 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 10.988 kg and 4.661 kg and initial signed speeds -5.494 and 18.084 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is 1.5286 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 909.69 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 6195.2 Hz and has spatial wavelength 3.949 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 0.00016142 s and the propagation speed is 24465 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

Physical setup: A mass of 18.935 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 255.41 N/m and displaced by 0.085 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 3.6727 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.58453 Hz, and turning-point energy is 0.92267 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Problem: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

Solution method: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 4.0366 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.0254 s^2.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.071 m^3 and material density 803.52 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1106.5 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 770.4 N and the weight is 559.47 N; their signed upward difference is 210.93 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Physical setup: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 58.43 W/(m K), thickness 0.566 m, area 2.328 m^2, and temperature difference 42.892 K.

Relevant law: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Calculated result: The conduction rate is 10308 W.

Interpretation: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Conditions of validity: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A force of magnitude 164.28 N acts at a distance of 2.159 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 128.06 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 279.27 N m.

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Linear thermal expansion

A rod with initial length 8.557 m has expansion coefficient 2.199e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 37.61 K.

For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

The calculated signed change in length is 7.077 mm.

For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.

## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 17248 Hz and has spatial wavelength 3.55 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 5.7979e-05 s and the propagation speed is 61229 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 1281 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 53.475 m below a surface at pressure 103.71 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

The pressure increase is 671.75 kPa and the absolute pressure is 775.47 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 8.71 m/s, emitting a tone of 715.01 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 733.64 Hz, a frequency increase of 18.63 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 16.68 kg and 22.132 kg and initial signed speeds 17.299 and -7.029 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 3.4263 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 2814.7 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 5.659 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 361.34 K, changing volume from 10.265 to 28.547 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is 17390 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 9.496 cm^2 and 6.728 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.938 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 4.1467 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0027899 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 9.633 kg block starts at 30.153 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.075. The surface extends for 19.355 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 618.09 m. After the available distance its speed is 29.677 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 0.7355 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 11.331 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -1.529 m/s^2 for 11.972 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is -6.9742 m/s, and the signed displacement is 26.08 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1311.9 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7682.9 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.2029 km/s and the orbital period is 111.7 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 69.182 m/s and elevation angle 74.935 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 13.624 s, the horizontal range is 244.98 m, and maximum height above launch is 227.54 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 19.139 kg is released from rest at a height of 43.905 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 29.345 m/s and the kinetic energy is 8240.5 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Small-angle pendulum

## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 1.682 kg changes signed velocity from 16.956 to -13.556 m/s during 0.94 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

## Ideal gas equation of state

## Worked example: Escape speed from a central mass

Physical setup: Consider a test object at altitude 1143 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Relevant law: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Calculated result: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.3 km/s.

Interpretation: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Conditions of validity: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 869.34 K and cold reservoir at 281.07 K, absorbing 7942.6 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 67.669 percent, corresponding to at most 5374.7 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 693.77 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7064.8 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 7.5114 km/s and the orbital period is 98.493 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Spring oscillator

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

## Quantitative physics problem: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Problem: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 47.794 W/(m K), thickness 0.307 m, area 2.193 m^2, and temperature difference 61.367 K.

Solution method: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Answer: The conduction rate is 20951 W.

Physical check: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Idealizations: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 9.499 m/s, emitting a tone of 1195.8 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 1229.9 Hz, a frequency increase of 34.061 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Worked example: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Physical setup: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 0.198 kg and radius 0.48 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 144.32 rad/s.

Relevant law: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Calculated result: The moment of inertia is 0.02281 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 237.55 J.

Interpretation: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Conditions of validity: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 1.478 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 420.48 K, changing volume from 44.321 to 32.62 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is -1583.9 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

The required energy is 3601.5 kJ.

The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Hooke-law force calibration

A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

The fitted slope is 213.9 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 213.68 N/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.048446 N.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.058 m^3 and material density 868.22 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 819.68 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 466.22 N and the weight is 493.83 N; their signed upward difference is -27.604 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

Answer: The speed of transverse waves is 100.49 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 13.219 Hz.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Lever arm and rotational effect

A force of magnitude 293.57 N acts at a distance of 1.398 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 166.76 degrees to the lever.

The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

The calculated torque magnitude is 93.984 N m.

For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Physical setup: A simple pendulum has length 7.072 m and an initial angular displacement of 7.974 degrees.

Relevant law: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Calculated result: The estimated oscillation period is 5.3357 s and its frequency is 0.18742 Hz.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Conditions of validity: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

## Reversible isothermal gas work

0.453 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 402.84 K, changing volume from 33.766 to 47.644 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 522.4 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Worked example: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Physical setup: A sample of mass 13.352 kg has specific heat capacity 1933.5 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 307.58 to 476.65 K.

Relevant law: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Calculated result: The required energy is 4364.6 kJ.

Interpretation: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Conditions of validity: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 10910 Hz and has spatial wavelength 4.259 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 9.1658e-05 s and the propagation speed is 46466 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 308.6 W/(m K), thickness 0.138 m, area 2.744 m^2, and temperature difference 71.35 K.

The conduction rate is 4.3782e+05 W.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

## Ideal gas equation of state

A vessel contains 1.879 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 264.77 K in volume 26.668 liters.

## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 169.48 kg follows a circle of radius 19.975 m at constant speed 59.486 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 177.15 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 30023 N, and rotation frequency is 0.47397 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1625.1 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7996.1 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 7.0604 km/s and the orbital period is 118.6 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 24.599 kg and 17.756 kg and initial signed speeds 16.57 and 7.77 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is 12.881 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 399.29 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.026 m^3 and material density 1419.7 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1312.9 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 334.75 N and the weight is 361.99 N; their signed upward difference is -27.235 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Problem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 4.05 cm^2 and 4.351 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.556 m/s.

Solution method: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Answer: The speed in the second section is 2.3792 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0010352 m^3/s.

Physical check: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Idealizations: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 26.148 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -2.8 m/s^2 for 14.321 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is -13.951 m/s, and the signed displacement is 87.338 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Worked example: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Physical setup: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 25.911 kg and radius 1.402 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 110.18 rad/s.

Relevant law: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Calculated result: The moment of inertia is 25.465 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 1.5457e+05 J.

Interpretation: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Conditions of validity: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 16.879 kg changes signed velocity from -14.272 to 0.595 m/s during 0.367 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is 250.94 N s and the average net force is 683.76 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Quantitative physics problem: Thermal conduction measurement

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Linear thermal expansion

## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 38.541 m/s, emitting a tone of 761.54 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Answer: The listener detects approximately 857.94 Hz, a frequency increase of 96.402 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 32.095 kg block starts at 31.991 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.067. The surface extends for 28.454 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 778.81 m. After the available distance its speed is 31.401 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 0.65705 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

Interpretation: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Conditions of validity: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.

## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 696.2 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.621 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 5.579 kg has specific heat capacity 4293.2 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 320.49 to 450.87 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 3122.8 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.075 m^3 and material density 897.79 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1053.7 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 774.96 N and the weight is 660.33 N; their signed upward difference is 114.63 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 216.39 kg follows a circle of radius 18.225 m at constant speed 45.443 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 113.31 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 24519 N, and rotation frequency is 0.39684 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 12756 Hz and has spatial wavelength 4.291 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 7.8397e-05 s and the propagation speed is 54734 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Linear thermal expansion

A rod with initial length 21.179 m has expansion coefficient 1.1593e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 161.7 K.

For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

The calculated signed change in length is 39.703 mm.

For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Worked example: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Physical setup: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 0.00019461 W/m^2.

Relevant law: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Calculated result: The ideal intensity level is 82.892 dB.

Interpretation: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Conditions of validity: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 38.656 m/s and elevation angle 62.392 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 6.986 s, the horizontal range is 125.15 m, and maximum height above launch is 59.826 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 1.786 m and an initial angular displacement of 5.107 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 2.6814 s and its frequency is 0.37294 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 24.98 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 201.55 N/m and displaced by 0.446 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 2.8405 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.45208 Hz, and turning-point energy is 20.046 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 24.109 kg changes signed velocity from -11.358 to 16.152 m/s during 0.15 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is 663.24 N s and the average net force is 4421.6 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Thermal conduction measurement

A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

The fitted slope is 4.5189 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.5531 W/K.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 37.651 W.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 41.593 m/s, emitting a tone of 841.17 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 957.25 Hz, a frequency increase of 116.08 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Problem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 4.841 m, tension 153.47 N, and linear mass density 0.026 kg/m.

Solution method: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Answer: The speed of transverse waves is 76.828 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 7.9351 Hz.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.

## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.0411 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.1165 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Pressure at depth

Physical setup: A stationary liquid has density 956.22 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 48.164 m below a surface at pressure 91.796 kPa.

Relevant law: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Calculated result: The pressure increase is 451.65 kPa and the absolute pressure is 543.44 kPa.

Interpretation: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Conditions of validity: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

Problem: A vessel contains 3.12 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 606.07 K in volume 198.2 liters.

Solution method: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Answer: The equilibrium pressure is 79.324 kPa.

Physical check: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 11.471 kg is released from rest at a height of 62.313 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 34.959 m/s and the kinetic energy is 7009.7 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 549.63 K and cold reservoir at 392.74 K, absorbing 817.38 J per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 18.284 kg block starts at 28.355 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.565. The surface extends for 24.319 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 72.554 m. After the available distance its speed is 23.12 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 5.5408 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 3.512 kg is released from rest at a height of 104.59 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 45.291 m/s and the kinetic energy is 3602.1 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1338.8 K and cold reservoir at 362.52 K, absorbing 3326.2 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 72.923 percent, corresponding to at most 2425.6 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 4.107 m and an initial angular displacement of 6.993 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 4.0661 s and its frequency is 0.24593 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Worked example: Linear thermal expansion

Calculated result: The calculated signed change in length is 32.531 mm.

Interpretation: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Conditions of validity: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.

## Worked example: Spring oscillator
