## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 13.764 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 2.606 m/s^2 for 15.785 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 54.9 m/s, and the signed displacement is 541.93 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 1457.9 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.091 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 322.55 N acts at a distance of 0.054 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 65.209 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 15.812 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Answer: The internal energy change is 5126.1 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.

## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 2.363 cm^2 and 1.015 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 3.841 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 8.9422 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.00090763 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Pressure at depth

Problem: A stationary liquid has density 922.94 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 199.03 m below a surface at pressure 103.95 kPa.

Solution method: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Answer: The pressure increase is 1801.4 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1905.3 kPa.

Physical check: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Idealizations: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

A sample of mass 5.449 kg has specific heat capacity 404.08 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 285.19 to 420.5 K.

For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

The required energy is 297.93 kJ.

The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.

## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 6.384 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 212.22 K, changing volume from 30.003 to 25.803 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is -1698.9 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 17.308 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 566.6 N/m and displaced by 0.017 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 5.7215 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.91061 Hz, and turning-point energy is 0.081873 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 15.402 kg is released from rest at a height of 112.11 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 46.891 m/s and the kinetic energy is 16933 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 39.728 m/s and elevation angle 30.881 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 4.1585 s, the horizontal range is 141.79 m, and maximum height above launch is 21.199 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 194.71 kg follows a circle of radius 21.728 m at constant speed 55.706 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 142.82 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 27808 N, and rotation frequency is 0.40804 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Standing wave on a stretched string

## Quantitative physics problem: Hooke-law force calibration

Problem: A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

Solution method: For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 127.39 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 127.1 N/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.11634 N.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 1.7785e-08 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 42.501 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.044 m^3 and material density 782.76 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1200.7 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 518.1 N and the weight is 337.76 N; their signed upward difference is 180.35 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 22.562 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 7.743 m/s^2 for 9.9 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 99.218 m/s, and the signed displacement is 602.81 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 3.985 kg has specific heat capacity 706.17 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 326.93 to 356.52 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 83.254 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 4.79 kg is released from rest at a height of 71.033 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 37.325 m/s and the kinetic energy is 3336.7 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Worked example: Linear thermal expansion

Physical setup: A rod with initial length 27.603 m has expansion coefficient 1.7003e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by -8.222 K.

Relevant law: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Calculated result: The calculated signed change in length is -3.8589 mm.

Interpretation: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Conditions of validity: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 30.6 kg and radius 0.74 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 4.38 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 8.3783 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 80.366 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 14.329 kg and 6.714 kg and initial signed speeds 11.871 and 18.54 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is 13.999 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 101.67 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

1.522 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 837.48 K to 942.79 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

The internal energy change is 1999 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 1.266 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 144.17 N/m and displaced by 0.078 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 10.671 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.6984 Hz, and turning-point energy is 0.43855 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 1305.6 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.191 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 7.519 m and an initial angular displacement of 4.82 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 5.5017 s and its frequency is 0.18176 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Worked example: Thermal conduction measurement

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 2.1184 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 2.1288 W/K.

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 2.2257 W.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 87.677 kg block starts at 4.937 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.471. The surface extends for 16.428 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 2.6385 m. After the available distance its speed is 0 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 4.6189 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 6.668 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 254.9 K, changing volume from 42.828 to 63.385 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is 5540.3 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 628.13 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 6999.1 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 7.5465 km/s and the orbital period is 97.124 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 80.936 Hz and has spatial wavelength 3.89 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 0.012355 s and the propagation speed is 314.84 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 9.884 kg changes signed velocity from 13.39 to 8.74 m/s during 1.476 s.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

The Carnot efficiency is 76.574 percent, corresponding to at most 3080.9 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 445.4 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 6816.4 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 7.647 km/s and the orbital period is 93.345 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 123.89 kg block starts at 23.94 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.103. The surface extends for 11.333 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 283.7 m. After the available distance its speed is 23.457 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.0101 m/s^2 while sliding.

## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 48.08 kg changes signed velocity from 13.75 to -2.658 m/s during 1.097 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is -788.9 N s and the average net force is -719.14 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 23.975 kg follows a circle of radius 7.574 m at constant speed 37.467 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 185.34 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 4443.6 N, and rotation frequency is 0.78731 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 26.949 m/s and elevation angle 39.996 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 3.5325 s, the horizontal range is 72.93 m, and maximum height above launch is 15.297 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Problem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 5.007 cm^2 and 3.537 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 3.252 m/s.

Solution method: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Answer: The speed in the second section is 4.6036 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0016283 m^3/s.

Physical check: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Idealizations: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 9.873 kg and 14.91 kg and initial signed speeds 10.673 and 10.255 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 10.422 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 0.51891 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 14.463 m/s, emitting a tone of 1061.4 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 1108.1 Hz, a frequency increase of 46.724 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Worked example: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Physical setup: 9.182 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 277.39 K to 774.74 K.

Relevant law: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Calculated result: The internal energy change is 56954 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Interpretation: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Conditions of validity: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 44.238 kg and radius 0.429 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 111.42 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 4.0708 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 25268 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Thermal conduction measurement

A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

The fitted slope is 3.0641 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 3.0555 W/K.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 3.4337 W.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 31.094 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 1.628 m/s^2 for 1.347 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 33.287 m/s, and the signed displacement is 43.361 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 7702.9 Hz and has spatial wavelength 2.452 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 0.00012982 s and the propagation speed is 18888 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 18.951 kg is released from rest at a height of 92.117 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 42.506 m/s and the kinetic energy is 17120 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 18.612 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 664.47 N/m and displaced by 0.164 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 5.9751 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.95096 Hz, and turning-point energy is 8.9358 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Solution method: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is 9.4983 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Lever arm and rotational effect

The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

The calculated torque magnitude is 266.27 N m.

For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Answer: The period is 0.00034011 s and the propagation speed is 4051.6 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 15.741 kg and radius 1.426 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 93.295 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 4.999 kg block starts at 25.873 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.318. The surface extends for 13.418 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 107.33 m. After the available distance its speed is 24.202 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 3.1185 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 1372.3 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Problem: A rod with initial length 22.008 m has expansion coefficient 5.876e-06 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 73.057 K.

Solution method: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is 9.4477 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

8.076 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 234.57 K to 851.13 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

The internal energy change is 62101 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.

## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 21.925 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 481.71 N/m and displaced by 0.132 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 4.6873 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.74601 Hz, and turning-point energy is 4.1966 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 5.983 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 349.51 K, changing volume from 47.985 to 59.789 liters.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 9.423 kg is released from rest at a height of 72.342 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 37.668 m/s and the kinetic energy is 6685 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 25.848 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -1.466 m/s^2 for 7.89 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 14.281 m/s, and the signed displacement is 158.31 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 67.941 kg changes signed velocity from -6.253 to -0.66 m/s during 1.002 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is 379.99 N s and the average net force is 379.24 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 23.244 kg and 18.239 kg and initial signed speeds 8.948 and -0.945 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 4.5983 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 500.11 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.021 m^3 and material density 1751.5 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 803.6 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 165.49 N and the weight is 360.7 N; their signed upward difference is -195.21 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

Physical setup: A mass of 182.39 kg follows a circle of radius 11.141 m at constant speed 59.512 m/s.

Relevant law: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Calculated result: The centripetal acceleration is 317.9 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 57982 N, and rotation frequency is 0.85016 Hz.

Interpretation: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Conditions of validity: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.014 m^3 and material density 867.82 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1371.7 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 188.32 N and the weight is 119.15 N; their signed upward difference is 69.178 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Lever arm and rotational effect

A force of magnitude 195.95 N acts at a distance of 0.279 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 174.13 degrees to the lever.

The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

The calculated torque magnitude is 5.594 N m.

For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Worked example: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Physical setup: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 43.806 kg and radius 1.606 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 127 rad/s.

Relevant law: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Calculated result: The moment of inertia is 56.493 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 4.5562e+05 J.

Interpretation: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Conditions of validity: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Quantitative physics problem: Pressure at depth

Problem: A stationary liquid has density 978.03 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 44.029 m below a surface at pressure 93.803 kPa.

Solution method: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Answer: The pressure increase is 422.29 kPa and the absolute pressure is 516.1 kPa.

Physical check: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Idealizations: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 17.812 m/s, emitting a tone of 1157.4 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 1220.8 Hz, a frequency increase of 63.398 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 147.1 kg block starts at 15.667 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.121. The surface extends for 13.045 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 103.43 m. After the available distance its speed is 14.646 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.1866 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Physical setup: A simple pendulum has length 3.551 m and an initial angular displacement of 2.914 degrees.

Relevant law: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Calculated result: The estimated oscillation period is 3.7809 s and its frequency is 0.26449 Hz.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Conditions of validity: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Problem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 0.671 m, tension 792.46 N, and linear mass density 0.008 kg/m.

Solution method: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Answer: The speed of transverse waves is 314.73 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 234.53 Hz.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Linear thermal expansion

A rod with initial length 20.228 m has expansion coefficient 5.841e-06 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 111.28 K.

For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

The calculated signed change in length is 13.147 mm.

For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Worked example: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Physical setup: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 7.4874e-05 W/m^2.

Relevant law: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Calculated result: The ideal intensity level is 78.743 dB.

Interpretation: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Conditions of validity: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Problem: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

Solution method: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 4.0227 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.02663 s^2.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 19.952 kg and 1.705 kg and initial signed speeds 19.368 and 8.9 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 18.544 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 86.062 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 5.391 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 510.18 K, changing volume from 46.113 to 74.426 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is 10947 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 34.683 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 2.141 m/s^2 for 2.882 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 40.853 m/s, and the signed displacement is 108.85 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 586.79 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 6957.8 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.5689 km/s and the orbital period is 96.264 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 40.398 kg changes signed velocity from -16.574 to 13.93 m/s during 0.422 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is 1232.3 N s and the average net force is 2920.1 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 7.178 kg is released from rest at a height of 28.648 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

Idealizations: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 46.683 kg and radius 0.571 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 130.84 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 7.6103 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 65146 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

Interpretation: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 63.392 m/s and elevation angle 60.356 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 11.236 s, the horizontal range is 352.3 m, and maximum height above launch is 154.77 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 2.373 kg is released from rest at a height of 49.778 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 31.246 m/s and the kinetic energy is 1158.4 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 15.896 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -0.511 m/s^2 for 7.676 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 11.974 m/s, and the signed displacement is 106.96 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 17.013 m/s, emitting a tone of 228.09 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 239.99 Hz, a frequency increase of 11.904 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 13.518 kg changes signed velocity from 18.114 to 1.828 m/s during 1.35 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is -220.15 N s and the average net force is -163.08 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Impulse and momentum change

## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 572.23 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 6943.2 km.

## Uniform circular motion

## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 23.413 kg and 23.769 kg and initial signed speeds -5.474 and 1.003 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is -2.2111 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 247.41 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Idealizations: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Problem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 7.166 cm^2 and 14.479 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 4.02 m/s.

Physical check: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

A sample of mass 1.747 kg has specific heat capacity 2720.1 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 299.44 to 429.16 K.

For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

The required energy is 616.42 kJ.

The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 131.36 kg block starts at 32.992 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.324. The surface extends for 24.955 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 171.29 m. After the available distance its speed is 30.494 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 3.1774 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.098 m^3 and material density 1668.8 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1289.3 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 1239.1 N and the weight is 1603.8 N; their signed upward difference is -364.75 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Problem: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

Solution method: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 3.9936 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.030373 s^2.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 1.126 m and an initial angular displacement of 4.714 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 2.1291 s and its frequency is 0.46969 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 12.032 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 314.05 N/m and displaced by 0.012 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 5.109 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.81312 Hz, and turning-point energy is 0.022612 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 11.752 cm^2 and 4.635 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 1.223 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 3.1009 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0014373 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Problem: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 5.7562e-05 W/m^2.

Solution method: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Answer: The ideal intensity level is 77.601 dB.

Physical check: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Idealizations: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Hooke-law force calibration

A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

The fitted slope is 547.36 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 552.7 N/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 1.5748 N.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Linear thermal expansion

Physical setup: A rod with initial length 2.022 m has expansion coefficient 6.489e-06 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 183.28 K.

Relevant law: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Calculated result: The calculated signed change in length is 2.4047 mm.

Interpretation: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Conditions of validity: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.

## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 12.103 m/s and elevation angle 31.931 degrees from level ground.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A force of magnitude 385.17 N acts at a distance of 2.104 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 172.86 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 100.74 N m.

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 22.499 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 5.992 m/s^2 for 13.439 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 103.03 m/s, and the signed displacement is 843.46 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 307.99 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 6679 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 7.7253 km/s and the orbital period is 90.537 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Worked example: Pressure at depth

Physical setup: A stationary liquid has density 1043.5 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 105.71 m below a surface at pressure 104.36 kPa.

Relevant law: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Calculated result: The pressure increase is 1081.7 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1186.1 kPa.

Interpretation: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Conditions of validity: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 515.11 K and cold reservoir at 398.03 K, absorbing 3451.4 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 22.729 percent, corresponding to at most 784.47 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.0193 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.11558 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

2.901 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 261.74 K to 928.08 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

The internal energy change is 24109 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Worked example: Uniform circular motion

Physical setup: A mass of 122.59 kg follows a circle of radius 23.437 m at constant speed 14.401 m/s.

Relevant law: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Calculated result: The centripetal acceleration is 8.8488 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 1084.8 N, and rotation frequency is 0.097794 Hz.

Interpretation: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Conditions of validity: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 20.417 kg changes signed velocity from 19.711 to -14.673 m/s during 1.566 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is -702.02 N s and the average net force is -448.29 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 7.086 m and an initial angular displacement of 5.526 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 5.341 s and its frequency is 0.18723 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Worked example: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Physical setup: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 269.45 W/(m K), thickness 0.124 m, area 1.214 m^2, and temperature difference 62.115 K.

Relevant law: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Calculated result: The conduction rate is 1.6386e+05 W.

Interpretation: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Conditions of validity: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

Problem: A vessel contains 8.307 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 567.86 K in volume 27.306 liters.

Solution method: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Answer: The equilibrium pressure is 1436.3 kPa.

Physical check: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 11100 Hz and has spatial wavelength 3.893 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 9.0088e-05 s and the propagation speed is 43213 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.014 m^3 and material density 1565.5 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1333.6 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 183.1 N and the weight is 214.93 N; their signed upward difference is -31.832 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 41.034 m/s, emitting a tone of 318.44 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 361.71 Hz, a frequency increase of 43.272 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 84.185 kg block starts at 28.547 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.38. The surface extends for 22.581 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 109.34 m. After the available distance its speed is 25.429 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 3.7265 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 1.691 kg is released from rest at a height of 115.23 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 47.541 m/s and the kinetic energy is 1910.9 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 18.2 kg and 18.814 kg and initial signed speeds 10.615 and 10.323 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 10.467 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 0.39439 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 6.976 cm^2 and 9.993 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 0.522 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 0.3644 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.00036415 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 10.924 kg has specific heat capacity 2218.3 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 322.34 to 367.61 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 1097.1 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 93.455 kg block starts at 22.043 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.057. The surface extends for 19.536 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 434.63 m. After the available distance its speed is 21.542 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 0.55898 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

Problem: A vessel contains 0.335 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 526.75 K in volume 40.225 liters.

Solution method: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Answer: The equilibrium pressure is 36.475 kPa.

Physical check: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 3.373 m and an initial angular displacement of 6.255 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 3.6849 s and its frequency is 0.27138 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Worked example: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Physical setup: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 4.7184e-09 W/m^2.

Relevant law: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Calculated result: The ideal intensity level is 36.738 dB.

Interpretation: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Conditions of validity: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Reversible isothermal gas work

8.57 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 234.76 K, changing volume from 35.613 to 64.958 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 10054 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 13.285 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 162.48 N/m and displaced by 0.184 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 3.4972 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.5566 Hz, and turning-point energy is 2.7505 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 79.538 m/s and elevation angle 32.901 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 8.8112 s, the horizontal range is 588.42 m, and maximum height above launch is 95.17 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 20.68 kg and radius 0.394 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 164.21 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 1.6051 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 21641 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

0.987 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 406.73 K to 343.47 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

The internal energy change is -778.79 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Worked example: Buoyant force on an immersed object

## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 13.076 kg changes signed velocity from 2.557 to 16.424 m/s during 0.603 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is 181.32 N s and the average net force is 300.7 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

The speed in the second section is 3.8357 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0023497 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Worked example: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Physical setup: A sample of mass 3.215 kg has specific heat capacity 768.3 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 287.77 to 469.21 K.

Relevant law: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Calculated result: The required energy is 448.17 kJ.

Interpretation: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Conditions of validity: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 17.516 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 3.06 m/s^2 for 8.847 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 44.588 m/s, and the signed displacement is 274.72 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 828.39 K and cold reservoir at 273.43 K, absorbing 3572.2 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 66.992 percent, corresponding to at most 2393.1 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1788.9 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 8159.9 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 6.9892 km/s and the orbital period is 122.26 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Lever arm and rotational effect

A force of magnitude 11.549 N acts at a distance of 0.796 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 7.66 degrees to the lever.

The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

The calculated torque magnitude is 1.2254 N m.

For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 8.928 kg is released from rest at a height of 73.504 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 37.969 m/s and the kinetic energy is 6435.6 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.
