## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A force of magnitude 232.92 N acts at a distance of 2.064 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 168.45 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 96.272 N m.

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 5.349 cm^2 and 7.548 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.044 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 1.4485 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0010933 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Physical setup: A simple pendulum has length 2.429 m and an initial angular displacement of 2.487 degrees.

Relevant law: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Calculated result: The estimated oscillation period is 3.127 s and its frequency is 0.31979 Hz.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Conditions of validity: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Problem: A rod with initial length 3.991 m has expansion coefficient 2.3905e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 71.107 K.

Solution method: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is 6.784 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.078 m^3 and material density 533.84 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1230.7 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 941.37 N and the weight is 408.34 N; their signed upward difference is 533.02 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Calculated result: The required energy is 1339.6 kJ.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 493.1 Hz and has spatial wavelength 0.733 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 0.002028 s and the propagation speed is 361.44 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 6.646 kg is released from rest at a height of 27.314 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 23.146 m/s and the kinetic energy is 1780.2 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 27.259 kg block starts at 19.657 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.291. The surface extends for 15.198 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 67.7 m. After the available distance its speed is 17.311 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 2.8537 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 7.774 kg and 17.581 kg and initial signed speeds -9.081 and 12.302 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 5.7458 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 1232.3 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 2035 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 8406 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 6.8861 km/s and the orbital period is 127.83 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 990.75 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.406 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 53.756 kg changes signed velocity from -3.039 to 16.795 m/s during 0.513 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 1066.2 N s and the average net force is 2078.4 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Conditions of validity: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 22.854 m/s, emitting a tone of 1599.6 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 1713.8 Hz, a frequency increase of 114.19 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 1181.7 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 6.637 m below a surface at pressure 107.53 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1387.9 K and cold reservoir at 226.27 K, absorbing 4276.7 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 83.696 percent, corresponding to at most 3579.4 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Spring oscillator

Problem: A force of magnitude 584.95 N acts at a distance of 3.596 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 83.587 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 2090.3 N m.

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

0.664 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 346.08 K to 231.78 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

The internal energy change is -946.57 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Worked example: Ideal gas equation of state

Calculated result: The equilibrium pressure is 718.39 kPa.

Interpretation: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Conditions of validity: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 38.94 kg block starts at 14.95 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.275. The surface extends for 3.506 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 41.438 m. After the available distance its speed is 14.304 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 2.6968 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Worked example: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Physical setup: A fully submerged body has volume 0.008 m^3 and material density 1766.5 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1388.3 kg/m^3.

Relevant law: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Calculated result: The upward buoyancy is 108.92 N and the weight is 138.59 N; their signed upward difference is -29.671 N.

Interpretation: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Conditions of validity: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Problem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 2.585 m, tension 708.48 N, and linear mass density 0.011 kg/m.

Solution method: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Answer: The speed of transverse waves is 253.79 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 49.088 Hz.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

The required energy is 2131.2 kJ.

## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.0197 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.41947 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 7.826 kg is released from rest at a height of 85.415 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 40.93 m/s and the kinetic energy is 6555.3 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 2080.3 Hz and has spatial wavelength 3.628 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 0.0004807 s and the propagation speed is 7547.3 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Thermal conduction measurement

A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

The fitted slope is 5.9121 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 5.8785 W/K.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 43.854 W.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1146 K and cold reservoir at 407.33 K, absorbing 8505.3 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 64.456 percent, corresponding to at most 5482.2 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 0.928 kg changes signed velocity from 0.723 to -10.311 m/s during 0.32 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -10.24 N s and the average net force is -31.999 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 14.694 cm^2 and 3.762 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 1.143 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 4.4644 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0016795 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Worked example: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Physical setup: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 4.946 kg and radius 1.459 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 103.87 rad/s.

Relevant law: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Calculated result: The moment of inertia is 5.2642 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 28400 J.

Interpretation: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Conditions of validity: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Small-angle pendulum

The estimated oscillation period is 3.7424 s and its frequency is 0.26721 Hz.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 22.158 m/s, emitting a tone of 1267.9 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 1355.5 Hz, a frequency increase of 87.564 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 1104.6 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.327 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 4.768 cm^2 and 12.332 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.604 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 1.0068 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0012416 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 58.091 kg block starts at 24.909 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.64. The surface extends for 15.848 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 49.429 m. After the available distance its speed is 20.531 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 6.2763 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 29.164 m/s and elevation angle 41.401 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 3.9334 s, the horizontal range is 86.047 m, and maximum height above launch is 18.966 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 26.437 m/s, emitting a tone of 1160.3 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 1257.2 Hz, a frequency increase of 96.904 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Lever arm and rotational effect

A force of magnitude 338.07 N acts at a distance of 3.943 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 20.612 degrees to the lever.

The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

The calculated torque magnitude is 469.28 N m.

For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.002 m^3 and material density 695.6 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1155.8 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 22.669 N and the weight is 13.643 N; their signed upward difference is 9.0259 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 19.776 kg and radius 1.212 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 17.172 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 14.525 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 2141.5 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Worked example: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Physical setup: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 1.1911e-07 W/m^2.

Relevant law: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Calculated result: The ideal intensity level is 50.759 dB.

Interpretation: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Conditions of validity: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 0.105 kg is released from rest at a height of 70.909 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 37.293 m/s and the kinetic energy is 73.015 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 5172.7 Hz and has spatial wavelength 2.232 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 0.00019332 s and the propagation speed is 11545 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Worked example: Uniform circular motion

Physical setup: A mass of 167.6 kg follows a circle of radius 9.311 m at constant speed 59.404 m/s.

Relevant law: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Calculated result: The centripetal acceleration is 379 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 63521 N, and rotation frequency is 1.0154 Hz.

Interpretation: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Conditions of validity: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Motion with constant acceleration

Interpretation: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 0.738 kg and 12.42 kg and initial signed speeds 3.005 and 12.948 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 12.39 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 34.434 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 0.129 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 197.9 N/m and displaced by 0.29 m.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 96.035 W/(m K), thickness 0.554 m, area 3.269 m^2, and temperature difference 9.754 K.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 5527.4 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Worked example: Uniform circular motion

Physical setup: A mass of 189.92 kg follows a circle of radius 14.673 m at constant speed 28.264 m/s.

Relevant law: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Calculated result: The centripetal acceleration is 54.444 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 10340 N, and rotation frequency is 0.30657 Hz.

Interpretation: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Problem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 3.103 m, tension 562.14 N, and linear mass density 0.057 kg/m.

Solution method: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Answer: The speed of transverse waves is 99.308 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 16.002 Hz.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

A sample of mass 7.661 kg has specific heat capacity 3381.6 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 280.32 to 471.62 K.

For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

The required energy is 4955.7 kJ.

The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 1.017 cm^2 and 4.214 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 0.582 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 0.14046 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 5.9189e-05 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A force of magnitude 214.11 N acts at a distance of 3.401 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 6.132 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 77.785 N m.

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 20.821 m/s and elevation angle 54.618 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 3.4621 s, the horizontal range is 41.738 m, and maximum height above launch is 14.693 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Worked example: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Physical setup: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 9.459e-07 W/m^2.

Relevant law: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Calculated result: The ideal intensity level is 59.758 dB.

Interpretation: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Conditions of validity: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.082 m^3 and material density 1168.4 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1063.5 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 855.2 N and the weight is 939.53 N; their signed upward difference is -84.332 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 27.569 kg block starts at 32.983 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.462. The surface extends for 28.535 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 120.06 m. After the available distance its speed is 28.798 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 4.5307 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Worked example: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Physical setup: 2.213 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 318.27 K to 644.45 K.

Relevant law: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Calculated result: The internal energy change is 9002.5 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Interpretation: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Conditions of validity: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 8.203 kg and 14.257 kg and initial signed speeds 15.696 and 19.127 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 20.598 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 418.8 N/m and displaced by 0.288 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 4.5091 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.71764 Hz, and turning-point energy is 17.368 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 543.61 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.737 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 58.004 kg changes signed velocity from -10.839 to 8.004 m/s during 0.602 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 1093 N s and the average net force is 1815.6 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Quantitative physics problem: Hooke-law force calibration

Problem: A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

Solution method: For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 647.88 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 640.09 N/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 1.4514 N.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 3.69 kg is released from rest at a height of 79.164 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 3.215 kg and radius 1.347 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 29.187 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 2.9167 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 1242.3 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 43.562 kg changes signed velocity from -14.894 to -5.013 m/s during 0.277 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is 430.44 N s and the average net force is 1553.9 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 3.758 cm^2 and 14.832 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.407 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 0.60986 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.00090455 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 26.053 m/s, emitting a tone of 206.62 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 223.6 Hz, a frequency increase of 16.984 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 19495 Hz and has spatial wavelength 0.037 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 5.1296e-05 s and the propagation speed is 721.3 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 393.12 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.856 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Worked example: Uniform circular motion

Physical setup: A mass of 141.13 kg follows a circle of radius 16.831 m at constant speed 14.003 m/s.

Relevant law: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Calculated result: The centripetal acceleration is 11.65 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 1644.2 N, and rotation frequency is 0.13241 Hz.

Interpretation: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Conditions of validity: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1101.9 K and cold reservoir at 325.37 K, absorbing 1148.7 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 70.473 percent, corresponding to at most 809.51 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 16.2 kg and 11.986 kg and initial signed speeds -1.039 and 11.656 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 4.3595 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 555.13 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 874.26 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7245.3 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 7.4173 km/s and the orbital period is 102.29 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 121.28 W/(m K), thickness 0.03 m, area 1.513 m^2, and temperature difference 60.218 K.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 3.6831e+05 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 60.01 kg block starts at 29.358 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.43. The surface extends for 29.262 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 102.2 m. After the available distance its speed is 24.801 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 4.2169 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 73.309 m/s and elevation angle 41.124 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 9.8331 s, the horizontal range is 543.01 m, and maximum height above launch is 118.52 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 826.57 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 153.15 m below a surface at pressure 98.755 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

The pressure increase is 1241.4 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1340.2 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 1.367 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 1.864 m/s^2 for 10.871 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 21.631 m/s, and the signed displacement is 125 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.082 m^3 and material density 630.99 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 746.95 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 600.66 N and the weight is 507.41 N; their signed upward difference is 93.249 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Ideal gas equation of state

A vessel contains 3.911 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 265.62 K in volume 67.811 liters.

The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

The equilibrium pressure is 127.38 kPa.

At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sound intensity and decibel scale

## Quantitative physics problem: Spring oscillator

Problem: A mass of 15.145 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 120.92 N/m and displaced by 0.189 m.

Solution method: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

8.656 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 679.89 K to 972.52 K.

## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 4.741 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 214.74 K, changing volume from 16.268 to 28.339 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is 4698.3 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.271 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Linear thermal expansion

A rod with initial length 6.249 m has expansion coefficient 2.4458e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by -6.909 K.

For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

The calculated signed change in length is -1.056 mm.

For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Worked example: Steady heat conduction through a slab

## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 12.257 m/s and elevation angle 57.125 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 2.0994 s, the horizontal range is 13.968 m, and maximum height above launch is 5.4029 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 3.612 kg changes signed velocity from -5.403 to -6.085 m/s during 0.459 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -2.4634 N s and the average net force is -5.3668 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Problem: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

Solution method: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 4.0358 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.09081 s^2.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 28.13 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 7.814 m/s^2 for 15.056 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 145.78 m/s, and the signed displacement is 1309.2 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 1.356 cm^2 and 11.386 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 0.812 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 0.096704 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.00011011 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 3.658 kg and 19.977 kg and initial signed speeds -1.727 and -6.299 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is -5.5914 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 32.315 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 14.635 kg follows a circle of radius 17.363 m at constant speed 62.559 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 225.4 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 3298.7 N, and rotation frequency is 0.57344 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 17.038 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 383.11 N/m and displaced by 0.123 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 4.7419 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.7547 Hz, and turning-point energy is 2.898 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.103 m^3 and material density 778.24 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1180.5 kg/m^3.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 0.582 kg is released from rest at a height of 49.614 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 31.194 m/s and the kinetic energy is 283.17 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Pressure at depth

The pressure increase is 1276.2 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1368.2 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Reversible isothermal gas work

1.546 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 507.91 K, changing volume from 26.662 to 41.299 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 2857 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 4.21 m/s, emitting a tone of 748.03 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 757.33 Hz, a frequency increase of 9.2955 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1505.6 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7876.6 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 7.1138 km/s and the orbital period is 115.95 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 182.3 kg follows a circle of radius 11.095 m at constant speed 57.697 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 300.04 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 54697 N, and rotation frequency is 0.82765 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 1.3851e-06 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 61.415 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 41.756 kg block starts at 24.541 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.119. The surface extends for 0.279 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 258.04 m. After the available distance its speed is 24.528 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.167 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 17.106 m/s and elevation angle 55.074 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 2.8603 s, the horizontal range is 28.013 m, and maximum height above launch is 10.029 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 565.02 N acts at a distance of 3.105 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 114.34 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 1598.5 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Problem: A rod with initial length 17.665 m has expansion coefficient 1.4836e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 121.38 K.

Solution method: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is 31.811 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 5.288 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 6.415 m/s^2 for 14.838 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 100.47 m/s, and the signed displacement is 784.65 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 465.16 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.799 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Quantitative physics problem: Pressure at depth

Problem: A stationary liquid has density 924.06 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 7.5 m below a surface at pressure 103.74 kPa.

Solution method: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Answer: The pressure increase is 67.964 kPa and the absolute pressure is 171.71 kPa.

Physical check: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Idealizations: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 34.201 kg changes signed velocity from 14.476 to -6.174 m/s during 1.568 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -706.25 N s and the average net force is -450.41 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 12.216 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 610.59 N/m and displaced by 0.354 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 7.0698 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.1252 Hz, and turning-point energy is 38.258 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Worked example: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Physical setup: A sample of mass 14.349 kg has specific heat capacity 2148 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 274.8 to 461.21 K.

Relevant law: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Calculated result: The required energy is 5745.6 kJ.

Interpretation: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Conditions of validity: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1254.9 K and cold reservoir at 402.83 K, absorbing 8000.6 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 67.898 percent, corresponding to at most 5432.2 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Worked example: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Physical setup: A fully submerged body has volume 0.111 m^3 and material density 1065.3 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 922.51 kg/m^3.

Relevant law: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Calculated result: The upward buoyancy is 1004.2 N and the weight is 1159.7 N; their signed upward difference is -155.47 N.

Interpretation: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Conditions of validity: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 17358 Hz and has spatial wavelength 0.298 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 5.761e-05 s and the propagation speed is 5172.7 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 9.642 kg and 5.154 kg and initial signed speeds -8.296 and 16.319 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 0.27832 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 1017.5 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Problem: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

Solution method: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 4.0166 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.042745 s^2.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Ideal gas equation of state

A vessel contains 3.498 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 947.8 K in volume 96.973 liters.

The equilibrium pressure is 284.26 kPa.

At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 14.102 cm^2 and 3.538 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 1.576 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 6.2817 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0022225 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Worked example: Thermal conduction measurement

Relevant law: For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 4.0742 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0487 W/K.

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 5.9045 W.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 3.2 kg and radius 1.702 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 119.58 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 4.6349 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 33135 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 1.9815e-10 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 22.97 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 11.685 cm^2 and 7.654 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 1.821 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 2.78 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0021278 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1556.8 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7927.8 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 7.0908 km/s and the orbital period is 117.08 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1413.8 K and cold reservoir at 429.92 K, absorbing 6125.2 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 69.592 percent, corresponding to at most 4262.6 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum

Problem: A simple pendulum has length 7.407 m and an initial angular displacement of 3.628 degrees.

Solution method: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Answer: The estimated oscillation period is 5.4606 s and its frequency is 0.18313 Hz.

Physical check: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Idealizations: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Linear thermal expansion

A rod with initial length 2.889 m has expansion coefficient 8.084e-06 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 193.89 K.

For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

The calculated signed change in length is 4.5283 mm.

For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Worked example: Hooke-law force calibration

Physical setup: A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

Relevant law: For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 737.03 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 734.47 N/m.

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 1.0226 N.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 22.661 kg and 22.149 kg and initial signed speeds 18.834 and 17.277 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is 18.064 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 13.577 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 15815 Hz and has spatial wavelength 4.099 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 6.3229e-05 s and the propagation speed is 64827 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Worked example: Standing wave on a stretched string

Physical setup: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 4.72 m, tension 751.75 N, and linear mass density 0.015 kg/m.

Relevant law: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Calculated result: The speed of transverse waves is 223.87 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 23.715 Hz.

Interpretation: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Conditions of validity: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.

## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 5.068 kg is released from rest at a height of 41.192 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 28.424 m/s and the kinetic energy is 2047.2 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 8.072 m/s, emitting a tone of 1055.6 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 1081 Hz, a frequency increase of 25.44 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Problem: 2.534 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 857.44 K to 342.5 K.

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Answer: The internal energy change is -16274 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.

## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 34.314 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 0.254 m/s^2 for 14.521 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 38.002 m/s, and the signed displacement is 525.05 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 3.765 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 676.83 K, changing volume from 4.403 to 11.76 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is 20816 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 233.62 W/(m K), thickness 0.152 m, area 0.389 m^2, and temperature difference 41.259 K.

The conduction rate is 24668 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.087 m^3 and material density 652.86 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1195.7 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 1020.1 N and the weight is 557 N; their signed upward difference is 463.12 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 81.497 m/s and elevation angle 23.244 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 6.5593 s, the horizontal range is 491.18 m, and maximum height above launch is 52.741 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 51.878 kg changes signed velocity from 13.269 to -2.604 m/s during 1.973 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -823.46 N s and the average net force is -417.36 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

Interpretation: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Conditions of validity: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Problem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 3.225 m, tension 690.61 N, and linear mass density 0.006 kg/m.

Solution method: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Answer: The speed of transverse waves is 339.27 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 52.599 Hz.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity
