Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 1.21 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 624.91 K, changing volume from 16.891 to 45.792 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is 6270.1 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Standing wave on a stretched string

A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 0.359 m, tension 312.56 N, and linear mass density 0.04 kg/m.

Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

The speed of transverse waves is 88.397 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 123.12 Hz.

The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Worked example: Escape speed from a central mass

Physical setup: Consider a test object at altitude 1486.9 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Relevant law: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Calculated result: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.072 km/s.

Interpretation: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Conditions of validity: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

Problem: A vessel contains 10.093 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 643.28 K in volume 8.355 liters.

Solution method: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Answer: The equilibrium pressure is 6461.1 kPa.

Physical check: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 36.454 kg and radius 1.061 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 70.392 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 20.519 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 50835 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 49.201 m/s and elevation angle 29.491 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 4.9397 s, the horizontal range is 211.55 m, and maximum height above launch is 29.911 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 0.819 m and an initial angular displacement of 3.683 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 1.8158 s and its frequency is 0.55073 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Worked example: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Physical setup: 7.739 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 641.01 K to 946.69 K.

Relevant law: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Calculated result: The internal energy change is 29504 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Interpretation: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Conditions of validity: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 9.501 kg is released from rest at a height of 118.03 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 48.113 m/s and the kinetic energy is 10997 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 58.97 W/(m K), thickness 0.446 m, area 0.809 m^2, and temperature difference 49.487 K.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 5293.4 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 9.312 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -0.644 m/s^2 for 6.278 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 5.269 m/s, and the signed displacement is 45.77 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 111.75 kg follows a circle of radius 18.311 m at constant speed 74.175 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 300.47 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 33576 N, and rotation frequency is 0.64471 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 21.928 m/s, emitting a tone of 633.02 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 676.25 Hz, a frequency increase of 43.233 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 9.3459e-07 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 59.706 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 503.63 K and cold reservoir at 400 K, absorbing 4486.2 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 20.576 percent, corresponding to at most 923.07 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Hooke-law force calibration

A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

The fitted slope is 454.76 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 452.54 N/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.29039 N.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Problem: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

Solution method: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 4.0318 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.29717 s^2.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 117.88 kg block starts at 34.52 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.179. The surface extends for 5.698 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 339.42 m. After the available distance its speed is 34.229 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.7554 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum

Problem: A simple pendulum has length 1.254 m and an initial angular displacement of 1.736 degrees.

Solution method: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Answer: The estimated oscillation period is 2.2468 s and its frequency is 0.44507 Hz.

Physical check: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Idealizations: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Circular Earth orbit

## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 228.32 kg follows a circle of radius 5.415 m at constant speed 51.328 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 486.53 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 1.1108e+05 N, and rotation frequency is 1.5086 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 62.342 kg changes signed velocity from -13.896 to -15.125 m/s during 0.802 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is -76.618 N s and the average net force is -95.534 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 12.113 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -1.622 m/s^2 for 16.36 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is -14.423 m/s, and the signed displacement is -18.895 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 253.73 W/(m K), thickness 0.033 m, area 2.923 m^2, and temperature difference 50.44 K.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 1.1336e+06 W.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 52.932 m/s, emitting a tone of 725.86 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 858.31 Hz, a frequency increase of 132.45 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 1051.1 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.364 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 8.141 cm^2 and 2.395 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 4.476 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 15.215 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0036439 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 5.483 kg has specific heat capacity 4079.3 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 328.53 to 454.98 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 2828.2 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Reversible isothermal gas work

8.711 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 517.82 K, changing volume from 14.397 to 40.153 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 38467 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 940.56 K and cold reservoir at 297.96 K, absorbing 3132.2 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 68.321 percent, corresponding to at most 2140 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 13672 Hz and has spatial wavelength 1.55 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 7.3143e-05 s and the propagation speed is 21191 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 22.113 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 278.3 N/m and displaced by 0.303 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 3.5476 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.56462 Hz, and turning-point energy is 12.775 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 7.457 kg is released from rest at a height of 52.061 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.09 m^3 and material density 1339.2 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 702.94 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 620.41 N and the weight is 1181.9 N; their signed upward difference is -561.54 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 1015.3 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.389 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 6.9858e-07 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 58.442 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 8.962 cm^2 and 13.568 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 4.149 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 2.7405 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0037183 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Problem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 1.928 m, tension 664.95 N, and linear mass density 0.007 kg/m.

Solution method: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Answer: The speed of transverse waves is 308.21 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 79.93 Hz.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.

## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Problem: 2.486 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 289.99 K to 541.4 K.

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Answer: The internal energy change is 7795 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 567.28 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 6938.3 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.5796 km/s and the orbital period is 95.86 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 26.956 kg changes signed velocity from 1.45 to -7.853 m/s during 0.014 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is -250.77 N s and the average net force is -17912 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 224.14 kg follows a circle of radius 3.431 m at constant speed 70.207 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 1436.6 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 3.22e+05 N, and rotation frequency is 3.2567 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 12.859 cm^2 and 5.113 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.189 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 5.5053 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0028148 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 27.839 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 4.418 m/s^2 for 4.728 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 48.727 m/s, and the signed displacement is 181 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 23.074 kg and radius 1.508 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 16.626 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 26.236 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 3626.1 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 11.23 kg changes signed velocity from -18.749 to 13.716 m/s during 0.221 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 364.58 N s and the average net force is 1649.7 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Linear thermal expansion

Physical setup: A rod with initial length 24.056 m has expansion coefficient 9.836e-06 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 114.6 K.

Relevant law: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Calculated result: The calculated signed change in length is 27.116 mm.

Interpretation: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Conditions of validity: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 7.809 m/s and elevation angle 27.889 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 0.74495 s, the horizontal range is 5.1417 m, and maximum height above launch is 0.68028 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Spring oscillator

Problem: A mass of 22.246 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 645.52 N/m and displaced by 0.283 m.

Solution method: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Answer: The angular frequency is 5.3868 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.85733 Hz, and turning-point energy is 25.85 J.

Physical check: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Idealizations: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 2.382 kg and 23.278 kg and initial signed speeds -1.462 and 6.513 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 5.7727 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 68.717 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Physical setup: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

Relevant law: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 4.0074 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.19642 s^2.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.146 m^3 and material density 456.79 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1149.2 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 1645.5 N and the weight is 654.01 N; their signed upward difference is 991.44 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Worked example: Ideal gas equation of state

Physical setup: A vessel contains 7.246 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 540.03 K in volume 128.15 liters.

Relevant law: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Calculated result: The equilibrium pressure is 253.88 kPa.

Interpretation: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Conditions of validity: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Hooke-law force calibration

Problem: A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

Solution method: For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 346.78 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 346.09 N/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.4453 N.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Worked example: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Physical setup: A sample of mass 0.965 kg has specific heat capacity 2109.5 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 301.27 to 413.55 K.

Relevant law: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Calculated result: The required energy is 228.57 kJ.

Interpretation: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Conditions of validity: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.

## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 802.99 K and cold reservoir at 422.81 K, absorbing 2309.1 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 47.346 percent, corresponding to at most 1093.3 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum

Problem: A simple pendulum has length 2.253 m and an initial angular displacement of 1.323 degrees.

Solution method: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Answer: The estimated oscillation period is 3.0116 s and its frequency is 0.33205 Hz.

Physical check: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Idealizations: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 0.528 kg is released from rest at a height of 39.981 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 28.003 m/s and the kinetic energy is 207.02 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 4.778 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 639.92 K, changing volume from 36.253 to 19.794 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is -15384 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 95.013 kg block starts at 34.075 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.186. The surface extends for 27.093 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 318.28 m. After the available distance its speed is 32.592 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.824 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Lever arm and rotational effect

A force of magnitude 518.48 N acts at a distance of 1.23 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 108.53 degrees to the lever.

The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

The calculated torque magnitude is 604.65 N m.

For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 28.826 m/s, emitting a tone of 645.88 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 705.14 Hz, a frequency increase of 59.261 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 3.908 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 258.48 K, changing volume from 5.228 to 11.868 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is 6885 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Lever arm and rotational effect

A force of magnitude 571.96 N acts at a distance of 2.001 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 101.53 degrees to the lever.

The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

The calculated torque magnitude is 1121.4 N m.

For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 9.387 kg changes signed velocity from -6.625 to -19.396 m/s during 1.075 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is -119.88 N s and the average net force is -111.52 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 215.47 kg follows a circle of radius 8.066 m at constant speed 73.127 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 662.98 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 1.4285e+05 N, and rotation frequency is 1.4429 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 12.831 kg block starts at 25.721 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.408. The surface extends for 24 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 82.673 m. After the available distance its speed is 21.668 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 4.0011 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.119 m^3 and material density 1483.1 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1328.5 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 1550.3 N and the weight is 1730.8 N; their signed upward difference is -180.46 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Problem: 7.04 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 320.88 K to 756.29 K.

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Answer: The internal energy change is 38229 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 975.34 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 123.25 m below a surface at pressure 104.44 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

The pressure increase is 1178.8 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1283.3 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 27.216 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 0.905 m/s^2 for 11.013 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 37.183 m/s, and the signed displacement is 354.61 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Quantitative physics problem: Spring oscillator

Problem: A mass of 18.649 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 56.65 N/m and displaced by 0.025 m.

Solution method: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Answer: The angular frequency is 1.7429 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.27739 Hz, and turning-point energy is 0.017703 J.

Physical check: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Idealizations: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 1237.6 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.236 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 5.6509e-07 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 57.521 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 662.53 K and cold reservoir at 243.36 K, absorbing 8060.4 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 63.268 percent, corresponding to at most 5099.6 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 972.66 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7343.7 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 7.3674 km/s and the orbital period is 104.38 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 32.881 m/s, emitting a tone of 361.17 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 399.46 Hz, a frequency increase of 38.294 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 11.875 cm^2 and 6.222 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 4.248 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 8.1075 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0050445 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 6.624 kg and 23.168 kg and initial signed speeds 4.831 and 10.852 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 9.5133 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 93.372 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Quantitative physics problem: Thermal conduction measurement

Problem: A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

Solution method: For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

Answer: The fitted slope is 2.1148 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 2.091 W/K.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 10.066 W.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 1.496 kg and radius 0.409 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 78.501 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 0.12513 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 385.54 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Physical setup: A simple pendulum has length 5.054 m and an initial angular displacement of 2.947 degrees.

Relevant law: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Calculated result: The estimated oscillation period is 4.5106 s and its frequency is 0.2217 Hz.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Conditions of validity: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

Interpretation: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Conditions of validity: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Problem: 0.975 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 462.83 K to 981.15 K.

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Answer: The internal energy change is 6302.7 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.

## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 473.89 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 6844.9 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.6311 km/s and the orbital period is 93.931 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Worked example: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Physical setup: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 26.06 kg and radius 0.057 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 144.49 rad/s.

Relevant law: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Calculated result: The moment of inertia is 0.042334 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 441.89 J.

Interpretation: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Conditions of validity: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 41.784 kg block starts at 34.075 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.506. The surface extends for 21.405 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 117 m. After the available distance its speed is 30.801 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 4.9622 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1138.7 K and cold reservoir at 352.56 K, absorbing 4544.2 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 69.038 percent, corresponding to at most 3137.2 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Lever arm and rotational effect

A force of magnitude 529.52 N acts at a distance of 3.3 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 25.827 degrees to the lever.

The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

The calculated torque magnitude is 761.27 N m.

For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Worked example: Standing wave on a stretched string

Physical setup: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 2.582 m, tension 680.16 N, and linear mass density 0.012 kg/m.

Relevant law: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Calculated result: The speed of transverse waves is 238.08 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 46.103 Hz.

Interpretation: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Conditions of validity: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 31.474 m/s, emitting a tone of 1410 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 1552.4 Hz, a frequency increase of 142.45 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Escape speed from a central mass

## Spring oscillator

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 18.4 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 236.74 N/m and displaced by 0.099 m.

The angular frequency is 3.5869 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.57088 Hz, and turning-point energy is 1.1601 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

## Quantitative physics problem: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Idealizations: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Worked example: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Physical setup: A fully submerged body has volume 0.011 m^3 and material density 546.58 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 730.72 kg/m^3.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 13.574 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 2.27 m/s^2 for 12.098 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 41.036 m/s, and the signed displacement is 330.34 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1296.9 K and cold reservoir at 395.91 K, absorbing 5111.3 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 69.472 percent, corresponding to at most 3550.9 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Hooke-law force calibration

Problem: A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

Solution method: For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 177.34 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 177.94 N/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.94321 N.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 15.906 kg changes signed velocity from -5.753 to -1.36 m/s during 0.794 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 69.875 N s and the average net force is 88.004 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 66.942 m/s and elevation angle 26.912 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 14.282 kg and 15.572 kg and initial signed speeds 18.226 and 3.892 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is 10.749 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 765.31 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

## Periodic wave propagation

## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 134.8 kg block starts at 23.75 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.596. The surface extends for 7.984 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 48.254 m. After the available distance its speed is 21.696 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 5.8448 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Worked example: Pressure at depth

Relevant law: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Calculated result: The pressure increase is 769.03 kPa and the absolute pressure is 861.79 kPa.

Interpretation: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Conditions of validity: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.148 m^3 and material density 365.06 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1107.3 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 1607.1 N and the weight is 529.84 N; their signed upward difference is 1077.3 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Lever arm and rotational effect

A force of magnitude 262.55 N acts at a distance of 0.167 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 103.48 degrees to the lever.

The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

The calculated torque magnitude is 42.637 N m.

For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 12.272 kg and 10.42 kg and initial signed speeds 8.56 and 3.557 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is 6.2627 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 70.525 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 52.315 kg block starts at 28.942 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.496. The surface extends for 11.421 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 86.104 m. After the available distance its speed is 26.954 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 4.8641 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Worked example: Ideal gas equation of state

Physical setup: A vessel contains 9.454 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 525.91 K in volume 5.087 liters.

Relevant law: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Calculated result: The equilibrium pressure is 8126.4 kPa.

Interpretation: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Conditions of validity: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Hooke-law force calibration

Problem: A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

Solution method: For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 661.07 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 669.51 N/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.54509 N.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 81.691 m/s and elevation angle 71.298 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 15.781 s, the horizontal range is 413.36 m, and maximum height above launch is 305.27 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 7.319 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 462.08 K, changing volume from 23.581 to 44.686 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is 17974 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 972.38 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.419 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 164.28 kg follows a circle of radius 16.364 m at constant speed 13.83 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 11.688 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 1920.1 N, and rotation frequency is 0.13451 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Worked example: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Physical setup: A sample of mass 9.298 kg has specific heat capacity 515.7 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 289.01 to 374.71 K.

Relevant law: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Calculated result: The required energy is 410.93 kJ.

Interpretation: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Conditions of validity: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Problem: A rod with initial length 1.681 m has expansion coefficient 1.4083e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 12.994 K.

Solution method: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is 0.30761 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 18.839 kg is released from rest at a height of 117.25 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 47.954 m/s and the kinetic energy is 21661 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Physical setup: A simple pendulum has length 6.323 m and an initial angular displacement of 6.703 degrees.

Relevant law: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Calculated result: The estimated oscillation period is 5.0452 s and its frequency is 0.19821 Hz.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Conditions of validity: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Problem: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 103.19 W/(m K), thickness 0.141 m, area 1.148 m^2, and temperature difference 39.636 K.

Solution method: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Answer: The conduction rate is 33302 W.

Physical check: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Idealizations: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 26.744 m/s, emitting a tone of 320.68 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 347.79 Hz, a frequency increase of 27.118 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 12.586 cm^2 and 3.329 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.289 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 8.6541 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0028809 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 9.752 kg changes signed velocity from 18.479 to -13.605 m/s during 1.945 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -312.88 N s and the average net force is -160.87 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 14.557 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 745.85 N/m and displaced by 0.092 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 7.158 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.1392 Hz, and turning-point energy is 3.1564 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 4347.6 Hz and has spatial wavelength 3.28 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 0.00023001 s and the propagation speed is 14260 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 131.32 kg block starts at 4.695 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.586. The surface extends for 14.392 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 1.9179 m. After the available distance its speed is 0 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 5.7467 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Quantitative physics problem: Pressure at depth

Problem: A stationary liquid has density 836.02 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 45.973 m below a surface at pressure 105.1 kPa.

Solution method: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Answer: The pressure increase is 376.91 kPa and the absolute pressure is 482.01 kPa.

Physical check: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Idealizations: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 750.35 K and cold reservoir at 369.77 K, absorbing 7220.3 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 50.72 percent, corresponding to at most 3662.2 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Worked example: Uniform circular motion

Physical setup: A mass of 187.75 kg follows a circle of radius 3.993 m at constant speed 6.945 m/s.

Relevant law: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Calculated result: The centripetal acceleration is 12.079 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 2267.8 N, and rotation frequency is 0.27682 Hz.

Interpretation: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Conditions of validity: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Problem: A rod with initial length 5.902 m has expansion coefficient 2.0881e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 165.87 K.

Solution method: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is 20.442 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 9.6731e-10 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 29.856 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1857 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 8228 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 6.9602 km/s and the orbital period is 123.79 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 13.876 kg changes signed velocity from -19.526 to -1.592 m/s during 0.15 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is 248.85 N s and the average net force is 1659 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 6.577 m/s, emitting a tone of 1494 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 1523.2 Hz, a frequency increase of 29.206 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 4.2 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 285.8 K, changing volume from 16.479 to 22.148 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is 2950.7 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 108.2 W/(m K), thickness 0.384 m, area 0.754 m^2, and temperature difference 65.635 K.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 13945 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 10.917 m/s and elevation angle 38.582 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 1.3885 s, the horizontal range is 11.849 m, and maximum height above launch is 2.3633 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.
