## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 358.73 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 6729.7 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.6961 km/s and the orbital period is 91.57 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 41.91 m/s and elevation angle 73.011 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 8.1743 s, the horizontal range is 100.1 m, and maximum height above launch is 81.908 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 4.573 kg and 15.671 kg and initial signed speeds 8.786 and 5.603 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is 6.322 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 17.933 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 6.813 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 0.295 m/s^2 for 16.983 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 11.823 m/s, and the signed displacement is 158.25 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 18.063 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 433.01 N/m and displaced by 0.2 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 4.8962 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.77925 Hz, and turning-point energy is 8.6603 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 3.285 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 572.99 K, changing volume from 31.24 to 33.739 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is 1204.4 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 233.1 W/(m K), thickness 0.153 m, area 2.36 m^2, and temperature difference 14.004 K.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 50352 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Worked example: Pressure at depth

## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 13.298 kg and radius 1.29 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 170.64 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 11.065 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 1.6109e+05 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 70.757 kg follows a circle of radius 1.186 m at constant speed 29.886 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 753.1 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 53287 N, and rotation frequency is 4.0105 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Worked example: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Physical setup: A sample of mass 10.544 kg has specific heat capacity 4409.2 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 282.85 to 400.46 K.

Relevant law: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Calculated result: The required energy is 5467.6 kJ.

Interpretation: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Conditions of validity: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.

## Sound intensity and decibel scale

## Escape speed from a central mass

## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 5.193 m and an initial angular displacement of 6.482 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 4.5722 s and its frequency is 0.21871 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Worked example: Periodic wave propagation

Physical setup: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 8542.1 Hz and has spatial wavelength 3.925 m.

Relevant law: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Calculated result: The period is 0.00011707 s and the propagation speed is 33528 m/s.

Interpretation: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Conditions of validity: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Quantitative physics problem: Thermal conduction measurement

Problem: A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

Solution method: For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

Answer: The fitted slope is 2.8913 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 2.8885 W/K.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 2.2512 W.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.134 m^3 and material density 524.63 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1286.4 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 1690.5 N and the weight is 689.41 N; their signed upward difference is 1001.1 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 10.236 m. After the available distance its speed is 0 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 3.6481 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 9561 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 10.493 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 3.4 m/s^2 for 10.955 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 47.74 m/s, and the signed displacement is 318.97 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Problem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 0.915 m, tension 429.61 N, and linear mass density 0.049 kg/m.

Solution method: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Answer: The speed of transverse waves is 93.635 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 51.167 Hz.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 0.00055457 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 87.44 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 67.23 kg block starts at 27.61 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.578. The surface extends for 22.982 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 67.244 m. After the available distance its speed is 22.4 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 5.6682 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum

Problem: A simple pendulum has length 0.224 m and an initial angular displacement of 6.144 degrees.

Solution method: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Answer: The estimated oscillation period is 0.94961 s and its frequency is 1.0531 Hz.

Physical check: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Idealizations: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 4.979 kg changes signed velocity from 10.787 to 17.309 m/s during 0.308 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 32.473 N s and the average net force is 105.43 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 294.54 N acts at a distance of 1.905 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 28.53 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 267.99 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 381.02 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.866 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 10.248 m/s, emitting a tone of 1440.9 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 1485.3 Hz, a frequency increase of 44.377 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 0.181 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 358.04 K, changing volume from 46.431 to 100.85 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is 417.93 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Problem: 9.002 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 577.48 K to 719.18 K.

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Answer: The internal energy change is 15908 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.

## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 4.621 cm^2 and 12.765 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.417 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 0.87497 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0011169 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 12.53 kg is released from rest at a height of 95.877 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 43.364 m/s and the kinetic energy is 11781 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1844.7 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 8215.7 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 6.9654 km/s and the orbital period is 123.52 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Linear thermal expansion

A rod with initial length 10.016 m has expansion coefficient 7.044e-06 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 31.115 K.

For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

The calculated signed change in length is 2.1952 mm.

For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 11.679 kg and 9.821 kg and initial signed speeds -1.705 and -7.779 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is -4.4795 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 98.411 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1261.6 K and cold reservoir at 246.29 K, absorbing 6693.9 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 80.479 percent, corresponding to at most 5387.1 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 24.498 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 480.53 N/m and displaced by 0.316 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 4.4289 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.70488 Hz, and turning-point energy is 23.992 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Physical setup: A simple pendulum has length 1.551 m and an initial angular displacement of 7.257 degrees.

Relevant law: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Calculated result: The estimated oscillation period is 2.4988 s and its frequency is 0.4002 Hz.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Conditions of validity: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

## Perfectly inelastic collision

## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 13.311 kg is released from rest at a height of 55.372 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 32.955 m/s and the kinetic energy is 7228.1 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 5.832 kg changes signed velocity from 1.482 to 16.481 m/s during 1.459 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 87.474 N s and the average net force is 59.955 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

## Motion with constant acceleration

## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 27.095 m/s and elevation angle 40.09 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 3.5586 s, the horizontal range is 73.765 m, and maximum height above launch is 15.523 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 64.316 kg block starts at 19.133 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.5. The surface extends for 7.246 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 37.329 m. After the available distance its speed is 17.176 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 4.9033 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Ideal gas equation of state

A vessel contains 6.842 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 326.83 K in volume 138.36 liters.

The equilibrium pressure is 134.38 kPa.

At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 4.1613e-10 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 26.192 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.0283 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.5306 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1081.3 K and cold reservoir at 350.4 K, absorbing 4213.6 J per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Standing wave on a stretched string

A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 0.775 m, tension 478.09 N, and linear mass density 0.056 kg/m.

Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

The speed of transverse waves is 92.397 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 59.611 Hz.

The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.

## Quantitative physics problem: Pressure at depth

Problem: A stationary liquid has density 1058.5 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 4.606 m below a surface at pressure 92.13 kPa.

Solution method: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Answer: The pressure increase is 47.814 kPa and the absolute pressure is 139.94 kPa.

Physical check: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Idealizations: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 22.527 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -0.248 m/s^2 for 10.574 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 19.905 m/s, and the signed displacement is 224.34 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 22.768 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 778.69 N/m and displaced by 0.049 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 5.8482 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.93076 Hz, and turning-point energy is 0.93482 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 8220.1 Hz and has spatial wavelength 3.203 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 0.00012165 s and the propagation speed is 26329 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 252.58 W/(m K), thickness 0.291 m, area 2.195 m^2, and temperature difference 47.652 K.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 90786 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 22.246 m/s, emitting a tone of 614.53 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 657.16 Hz, a frequency increase of 42.621 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 5.644 cm^2 and 3.688 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 0.323 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 0.49431 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0001823 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

Calculated result: The calculated signed change in length is 6.0529 mm.

Interpretation: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Conditions of validity: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.123 m^3 and material density 1447.5 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 802.18 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 967.61 N and the weight is 1746 N; their signed upward difference is -778.42 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 245.05 N acts at a distance of 0.451 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 7.243 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 13.934 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 21.083 kg and radius 0.71 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 107.9 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 5.314 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 30933 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 63.451 m/s and elevation angle 42.979 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 8.8219 s, the horizontal range is 409.52 m, and maximum height above launch is 95.401 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1614.2 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7985.2 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 7.0652 km/s and the orbital period is 118.36 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 8.521 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 508.07 K, changing volume from 24.963 to 50.051 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is 25040 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1415.4 K and cold reservoir at 308.98 K, absorbing 8767.9 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 78.169 percent, corresponding to at most 6853.9 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 397.35 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.853 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 18.072 kg and 0.849 kg and initial signed speeds 0.331 and 14.215 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is 0.95399 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 78.157 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 2.01 kg is released from rest at a height of 88.943 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 41.767 m/s and the kinetic energy is 1753.2 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Small-angle pendulum

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 10.201 kg block starts at 32.675 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.176. The surface extends for 8.216 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 309.29 m. After the available distance its speed is 32.238 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.726 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 530.08 K and cold reservoir at 334.95 K, absorbing 6256.8 J per cycle.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 36.812 percent, corresponding to at most 2303.3 J of work per cycle.

## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 18598 Hz and has spatial wavelength 2.015 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 5.377e-05 s and the propagation speed is 37474 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1366.3 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7737.3 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.1775 km/s and the orbital period is 112.89 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Worked example: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Physical setup: A fully submerged body has volume 0.1 m^3 and material density 249.34 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1269.7 kg/m^3.

Relevant law: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Calculated result: The upward buoyancy is 1245.2 N and the weight is 244.52 N; their signed upward difference is 1000.6 N.

Interpretation: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Conditions of validity: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Hooke-law force calibration

A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

The fitted slope is 86.566 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 86.686 N/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.17664 N.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Linear thermal expansion

Physical setup: A rod with initial length 20.54 m has expansion coefficient 2.0489e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 0.705 K.

Relevant law: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Calculated result: The calculated signed change in length is 0.2967 mm.

Interpretation: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Conditions of validity: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 18.244 kg is released from rest at a height of 116.68 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 47.839 m/s and the kinetic energy is 20876 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 8.955 kg has specific heat capacity 4308.9 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 276.38 to 411.36 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 5208.7 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 82.121 kg block starts at 25.17 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.181. The surface extends for 24.484 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 178.46 m. After the available distance its speed is 23.38 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.775 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Standing wave on a stretched string

A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 0.97 m, tension 742.04 N, and linear mass density 0.039 kg/m.

Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

The speed of transverse waves is 137.94 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 71.102 Hz.

The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.

## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 42.781 m/s, emitting a tone of 435.55 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 497.61 Hz, a frequency increase of 62.065 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Escape speed from a central mass

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 16.291 kg changes signed velocity from 9.023 to 11.482 m/s during 0.107 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 40.06 N s and the average net force is 374.39 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 4.366 cm^2 and 5.024 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 4.402 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 3.8255 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0019219 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 6.65 kg has specific heat capacity 4446.4 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 295.48 to 431.13 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 4011 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Ideal gas equation of state

A vessel contains 11.126 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 969.36 K in volume 116.64 liters.

The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

The equilibrium pressure is 768.79 kPa.

At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 48.502 kg and radius 1.385 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 52.472 rad/s.

The moment of inertia is 46.519 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 64040 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 3.524 kg is released from rest at a height of 40.575 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 28.21 m/s and the kinetic energy is 1402.2 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 17.076 kg and 15.805 kg and initial signed speeds 12.961 and 6.729 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is 9.9654 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 159.39 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 27.316 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 0.926 m/s^2 for 16.2 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 42.317 m/s, and the signed displacement is 564.03 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Reversible isothermal gas work

6.714 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 373.51 K, changing volume from 46.21 to 61.644 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 6008.7 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Worked example: Thermal conduction measurement

Physical setup: A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

Relevant law: For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 5.0112 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.9853 W/K.

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 25.076 W.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 11.058 m/s, emitting a tone of 948.2 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 979.79 Hz, a frequency increase of 31.587 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 266.78 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 6637.8 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 7.7492 km/s and the orbital period is 89.7 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 240.87 kg follows a circle of radius 11.995 m at constant speed 76.348 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 485.95 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 1.1705e+05 N, and rotation frequency is 1.013 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 48.012 kg changes signed velocity from -18.895 to 3.287 m/s during 1.198 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 1065 N s and the average net force is 888.98 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Periodic wave propagation

Physical setup: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 8551 Hz and has spatial wavelength 0.333 m.

Relevant law: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Calculated result: The period is 0.00011695 s and the propagation speed is 2847.5 m/s.

Interpretation: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Conditions of validity: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.018 m^3 and material density 1715.1 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 826.11 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 145.82 N and the weight is 302.75 N; their signed upward difference is -156.92 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 144.06 kg block starts at 28.273 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.094. The surface extends for 29.682 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 433.58 m. After the available distance its speed is 27.288 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 0.92183 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 1.738 kg and 20.263 kg and initial signed speeds 11.361 and 12.426 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 12.342 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 0.90778 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Ideal gas equation of state

A vessel contains 8.575 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 321.64 K in volume 47.778 liters.

The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

The equilibrium pressure is 479.96 kPa.

At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 65.142 m/s and elevation angle 19.43 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 4.4194 s, the horizontal range is 271.49 m, and maximum height above launch is 23.942 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 1127 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Linear thermal expansion

A rod with initial length 11.896 m has expansion coefficient 2.3699e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 72.294 K.

For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

The calculated signed change in length is 20.381 mm.

For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Worked example: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Physical setup: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 61.595 W/(m K), thickness 0.251 m, area 1.462 m^2, and temperature difference 84.821 K.

Relevant law: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Calculated result: The conduction rate is 30431 W.

Interpretation: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Conditions of validity: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 47.985 kg and radius 0.313 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 137.21 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Periodic wave propagation

## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 62.243 kg block starts at 19.112 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.26. The surface extends for 23.688 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 71.629 m. After the available distance its speed is 15.636 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 2.5497 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 14.684 cm^2 and 11.476 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 1.722 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 2.2034 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0025286 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Worked example: Escape speed from a central mass

## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 606.2 K and cold reservoir at 345.88 K, absorbing 7260.7 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 42.944 percent, corresponding to at most 3118 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.128 m^3 and material density 299.34 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1336.3 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 1677.5 N and the weight is 375.75 N; their signed upward difference is 1301.7 N.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 30.315 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 3.808 m/s^2 for 13.171 s.

## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 28.807 kg changes signed velocity from -4.767 to -13.399 m/s during 1.827 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -248.66 N s and the average net force is -136.1 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 452.7 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 3.511 kg changes signed velocity from 6.658 to 8.637 m/s during 1.168 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is 6.9483 N s and the average net force is 5.9489 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 701.9 K and cold reservoir at 327.65 K, absorbing 2960.9 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 53.32 percent, corresponding to at most 1578.8 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Worked example: Escape speed from a central mass

Physical setup: Consider a test object at altitude 129.83 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Relevant law: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Calculated result: The minimum escape speed at that position is 11.074 km/s.

Interpretation: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Conditions of validity: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Quantitative physics problem: Pressure at depth

Problem: A stationary liquid has density 906.91 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 119.94 m below a surface at pressure 102.92 kPa.

Solution method: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Answer: The pressure increase is 1066.7 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1169.6 kPa.

Physical check: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Idealizations: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 2.737 m and an initial angular displacement of 1.006 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 3.3194 s and its frequency is 0.30126 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 34.365 m/s and elevation angle 15.427 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 1.8643 s, the horizontal range is 61.76 m, and maximum height above launch is 4.2607 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 58.265 kg block starts at 22.68 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.236. The surface extends for 3.096 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 111.13 m. After the available distance its speed is 22.362 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 2.3144 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

8.986 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 610.4 K to 218.96 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

The internal energy change is -43869 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 8.495 cm^2 and 10.435 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 3.558 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 2.8965 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0030225 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Problem: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 5.7403e-07 W/m^2.

Solution method: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Answer: The ideal intensity level is 57.589 dB.

Physical check: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Idealizations: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Spring oscillator

A mass of 1.019 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 530.9 N/m and displaced by 0.403 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 22.825 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 3.6328 Hz, and turning-point energy is 43.111 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 0.895 kg has specific heat capacity 2278.5 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 329.43 to 356.06 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 54.318 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Reversible isothermal gas work

8.135 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 434.89 K, changing volume from 33.529 to 44.225 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 8144.4 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 7.557 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 6.775 m/s^2 for 9.146 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 69.521 m/s, and the signed displacement is 352.48 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Worked example: Standing wave on a stretched string

## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 16794 Hz and has spatial wavelength 0.533 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 5.9546e-05 s and the propagation speed is 8951 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Worked example: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Physical setup: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 7.603 kg and radius 1.51 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 174.06 rad/s.

Relevant law: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Calculated result: The moment of inertia is 8.6678 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 1.313e+05 J.

Interpretation: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Conditions of validity: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 54.83 m/s, emitting a tone of 477.01 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 567.77 Hz, a frequency increase of 90.761 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 12.674 kg is released from rest at a height of 72.047 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 0.531 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1215.9 K and cold reservoir at 329.7 K, absorbing 3768.2 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 72.885 percent, corresponding to at most 2746.4 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 293.78 W/(m K), thickness 0.302 m, area 1.428 m^2, and temperature difference 60.222 K.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 83656 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 12.25 cm^2 and 13.278 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 4.283 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 3.9514 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0052467 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 5.048 m/s, emitting a tone of 681.67 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 691.85 Hz, a frequency increase of 10.182 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 57.692 kg block starts at 33.393 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.223. The surface extends for 27.092 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 254.95 m. After the available distance its speed is 31.569 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 2.1869 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 5.573 kg has specific heat capacity 1640.2 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 338.21 to 350.29 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 110.38 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 4.3746e-07 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 56.409 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 20.54 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 195.26 N/m and displaced by 0.112 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 3.0832 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.49071 Hz, and turning-point energy is 1.2247 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 20.45 kg and 22.559 kg and initial signed speeds 18.455 and 1.708 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is 9.6709 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 1504.2 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.123 m^3 and material density 498.54 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1396.6 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 1684.7 N and the weight is 601.34 N; their signed upward difference is 1083.3 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Periodic wave propagation

Interpretation: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Conditions of validity: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Thermal conduction measurement

A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

The fitted slope is 3.8663 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 3.9062 W/K.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 31.842 W.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 31.458 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -0.903 m/s^2 for 4.58 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 27.322 m/s, and the signed displacement is 134.61 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Problem: A rod with initial length 11.999 m has expansion coefficient 1.9291e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 56.146 K.

Solution method: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is 12.996 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.

## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 7.237 kg is released from rest at a height of 70.6 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).
