## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 368.47 N acts at a distance of 0.305 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 103.24 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 109.39 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 50.269 m/s, emitting a tone of 760.73 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 891.36 Hz, a frequency increase of 130.64 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 188.2 W/(m K), thickness 0.405 m, area 1.176 m^2, and temperature difference 47.147 K.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 25764 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Worked example: Standing wave on a stretched string

Physical setup: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 1.224 m, tension 860.05 N, and linear mass density 0.051 kg/m.

Relevant law: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Calculated result: The speed of transverse waves is 129.86 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 53.048 Hz.

Interpretation: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Conditions of validity: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 705.82 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.614 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1059.6 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7430.6 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.3242 km/s and the orbital period is 106.24 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.089 m^3 and material density 1672.7 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1221.2 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 1065.9 N and the weight is 1459.9 N; their signed upward difference is -394.05 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 49.012 kg changes signed velocity from -14.372 to 8.017 m/s during 0.568 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is 1097.3 N s and the average net force is 1931.9 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Problem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 14.523 cm^2 and 11.286 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 4.554 m/s.

Solution method: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Answer: The speed in the second section is 5.8602 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0066138 m^3/s.

Physical check: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Idealizations: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Thermal conduction measurement

A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

The fitted slope is 1.5476 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 1.5488 W/K.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 1.6793 W.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Uniform circular motion

Physical setup: A mass of 186.95 kg follows a circle of radius 23.561 m at constant speed 20.144 m/s.

Relevant law: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Calculated result: The centripetal acceleration is 17.223 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 3219.7 N, and rotation frequency is 0.13607 Hz.

Interpretation: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Conditions of validity: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Worked example: Periodic wave propagation

Physical setup: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 12661 Hz and has spatial wavelength 4.591 m.

Relevant law: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Calculated result: The period is 7.8983e-05 s and the propagation speed is 58126 m/s.

Interpretation: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Conditions of validity: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

Problem: A vessel contains 8.009 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 444.98 K in volume 134.11 liters.

Solution method: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Answer: The equilibrium pressure is 220.95 kPa.

Physical check: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Physical setup: A simple pendulum has length 1.758 m and an initial angular displacement of 1.013 degrees.

Relevant law: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Calculated result: The estimated oscillation period is 2.6603 s and its frequency is 0.3759 Hz.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Conditions of validity: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 58.739 m/s and elevation angle 60.889 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 10.466 s, the horizontal range is 299.09 m, and maximum height above launch is 134.28 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 24.026 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 0.142 m/s^2 for 11.403 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 25.645 m/s, and the signed displacement is 283.2 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 8.605 kg block starts at 25.999 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.23. The surface extends for 17.399 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 149.84 m. After the available distance its speed is 24.443 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 2.2555 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 60.895 kg changes signed velocity from 0.489 to 9.578 m/s during 1.78 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 553.47 N s and the average net force is 310.94 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 13.531 kg and 2.412 kg and initial signed speeds 10.474 and 7.027 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is 9.9525 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 12.162 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 5.443 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 395.67 K, changing volume from 19.104 to 50.454 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is 17390 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 10981 Hz and has spatial wavelength 3.849 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 9.1063e-05 s and the propagation speed is 42268 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 6.108 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 280.71 K, changing volume from 17.397 to 23.938 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is 4550.2 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 352.33 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.889 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1298.8 K and cold reservoir at 223.2 K, absorbing 5478.9 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 82.814 percent, corresponding to at most 4537.3 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Worked example: Periodic wave propagation

Physical setup: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 15316 Hz and has spatial wavelength 0.15 m.

Calculated result: The period is 6.5291e-05 s and the propagation speed is 2297.4 m/s.

## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.081 m^3 and material density 1273.9 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 781.73 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 620.96 N and the weight is 1011.9 N; their signed upward difference is -390.97 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

6.107 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 313.19 K to 400.65 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

The internal energy change is 6661.7 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Worked example: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Physical setup: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 302.07 W/(m K), thickness 0.263 m, area 0.639 m^2, and temperature difference 12.884 K.

Relevant law: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Calculated result: The conduction rate is 9455.8 W.

Interpretation: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Conditions of validity: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 18.802 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 1.831 m/s^2 for 15.202 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 46.637 m/s, and the signed displacement is 497.4 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 843.74 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 172.93 m below a surface at pressure 99.718 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

The pressure increase is 1430.8 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1530.6 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 23.235 kg and radius 0.225 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 19.212 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 0.58814 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 108.54 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Spring oscillator

A mass of 8.119 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 105.91 N/m and displaced by 0.222 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 3.6117 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.57482 Hz, and turning-point energy is 2.6097 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Worked example: Linear thermal expansion

Physical setup: A rod with initial length 22.639 m has expansion coefficient 7.093e-06 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 101.12 K.

Relevant law: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Calculated result: The calculated signed change in length is 16.238 mm.

Interpretation: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Conditions of validity: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 14.463 kg is released from rest at a height of 19.351 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 19.482 m/s and the kinetic energy is 2744.6 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum

Problem: A simple pendulum has length 1.484 m and an initial angular displacement of 3.72 degrees.

Solution method: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Answer: The estimated oscillation period is 2.4442 s and its frequency is 0.40913 Hz.

Physical check: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Idealizations: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

A sample of mass 7.636 kg has specific heat capacity 1431.9 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 277.45 to 432.95 K.

For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

The required energy is 1700.3 kJ.

The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

Problem: A vessel contains 10.078 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 451.01 K in volume 43.084 liters.

Answer: The equilibrium pressure is 877.17 kPa.

Physical check: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 2.351e-06 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 63.713 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 14.253 m/s and elevation angle 62.455 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 2.5773 s, the horizontal range is 16.988 m, and maximum height above launch is 8.1426 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 91.371 kg block starts at 11.159 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.544. The surface extends for 4.047 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 11.671 m. After the available distance its speed is 9.0191 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 5.3348 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 201.01 kg follows a circle of radius 20.764 m at constant speed 3.493 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 0.58761 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 118.11 N, and rotation frequency is 0.026774 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1249.8 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7620.8 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 7.2322 km/s and the orbital period is 110.35 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A force of magnitude 414.7 N acts at a distance of 3.772 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 151.28 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 751.57 N m.

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Standing wave on a stretched string

A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 4.884 m, tension 332.25 N, and linear mass density 0.041 kg/m.

Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

The speed of transverse waves is 90.02 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 9.2159 Hz.

The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 14.714 cm^2 and 1.931 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 4.993 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 38.046 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0073467 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

Problem: A mass of 114.95 kg follows a circle of radius 22.241 m at constant speed 19.348 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 16.831 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 1934.7 N, and rotation frequency is 0.13845 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Standing wave on a stretched string

A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 0.902 m, tension 850.07 N, and linear mass density 0.009 kg/m.

Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

The speed of transverse waves is 307.33 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 170.36 Hz.

The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Worked example: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Physical setup: 2.051 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 644.63 K to 700.28 K.

Relevant law: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Calculated result: The internal energy change is 1423.5 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Interpretation: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Conditions of validity: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Problem: A rod with initial length 17.643 m has expansion coefficient 1.9072e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 34.91 K.

Solution method: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is 11.747 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 11.622 kg and radius 0.485 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 42.858 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 1.3669 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 1255.4 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 13.517 cm^2 and 14.049 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 1.126 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 1.0834 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.001522 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum

Problem: A simple pendulum has length 3.174 m and an initial angular displacement of 4.355 degrees.

Solution method: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Answer: The estimated oscillation period is 3.5746 s and its frequency is 0.27975 Hz.

Physical check: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Idealizations: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 70.343 kg changes signed velocity from -17.113 to -18.555 m/s during 1.745 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is -101.43 N s and the average net force is -58.129 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 3.323 kg has specific heat capacity 1417.2 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 273.46 to 441.35 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 790.66 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 140.98 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 11.064 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

Interpretation: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Conditions of validity: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 11.239 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -1.64 m/s^2 for 6.451 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 0.65936 m/s, and the signed displacement is 38.378 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Worked example: Pressure at depth

Physical setup: A stationary liquid has density 1091 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 90.277 m below a surface at pressure 97.604 kPa.

Relevant law: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Calculated result: The pressure increase is 965.88 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1063.5 kPa.

Interpretation: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Conditions of validity: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.055 m^3 and material density 926.43 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1191.1 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 642.45 N and the weight is 499.68 N; their signed upward difference is 142.77 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 718.68 K and cold reservoir at 421.91 K, absorbing 6728.9 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 41.294 percent, corresponding to at most 2778.6 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Worked example: Hooke-law force calibration

Physical setup: A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

Relevant law: For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 231.31 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 232.24 N/m.

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.26902 N.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 4.28 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 393.51 K, changing volume from 23.478 to 55.831 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is 12131 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 6.709 kg and 17.878 kg and initial signed speeds 12.152 and -0.012 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 3.3072 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 360.91 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 2.983 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 779.61 N/m and displaced by 0.034 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 16.166 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 2.573 Hz, and turning-point energy is 0.45062 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 137.25 kg block starts at 22.125 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.081. The surface extends for 1.968 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 308.13 m. After the available distance its speed is 22.054 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 0.79434 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 3.663 kg is released from rest at a height of 73.522 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 37.974 m/s and the kinetic energy is 2641 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 13.016 m/s, emitting a tone of 1547.3 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 1608.4 Hz, a frequency increase of 61.034 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 278.71 Hz and has spatial wavelength 3.572 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 0.0035879 s and the propagation speed is 995.56 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 1092.9 N and the weight is 282.49 N; their signed upward difference is 810.38 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 11333 Hz and has spatial wavelength 0.074 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 8.8239e-05 s and the propagation speed is 838.63 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 27.369 kg changes signed velocity from 15.625 to 1.673 m/s during 1.873 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is -381.85 N s and the average net force is -203.87 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Problem: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

Solution method: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 4.0595 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.42755 s^2.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 1.39 kg follows a circle of radius 9.184 m at constant speed 21.208 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 48.974 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 68.074 N, and rotation frequency is 0.36753 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Worked example: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Physical setup: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 2.3389e-10 W/m^2.

Relevant law: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Calculated result: The ideal intensity level is 23.69 dB.

Interpretation: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Conditions of validity: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 391.05 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 6762.1 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 7.6777 km/s and the orbital period is 92.231 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

8.657 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 529.83 K to 500.46 K.

## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 15.039 m/s and elevation angle 32.484 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 1.6472 s, the horizontal range is 20.897 m, and maximum height above launch is 3.3261 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Physical setup: A simple pendulum has length 2.691 m and an initial angular displacement of 3.127 degrees.

Relevant law: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Calculated result: The estimated oscillation period is 3.2914 s and its frequency is 0.30383 Hz.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Conditions of validity: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Spring oscillator

Problem: A mass of 12.802 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 313.93 N/m and displaced by 0.337 m.

Solution method: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Answer: The angular frequency is 4.952 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.78813 Hz, and turning-point energy is 17.827 J.

Physical check: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Idealizations: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Linear thermal expansion

## Worked example: Escape speed from a central mass

## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 10.107 m/s, emitting a tone of 1681.3 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Answer: The listener detects approximately 1732.3 Hz, a frequency increase of 51.045 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 68.042 kg block starts at 9.928 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.495. The surface extends for 11.85 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 10.152 m. After the available distance its speed is 0 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 4.8543 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 8.527 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 1.505 m/s^2 for 2.665 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 12.538 m/s, and the signed displacement is 28.069 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 15.757 kg and 11.763 kg and initial signed speeds -5.618 and 13.966 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is 2.7529 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 1291.6 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 8.77 kg is released from rest at a height of 84.933 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 40.814 m/s and the kinetic energy is 7304.6 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.009 m^3 and material density 484.16 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 753.77 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 66.528 N and the weight is 42.732 N; their signed upward difference is 23.796 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 53.566 kg changes signed velocity from -0.733 to -1.92 m/s during 0.241 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -63.583 N s and the average net force is -263.83 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Ideal gas equation of state

Physical setup: A vessel contains 9.783 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 435.25 K in volume 93.916 liters.

Relevant law: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Calculated result: The equilibrium pressure is 376.97 kPa.

Interpretation: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Conditions of validity: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Problem: A rod with initial length 13.557 m has expansion coefficient 1.0992e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 118.46 K.

Solution method: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is 17.652 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 23.552 kg and 20.997 kg and initial signed speeds 14.962 and -3.599 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 6.2138 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 1912.1 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Worked example: Pressure at depth

Physical setup: A stationary liquid has density 1037 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 31.856 m below a surface at pressure 102.03 kPa.

Relevant law: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Calculated result: The pressure increase is 323.95 kPa and the absolute pressure is 425.99 kPa.

Interpretation: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Conditions of validity: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 9418.9 Hz and has spatial wavelength 4.853 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 0.00010617 s and the propagation speed is 45710 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 1.827 kg is released from rest at a height of 33.716 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 25.715 m/s and the kinetic energy is 604.08 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Problem: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 6.982 W/(m K), thickness 0.108 m, area 3.301 m^2, and temperature difference 83.455 K.

Solution method: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Answer: The conduction rate is 17810 W.

Physical check: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Idealizations: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 16.682 kg and radius 1.349 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 137.68 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 15.179 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 1.4387e+05 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Worked example: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Physical setup: A sample of mass 4.946 kg has specific heat capacity 2380.9 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 312.17 to 379.02 K.

Relevant law: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Calculated result: The required energy is 787.28 kJ.

Interpretation: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Conditions of validity: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Problem: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 4.2338e-09 W/m^2.

Solution method: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Answer: The ideal intensity level is 36.267 dB.

Physical check: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Idealizations: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Problem: 9.279 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 290.95 K to 728.25 K.

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Answer: The internal energy change is 50606 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Lever arm and rotational effect

A force of magnitude 386.14 N acts at a distance of 2.311 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 94.619 degrees to the lever.

The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

The calculated torque magnitude is 889.47 N m.

For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Quantitative physics problem: Hooke-law force calibration

Problem: A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

Solution method: For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 388.06 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 386.34 N/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.50645 N.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Physical setup: A simple pendulum has length 1.71 m and an initial angular displacement of 4.944 degrees.

Relevant law: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Calculated result: The estimated oscillation period is 2.6237 s and its frequency is 0.38114 Hz.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Conditions of validity: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 37.363 m/s and elevation angle 49 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 5.7508 s, the horizontal range is 140.97 m, and maximum height above launch is 40.541 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Spring oscillator

A mass of 12.2 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 405.02 N/m and displaced by 0.212 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 5.7618 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.91702 Hz, and turning-point energy is 9.1017 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 225.56 kg follows a circle of radius 12.364 m at constant speed 8.716 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 6.1443 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 1385.9 N, and rotation frequency is 0.1122 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1846.5 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 8217.5 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 6.9646 km/s and the orbital period is 123.56 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 144.91 kg block starts at 13.403 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.051. The surface extends for 6.007 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 179.59 m. After the available distance its speed is 13.177 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 0.50014 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1475.2 K and cold reservoir at 274.42 K, absorbing 8749.9 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 81.398 percent, corresponding to at most 7122.2 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

Problem: An object is launched at speed 38.433 m/s and elevation angle 23.62 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 3.1405 s, the horizontal range is 110.59 m, and maximum height above launch is 12.09 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.006 m^3 and material density 1275 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1353.2 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 79.619 N and the weight is 75.02 N; their signed upward difference is 4.5998 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.0384 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.64046 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 53.498 kg block starts at 23.352 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.469. The surface extends for 18.282 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 59.282 m. After the available distance its speed is 19.42 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 4.5993 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 5.541 m and an initial angular displacement of 2.969 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 4.723 s and its frequency is 0.21173 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 12.004 kg has specific heat capacity 2466.6 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 309.97 to 380.52 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 2088.9 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 17.811 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 385.98 N/m and displaced by 0.114 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 4.6552 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.7409 Hz, and turning-point energy is 2.5081 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Worked example: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Interpretation: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

## Quantitative physics problem: Pressure at depth

Problem: A stationary liquid has density 1117.2 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 41.823 m below a surface at pressure 108.35 kPa.

Solution method: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Answer: The pressure increase is 458.23 kPa and the absolute pressure is 566.57 kPa.

Physical check: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Idealizations: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 8.317 kg is released from rest at a height of 106.38 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 45.677 m/s and the kinetic energy is 8676.4 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 8.232 kg changes signed velocity from 19.828 to -9.772 m/s during 1.087 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is -243.67 N s and the average net force is -224.16 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 0.551 kg and radius 0.973 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 140.37 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 0.26082 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 2569.7 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 118.3 kg follows a circle of radius 3.605 m at constant speed 60.348 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 1010.2 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 1.1951e+05 N, and rotation frequency is 2.6643 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 11.795 cm^2 and 11.671 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 4.625 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 4.6741 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0054552 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 19.217 kg and 16.499 kg and initial signed speeds 10.134 and 7.438 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 8.8886 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 32.262 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 37.933 m/s, emitting a tone of 1608 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 1808 Hz, a frequency increase of 199.95 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 826.85 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7197.8 km.

The circular speed is 7.4416 km/s and the orbital period is 101.29 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

## Worked example: Ideal gas equation of state

Calculated result: The equilibrium pressure is 162.98 kPa.

## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum

Problem: A simple pendulum has length 6.761 m and an initial angular displacement of 1.683 degrees.

Solution method: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Answer: The estimated oscillation period is 5.217 s and its frequency is 0.19168 Hz.

Physical check: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Idealizations: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 2116.2 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 8487.2 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 6.8531 km/s and the orbital period is 129.69 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 5.238 kg and radius 1.072 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 111.86 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 3.0097 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 18828 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 423.24 N acts at a distance of 2.84 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 39.578 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 765.83 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.106 m^3 and material density 1752.3 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 723.15 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 751.72 N and the weight is 1821.6 N; their signed upward difference is -1069.9 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Spring oscillator

A mass of 23.174 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 45.436 N/m and displaced by 0.244 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 1.4002 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.22285 Hz, and turning-point energy is 1.3525 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 8.225 kg is released from rest at a height of 54.182 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 32.599 m/s and the kinetic energy is 4370.3 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 106.49 kg block starts at 3.01 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.616. The surface extends for 12.368 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 0.7499 m. After the available distance its speed is 0 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 6.0409 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 22.386 kg and 16.43 kg and initial signed speeds 17.34 and 13.765 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is 15.827 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 60.552 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 1.2239e-10 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 20.877 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 38.532 m/s, emitting a tone of 1486.5 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 1674.6 Hz, a frequency increase of 188.12 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

At the lower level the speed is 45.733 m/s and the kinetic energy is 364.97 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 43.669 kg and radius 1.493 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 36.95 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 31.822 kg block starts at 19.735 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.497. The surface extends for 5.909 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 39.955 m. After the available distance its speed is 18.217 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 4.8739 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 30.019 m/s and elevation angle 51.694 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 4.8041 s, the horizontal range is 89.394 m, and maximum height above launch is 28.292 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Problem: A rod with initial length 5.059 m has expansion coefficient 9.42e-06 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 99.375 K.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is 4.7358 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.
