## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 32.704 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 1.186 m/s^2 for 1.028 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 33.923 m/s, and the signed displacement is 34.246 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Worked example: Escape speed from a central mass

Physical setup: Consider a test object at altitude 882.72 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Relevant law: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Calculated result: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.483 km/s.

Interpretation: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Conditions of validity: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 1.671 kg is released from rest at a height of 83.208 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 40.398 m/s and the kinetic energy is 1363.5 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 7.481 cm^2 and 4.008 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.668 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 4.9799 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0019959 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 9.434 m/s and elevation angle 23.986 degrees from level ground.

The nonzero return time is 0.78213 s, the horizontal range is 6.7415 m, and maximum height above launch is 0.74988 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Worked example: Hooke-law force calibration

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 111.4 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 112.55 N/m.

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.43489 N.

## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 51.112 kg changes signed velocity from -15.118 to 16.133 m/s during 0.809 s.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

## Reversible isothermal gas work

4.691 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 674.83 K, changing volume from 18.532 to 11.119 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is -13445 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 6.981 kg and 8.451 kg and initial signed speeds -2.402 and 3.328 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 0.73591 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 62.76 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Worked example: Linear thermal expansion

Physical setup: A rod with initial length 12.132 m has expansion coefficient 1.0482e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 11.88 K.

Relevant law: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Calculated result: The calculated signed change in length is 1.5108 mm.

Interpretation: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1958.9 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 8329.9 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 6.9175 km/s and the orbital period is 126.1 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Spring oscillator

Problem: A mass of 5.566 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 512.94 N/m and displaced by 0.141 m.

Solution method: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Answer: The angular frequency is 9.5998 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.5279 Hz, and turning-point energy is 5.0989 J.

Physical check: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Idealizations: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 9887.4 Hz and has spatial wavelength 1.328 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 0.00010114 s and the propagation speed is 13130 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 1.995 kg is released from rest at a height of 72.743 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 37.772 m/s and the kinetic energy is 1423.2 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum

Problem: A simple pendulum has length 2.349 m and an initial angular displacement of 3.058 degrees.

Solution method: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Answer: The estimated oscillation period is 3.0751 s and its frequency is 0.32519 Hz.

Physical check: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Idealizations: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 1.075 kg and radius 0.025 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 51.802 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 0.00033594 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 0.45074 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 58.463 m/s and elevation angle 42.243 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 8.0156 s, the horizontal range is 346.92 m, and maximum height above launch is 78.76 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Problem: 7.667 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 810.06 K to 685.27 K.

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Answer: The internal energy change is -11932 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.

## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 17.769 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 6.042 m/s^2 for 7.736 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 64.51 m/s, and the signed displacement is 318.25 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 144.77 W/(m K), thickness 0.505 m, area 2.41 m^2, and temperature difference 71.296 K.

The conduction rate is 49257 W.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Worked example: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Physical setup: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 2.3812e-08 W/m^2.

Relevant law: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Calculated result: The ideal intensity level is 43.768 dB.

Interpretation: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Conditions of validity: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 25.404 kg changes signed velocity from -18.407 to -7.27 m/s during 1.606 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 282.92 N s and the average net force is 176.17 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 128.29 kg block starts at 11.474 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.324. The surface extends for 3.129 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 20.717 m. After the available distance its speed is 10.572 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 3.1774 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 22.414 m/s, emitting a tone of 1642.2 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 1757 Hz, a frequency increase of 114.81 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Thermal conduction measurement

A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

The fitted slope is 1.6085 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 1.6025 W/K.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 4.5645 W.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Standing wave on a stretched string

Physical setup: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 4.935 m, tension 493.99 N, and linear mass density 0.002 kg/m.

Relevant law: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Calculated result: The speed of transverse waves is 496.99 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 50.353 Hz.

Interpretation: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Conditions of validity: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 11.076 kg block starts at 4.093 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.447. The surface extends for 2.37 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 1.9108 m. After the available distance its speed is 0 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 4.3836 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.031 m^3 and material density 302.24 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1232.3 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 374.62 N and the weight is 91.882 N; their signed upward difference is 282.74 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 14.089 cm^2 and 3.936 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.382 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 8.5264 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.003356 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1371.5 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7742.5 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 7.1751 km/s and the orbital period is 113 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Spring oscillator

A mass of 10.874 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 545.98 N/m and displaced by 0.382 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 7.0858 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.1277 Hz, and turning-point energy is 39.835 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 16.801 kg is released from rest at a height of 22.781 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 21.138 m/s and the kinetic energy is 3753.4 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 26.337 m/s, emitting a tone of 1475.6 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 1598.3 Hz, a frequency increase of 122.73 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 9.058 kg and 8.652 kg and initial signed speeds -4.347 and -6.759 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is -5.5254 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 12.872 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Worked example: Uniform circular motion

Physical setup: A mass of 96.188 kg follows a circle of radius 4.586 m at constant speed 53.499 m/s.

Relevant law: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Calculated result: The centripetal acceleration is 624.1 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 60031 N, and rotation frequency is 1.8567 Hz.

Interpretation: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Conditions of validity: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 5.111 kg has specific heat capacity 4208.2 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 289.75 to 439.79 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 3226.9 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.

## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 7.749 m and an initial angular displacement of 2.873 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 5.5852 s and its frequency is 0.17904 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Worked example: Periodic wave propagation

Physical setup: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 6828.9 Hz and has spatial wavelength 2.616 m.

Relevant law: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Calculated result: The period is 0.00014644 s and the propagation speed is 17864 m/s.

Interpretation: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Conditions of validity: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Problem: 5.181 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 203.94 K to 900.46 K.

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Answer: The internal energy change is 45006 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.

## Projectile trajectory above level ground

## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 149.97 N acts at a distance of 0.999 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 96.909 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 148.73 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

Problem: A vessel contains 9.674 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 682.53 K in volume 115.71 liters.

Solution method: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Answer: The equilibrium pressure is 474.44 kPa.

Physical check: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 15.329 kg changes signed velocity from 9.971 to 4.269 m/s during 0.064 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is -87.406 N s and the average net force is -1365.7 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 12.344 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -0.714 m/s^2 for 7.448 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 7.0261 m/s, and the signed displacement is 72.134 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1371.1 K and cold reservoir at 317.56 K, absorbing 2206.4 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 76.839 percent, corresponding to at most 1695.4 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

Interpretation: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Conditions of validity: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Worked example: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Interpretation: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Conditions of validity: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 22.412 m. After the available distance its speed is 8.9019 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 5.6584 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Reversible isothermal gas work

1.462 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 576.41 K, changing volume from 35.773 to 103.46 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 7440.7 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 24.793 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 6.452 m/s^2 for 13.633 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 112.75 m/s, and the signed displacement is 937.58 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 12.72 kg is released from rest at a height of 78.696 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 39.287 m/s and the kinetic energy is 9816.6 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.058 m^3 and material density 206.12 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1267.2 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 720.79 N and the weight is 117.24 N; their signed upward difference is 603.55 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 17.119 m/s and elevation angle 70.204 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 3.285 s, the horizontal range is 19.045 m, and maximum height above launch is 13.228 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 73.072 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 11.123 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 5120.9 Hz and has spatial wavelength 1.658 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 0.00019528 s and the propagation speed is 8490.4 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

## Quantitative physics problem: Spring oscillator

Problem: A mass of 11.025 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 746.37 N/m and displaced by 0.199 m.

Solution method: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Answer: The angular frequency is 8.2279 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.3095 Hz, and turning-point energy is 14.778 J.

Physical check: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Idealizations: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 17.469 m/s, emitting a tone of 1712.3 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 1804.2 Hz, a frequency increase of 91.89 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Worked example: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Physical setup: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 47.263 W/(m K), thickness 0.051 m, area 3.398 m^2, and temperature difference 63.017 K.

Relevant law: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Calculated result: The conduction rate is 1.9844e+05 W.

Interpretation: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Conditions of validity: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Quantitative physics problem: Pressure at depth

Problem: A stationary liquid has density 1287 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 41.811 m below a surface at pressure 105.79 kPa.

Solution method: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Answer: The pressure increase is 527.71 kPa and the absolute pressure is 633.5 kPa.

Physical check: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Idealizations: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

A sample of mass 10.042 kg has specific heat capacity 2045.6 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 318.77 to 459.82 K.

For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

The required energy is 2897.3 kJ.

The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 384.79 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 6755.8 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 7.6812 km/s and the orbital period is 92.103 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1064.4 K and cold reservoir at 345.64 K, absorbing 7605.6 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 67.527 percent, corresponding to at most 5135.9 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Worked example: Ideal gas equation of state

Relevant law: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Calculated result: The equilibrium pressure is 188.47 kPa.

Interpretation: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 6.7948e-05 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 78.322 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Physical setup: A simple pendulum has length 5.829 m and an initial angular displacement of 3.016 degrees.

Relevant law: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Calculated result: The estimated oscillation period is 4.8441 s and its frequency is 0.20644 Hz.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Conditions of validity: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A force of magnitude 530.72 N acts at a distance of 1.254 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 123.36 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 555.86 N m.

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

4.715 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 460.38 K to 364.52 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

The internal energy change is -5636.7 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Worked example: Standing wave on a stretched string

Physical setup: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 2.644 m, tension 697.85 N, and linear mass density 0.033 kg/m.

Relevant law: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Calculated result: The speed of transverse waves is 145.42 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 27.5 Hz.

Interpretation: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Conditions of validity: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Problem: A rod with initial length 22.341 m has expansion coefficient 1.3309e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 74.25 K.

Solution method: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is 22.077 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 4.663 kg and 8.248 kg and initial signed speeds 9.118 and -5.39 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is -0.15022 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 313.5 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Worked example: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Physical setup: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 3.86 kg and radius 1.405 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 172.93 rad/s.

Relevant law: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Calculated result: The moment of inertia is 3.8099 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 56969 J.

Interpretation: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Conditions of validity: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Thermal conduction measurement

A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

The fitted slope is 4.2748 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.2131 W/K.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 14.26 W.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

The period is 8.5489e-05 s and the propagation speed is 5918.9 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1216.9 K and cold reservoir at 379.77 K, absorbing 3071.2 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 68.791 percent, corresponding to at most 2112.7 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 1129.7 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 48.561 m below a surface at pressure 95.759 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

The pressure increase is 537.97 kPa and the absolute pressure is 633.73 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Physical setup: A simple pendulum has length 1.016 m and an initial angular displacement of 1.471 degrees.

Relevant law: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Calculated result: The estimated oscillation period is 2.0224 s and its frequency is 0.49446 Hz.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Conditions of validity: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 4.307 kg changes signed velocity from 9.092 to 11.089 m/s during 1.281 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is 8.6011 N s and the average net force is 6.7143 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 48.173 m/s, emitting a tone of 365.86 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 425.64 Hz, a frequency increase of 59.779 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 8.682 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 204.42 K, changing volume from 12.756 to 36.839 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is 15650 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 100.5 kg follows a circle of radius 18.64 m at constant speed 61.684 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 204.13 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 20514 N, and rotation frequency is 0.52668 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Lever arm and rotational effect

A force of magnitude 557.59 N acts at a distance of 2.181 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 167.66 degrees to the lever.

The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

The calculated torque magnitude is 259.79 N m.

For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Worked example: Linear thermal expansion

Physical setup: A rod with initial length 12.123 m has expansion coefficient 1.8651e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by -21.693 K.

Relevant law: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Calculated result: The calculated signed change in length is -4.9049 mm.

Interpretation: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Conditions of validity: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 7.08 kg and 20.559 kg and initial signed speeds -2.907 and 4.299 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is 2.4531 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 136.73 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

0.831 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 757.96 K to 411.21 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

The internal energy change is -3593.7 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.

## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 5.574 cm^2 and 10.266 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.972 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 1.6137 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0016566 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 5.046 kg is released from rest at a height of 75.593 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 38.505 m/s and the kinetic energy is 3740.7 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 124.73 kg block starts at 19.337 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.472. The surface extends for 17.281 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 40.391 m. After the available distance its speed is 14.627 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 4.6287 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.13 m^3 and material density 691.91 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1087.5 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 1386.4 N and the weight is 882.09 N; their signed upward difference is 504.27 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 1.707 s, the horizontal range is 19.785 m, and maximum height above launch is 3.5718 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.025 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.50732 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 1524.8 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.048 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 5.197 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 551.19 K, changing volume from 48.911 to 33.944 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is -8699.9 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 140.44 kg block starts at 14.806 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.167. The surface extends for 2.067 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 66.928 m. After the available distance its speed is 14.576 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.6377 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 20.072 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 768.28 N/m and displaced by 0.274 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 6.1868 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.98466 Hz, and turning-point energy is 28.84 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.123 m^3 and material density 1149.9 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1033.3 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 1246.4 N and the weight is 1387 N; their signed upward difference is -140.55 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1366.6 K and cold reservoir at 393.19 K, absorbing 2513.6 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 71.229 percent, corresponding to at most 1790.4 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 10.195 cm^2 and 13.557 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 1.69 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 1.2709 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.001723 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 117.58 kg follows a circle of radius 3.341 m at constant speed 44.372 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 589.31 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 69290 N, and rotation frequency is 2.1137 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Worked example: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Calculated result: The conduction rate is 1480.7 W.

Interpretation: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Conditions of validity: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1209.6 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7580.6 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 7.2513 km/s and the orbital period is 109.48 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Small-angle pendulum

## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.0238 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.10275 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 39.99 m/s, emitting a tone of 1528.8 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 1730.6 Hz, a frequency increase of 201.76 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

Interpretation: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Conditions of validity: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

## Standing wave on a stretched string

A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 1.719 m, tension 774.65 N, and linear mass density 0.033 kg/m.

Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

The speed of transverse waves is 153.21 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 44.565 Hz.

The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Worked example: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Physical setup: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 36.123 kg and radius 1.929 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 88.871 rad/s.

Relevant law: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Calculated result: The moment of inertia is 67.208 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 2.654e+05 J.

Interpretation: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Conditions of validity: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Problem: A rod with initial length 17.193 m has expansion coefficient 2.5191e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 21.17 K.

Solution method: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is 9.1689 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 145.33 W/(m K), thickness 0.377 m, area 3.746 m^2, and temperature difference 26.18 K.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 37804 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Worked example: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Physical setup: 6.938 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 325.45 K to 829.88 K.

Relevant law: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Calculated result: The internal energy change is 43648 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Interpretation: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Conditions of validity: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.

## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 10941 Hz and has spatial wavelength 2.051 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 9.14e-05 s and the propagation speed is 22440 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 2.729 kg is released from rest at a height of 15.601 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 17.492 m/s and the kinetic energy is 417.52 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1637.8 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 8008.8 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.0548 km/s and the orbital period is 118.88 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 17.006 kg and 5.287 kg and initial signed speeds 18.598 and 13.563 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is 17.404 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 51.122 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 2.5877e-05 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 74.129 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 1.268 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 658.34 K, changing volume from 35.742 to 88.39 liters.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 12.05 kg changes signed velocity from -1.268 to 5.625 m/s during 0.387 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is 83.061 N s and the average net force is 214.63 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Answer: The nonzero return time is 5.4767 s, the horizontal range is 91.532 m, and maximum height above launch is 36.767 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 147.54 kg block starts at 9.741 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.363. The surface extends for 7.514 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 13.328 m. After the available distance its speed is 6.4335 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 3.5598 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 7.299 kg is released from rest at a height of 22.053 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 20.797 m/s and the kinetic energy is 1578.5 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Problem: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

Solution method: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 4.0292 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.20355 s^2.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Quantitative physics problem: Spring oscillator

Solution method: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Answer: The angular frequency is 4.8588 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.7733 Hz, and turning-point energy is 21.889 J.

Physical check: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Idealizations: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 2.287 kg changes signed velocity from -5.047 to -7.961 m/s during 1.422 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -6.6643 N s and the average net force is -4.6866 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 17.937 kg and 12.033 kg and initial signed speeds -6.523 and 6.058 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is -1.4717 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 569.95 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Worked example: Pressure at depth

Physical setup: A stationary liquid has density 872.71 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 41.797 m below a surface at pressure 103.01 kPa.

Calculated result: The pressure increase is 357.71 kPa and the absolute pressure is 460.72 kPa.

Interpretation: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Problem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 4.56 cm^2 and 4.209 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.814 m/s.

Solution method: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Answer: The speed in the second section is 3.0487 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0012832 m^3/s.

Physical check: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Idealizations: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Lever arm and rotational effect

## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 559.49 K and cold reservoir at 294.48 K, absorbing 6232.8 J per cycle.

## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 38.126 m/s, emitting a tone of 939.84 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 1057.4 Hz, a frequency increase of 117.53 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 4.5213e-10 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 26.553 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 39.632 kg block starts at 34.183 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.355. The surface extends for 26.889 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 167.82 m. After the available distance its speed is 31.325 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 3.4814 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Hooke-law force calibration

A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

The fitted slope is 754.57 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 749.63 N/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 2.8435 N.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

5.994 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 286.98 K to 466.72 K.

The internal energy change is 13437 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 4.607 kg and 16.818 kg and initial signed speeds 0.259 and 8.293 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is 6.5655 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 116.71 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 36.864 kg and radius 1.292 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 74.662 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 30.768 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 85756 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 3.764 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 339.35 K, changing volume from 28.901 to 31.907 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is 1050.7 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 364.67 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 365.48 N/m.

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 1.1408 N.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 3.55 kg and radius 1.489 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 70.034 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 3.9354 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 9651.1 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Reversible heat engine upper bound

## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 11.435 kg is released from rest at a height of 72.159 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 37.62 m/s and the kinetic energy is 8091.8 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Problem: 6.658 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 504.42 K to 557.97 K.

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Answer: The internal energy change is 4446.8 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.

## Worked example: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Physical setup: A sample of mass 13.161 kg has specific heat capacity 2612.7 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 335.83 to 427.06 K.

Relevant law: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Calculated result: The required energy is 3137.1 kJ.

Interpretation: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Conditions of validity: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Spring oscillator

Problem: A mass of 15.408 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 620.89 N/m and displaced by 0.383 m.

Solution method: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Answer: The angular frequency is 6.348 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.0103 Hz, and turning-point energy is 45.539 J.

Physical check: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Idealizations: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 14.14 cm^2 and 10.347 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 1.596 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 2.1811 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0022567 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1610.6 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7981.6 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 7.0669 km/s and the orbital period is 118.27 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.112 m^3 and material density 398.01 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1377.4 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 1512.9 N and the weight is 437.15 N; their signed upward difference is 1075.7 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A force of magnitude 442.49 N acts at a distance of 1.143 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 61.433 degrees to the lever.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 27.706 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 3.582 m/s^2 for 9.526 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 61.828 m/s, and the signed displacement is 426.45 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.
