## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 53.486 kg changes signed velocity from 16.458 to 18.256 m/s during 1.078 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is 96.168 N s and the average net force is 89.209 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 3.199 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 699.22 K, changing volume from 21.269 to 37.923 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is 10755 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 15.134 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 722.68 N/m and displaced by 0.314 m.

The angular frequency is 6.9103 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.0998 Hz, and turning-point energy is 35.627 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 50.842 m/s, emitting a tone of 1471.6 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 1727.7 Hz, a frequency increase of 256.1 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Hooke-law force calibration

Problem: A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

Solution method: For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 345.95 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 348.98 N/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.29292 N.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Motion with constant acceleration

## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 136.05 kg block starts at 31.371 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.489. The surface extends for 16.585 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 102.61 m. After the available distance its speed is 28.724 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 4.7955 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 3.23 kg and 16.31 kg and initial signed speeds -2.865 and 16.909 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is 13.64 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 527.1 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.037 m^3 and material density 1792.5 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1023.4 kg/m^3.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 371.33 N and the weight is 650.39 N; their signed upward difference is -279.05 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 11.836 kg is released from rest at a height of 5.515 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 10.4 m/s and the kinetic energy is 640.13 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1558.5 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7929.5 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.09 km/s and the orbital period is 117.12 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Worked example: Ideal gas equation of state

Physical setup: A vessel contains 9.602 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 342.95 K in volume 110.53 liters.

Relevant law: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Calculated result: The equilibrium pressure is 247.72 kPa.

Interpretation: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Conditions of validity: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 2133.9 Hz and has spatial wavelength 3.929 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 0.00046862 s and the propagation speed is 8384.2 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.0202 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.062973 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Physical setup: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 396.99 W/(m K), thickness 0.245 m, area 1.103 m^2, and temperature difference 54.227 K.

Relevant law: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Calculated result: The conduction rate is 96917 W.

Interpretation: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Conditions of validity: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 176.49 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 11.034 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 36.182 m/s and elevation angle 27.934 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 3.4568 s, the horizontal range is 110.5 m, and maximum height above launch is 14.648 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 5.823 kg is released from rest at a height of 50.02 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 31.322 m/s and the kinetic energy is 2856.3 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1330.5 K and cold reservoir at 256.43 K, absorbing 6289.5 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 80.726 percent, corresponding to at most 5077.3 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

A sample of mass 2.18 kg has specific heat capacity 1563.7 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 273.86 to 489.85 K.

For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

The required energy is 736.3 kJ.

The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 9.702 m/s, emitting a tone of 827.72 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 851.82 Hz, a frequency increase of 24.094 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.069 m^3 and material density 213.42 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 785.74 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 531.67 N and the weight is 144.41 N; their signed upward difference is 387.26 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 14.788 W/(m K), thickness 0.302 m, area 0.054 m^2, and temperature difference 24.503 K.

The conduction rate is 64.791 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 425.36 N acts at a distance of 0.057 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 101.71 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 23.741 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 9.581 cm^2 and 8.265 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 1.613 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 1.8698 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0015454 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Thermal conduction measurement

A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

The fitted slope is 1.5245 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 1.5089 W/K.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 4.8766 W.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 17.17 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 2.686 m/s^2 for 16.507 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 61.508 m/s, and the signed displacement is 649.37 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Linear thermal expansion

A rod with initial length 27.04 m has expansion coefficient 2.0092e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 39.632 K.

For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

The calculated signed change in length is 21.532 mm.

For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Worked example: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Physical setup: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 0.00021636 W/m^2.

Relevant law: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Calculated result: The ideal intensity level is 83.352 dB.

Interpretation: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Conditions of validity: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 8.746 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 447.62 K, changing volume from 34.766 to 80.657 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is 27393 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 13.088 kg block starts at 16.6 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.145. The surface extends for 27.606 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 96.894 m. After the available distance its speed is 14.037 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.422 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 98.008 kg follows a circle of radius 0.847 m at constant speed 53.44 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 3371.7 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 3.3045e+05 N, and rotation frequency is 10.042 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 48.175 kg changes signed velocity from 13.283 to 12.903 m/s during 1.839 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is -18.306 N s and the average net force is -9.9546 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum

Problem: A simple pendulum has length 6.14 m and an initial angular displacement of 3.905 degrees.

Solution method: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Answer: The estimated oscillation period is 4.9717 s and its frequency is 0.20114 Hz.

Physical check: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Idealizations: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 10.168 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 297.07 N/m and displaced by 0.157 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 5.4052 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.86027 Hz, and turning-point energy is 3.6613 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

8.56 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 528.95 K to 883.33 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

The internal energy change is 37832 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Pressure at depth

Problem: A stationary liquid has density 990.29 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 37.197 m below a surface at pressure 96.22 kPa.

Solution method: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Answer: The pressure increase is 361.24 kPa and the absolute pressure is 457.46 kPa.

Physical check: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Idealizations: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 7.8209 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.2447 Hz, and turning-point energy is 20.501 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 8.82 kg is released from rest at a height of 91.108 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 42.272 m/s and the kinetic energy is 7880.4 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 8.335 kg and 0.571 kg and initial signed speeds 13.636 and 16.183 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 13.799 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 1.7334 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 5.688 kg block starts at 13.513 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.509. The surface extends for 11.473 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 18.291 m. After the available distance its speed is 8.2501 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 4.9916 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

2.772 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 482.43 K to 943.32 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

The internal energy change is 15934 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.

## Ideal gas equation of state

A vessel contains 7.455 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 588.89 K in volume 5.206 liters.

The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

The equilibrium pressure is 7011.6 kPa.

At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Worked example: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Physical setup: A fully submerged body has volume 0.014 m^3 and material density 804.59 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1189.6 kg/m^3.

Relevant law: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Calculated result: The upward buoyancy is 163.33 N and the weight is 110.46 N; their signed upward difference is 52.864 N.

Interpretation: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Conditions of validity: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Problem: A rod with initial length 9.957 m has expansion coefficient 2.1315e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 53.08 K.

Solution method: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is 11.265 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.

## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 92.799 N acts at a distance of 3.47 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 129.77 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 247.5 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 6.644 kg has specific heat capacity 4229.3 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 339.97 to 450.78 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 3113.7 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.

## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 740.8 K and cold reservoir at 303.74 K, absorbing 5129.1 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 58.998 percent, corresponding to at most 3026.1 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Reversible isothermal gas work

3.061 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 213.74 K, changing volume from 11.632 to 33.279 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 5718.1 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Worked example: Escape speed from a central mass

Physical setup: Consider a test object at altitude 248.5 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Relevant law: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Calculated result: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.974 km/s.

Interpretation: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Conditions of validity: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 22.263 kg and radius 1.28 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 11.784 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 18.238 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 1266.3 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 18405 Hz and has spatial wavelength 4.178 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 5.4332e-05 s and the propagation speed is 76898 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 96.957 kg follows a circle of radius 0.689 m at constant speed 25.837 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 968.87 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 93939 N, and rotation frequency is 5.9682 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Worked example: Pressure at depth

Physical setup: A stationary liquid has density 1104.7 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 174.58 m below a surface at pressure 90.356 kPa.

Calculated result: The pressure increase is 1891.3 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1981.7 kPa.

Interpretation: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Conditions of validity: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 18.146 m/s and elevation angle 68.146 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 3.4348 s, the horizontal range is 23.201 m, and maximum height above launch is 14.462 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 828.92 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7199.9 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 7.4406 km/s and the orbital period is 101.33 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum

Problem: A simple pendulum has length 6.778 m and an initial angular displacement of 6.129 degrees.

Solution method: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Answer: The estimated oscillation period is 5.2236 s and its frequency is 0.19144 Hz.

Physical check: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Idealizations: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 65.812 kg changes signed velocity from -8.725 to 18.695 m/s during 1.299 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 1804.6 N s and the average net force is 1389.2 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 5.5556e-10 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 27.447 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

Problem: A body with mass 26.001 kg changes signed velocity from -18.44 to 17.487 m/s during 1.226 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is 934.14 N s and the average net force is 761.94 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.104 m^3 and material density 795.53 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1256.2 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 1281.1 N and the weight is 811.36 N; their signed upward difference is 469.79 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Physical setup: A sample of mass 14.462 kg has specific heat capacity 4433 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 283.9 to 384.21 K.

Relevant law: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Calculated result: The required energy is 6430.5 kJ.

Interpretation: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Conditions of validity: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Problem: 5.81 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 636.85 K to 368.72 K.

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Answer: The internal energy change is -19429 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Reversible isothermal gas work

7.148 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 341.45 K, changing volume from 6.694 to 18.656 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 20800 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 10.406 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Projectile trajectory above level ground

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 33.372 kg block starts at 12.085 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.076. The surface extends for 9.462 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 97.978 m. After the available distance its speed is 11.487 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 0.74531 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Worked example: Standing wave on a stretched string

Physical setup: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 0.46 m, tension 154.2 N, and linear mass density 0.004 kg/m.

Relevant law: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Calculated result: The speed of transverse waves is 196.34 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 213.41 Hz.

Interpretation: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Conditions of validity: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 90 kg follows a circle of radius 13.599 m at constant speed 79.856 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 468.93 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 42204 N, and rotation frequency is 0.93459 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 19.936 kg and 0.391 kg and initial signed speeds -3.24 and 8.256 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is -3.0189 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 25.34 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 1.933 kg is released from rest at a height of 46.727 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 30.273 m/s and the kinetic energy is 885.77 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.0249 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.56383 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 18660 Hz and has spatial wavelength 4.507 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 5.3591e-05 s and the propagation speed is 84100 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is 10.368 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 572.09 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Quantitative physics problem: Pressure at depth

Problem: A stationary liquid has density 1030.7 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 170.35 m below a surface at pressure 105.99 kPa.

Solution method: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Answer: The pressure increase is 1721.9 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1827.9 kPa.

Physical check: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Idealizations: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 386.1 W/(m K), thickness 0.34 m, area 0.323 m^2, and temperature difference 39.468 K.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 14477 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 106.92 kg block starts at 17.989 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.139. The surface extends for 22.179 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 118.7 m. After the available distance its speed is 16.222 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.3631 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 2135 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 8506 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 6.8455 km/s and the orbital period is 130.12 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Worked example: Standing wave on a stretched string

## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 54.495 m/s, emitting a tone of 387.34 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 460.5 Hz, a frequency increase of 73.164 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Reversible isothermal gas work

6.444 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 609.17 K, changing volume from 48.713 to 118.66 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 29060 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 23.065 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 184.46 N/m and displaced by 0.489 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 2.828 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.45009 Hz, and turning-point energy is 22.055 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 28.317 kg changes signed velocity from 10.798 to 2.917 m/s during 1.963 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -223.17 N s and the average net force is -113.69 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Physical setup: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 24.781 kg and radius 0.112 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 112.19 rad/s.

Relevant law: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Calculated result: The moment of inertia is 0.15543 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 978.08 J.

Interpretation: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Conditions of validity: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A force of magnitude 548.66 N acts at a distance of 1.21 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 26.817 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 299.51 N m.

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.032 m^3 and material density 860.66 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1124.3 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 352.82 N and the weight is 270.09 N; their signed upward difference is 82.737 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 16003 Hz and has spatial wavelength 4.41 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 6.2487e-05 s and the propagation speed is 70574 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 12.295 kg is released from rest at a height of 83.846 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Hooke-law force calibration

A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

The fitted slope is 269.13 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 266.8 N/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.47483 N.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 2113.6 Hz and has spatial wavelength 2.384 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 0.00047313 s and the propagation speed is 5038.7 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 1256.5 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.223 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1224 K and cold reservoir at 413.96 K, absorbing 8035.8 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 66.179 percent, corresponding to at most 5318 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Hooke-law force calibration

A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

The fitted slope is 190.58 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 190.62 N/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.064979 N.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 36.085 m/s, emitting a tone of 453.15 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 506.43 Hz, a frequency increase of 53.279 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 12.037 kg has specific heat capacity 4095.8 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 321.05 to 370.11 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 2418.5 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 3.321 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 0.748 m/s^2 for 6.839 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 8.4366 m/s, and the signed displacement is 40.205 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 64.659 kg block starts at 16.556 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.211. The surface extends for 14.876 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 66.234 m. After the available distance its speed is 14.579 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 2.0692 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 32.46 kg changes signed velocity from 10.702 to 18.945 m/s during 0.411 s.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is 267.57 N s and the average net force is 651.02 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A force of magnitude 92.998 N acts at a distance of 2.011 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 13.348 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 43.176 N m.

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

9.566 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 401.58 K to 859.6 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

The internal energy change is 54644 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 7.589 kg and 17.341 kg and initial signed speeds 1.61 and -8.694 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is -5.5573 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 280.23 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 17.559 m/s and elevation angle 45.401 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 2.5498 s, the horizontal range is 31.437 m, and maximum height above launch is 7.9699 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Physical setup: A simple pendulum has length 5.247 m and an initial angular displacement of 2.857 degrees.

Relevant law: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Calculated result: The estimated oscillation period is 4.5959 s and its frequency is 0.21758 Hz.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Conditions of validity: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 94.292 kg follows a circle of radius 5.637 m at constant speed 62.223 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 686.84 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 64763 N, and rotation frequency is 1.7568 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 13.722 cm^2 and 3.163 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.131 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 9.2449 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0029242 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

Answer: The equilibrium pressure is 425.58 kPa.

Physical check: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 4.3114e-05 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 76.346 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Worked example: Pressure at depth

Physical setup: A stationary liquid has density 1097.8 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 27.536 m below a surface at pressure 108.2 kPa.

Relevant law: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Calculated result: The pressure increase is 296.46 kPa and the absolute pressure is 404.66 kPa.

Interpretation: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Conditions of validity: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 33.353 kg and radius 1.917 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 136.63 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 61.284 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 5.7201e+05 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Worked example: Standing wave on a stretched string

Physical setup: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 2.296 m, tension 76.033 N, and linear mass density 0.024 kg/m.

Relevant law: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Calculated result: The speed of transverse waves is 56.285 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 12.257 Hz.

Interpretation: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Conditions of validity: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 1.873 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 691.96 K, changing volume from 15.326 to 21.778 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is 3786.2 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

Problem: A mass of 232.87 kg follows a circle of radius 8.924 m at constant speed 12.177 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 16.616 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 3869.3 N, and rotation frequency is 0.21717 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 301.68 W/(m K), thickness 0.169 m, area 3.148 m^2, and temperature difference 72.895 K.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 4.0963e+05 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 9.577 kg and 24.481 kg and initial signed speeds 14.091 and -4.94 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is 0.41146 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 1246.6 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 72.992 m/s and elevation angle 36.769 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 8.9107 s, the horizontal range is 521.02 m, and maximum height above launch is 97.333 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 14.314 kg has specific heat capacity 4448.6 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 328.44 to 453.09 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 7937.5 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 38.907 kg changes signed velocity from -16.749 to 10.99 m/s during 0.773 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 1079.2 N s and the average net force is 1396.2 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 575.25 N acts at a distance of 0.537 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 118.18 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 272.31 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 4573.5 Hz and has spatial wavelength 3.805 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 0.00021865 s and the propagation speed is 17402 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 2.3864e-09 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 33.777 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Worked example: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Physical setup: A fully submerged body has volume 0.013 m^3 and material density 884.96 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 821.59 kg/m^3.

Relevant law: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Calculated result: The upward buoyancy is 104.74 N and the weight is 112.82 N; their signed upward difference is -8.0789 N.

Interpretation: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Conditions of validity: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 58.125 kg block starts at 27.674 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.221. The surface extends for 6.056 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 176.69 m. After the available distance its speed is 27.196 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 2.1673 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 1205.6 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 10.437 m below a surface at pressure 98.207 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

The pressure increase is 123.4 kPa and the absolute pressure is 221.6 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 1.522 kg is released from rest at a height of 23.937 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 21.668 m/s and the kinetic energy is 357.28 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Problem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 1.443 m, tension 439.99 N, and linear mass density 0.04 kg/m.

Solution method: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Answer: The speed of transverse waves is 104.88 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 36.341 Hz.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 6.919 m/s, emitting a tone of 475.91 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 485.7 Hz, a frequency increase of 9.7976 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Worked example: Escape speed from a central mass

Physical setup: Consider a test object at altitude 1484 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Relevant law: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Calculated result: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.074 km/s.

Interpretation: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Conditions of validity: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 348.12 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 6719.1 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 7.7022 km/s and the orbital period is 91.354 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 696.26 K and cold reservoir at 419.58 K, absorbing 5007.6 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 39.738 percent, corresponding to at most 1989.9 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Problem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 6.968 cm^2 and 4.769 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.298 m/s.

Solution method: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Answer: The speed in the second section is 3.3576 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0016012 m^3/s.

Physical check: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Idealizations: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 11.726 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 0.263 m/s^2 for 14.955 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 15.659 m/s, and the signed displacement is 204.77 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 45.832 kg and radius 1.339 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 89.255 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 41.087 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 1.6366e+05 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

Calculated result: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.438 km/s.

Interpretation: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Conditions of validity: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 13867 Hz and has spatial wavelength 2.557 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 7.2113e-05 s and the propagation speed is 35458 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Worked example: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Physical setup: A fully submerged body has volume 0.059 m^3 and material density 374.43 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1175.1 kg/m^3.

Relevant law: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Calculated result: The upward buoyancy is 679.91 N and the weight is 216.64 N; their signed upward difference is 463.27 N.

Interpretation: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Conditions of validity: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 30.064 m/s, emitting a tone of 1482.7 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 1625.2 Hz, a frequency increase of 142.45 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 190.78 W/(m K), thickness 0.089 m, area 1.338 m^2, and temperature difference 19.475 K.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 55857 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1051.4 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7422.4 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 7.3282 km/s and the orbital period is 106.07 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 7.161 m and an initial angular displacement of 7.633 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 5.3692 s and its frequency is 0.18625 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 7.347 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 3.416 m/s^2 for 2.806 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 16.932 m/s, and the signed displacement is 34.064 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Problem: 4.773 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 586.5 K to 399.23 K.

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Answer: The internal energy change is -11148 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.
