## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.0248 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.68693 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 45.068 kg changes signed velocity from -3.686 to 13.989 m/s during 1.395 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is 796.58 N s and the average net force is 571.02 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 16.065 kg block starts at 21.931 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.296. The surface extends for 19.524 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 82.847 m. After the available distance its speed is 19.173 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 2.9028 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 943.06 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 56.405 m below a surface at pressure 90.792 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

The pressure increase is 521.65 kPa and the absolute pressure is 612.44 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 22.846 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 129.99 N/m and displaced by 0.033 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 2.3853 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.37963 Hz, and turning-point energy is 0.070777 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

Problem: 4.29 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 632.25 K to 963.28 K.

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Answer: The internal energy change is 17711 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1363.1 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7734.1 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.179 km/s and the orbital period is 112.82 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 32.192 kg changes signed velocity from 4.268 to -15.689 m/s during 1.876 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is -642.46 N s and the average net force is -342.46 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 12.521 kg has specific heat capacity 2609.9 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 273.71 to 353.69 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 2613.5 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Reversible isothermal gas work

3.396 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 339.33 K, changing volume from 24.28 to 40.912 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 4999.2 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Worked example: Uniform circular motion

Physical setup: A mass of 207.26 kg follows a circle of radius 6.233 m at constant speed 54.934 m/s.

Interpretation: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1243 K and cold reservoir at 336.12 K, absorbing 8851 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 72.959 percent, corresponding to at most 6457.6 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 24.565 kg and 9.239 kg and initial signed speeds -3.017 and 18.19 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is 2.7791 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 1509.7 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Problem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 0.528 m, tension 378.69 N, and linear mass density 0.028 kg/m.

Solution method: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Answer: The speed of transverse waves is 116.3 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 110.13 Hz.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 19.338 m/s, emitting a tone of 871.77 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 923.85 Hz, a frequency increase of 52.086 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Worked example: Buoyant force on an immersed object

## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.0055 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.21693 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 356.98 W/(m K), thickness 0.118 m, area 1.804 m^2, and temperature difference 71.507 K.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 3.9025e+05 W.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 4.638 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -0.212 m/s^2 for 8.185 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 2.9028 m/s, and the signed displacement is 30.861 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 58.153 m/s and elevation angle 26.073 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 5.2126 s, the horizontal range is 272.28 m, and maximum height above launch is 33.308 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

Answer: The ideal intensity level is 37.41 dB.

## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 962.6 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7333.6 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.3724 km/s and the orbital period is 104.17 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 3.312 kg is released from rest at a height of 62.404 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 34.985 m/s and the kinetic energy is 2026.9 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 178.13 kg follows a circle of radius 9.65 m at constant speed 18.438 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 35.229 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 6275.5 N, and rotation frequency is 0.30409 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 4.066 kg changes signed velocity from 12.346 to 15.533 m/s during 1.929 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 12.958 N s and the average net force is 6.7176 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 13.209 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 469.96 N/m and displaced by 0.232 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 5.9648 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.94933 Hz, and turning-point energy is 12.648 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Worked example: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Physical setup: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 12.1 kg and radius 1.388 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 134.38 rad/s.

Relevant law: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Calculated result: The moment of inertia is 11.656 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 1.0523e+05 J.

Interpretation: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Conditions of validity: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum

Problem: A simple pendulum has length 7.574 m and an initial angular displacement of 6.332 degrees.

Solution method: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Answer: The estimated oscillation period is 5.5218 s and its frequency is 0.1811 Hz.

Physical check: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Idealizations: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.017 m^3 and material density 803.07 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 749.76 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 124.99 N and the weight is 133.88 N; their signed upward difference is -8.8883 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 347.18 W/(m K), thickness 0.233 m, area 0.332 m^2, and temperature difference 48.039 K.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 34.153 m/s, emitting a tone of 1761.4 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 1956.2 Hz, a frequency increase of 194.78 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 237.81 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.983 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Problem: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

Solution method: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 3.9676 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.7278 s^2.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 0.31 kg and 24.822 kg and initial signed speeds 7.296 and 6.242 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is 6.255 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 0.17007 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 70.237 m/s, and the signed displacement is 567.1 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 18164 Hz and has spatial wavelength 1.136 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 5.5054e-05 s and the propagation speed is 20634 m/s.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

Problem: A cart begins at 17.103 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 0.236 m/s^2 for 4.138 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 18.08 m/s, and the signed displacement is 72.793 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Reversible isothermal gas work

8.643 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 284.93 K, changing volume from 33.79 to 55.686 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 10229 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 23.068 kg and 21.776 kg and initial signed speeds -8.59 and 11.434 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 68.571 m/s and elevation angle 39.946 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 8.979 s, the horizontal range is 472.03 m, and maximum height above launch is 98.83 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 12.59 kg is released from rest at a height of 99.005 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 44.066 m/s and the kinetic energy is 12224 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Worked example: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Physical setup: A fully submerged body has volume 0.092 m^3 and material density 940.67 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 915.11 kg/m^3.

## Hooke-law force calibration

A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

The fitted slope is 648.95 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 651.76 N/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.64482 N.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Spring oscillator

## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 31.583 m/s, emitting a tone of 297.59 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 327.77 Hz, a frequency increase of 30.181 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 1711.7 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 39.632 kg and radius 1.743 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 140.79 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 60.202 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 5.9666e+05 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.045 m^3 and material density 1351.2 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1060.2 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 467.85 N and the weight is 596.29 N; their signed upward difference is -128.45 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Relevant law: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Calculated result: The estimated oscillation period is 4.1523 s and its frequency is 0.24083 Hz.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Conditions of validity: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Problem: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 44.548 W/(m K), thickness 0.034 m, area 1.029 m^2, and temperature difference 46.277 K.

Solution method: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Answer: The conduction rate is 62392 W.

Physical check: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Idealizations: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Spring oscillator

A mass of 17.445 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 258.58 N/m and displaced by 0.417 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 3.85 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.61275 Hz, and turning-point energy is 22.482 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 21.895 kg and 13.998 kg and initial signed speeds 2.582 and -6.089 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is -0.79962 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 321 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 15097 Hz and has spatial wavelength 4.015 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 6.6238e-05 s and the propagation speed is 60615 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 24.845 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -2.114 m/s^2 for 9.39 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 4.9945 m/s, and the signed displacement is 140.1 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Reversible isothermal gas work

2.454 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 513.34 K, changing volume from 36.168 to 92.699 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 9857.9 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 19.035 kg block starts at 13.192 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.409. The surface extends for 11.017 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 21.694 m. After the available distance its speed is 9.2549 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 4.0109 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Linear thermal expansion

The calculated signed change in length is 16.143 mm.

The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Worked example: Hooke-law force calibration

Physical setup: A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

Relevant law: For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 699.11 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 697.48 N/m.

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.67021 N.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 16.775 kg is released from rest at a height of 70.745 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 37.25 m/s and the kinetic energy is 11638 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 715.18 K and cold reservoir at 424.3 K, absorbing 7670 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 40.673 percent, corresponding to at most 3119.6 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1998.9 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 8369.9 km.

The circular speed is 6.901 km/s and the orbital period is 127.01 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 6.338 cm^2 and 14.218 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.043 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 0.91071 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0012949 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A vessel contains 1.68 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 330.81 K in volume 22.869 liters.

Solution method: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Answer: The equilibrium pressure is 202.06 kPa.

Physical check: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 14.29 cm^2 and 4.899 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.3 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 6.7089 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0032867 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 10212 Hz and has spatial wavelength 2.736 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 9.7926e-05 s and the propagation speed is 27939 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 671.89 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7042.9 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 7.5231 km/s and the orbital period is 98.036 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.128 m^3 and material density 410.83 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 855.05 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 1073.3 N and the weight is 515.69 N; their signed upward difference is 557.61 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 6.643 kg is released from rest at a height of 25.518 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 22.372 m/s and the kinetic energy is 1662.4 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 13.858 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -1.397 m/s^2 for 4.016 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 8.2476 m/s, and the signed displacement is 44.388 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Problem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 0.911 m, tension 841.14 N, and linear mass density 0.032 kg/m.

Solution method: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Answer: The speed of transverse waves is 162.13 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 88.984 Hz.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.

## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 54.191 m/s and elevation angle 29.748 degrees from level ground.

## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A force of magnitude 305.68 N acts at a distance of 1.936 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 83.635 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 588.16 N m.

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Spring oscillator

A mass of 2.89 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 712.36 N/m and displaced by 0.186 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 15.7 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 2.4987 Hz, and turning-point energy is 12.322 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 56.914 kg changes signed velocity from -19.587 to -19.855 m/s during 0.033 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 93.29 W/(m K), thickness 0.595 m, area 0.32 m^2, and temperature difference 51.561 K.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 2587 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Worked example: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Physical setup: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 20.483 kg and radius 1.637 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 73.615 rad/s.

Relevant law: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Calculated result: The moment of inertia is 27.445 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 74364 J.

Interpretation: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Conditions of validity: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 151.83 kg follows a circle of radius 24.735 m at constant speed 4.975 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 1.0006 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 151.93 N, and rotation frequency is 0.032011 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 0.00046645 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 86.688 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 1.663 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 679.64 K, changing volume from 49.527 to 116.64 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is 8049.2 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 968.54 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 103.62 m below a surface at pressure 101.36 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

The pressure increase is 984.19 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1085.6 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

Interpretation: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 14.616 kg and 6.206 kg and initial signed speeds 12.289 and 16.99 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is 13.69 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 48.136 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 88.573 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 6.462 m and an initial angular displacement of 3.775 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 5.1004 s and its frequency is 0.19606 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Worked example: Ideal gas equation of state

Physical setup: A vessel contains 10.117 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 253.42 K in volume 114.07 liters.

Relevant law: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Calculated result: The equilibrium pressure is 186.87 kPa.

Interpretation: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Conditions of validity: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Pressure at depth

Problem: A stationary liquid has density 1156.8 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 70.225 m below a surface at pressure 99.937 kPa.

Solution method: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Answer: The pressure increase is 796.69 kPa and the absolute pressure is 896.63 kPa.

Physical check: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Idealizations: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.129 m^3 and material density 1321.7 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 722.31 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 913.76 N and the weight is 1672 N; their signed upward difference is -758.23 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 19.878 kg and 16.242 kg and initial signed speeds 2.613 and -2.865 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is 0.14972 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 134.12 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 9.268 m/s and elevation angle 20.936 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 0.6754 s, the horizontal range is 5.8463 m, and maximum height above launch is 0.55918 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1513.5 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7884.5 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.1102 km/s and the orbital period is 116.12 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 16.039 m/s, emitting a tone of 553.67 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 580.83 Hz, a frequency increase of 27.16 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Problem: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 5.0726e-08 W/m^2.

Solution method: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Answer: The ideal intensity level is 47.052 dB.

Physical check: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Idealizations: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 11.681 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 3.216 m/s^2 for 11.566 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 48.877 m/s, and the signed displacement is 350.21 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 19792 Hz and has spatial wavelength 3.72 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 5.0526e-05 s and the propagation speed is 73625 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 9.468 kg is released from rest at a height of 49.87 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 31.275 m/s and the kinetic energy is 4630.4 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Worked example: Uniform circular motion

Physical setup: A mass of 168.91 kg follows a circle of radius 5.645 m at constant speed 55.138 m/s.

Relevant law: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Calculated result: The centripetal acceleration is 538.56 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 90966 N, and rotation frequency is 1.5546 Hz.

Interpretation: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Conditions of validity: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 44.927 kg changes signed velocity from 16.048 to -5.444 m/s during 0.542 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is -965.57 N s and the average net force is -1781.5 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Problem: 2.092 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 662.04 K to 991.83 K.

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Answer: The internal energy change is 8604.2 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 9.521 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 149.94 N/m and displaced by 0.296 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 3.9684 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.63159 Hz, and turning-point energy is 6.5685 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A force of magnitude 329.65 N acts at a distance of 1.124 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 137.4 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 250.81 N m.

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.

## Worked example: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Physical setup: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 32.42 W/(m K), thickness 0.194 m, area 2.541 m^2, and temperature difference 33.238 K.

Relevant law: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Calculated result: The conduction rate is 14114 W.

Interpretation: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Conditions of validity: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Worked example: Standing wave on a stretched string

Physical setup: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 2.448 m, tension 128 N, and linear mass density 0.002 kg/m.

Calculated result: The speed of transverse waves is 252.98 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 51.671 Hz.

## Small-angle pendulum

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

## Worked example: Uniform circular motion

Physical setup: A mass of 75.114 kg follows a circle of radius 3.663 m at constant speed 16.564 m/s.

Relevant law: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Calculated result: The centripetal acceleration is 74.902 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 5626.2 N, and rotation frequency is 0.71969 Hz.

Interpretation: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Conditions of validity: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 125.52 W/(m K), thickness 0.533 m, area 2.413 m^2, and temperature difference 77.037 K.

The conduction rate is 43776 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 26.026 m/s and elevation angle 55.649 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 4.3821 s, the horizontal range is 64.353 m, and maximum height above launch is 23.54 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 1390.6 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.135 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 6.591 kg and 7.54 kg and initial signed speeds 0.383 and 2.585 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is 1.5579 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 8.5262 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 5.218 kg is released from rest at a height of 78.583 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 39.259 m/s and the kinetic energy is 4021.2 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 118.33 kg block starts at 31.354 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.096. The surface extends for 9.938 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 522.11 m. After the available distance its speed is 31.054 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 0.94144 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 33.676 kg changes signed velocity from 14.275 to -5.564 m/s during 1.698 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -668.1 N s and the average net force is -393.46 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Ideal gas equation of state

Physical setup: A vessel contains 4.065 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 809.28 K in volume 34.572 liters.

Relevant law: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Calculated result: The equilibrium pressure is 791.17 kPa.

Interpretation: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Conditions of validity: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 37.13 m/s, emitting a tone of 1204.9 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 1351.2 Hz, a frequency increase of 146.26 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 6369.8 Hz and has spatial wavelength 1.668 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 0.00015699 s and the propagation speed is 10625 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.019 m^3 and material density 1489.4 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 704.43 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 131.25 N and the weight is 277.51 N; their signed upward difference is -146.25 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Periodic wave propagation

Physical setup: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 13771 Hz and has spatial wavelength 1.492 m.

Relevant law: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Calculated result: The period is 7.2615e-05 s and the propagation speed is 20547 m/s.

Interpretation: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Conditions of validity: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 5.057 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 696.56 K, changing volume from 15.929 to 39.998 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is 26965 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.0375 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.07722 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 24.057 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 273.08 N/m and displaced by 0.142 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 3.3692 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.53622 Hz, and turning-point energy is 2.7532 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Problem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 9.639 cm^2 and 3.651 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.442 m/s.

Solution method: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Answer: The speed in the second section is 6.4471 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0023538 m^3/s.

Physical check: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Idealizations: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1125.6 K and cold reservoir at 430.89 K, absorbing 4854.2 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 61.719 percent, corresponding to at most 2996 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 49.367 m/s and elevation angle 54.067 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 8.1522 s, the horizontal range is 236.17 m, and maximum height above launch is 81.466 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 17.532 kg is released from rest at a height of 2.502 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 7.0052 m/s and the kinetic energy is 430.17 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Lever arm and rotational effect

A force of magnitude 253.92 N acts at a distance of 0.72 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 25.735 degrees to the lever.

The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

The calculated torque magnitude is 79.384 N m.

For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Physical setup: A simple pendulum has length 5.481 m and an initial angular displacement of 4.257 degrees.

Relevant law: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Calculated result: The estimated oscillation period is 4.6973 s and its frequency is 0.21289 Hz.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Conditions of validity: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum

Solution method: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Answer: The estimated oscillation period is 2.4185 s and its frequency is 0.41347 Hz.

## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

A sample of mass 7.954 kg has specific heat capacity 3803.1 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 321.84 to 444.43 K.

For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

The required energy is 3708.3 kJ.

The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Worked example: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Physical setup: 6.593 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 537.3 K to 220.95 K.

Relevant law: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Calculated result: The internal energy change is -26012 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Interpretation: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Conditions of validity: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

Problem: A vessel contains 4.964 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 876.27 K in volume 149.36 liters.

Solution method: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Answer: The equilibrium pressure is 242.15 kPa.

Physical check: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 26.968 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -2.797 m/s^2 for 3.752 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 16.474 m/s, and the signed displacement is 81.497 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1333.8 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7704.8 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.1926 km/s and the orbital period is 112.18 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 16.786 m/s, emitting a tone of 961.91 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 1011.4 Hz, a frequency increase of 49.497 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 6.675 kg and 15.851 kg and initial signed speeds 18.508 and 8.614 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is 11.546 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 229.9 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 5.176 kg block starts at 17.962 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.159. The surface extends for 24.774 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 103.46 m. After the available distance its speed is 15.664 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.5593 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 10.744 kg and radius 1.631 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 106.89 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 14.29 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 81640 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 7.3136e-06 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 68.641 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Worked example: Uniform circular motion

Physical setup: A mass of 245.01 kg follows a circle of radius 24.069 m at constant speed 71.405 m/s.

Relevant law: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Calculated result: The centripetal acceleration is 211.84 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 51903 N, and rotation frequency is 0.47216 Hz.

Interpretation: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Conditions of validity: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Answer: The speed of transverse waves is 152.92 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 76.23 Hz.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.

For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Worked example: Linear thermal expansion

Calculated result: The calculated signed change in length is 8.4024 mm.

Interpretation: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 53.516 m/s, emitting a tone of 285.26 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 338 Hz, a frequency increase of 52.735 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Quantitative physics problem: Spring oscillator

Problem: A mass of 10.732 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 785.77 N/m and displaced by 0.095 m.

Solution method: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Answer: The angular frequency is 8.5567 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.3618 Hz, and turning-point energy is 3.5458 J.

Physical check: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Idealizations: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 2.8667e-06 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 64.574 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 132.13 kg block starts at 14.717 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.297. The surface extends for 26.733 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 37.182 m. After the available distance its speed is 7.8017 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 2.9126 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 33.234 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 6.03 m/s^2 for 10.305 s.

The final signed velocity is 95.373 m/s, and the signed displacement is 662.65 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Worked example: Pressure at depth

Physical setup: A stationary liquid has density 976.66 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 132.56 m below a surface at pressure 103.78 kPa.

Relevant law: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Calculated result: The pressure increase is 1269.6 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1373.4 kPa.

Interpretation: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Conditions of validity: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 13641 Hz and has spatial wavelength 0.445 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 7.3311e-05 s and the propagation speed is 6070.1 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 7.592 kg is released from rest at a height of 6.648 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 11.419 m/s and the kinetic energy is 494.96 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.
