## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 5.373 kg and 5.587 kg and initial signed speeds 6.323 and 7.546 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 26.449 m/s and elevation angle 40.663 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 3.5148 s, the horizontal range is 70.518 m, and maximum height above launch is 15.144 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Problem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 14.859 cm^2 and 8.016 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 1.918 m/s.

Solution method: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Answer: The speed in the second section is 3.5553 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.00285 m^3/s.

Physical check: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Idealizations: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1277.2 K and cold reservoir at 346.46 K, absorbing 4535.1 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 72.873 percent, corresponding to at most 3304.9 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

## Reversible isothermal gas work

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 2.944 kg and 0.403 kg and initial signed speeds 10.628 and 0.256 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 62.106 kg changes signed velocity from 5.269 to -18.162 m/s during 0.246 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is -1455.2 N s and the average net force is -5915.5 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Spring oscillator

A mass of 18.201 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 770.5 N/m and displaced by 0.304 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 6.5064 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.0355 Hz, and turning-point energy is 35.603 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 0.389 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 209.48 K, changing volume from 8.924 to 21.409 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is 592.88 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 131.51 kg block starts at 7.109 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.145. The surface extends for 6.663 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 17.77 m. After the available distance its speed is 5.6204 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.422 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 1432 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.108 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Worked example: Uniform circular motion

Physical setup: A mass of 105.24 kg follows a circle of radius 3.764 m at constant speed 74.641 m/s.

Relevant law: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Calculated result: The centripetal acceleration is 1480.1 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 1.5577e+05 N, and rotation frequency is 3.1561 Hz.

Interpretation: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Conditions of validity: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A force of magnitude 367.09 N acts at a distance of 3.439 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 88.886 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 1262.2 N m.

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1571.4 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7942.4 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.0843 km/s and the orbital period is 117.41 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 3.01 kg is released from rest at a height of 30.568 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 24.485 m/s and the kinetic energy is 902.31 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Problem: 6.782 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 779.21 K to 852.95 K.

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Answer: The internal energy change is 6237 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1323.4 K and cold reservoir at 377.07 K, absorbing 8674.7 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 71.507 percent, corresponding to at most 6203 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Worked example: Periodic wave propagation

Physical setup: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 5045.9 Hz and has spatial wavelength 3.485 m.

Relevant law: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Calculated result: The period is 0.00019818 s and the propagation speed is 17585 m/s.

Interpretation: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Conditions of validity: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Quantitative physics problem: Pressure at depth

Problem: A stationary liquid has density 1064.9 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 52.215 m below a surface at pressure 96.758 kPa.

Solution method: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Answer: The pressure increase is 545.28 kPa and the absolute pressure is 642.04 kPa.

Physical check: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Idealizations: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Physical setup: A simple pendulum has length 2.871 m and an initial angular displacement of 4.033 degrees.

Relevant law: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Calculated result: The estimated oscillation period is 3.3997 s and its frequency is 0.29415 Hz.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Conditions of validity: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 11.53 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 6.311 m/s^2 for 4.175 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 37.878 m/s, and the signed displacement is 103.14 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 13.598 kg is released from rest at a height of 108.35 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 46.098 m/s and the kinetic energy is 14448 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

1.373 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 841.99 K to 447.15 K.

## Linear thermal expansion

## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 237.26 kg follows a circle of radius 5.029 m at constant speed 41.917 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 349.38 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 82895 N, and rotation frequency is 1.3266 Hz.

## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 54.028 m/s, emitting a tone of 1073.3 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 1274 Hz, a frequency increase of 200.68 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 133.1 kg block starts at 19.567 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.461. The surface extends for 6.177 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 42.344 m. After the available distance its speed is 18.084 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 4.5209 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Hooke-law force calibration

A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

The fitted slope is 471.53 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 471.15 N/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.28323 N.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

A 36.656 kg block starts at 30.936 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.54. The surface extends for 17.516 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 90.362 m. After the available distance its speed is 27.776 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 5.2956 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 10.641 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 307.07 N/m and displaced by 0.31 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 5.3719 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.85497 Hz, and turning-point energy is 14.755 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 42.078 kg and radius 0.858 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 6.7 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 15.488 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 347.63 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Standing wave on a stretched string

A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 2.225 m, tension 190.69 N, and linear mass density 0.028 kg/m.

Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

The speed of transverse waves is 82.525 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 18.545 Hz.

The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.

## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 6.997 kg is released from rest at a height of 76.149 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 38.646 m/s and the kinetic energy is 5225.1 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 68.643 m/s and elevation angle 71.409 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 13.269 s, the horizontal range is 290.38 m, and maximum height above launch is 215.82 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.084 m^3 and material density 391.21 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1138.8 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 938.08 N and the weight is 322.26 N; their signed upward difference is 615.82 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 1.0255e-07 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 50.109 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Physical setup: A simple pendulum has length 3.343 m and an initial angular displacement of 4.758 degrees.

Relevant law: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Calculated result: The estimated oscillation period is 3.6685 s and its frequency is 0.27259 Hz.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Conditions of validity: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

## Ideal gas equation of state

A vessel contains 2.301 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 216.53 K in volume 22.792 liters.

The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

The equilibrium pressure is 181.75 kPa.

At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Worked example: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Physical setup: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 384.49 W/(m K), thickness 0.513 m, area 1.522 m^2, and temperature difference 12.169 K.

Relevant law: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Calculated result: The conduction rate is 13882 W.

Interpretation: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Conditions of validity: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 2.678 kg has specific heat capacity 3420.6 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 326.91 to 485.43 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 1452.1 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.

## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 4.431 m/s, emitting a tone of 804.19 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 814.71 Hz, a frequency increase of 10.525 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Worked example: Escape speed from a central mass

Physical setup: Consider a test object at altitude 247.38 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Relevant law: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Calculated result: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.975 km/s.

Interpretation: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Conditions of validity: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 3428.8 Hz and has spatial wavelength 1.809 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 0.00029165 s and the propagation speed is 6202.6 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 3.491 kg and 12.151 kg and initial signed speeds 3.713 and -5.651 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is -3.5611 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 118.89 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 6.365 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 328.73 K, changing volume from 41.975 to 107.92 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is 16428 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 46.484 kg changes signed velocity from 15.346 to -3.385 m/s during 1.678 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -870.69 N s and the average net force is -518.89 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1874.3 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 8245.3 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 6.9529 km/s and the orbital period is 124.18 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 156.38 kg follows a circle of radius 5.288 m at constant speed 31.682 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 189.82 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 29684 N, and rotation frequency is 0.95355 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Physical setup: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

Relevant law: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 4.044 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.19029 s^2.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

An object is launched at speed 39.674 m/s and elevation angle 40.879 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 5.2954 s, the horizontal range is 158.85 m, and maximum height above launch is 34.374 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Worked example: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Relevant law: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Calculated result: The conduction rate is 19258 W.

Conditions of validity: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 14.226 kg has specific heat capacity 554.9 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 321.7 to 359.07 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 294.98 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 29.796 kg and radius 0.629 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 83.765 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 5.8943 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 20679 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Worked example: Pressure at depth

Calculated result: The pressure increase is 21.435 kPa and the absolute pressure is 129.19 kPa.

Interpretation: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Conditions of validity: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 27.098 kg changes signed velocity from 0.843 to -4.483 m/s during 0.734 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -144.32 N s and the average net force is -196.63 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Escape speed from a central mass

Physical setup: Consider a test object at altitude 0.777 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Relevant law: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Calculated result: The minimum escape speed at that position is 11.185 km/s.

Interpretation: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Conditions of validity: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

Problem: A vessel contains 1.439 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 390.53 K in volume 165.21 liters.

Solution method: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Answer: The equilibrium pressure is 28.282 kPa.

Physical check: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Sound intensity and decibel scale

## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1130.3 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7501.3 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 7.2896 km/s and the orbital period is 107.76 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 5.339 m and an initial angular displacement of 1.339 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 4.6361 s and its frequency is 0.2157 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 19.897 kg is released from rest at a height of 87.164 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 41.347 m/s and the kinetic energy is 17008 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 115.09 kg block starts at 24.34 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.052. The surface extends for 24.594 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 580.88 m. After the available distance its speed is 23.819 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 0.50995 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

Calculated result: The centripetal acceleration is 69.469 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 8339 N, and rotation frequency is 0.29978 Hz.

Interpretation: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 17.704 kg and 3.037 kg and initial signed speeds 8.837 and 7.631 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.092 m^3 and material density 953.49 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1048.8 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 946.25 N and the weight is 860.25 N; their signed upward difference is 85.998 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 29.168 m/s, emitting a tone of 808.71 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 883.87 Hz, a frequency increase of 75.162 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 5.2979 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.84318 Hz, and turning-point energy is 7.7939 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Problem: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 104.43 W/(m K), thickness 0.357 m, area 0.866 m^2, and temperature difference 52.224 K.

Solution method: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Answer: The conduction rate is 13230 W.

Physical check: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Idealizations: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 4.17 kg and 2.085 kg and initial signed speeds 5.85 and -6.45 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 1.75 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 105.15 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 71.432 kg changes signed velocity from 19.489 to 16.539 m/s during 0.897 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is -210.72 N s and the average net force is -234.92 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 52.775 kg follows a circle of radius 17.274 m at constant speed 75.953 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 333.96 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 17625 N, and rotation frequency is 0.6998 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 61.363 m/s and elevation angle 62.706 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 11.121 s, the horizontal range is 312.93 m, and maximum height above launch is 151.61 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 1059.5 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 58.207 m below a surface at pressure 106.63 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

The pressure increase is 604.75 kPa and the absolute pressure is 711.38 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1473.4 K and cold reservoir at 291.86 K, absorbing 4925.9 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 80.191 percent, corresponding to at most 3950.1 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 3881.2 Hz and has spatial wavelength 1.583 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 0.00025765 s and the propagation speed is 6143.9 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1600 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7971 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 7.0715 km/s and the orbital period is 118.04 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Problem: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

Solution method: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 3.9614 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.32162 s^2.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 2.16 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 443.87 K, changing volume from 25.711 to 22.6 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is -1028.1 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Problem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 1.07 m, tension 734.83 N, and linear mass density 0.038 kg/m.

Solution method: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Answer: The speed of transverse waves is 139.06 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 64.981 Hz.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.

## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 7.772 cm^2 and 10.403 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 4.604 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 3.4396 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0035782 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.086 m^3 and material density 827.21 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 784.47 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 661.6 N and the weight is 697.65 N; their signed upward difference is -36.047 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 42.043 kg and radius 1.748 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 7.749 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 64.231 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 1928.4 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Linear thermal expansion

For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

The calculated signed change in length is 53.042 mm.

The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.

## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 98.603 kg block starts at 27.596 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.112. The surface extends for 27.557 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 346.68 m. After the available distance its speed is 26.476 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.0983 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 7.373 kg is released from rest at a height of 55.211 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 32.907 m/s and the kinetic energy is 3992 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Small-angle pendulum

The estimated oscillation period is 3.9679 s and its frequency is 0.25202 Hz.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

Physical setup: 5.466 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 284.44 K, changing volume from 47.525 to 94.432 liters.

Calculated result: The work by the gas is 8875.9 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 44.491 m/s, emitting a tone of 943.31 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 1083.9 Hz, a frequency increase of 140.6 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Worked example: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Physical setup: A fully submerged body has volume 0.039 m^3 and material density 1746.9 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 769.79 kg/m^3.

Relevant law: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Calculated result: The upward buoyancy is 294.42 N and the weight is 668.12 N; their signed upward difference is -373.71 N.

Interpretation: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Conditions of validity: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 6.48 kg and 8.301 kg and initial signed speeds 6.204 and -7.623 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is -1.5612 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 347.88 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 6.015 kg is released from rest at a height of 9.552 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 13.687 m/s and the kinetic energy is 563.44 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Idealizations: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Thermal conduction measurement

A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

The fitted slope is 1.0121 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 1.0002 W/K.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 11.071 W.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 2.611 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 619.33 N/m and displaced by 0.152 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 15.401 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 2.4512 Hz, and turning-point energy is 7.1544 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Problem: A rod with initial length 16.037 m has expansion coefficient 5.664e-06 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 176.19 K.

Solution method: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is 16.004 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.

## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 65.64 kg block starts at 32.346 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.588. The surface extends for 19.113 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 90.722 m. After the available distance its speed is 28.737 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 5.7663 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Problem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 1.729 m, tension 325.1 N, and linear mass density 0.054 kg/m.

Solution method: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Answer: The speed of transverse waves is 77.591 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 22.438 Hz.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 30.946 kg and radius 0.3 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 132.67 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 1.3926 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 12256 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 27.34 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -1.816 m/s^2 for 6.351 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 15.807 m/s, and the signed displacement is 137.01 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 1290.6 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 12.479 m below a surface at pressure 96.372 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

The pressure increase is 157.94 kPa and the absolute pressure is 254.31 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 48.95 kg follows a circle of radius 19.328 m at constant speed 44.631 m/s.

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.045 m^3 and material density 1460.4 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1011.9 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 446.55 N and the weight is 644.46 N; their signed upward difference is -197.91 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 67.744 kg block starts at 30.24 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.601. The surface extends for 2.348 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 77.578 m. After the available distance its speed is 29.779 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 5.8938 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 29.363 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 0.614 m/s^2 for 16.062 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 39.225 m/s, and the signed displacement is 550.83 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 35.19 m/s and elevation angle 73.279 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 6.8733 s, the horizontal range is 69.589 m, and maximum height above launch is 57.911 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 248.18 kg follows a circle of radius 5.362 m at constant speed 24.201 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 109.23 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 27108 N, and rotation frequency is 0.71833 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Problem: A rod with initial length 0.176 m has expansion coefficient 1.4163e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 190.55 K.

Solution method: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is 0.47499 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 15.291 kg is released from rest at a height of 90.579 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 42.149 m/s and the kinetic energy is 13583 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Worked example: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Interpretation: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Conditions of validity: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 33.689 m/s, emitting a tone of 1622.6 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 1799.4 Hz, a frequency increase of 176.73 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Spring oscillator

A mass of 13.844 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 389.92 N/m and displaced by 0.366 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 5.3071 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.84465 Hz, and turning-point energy is 26.116 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1933 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 8304 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 6.9283 km/s and the orbital period is 125.51 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Steady heat conduction through a slab

The conduction rate is 1.1149e+05 W.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.0407 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.22175 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Reversible isothermal gas work

7.902 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 503.02 K, changing volume from 11.72 to 7.993 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is -12649 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Physical setup: A simple pendulum has length 6.794 m and an initial angular displacement of 6.303 degrees.

Calculated result: The estimated oscillation period is 5.2298 s and its frequency is 0.19121 Hz.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Conditions of validity: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 43.762 kg changes signed velocity from 0.286 to -18.74 m/s during 0.974 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is -832.62 N s and the average net force is -854.84 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 1082.6 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.342 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 7.099 kg and radius 1.516 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 94.922 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 8.1577 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 36751 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 9.244 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 589.83 N/m and displaced by 0.061 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 7.9879 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.2713 Hz, and turning-point energy is 1.0974 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1453.9 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7824.9 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 7.1372 km/s and the orbital period is 114.81 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Reversible isothermal gas work

2.758 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 570.62 K, changing volume from 30.738 to 43.802 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 4634.4 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 11.896 m/s, emitting a tone of 1618 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 1676.2 Hz, a frequency increase of 58.133 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 1.849 kg and 0.309 kg and initial signed speeds -9.566 and 4.556 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is -7.5439 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 26.4 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 3.865 kg is released from rest at a height of 92.407 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 42.572 m/s and the kinetic energy is 3502.5 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Pressure at depth

Problem: A stationary liquid has density 1260.9 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 142.93 m below a surface at pressure 97.724 kPa.

Solution method: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Answer: The pressure increase is 1767.4 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1865.1 kPa.

Physical check: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Idealizations: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Thermal conduction measurement

A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

The fitted slope is 3.6819 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 3.6711 W/K.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 8.9106 W.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Linear thermal expansion

Physical setup: A rod with initial length 15.003 m has expansion coefficient 2.2956e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 56.197 K.

Relevant law: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Calculated result: The calculated signed change in length is 19.355 mm.

Interpretation: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Conditions of validity: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.106 m^3 and material density 1640.8 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 997.1 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 1036.5 N and the weight is 1705.6 N; their signed upward difference is -669.08 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Hooke-law force calibration

A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

The fitted slope is 701.43 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 700.54 N/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 1.028 N.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 141.13 kg block starts at 3.458 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.124. The surface extends for 3.147 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 4.9167 m. After the available distance its speed is 2.0746 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.216 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 2.8994e-05 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 74.623 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 37.35 kg changes signed velocity from -1.088 to -13.835 m/s during 1.836 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is -476.1 N s and the average net force is -259.31 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 1509.6 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.058 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Ideal gas equation of state

Consider a test object at altitude 1245.7 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.231 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Worked example: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Relevant law: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Calculated result: The internal energy change is -15478 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Interpretation: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Conditions of validity: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A force of magnitude 570.83 N acts at a distance of 2.973 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 99.914 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 1671.7 N m.

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Linear thermal expansion

A rod with initial length 28.469 m has expansion coefficient 1.6751e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 143.07 K.

For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

The calculated signed change in length is 68.229 mm.

For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.

## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 142.5 kg block starts at 23.425 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.246. The surface extends for 3.654 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 113.73 m. After the available distance its speed is 23.046 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 2.4124 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 9.319 kg is released from rest at a height of 101.41 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 44.598 m/s and the kinetic energy is 9267.9 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 2.511 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 486.17 K, changing volume from 9.343 to 12.912 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is 3283.9 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 3.9705 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.25541 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Sound intensity and decibel scale

## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 10.895 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 511.52 N/m and displaced by 0.346 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 6.852 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.0905 Hz, and turning-point energy is 30.618 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Ideal gas equation of state

At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Steady heat conduction through a slab

## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 19.931 m/s, emitting a tone of 1088.1 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 1155.2 Hz, a frequency increase of 67.127 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Worked example: Standing wave on a stretched string

Physical setup: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 3.893 m, tension 483.13 N, and linear mass density 0.032 kg/m.
