## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 920.95 K and cold reservoir at 348.38 K, absorbing 278.16 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 62.171 percent, corresponding to at most 172.94 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Worked example: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Physical setup: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 244.11 W/(m K), thickness 0.584 m, area 1.16 m^2, and temperature difference 59.387 K.

Relevant law: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Calculated result: The conduction rate is 28796 W.

Interpretation: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Conditions of validity: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 29.724 m/s, emitting a tone of 1425.2 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 1560.4 Hz, a frequency increase of 135.22 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 14.35 kg is released from rest at a height of 78.71 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 39.291 m/s and the kinetic energy is 11076 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Worked example: Escape speed from a central mass

Physical setup: Consider a test object at altitude 30.515 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Relevant law: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Calculated result: The minimum escape speed at that position is 11.159 km/s.

Interpretation: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Conditions of validity: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Problem: 8.246 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 229.31 K to 572.26 K.

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Answer: The internal energy change is 35269 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Reversible isothermal gas work

0.133 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 665.19 K, changing volume from 40.214 to 67.278 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 378.55 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Worked example: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Physical setup: A fully submerged body has volume 0.059 m^3 and material density 749.61 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1276.4 kg/m^3.

Relevant law: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Calculated result: The upward buoyancy is 738.54 N and the weight is 433.72 N; their signed upward difference is 304.83 N.

Interpretation: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Conditions of validity: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 112.79 kg follows a circle of radius 23.556 m at constant speed 62.749 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 167.15 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 18853 N, and rotation frequency is 0.42396 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

A sample of mass 11.149 kg has specific heat capacity 3325.8 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 334.55 to 452.46 K.

For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

The required energy is 4372.2 kJ.

The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 6.371 cm^2 and 6.848 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 0.351 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 0.32655 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.00022362 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Physical setup: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

Relevant law: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 3.9947 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.19104 s^2.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Lever arm and rotational effect

A force of magnitude 510.64 N acts at a distance of 0.894 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 103.19 degrees to the lever.

The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

The calculated torque magnitude is 444.48 N m.

For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Worked example: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Physical setup: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 44.446 kg and radius 1.826 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 118.32 rad/s.

Relevant law: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Calculated result: The moment of inertia is 74.098 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 5.1863e+05 J.

Interpretation: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Conditions of validity: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 5.473 kg block starts at 19.594 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.202. The surface extends for 29.261 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 96.905 m. After the available distance its speed is 16.371 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.9809 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 57.233 m/s and elevation angle 71.039 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 11.039 s, the horizontal range is 205.28 m, and maximum height above launch is 149.38 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 13.631 kg and 8.548 kg and initial signed speeds -6.852 and -6.313 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is -6.6443 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 0.76313 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Answer: The ideal intensity level is 74.403 dB.

Physical check: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 6.353 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 7.627 m/s^2 for 9.764 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 80.823 m/s, and the signed displacement is 425.59 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

Problem: A vessel contains 2.13 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 394.38 K in volume 187.06 liters.

Solution method: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Answer: The equilibrium pressure is 37.337 kPa.

Physical check: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 24.014 kg and radius 0.636 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 31.195 rad/s.

## Ideal gas equation of state

## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 970.58 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 101.53 m below a surface at pressure 95.841 kPa.

## Worked example: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum

Idealizations: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 19.182 kg is released from rest at a height of 7.843 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 12.403 m/s and the kinetic energy is 1475.4 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 31.082 kg block starts at 14.765 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.257. The surface extends for 13.257 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 43.25 m. After the available distance its speed is 12.296 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 2.5203 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

## Steady heat conduction through a slab

## Worked example: Standing wave on a stretched string

## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 34.212 m/s, emitting a tone of 871.94 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 968.54 Hz, a frequency increase of 96.606 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Worked example: Periodic wave propagation

Calculated result: The period is 5.6732e-05 s and the propagation speed is 12480 m/s.

Interpretation: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Conditions of validity: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 26.201 kg changes signed velocity from 9.071 to 17.213 m/s during 1.722 s.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 2.1695e-06 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 63.364 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Thermal conduction measurement

A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.0152 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.076398 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 24.798 m/s, emitting a tone of 993.46 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 1070.9 Hz, a frequency increase of 77.422 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.094 m^3 and material density 1557.3 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 990.71 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 913.26 N and the weight is 1435.5 N; their signed upward difference is -522.28 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 42.16 kg block starts at 14.722 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.529. The surface extends for 6.665 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 20.889 m. After the available distance its speed is 12.148 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 5.1877 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 51.569 kg changes signed velocity from -12.04 to 9.451 m/s during 0.695 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is 1108.3 N s and the average net force is 1594.6 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 1.296 kg is released from rest at a height of 19.27 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 19.441 m/s and the kinetic energy is 244.91 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 19.638 kg and radius 0.519 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 30.207 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 2.6449 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 1206.7 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 387.76 N acts at a distance of 2.795 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 64.677 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 979.66 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Quantitative physics problem: Spring oscillator

Problem: A mass of 5.014 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 13.992 N/m and displaced by 0.063 m.

Solution method: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Answer: The angular frequency is 1.6705 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.26587 Hz, and turning-point energy is 0.027767 J.

Physical check: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Idealizations: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 33.727 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 2.878 m/s^2 for 13.84 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 73.559 m/s, and the signed displacement is 742.42 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Worked example: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Physical setup: A sample of mass 2.864 kg has specific heat capacity 3502.9 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 297.58 to 404.97 K.

Relevant law: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Calculated result: The required energy is 1077.3 kJ.

Interpretation: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Conditions of validity: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Problem: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 164.96 W/(m K), thickness 0.542 m, area 1.001 m^2, and temperature difference 9.4 K.

Solution method: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Answer: The conduction rate is 2863.7 W.

Physical check: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Idealizations: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 11.144 cm^2 and 12.212 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 0.583 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 0.53201 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0006497 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 957.65 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7328.7 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 7.3749 km/s and the orbital period is 104.06 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 86.825 kg follows a circle of radius 17.537 m at constant speed 54.856 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 171.59 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 14898 N, and rotation frequency is 0.49784 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 9.882 kg and 8.254 kg and initial signed speeds -5.571 and 10.63 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is 1.8023 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 590.23 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Worked example: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Physical setup: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 3.4492e-10 W/m^2.

Relevant law: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Calculated result: The ideal intensity level is 25.377 dB.

Interpretation: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Conditions of validity: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 967.58 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.423 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 892.09 K and cold reservoir at 318.89 K, absorbing 1090.2 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 64.254 percent, corresponding to at most 700.47 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Problem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 2.638 m, tension 749.52 N, and linear mass density 0.025 kg/m.

Solution method: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Answer: The speed of transverse waves is 173.15 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 32.818 Hz.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 8960.9 Hz and has spatial wavelength 4.433 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 0.0001116 s and the propagation speed is 39724 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Physical setup: A simple pendulum has length 6.179 m and an initial angular displacement of 3.924 degrees.

Relevant law: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Calculated result: The estimated oscillation period is 4.9875 s and its frequency is 0.2005 Hz.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Conditions of validity: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

Physical check: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Idealizations: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Worked example: Thermal conduction measurement

Physical setup: A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

Relevant law: For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 4.7424 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.7658 W/K.

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 11.566 W.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 24.471 kg changes signed velocity from 0.548 to 10.017 m/s during 0.285 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is 231.72 N s and the average net force is 813.04 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

3.936 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 756.52 K to 945.68 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

The internal energy change is 9285.6 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.

Relevant law: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Interpretation: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 78.123 m/s and elevation angle 25.617 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 6.8885 s, the horizontal range is 485.26 m, and maximum height above launch is 58.168 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 171.3 kg follows a circle of radius 24.06 m at constant speed 2.891 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 0.34738 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 59.506 N, and rotation frequency is 0.019124 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 14.287 cm^2 and 3.841 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 4.624 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 17.199 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0066063 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 11.571 kg and radius 1.357 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 6.444 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 10.654 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 221.2 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 16.892 kg and 23.022 kg and initial signed speeds -1.84 and -7.638 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is -5.1842 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 163.77 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Worked example: Pressure at depth

Interpretation: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Conditions of validity: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 10.305 kg is released from rest at a height of 84.308 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 40.664 m/s and the kinetic energy is 8520 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 765.69 K and cold reservoir at 231.16 K, absorbing 2891.2 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 69.811 percent, corresponding to at most 2018.4 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Worked example: Escape speed from a central mass

Physical setup: Consider a test object at altitude 547.75 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Calculated result: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.734 km/s.

Interpretation: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Conditions of validity: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 18245 Hz and has spatial wavelength 2.248 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 5.4809e-05 s and the propagation speed is 41015 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 5.914 m/s, emitting a tone of 402.49 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 409.55 Hz, a frequency increase of 7.0615 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Worked example: Buoyant force on an immersed object

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1414.8 K and cold reservoir at 380.13 K, absorbing 6694.5 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 73.131 percent, corresponding to at most 4895.8 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Worked example: Periodic wave propagation

Relevant law: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Calculated result: The period is 0.0019384 s and the propagation speed is 2000.6 m/s.

Interpretation: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Conditions of validity: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Quantitative physics problem: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Problem: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 127.05 W/(m K), thickness 0.294 m, area 2.912 m^2, and temperature difference 64.157 K.

Solution method: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Answer: The conduction rate is 80734 W.

Physical check: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Idealizations: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 36.478 m/s, emitting a tone of 1340 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 1499.5 Hz, a frequency increase of 159.47 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.0325 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.1099 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Problem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 10.332 cm^2 and 9.644 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 3.737 m/s.

Solution method: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Answer: The speed in the second section is 4.0036 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0038611 m^3/s.

Physical check: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 4.499 kg and 19.238 kg and initial signed speeds -7.451 and 17.103 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 12.449 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 1099.2 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 8.563 kg is released from rest at a height of 98.921 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 44.047 m/s and the kinetic energy is 8306.8 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 24.58 kg and radius 1.012 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 36.7 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 12.587 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 8476.5 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

Physical check: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Idealizations: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1113.9 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7484.9 km.

The circular speed is 7.2976 km/s and the orbital period is 107.41 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.039 m^3 and material density 1030 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1339.3 kg/m^3.

## Impulse and momentum change

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 55.643 kg changes signed velocity from -6.883 to 1.289 m/s during 0.447 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 454.71 N s and the average net force is 1017.3 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 10.981 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 5.847 m/s^2 for 15.888 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 103.88 m/s, and the signed displacement is 912.44 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 26.466 m/s and elevation angle 32.908 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 2.9325 s, the horizontal range is 65.157 m, and maximum height above launch is 10.541 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 3.011 m and an initial angular displacement of 1.854 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 3.4816 s and its frequency is 0.28723 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 14.946 kg block starts at 15.78 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.092. The surface extends for 7.452 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 138 m. After the available distance its speed is 15.348 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 0.90221 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 9.753 kg and radius 0.724 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 25.482 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 2.5561 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 829.89 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 19.543 kg and 12.292 kg and initial signed speeds 10.585 and 14.102 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is 11.943 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 46.668 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Problem: A rod with initial length 23.422 m has expansion coefficient 2.2141e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 23.003 K.

Solution method: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is 11.929 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.003 m^3 and material density 1344.1 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 885.93 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 26.064 N and the weight is 39.542 N; their signed upward difference is -13.478 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Quantitative physics problem: Spring oscillator

## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 12.893 kg is released from rest at a height of 86.335 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 41.15 m/s and the kinetic energy is 10916 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 1754.3 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 9.9053 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 44.491 m/s and the kinetic energy is 4445.8 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Worked example: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Physical setup: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 1.7544e-08 W/m^2.

Relevant law: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Calculated result: The ideal intensity level is 42.441 dB.

Interpretation: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Conditions of validity: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 35.556 m/s, emitting a tone of 1008.5 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 1125.1 Hz, a frequency increase of 116.63 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

6.843 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 370.61 K to 425.6 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

The internal energy change is 4693.6 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Worked example: Thermal conduction measurement

Physical setup: A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

Relevant law: For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 3.9912 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 3.9484 W/K.

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 26.537 W.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Quantitative physics problem: Pressure at depth

Problem: A stationary liquid has density 1156.2 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 85.829 m below a surface at pressure 107.12 kPa.

Solution method: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Answer: The pressure increase is 973.2 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1080.3 kPa.

Physical check: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Idealizations: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 603.79 K and cold reservoir at 387.3 K, absorbing 7664.5 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 35.854 percent, corresponding to at most 2748.1 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

Problem: A vessel contains 9.969 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 789.86 K in volume 135.25 liters.

Solution method: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Answer: The equilibrium pressure is 484.05 kPa.

Physical check: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 131.55 N acts at a distance of 2.627 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 71.49 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 327.7 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Quantitative physics problem: Hooke-law force calibration

Problem: A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

Solution method: For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 152.9 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 151.57 N/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.12092 N.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 70.497 kg changes signed velocity from -11.533 to -15.937 m/s during 0.216 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -310.47 N s and the average net force is -1437.4 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 147.67 kg block starts at 21.651 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.303. The surface extends for 8.896 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 78.879 m. After the available distance its speed is 20.394 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 2.9714 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1510.7 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7881.7 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 7.1115 km/s and the orbital period is 116.06 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.033 m^3 and material density 241.86 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1106.4 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 358.06 N and the weight is 78.272 N; their signed upward difference is 279.79 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Problem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 3.234 m, tension 534.26 N, and linear mass density 0.033 kg/m.

Solution method: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Answer: The speed of transverse waves is 127.24 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 19.672 Hz.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 19.843 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -1.828 m/s^2 for 4.27 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 12.037 m/s, and the signed displacement is 68.065 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 1412.6 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.12 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 5.721 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 450.43 K, changing volume from 3.376 to 1.4247 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is -18485 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Linear thermal expansion

A rod with initial length 2.421 m has expansion coefficient 2.0235e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by -18.29 K.

For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

The calculated signed change in length is -0.89601 mm.

For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 13.108 kg has specific heat capacity 3291.5 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 291.98 to 441.9 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 6468.1 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.

## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 5.456 kg and 0.47 kg and initial signed speeds -5.586 and -6.001 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is -5.6189 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 0.037263 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 15.839 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 172.75 N/m and displaced by 0.259 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 3.3025 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.52561 Hz, and turning-point energy is 5.7941 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 33.903 kg follows a circle of radius 18.988 m at constant speed 51.61 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 140.28 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 4755.8 N, and rotation frequency is 0.43259 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 37.351 m/s and elevation angle 24.818 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 3.1973 s, the horizontal range is 108.39 m, and maximum height above launch is 12.532 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 1.637 cm^2 and 3.851 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 0.336 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 0.14283 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 5.5003e-05 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Worked example: Periodic wave propagation

Physical setup: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 11928 Hz and has spatial wavelength 3.791 m.

Relevant law: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Calculated result: The period is 8.384e-05 s and the propagation speed is 45217 m/s.

Interpretation: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Conditions of validity: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 5.646 m and an initial angular displacement of 1.086 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 4.7675 s and its frequency is 0.20975 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 14.284 kg is released from rest at a height of 87.609 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 41.452 m/s and the kinetic energy is 12272 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 137.32 kg block starts at 31.768 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.414. The surface extends for 3.354 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 124.29 m. After the available distance its speed is 31.336 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 4.06 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A force of magnitude 54.929 N acts at a distance of 3.927 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 134.46 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 153.95 N m.

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Spring oscillator

A mass of 15.091 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 49.946 N/m and displaced by 0.224 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 1.8192 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.28954 Hz, and turning-point energy is 1.253 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1406.4 K and cold reservoir at 226.01 K, absorbing 4987.2 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 83.93 percent, corresponding to at most 4185.8 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Hooke-law force calibration

Problem: A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

Solution method: For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 397.75 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 394.78 N/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 2.4563 N.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.0047 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.03614 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Physical setup: 2.027 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 247.43 K to 888.29 K.

Relevant law: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Calculated result: The internal energy change is 16201 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Interpretation: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Conditions of validity: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 0.888 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 343.7 K, changing volume from 36.362 to 15.417 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is -2177.3 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Worked example: Escape speed from a central mass

Physical setup: Consider a test object at altitude 111.77 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Relevant law: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Calculated result: The minimum escape speed at that position is 11.089 km/s.

Interpretation: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Conditions of validity: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Problem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 0.429 m, tension 386.23 N, and linear mass density 0.055 kg/m.

Solution method: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Answer: The speed of transverse waves is 83.799 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 97.668 Hz.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Thermal conduction measurement

## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 13.44 cm^2 and 2.597 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 3.171 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 16.411 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0042618 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Linear thermal expansion

## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 13583 Hz and has spatial wavelength 3.257 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 7.3621e-05 s and the propagation speed is 44240 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

Problem: A vessel contains 0.562 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 966.83 K in volume 183.72 liters.

Physical check: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Steady heat conduction through a slab

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 4.846 kg and 2.668 kg and initial signed speeds -6.962 and 2.915 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is -3.455 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 83.93 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 44.867 m/s, emitting a tone of 1400.2 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 1610.9 Hz, a frequency increase of 210.72 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 201.64 kg follows a circle of radius 16.859 m at constant speed 50.013 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 148.37 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 29917 N, and rotation frequency is 0.47214 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Worked example: Pressure at depth

Physical setup: A stationary liquid has density 1034.7 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 64.595 m below a surface at pressure 107.1 kPa.

Relevant law: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Calculated result: The pressure increase is 655.41 kPa and the absolute pressure is 762.51 kPa.

Interpretation: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Conditions of validity: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 495.63 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 6866.6 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 7.619 km/s and the orbital period is 94.379 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Worked example: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Physical setup: A fully submerged body has volume 0.112 m^3 and material density 252.14 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 836.2 kg/m^3.

Relevant law: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Calculated result: The upward buoyancy is 918.44 N and the weight is 276.93 N; their signed upward difference is 641.5 N.

Interpretation: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 52.542 kg changes signed velocity from 2.455 to -4.881 m/s during 1.19 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -385.45 N s and the average net force is -323.91 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 67.379 m/s and elevation angle 43.445 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 9.4494 s, the horizontal range is 462.26 m, and maximum height above launch is 109.46 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 12.799 kg is released from rest at a height of 1.255 m.
