Answer: At the lower level the speed is 4.9613 m/s and the kinetic energy is 157.52 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.113 m^3 and material density 1314.3 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1266.5 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 1403.4 N and the weight is 1456.5 N; their signed upward difference is -53.047 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Calculated result: The required energy is 2707.4 kJ.

Interpretation: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Conditions of validity: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 15.524 kg and radius 0.475 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 114.12 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 1.7513 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 11405 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 67.13 m. After the available distance its speed is 14.882 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 2.383 m/s^2 while sliding.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 18.839 m/s, emitting a tone of 614.23 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 649.92 Hz, a frequency increase of 35.697 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Uniform circular motion

The centripetal acceleration is 0.22006 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 44.459 N, and rotation frequency is 0.020175 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Escape speed from a central mass

## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 3.163e-07 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 55.001 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 9.723 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -2.739 m/s^2 for 15.743 s.

Answer: The final signed velocity is -33.397 m/s, and the signed displacement is -186.35 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Circular Earth orbit

Relevant law: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Calculated result: The required energy is 3479.7 kJ.

Interpretation: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Conditions of validity: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Problem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 3.496 cm^2 and 4.439 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.764 m/s.

Solution method: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Answer: The speed in the second section is 2.1768 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.00096629 m^3/s.

Physical check: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Idealizations: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 21.497 kg and 1.216 kg and initial signed speeds 6.472 and 9.07 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 6.6111 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 3.8841 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 38.297 kg changes signed velocity from 2.539 to -12.649 m/s during 0.042 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is -581.65 N s and the average net force is -13849 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 207.04 kg follows a circle of radius 6.715 m at constant speed 27.948 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 116.32 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 24083 N, and rotation frequency is 0.66241 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 34.257 m/s and elevation angle 71.672 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 6.6321 s, the horizontal range is 71.443 m, and maximum height above launch is 53.917 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Problem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 0.727 m, tension 743.19 N, and linear mass density 0.019 kg/m.

Solution method: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Answer: The speed of transverse waves is 197.78 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 136.02 Hz.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.

## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 319.16 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 6690.2 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 7.7188 km/s and the orbital period is 90.764 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Problem: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 4.0249e-10 W/m^2.

Solution method: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Answer: The ideal intensity level is 26.048 dB.

Physical check: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Idealizations: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Spring oscillator

A mass of 14.379 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 504.46 N/m and displaced by 0.389 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 5.9231 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.9427 Hz, and turning-point energy is 38.168 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 25.137 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -0.8 m/s^2 for 11.322 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 16.079 m/s, and the signed displacement is 233.33 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Problem: A rod with initial length 27.152 m has expansion coefficient 8.01e-06 K^-1. Its temperature changes by -18.408 K.

Solution method: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is -4.0035 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Ideal gas equation of state

A vessel contains 1.44 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 521.89 K in volume 65.41 liters.

The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

The equilibrium pressure is 95.529 kPa.

At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Hooke-law force calibration

Problem: A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

Solution method: For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 707.6 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 721.29 N/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 5.4793 N.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 27.202 kg and radius 1.315 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 112.54 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 23.519 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 1.4894e+05 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 354.63 N acts at a distance of 1.266 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 112.78 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 413.94 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 128.06 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 11.075 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 94.896 kg block starts at 22.898 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.366. The surface extends for 15.892 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 73.04 m. After the available distance its speed is 20.254 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 3.5892 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Reversible isothermal gas work

7.241 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 665.09 K, changing volume from 39.976 to 17.19 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is -33794 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Quantitative physics problem: Pressure at depth

Problem: A stationary liquid has density 879.97 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 54.597 m below a surface at pressure 99.734 kPa.

Solution method: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Answer: The pressure increase is 471.15 kPa and the absolute pressure is 570.88 kPa.

Physical check: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Idealizations: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 8.275 kg is released from rest at a height of 19.662 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 19.638 m/s and the kinetic energy is 1595.6 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.122 m^3 and material density 1718.2 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1199.4 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 1435 N and the weight is 2055.7 N; their signed upward difference is -620.72 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 38.221 m/s, emitting a tone of 915.26 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 1030 Hz, a frequency increase of 114.78 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum

Problem: A simple pendulum has length 2.896 m and an initial angular displacement of 4.304 degrees.

Solution method: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Answer: The estimated oscillation period is 3.4144 s and its frequency is 0.29287 Hz.

Physical check: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Idealizations: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 66.072 kg changes signed velocity from 19.509 to 9.07 m/s during 1.621 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -689.73 N s and the average net force is -425.49 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 10.811 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 380.13 N/m and displaced by 0.312 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 5.9297 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.94375 Hz, and turning-point energy is 18.502 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 1116.8 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.318 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 8723.7 Hz and has spatial wavelength 0.417 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 0.00011463 s and the propagation speed is 3637.8 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum

Problem: A simple pendulum has length 5.88 m and an initial angular displacement of 1.359 degrees.

Solution method: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Answer: The estimated oscillation period is 4.8653 s and its frequency is 0.20554 Hz.

Physical check: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Idealizations: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Hooke-law force calibration

A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

The fitted slope is 201.34 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 201.72 N/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.19609 N.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 537.96 N acts at a distance of 0.673 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 95.745 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 360.23 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 599.58 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 6.545 kg is released from rest at a height of 3.766 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 8.5944 m/s and the kinetic energy is 241.72 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 18.974 m/s and elevation angle 21.407 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 1.4124 s, the horizontal range is 24.95 m, and maximum height above launch is 2.4453 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 18.173 kg and radius 1.707 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 135.32 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 26.477 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 2.4242e+05 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 864.21 K and cold reservoir at 252.99 K, absorbing 7940.8 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 70.726 percent, corresponding to at most 5616.2 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 33.097 m/s, emitting a tone of 1673.3 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 1852 Hz, a frequency increase of 178.7 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1709.4 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 8080.4 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 7.0235 km/s and the orbital period is 120.48 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 15.49 kg and 17.375 kg and initial signed speeds -9.419 and 14.456 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 3.2032 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 2334 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 29.492 kg and radius 0.441 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 168.01 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 2.8678 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 40475 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 8.014 m/s, emitting a tone of 1648.3 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 1687.8 Hz, a frequency increase of 39.434 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Worked example: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Physical setup: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 0.00030795 W/m^2.

Relevant law: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Calculated result: The ideal intensity level is 84.885 dB.

Interpretation: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Conditions of validity: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Problem: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

Solution method: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 4.0019 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.29207 s^2.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.132 m^3 and material density 1378.8 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1063 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 1376 N and the weight is 1784.9 N; their signed upward difference is -408.91 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Worked example: Linear thermal expansion

Physical setup: A rod with initial length 1.618 m has expansion coefficient 6.595e-06 K^-1. Its temperature changes by -18.331 K.

Relevant law: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Calculated result: The calculated signed change in length is -0.1956 mm.

Interpretation: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Conditions of validity: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 5.958 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 321.41 K, changing volume from 48.254 to 83.238 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is 8681.1 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 242.16 W/(m K), thickness 0.554 m, area 1.456 m^2, and temperature difference 75.426 K.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 48005 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 10.223 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 358.56 N/m and displaced by 0.261 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 5.9223 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.94256 Hz, and turning-point energy is 12.213 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 86.74 kg block starts at 14.569 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.149. The surface extends for 12.182 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 72.631 m. After the available distance its speed is 13.291 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.4612 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Worked example: Standing wave on a stretched string

Physical setup: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 0.898 m, tension 813.8 N, and linear mass density 0.025 kg/m.

Relevant law: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Calculated result: The speed of transverse waves is 180.42 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 100.46 Hz.

Interpretation: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Conditions of validity: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 19.048 m/s and elevation angle 15.01 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 1.0061 s, the horizontal range is 18.51 m, and maximum height above launch is 1.2408 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 45.398 kg changes signed velocity from 6.768 to 18.836 m/s during 1.972 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 547.86 N s and the average net force is 277.82 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Physical setup: 3.691 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 602.4 K to 978.54 K.

Relevant law: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Calculated result: The internal energy change is 17315 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Interpretation: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Conditions of validity: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

Problem: A vessel contains 11.956 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 656.44 K in volume 39.157 liters.

Solution method: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Answer: The equilibrium pressure is 1666.5 kPa.

Physical check: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 0.732 m and an initial angular displacement of 5.755 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 1.7166 s and its frequency is 0.58254 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 26.529 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 7.412 m/s^2 for 4.678 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 61.202 m/s, and the signed displacement is 205.2 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 810.34 K and cold reservoir at 319.28 K, absorbing 1816 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 60.599 percent, corresponding to at most 1100.5 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 38.131 kg changes signed velocity from 17.728 to 18.184 m/s during 1.625 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 17.388 N s and the average net force is 10.7 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

## Worked example: Escape speed from a central mass

## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A force of magnitude 333.7 N acts at a distance of 0.161 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 6.271 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 5.8685 N m.

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1034.3 K and cold reservoir at 389.33 K, absorbing 5831.9 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 62.356 percent, corresponding to at most 3636.5 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 14.871 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 3.115 m/s^2 for 12.472 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 53.721 m/s, and the signed displacement is 427.74 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 180.42 kg follows a circle of radius 5.807 m at constant speed 14.711 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 37.268 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 6723.9 N, and rotation frequency is 0.40319 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 16200 Hz and has spatial wavelength 4.566 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 6.1728e-05 s and the propagation speed is 73969 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Spring oscillator

A mass of 5.774 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 323.92 N/m and displaced by 0.074 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 7.49 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.1921 Hz, and turning-point energy is 0.8869 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.0322 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.1045 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 5.9345 s, the horizontal range is 222.57 m, and maximum height above launch is 43.171 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 13.435 kg and radius 1.079 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 20.418 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 7.8208 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 1630.2 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 1.475 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 530.08 K, changing volume from 11.593 to 13.112 liters.

Calculated result: The work by the gas is 800.26 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Quantitative physics problem: Pressure at depth

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.098 m^3 and material density 1280.7 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1386.4 kg/m^3.

## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 8.69 cm^2 and 2.547 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.074 m/s.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

Problem: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 102.56 W/(m K), thickness 0.572 m, area 0.354 m^2, and temperature difference 79.844 K.

Solution method: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Answer: The conduction rate is 5068.1 W.

Physical check: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Idealizations: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 2.579 kg is released from rest at a height of 113.5 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 47.181 m/s and the kinetic energy is 2870.5 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 21.482 kg and 1.526 kg and initial signed speeds 1.755 and 0.909 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is 1.6989 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 0.50987 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A force of magnitude 364.78 N acts at a distance of 3.284 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 92.279 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 1197 N m.

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 2.678 kg changes signed velocity from 8.791 to 6.302 m/s during 1.316 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -6.6655 N s and the average net force is -5.065 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1178.5 K and cold reservoir at 316.8 K, absorbing 6606.9 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 73.118 percent, corresponding to at most 4830.8 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 3.353 kg has specific heat capacity 883.31 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 313.04 to 473 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 473.76 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Spring oscillator

A mass of 20.045 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 589.89 N/m and displaced by 0.07 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 5.4248 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.86338 Hz, and turning-point energy is 1.4452 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Physical setup: A simple pendulum has length 6.55 m and an initial angular displacement of 7.967 degrees.

Relevant law: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Calculated result: The estimated oscillation period is 5.135 s and its frequency is 0.19474 Hz.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Conditions of validity: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 7.321 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 218.56 K, changing volume from 29.344 to 30.899 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is 687.07 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 5.374 cm^2 and 13.61 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 1.993 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 0.78695 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.001071 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 6.014 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 2.745 m/s^2 for 14.626 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 46.162 m/s, and the signed displacement is 381.57 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 45.988 m/s and elevation angle 18.006 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 2.8992 s, the horizontal range is 126.8 m, and maximum height above launch is 10.303 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Worked example: Linear thermal expansion

Physical setup: A rod with initial length 26.013 m has expansion coefficient 8.346e-06 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 172.65 K.

Relevant law: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Calculated result: The calculated signed change in length is 37.482 mm.

Interpretation: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Conditions of validity: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.

## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

1.323 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 802.11 K to 807.28 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

The internal energy change is 85.454 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 16155 Hz and has spatial wavelength 4.742 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 6.1899e-05 s and the propagation speed is 76609 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Ideal gas equation of state

A vessel contains 6.898 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 603.4 K in volume 19.044 liters.

The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

The equilibrium pressure is 1817.2 kPa.

At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Worked example: Standing wave on a stretched string

Physical setup: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 0.36 m, tension 604.71 N, and linear mass density 0.059 kg/m.

Relevant law: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Calculated result: The speed of transverse waves is 101.24 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 140.61 Hz.

Interpretation: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Conditions of validity: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Quantitative physics problem: Thermal conduction measurement

Problem: A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

Solution method: For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

Answer: The fitted slope is 2.9559 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 2.9471 W/K.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 10.037 W.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 8.427 m/s, emitting a tone of 1399.7 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 1434.9 Hz, a frequency increase of 35.254 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 2143.7 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 8514.7 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 6.842 km/s and the orbital period is 130.32 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

## Quantitative physics problem: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Answer: The ideal intensity level is 69.749 dB.

Physical check: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 78.462 kg block starts at 13.94 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.329. The surface extends for 21.416 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 30.115 m. After the available distance its speed is 7.4921 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 3.2264 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Reversible heat engine upper bound

## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 50.616 kg changes signed velocity from 7.877 to 8.947 m/s during 0.863 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is 54.159 N s and the average net force is 62.757 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 24.34 m/s, emitting a tone of 981.87 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 1056.9 Hz, a frequency increase of 74.998 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Projectile trajectory above level ground

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

## Standing wave on a stretched string

A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 4.682 m, tension 25.438 N, and linear mass density 0.001 kg/m.

Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

The speed of transverse waves is 159.49 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 17.033 Hz.

The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 12.068 kg and 19.748 kg and initial signed speeds 1.195 and 18.559 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is 11.973 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 1129.2 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 6.212 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 3.698 m/s^2 for 11.072 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 47.156 m/s, and the signed displacement is 295.45 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Worked example: Periodic wave propagation

Calculated result: The period is 7.9899e-05 s and the propagation speed is 3955 m/s.

Interpretation: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Conditions of validity: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A force of magnitude 24.878 N acts at a distance of 2.866 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 110.2 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 66.914 N m.

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 473 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 6844 km.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

The required energy is 2537.7 kJ.

The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Worked example: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Physical setup: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 37.417 kg and radius 0.923 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 48.304 rad/s.

Relevant law: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Calculated result: The moment of inertia is 15.938 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 18594 J.

Conditions of validity: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 58.722 kg block starts at 20.731 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.131. The surface extends for 10.272 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 167.27 m. After the available distance its speed is 20.084 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.2847 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 102.78 kg follows a circle of radius 12.473 m at constant speed 21.852 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 38.283 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 3934.9 N, and rotation frequency is 0.27883 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1304.6 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7675.6 km.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

## Reversible isothermal gas work

1.387 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 523.16 K, changing volume from 6.319 to 8.2273 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 1592.2 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Worked example: Hooke-law force calibration

Physical setup: A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

Relevant law: For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 555.62 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 556.09 N/m.

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.92995 N.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Answer: The nonzero return time is 7.7963 s, the horizontal range is 144.07 m, and maximum height above launch is 74.509 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 8.393 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 551.85 N/m and displaced by 0.159 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 8.1087 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.2905 Hz, and turning-point energy is 6.9757 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1352.4 K and cold reservoir at 291.72 K, absorbing 2635.7 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 78.429 percent, corresponding to at most 2067.1 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 12.262 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -1.036 m/s^2 for 11.999 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is -0.16896 m/s, and the signed displacement is 72.552 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 3.423 kg and 5.776 kg and initial signed speeds 11.763 and 18.009 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is 15.685 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 41.924 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 17.238 kg changes signed velocity from -0.675 to 9.572 m/s during 0.985 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 176.64 N s and the average net force is 179.33 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 6125.7 Hz and has spatial wavelength 4.973 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 0.00016325 s and the propagation speed is 30463 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Standing wave on a stretched string

A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 4.606 m, tension 383.95 N, and linear mass density 0.048 kg/m.

Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

The speed of transverse waves is 89.437 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 9.7088 Hz.

The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.

Idealizations: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 25.048 m/s, emitting a tone of 868.59 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 937.01 Hz, a frequency increase of 68.426 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: A body with mass 25.244 kg changes signed velocity from -9.312 to 17.936 m/s during 0.791 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is 687.85 N s and the average net force is 869.59 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 28.593 kg and radius 1.578 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 68.029 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 35.599 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 82376 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Circular Earth orbit

## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 2969.1 Hz and has spatial wavelength 2.23 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 0.0003368 s and the propagation speed is 6621.1 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Linear thermal expansion

## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 22.342 kg and 3.103 kg and initial signed speeds -8.671 and 17.242 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is -5.5109 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 914.76 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 9.763 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 543.98 N/m and displaced by 0.37 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 7.4645 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.188 Hz, and turning-point energy is 37.236 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Worked example: Escape speed from a central mass

Calculated result: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.29 km/s.

Interpretation: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Conditions of validity: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Worked example: Hooke-law force calibration

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.04943 N.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

Idealizations: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.

Solution method: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Answer: The equilibrium pressure is 69.175 kPa.

Physical check: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 33.906 m/s, emitting a tone of 937.89 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 1040.8 Hz, a frequency increase of 102.88 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Worked example: Standing wave on a stretched string

Physical setup: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 4.283 m, tension 153.82 N, and linear mass density 0.056 kg/m.

Relevant law: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Calculated result: The speed of transverse waves is 52.41 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 6.1184 Hz.

Interpretation: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Conditions of validity: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 22.184 kg and 4.855 kg and initial signed speeds 1.018 and 18.969 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is 4.2412 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 641.78 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Worked example: Linear thermal expansion

Physical setup: A rod with initial length 6.172 m has expansion coefficient 1.2502e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 120.72 K.

Relevant law: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Calculated result: The calculated signed change in length is 9.315 mm.

Interpretation: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Conditions of validity: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 53.57 kg changes signed velocity from -4.007 to -8.808 m/s during 1.498 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is -257.19 N s and the average net force is -171.69 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 11.448 kg and 18.794 kg and initial signed speeds -8.083 and -0.067 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is -3.1014 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 228.57 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 2.667 kg is released from rest at a height of 49.981 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 31.31 m/s and the kinetic energy is 1307.2 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 1.995 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 498.89 K, changing volume from 10.374 to 11.059 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is 528.9 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1203.4 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7574.4 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.2543 km/s and the orbital period is 109.34 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.
