The ideal stopping distance is 5.1799 m. After the available distance its speed is 0 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 4.1678 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 6.836 kg is released from rest at a height of 65.226 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 35.767 m/s and the kinetic energy is 4372.6 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 1.978 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 225.22 K, changing volume from 16.048 to 15.342 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is -166.67 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

A sample of mass 7.164 kg has specific heat capacity 1686 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 292.84 to 402 K.

For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

The required energy is 1318.5 kJ.

The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Worked example: Thermal conduction measurement

Physical setup: A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

Relevant law: For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 1.9227 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 1.937 W/K.

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 8.5633 W.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Quantitative physics problem: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Problem: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 326.89 W/(m K), thickness 0.027 m, area 0.522 m^2, and temperature difference 42.539 K.

Solution method: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Answer: The conduction rate is 2.6884e+05 W.

Physical check: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Idealizations: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Worked example: Uniform circular motion

Physical setup: A mass of 197.59 kg follows a circle of radius 20.995 m at constant speed 7.729 m/s.

Relevant law: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Calculated result: The centripetal acceleration is 2.8453 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 562.21 N, and rotation frequency is 0.058591 Hz.

Interpretation: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Conditions of validity: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

Problem: A vessel contains 3.877 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 537.51 K in volume 107.65 liters.

Solution method: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Answer: The equilibrium pressure is 160.95 kPa.

Physical check: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 3.443 m and an initial angular displacement of 4.623 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 3.723 s and its frequency is 0.2686 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.137 m^3 and material density 1299.4 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 909.32 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 1221.7 N and the weight is 1745.8 N; their signed upward difference is -524.12 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1866.4 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 8237.4 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 6.9562 km/s and the orbital period is 124.01 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 16.787 m/s and elevation angle 71.564 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 3.2479 s, the horizontal range is 17.242 m, and maximum height above launch is 12.931 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 2438.4 Hz and has spatial wavelength 1.661 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 0.00041011 s and the propagation speed is 4050.1 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Lever arm and rotational effect

A force of magnitude 472.53 N acts at a distance of 3.049 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 18.127 degrees to the lever.

The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

The calculated torque magnitude is 448.25 N m.

For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Worked example: Pressure at depth

Conditions of validity: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 22.222 m/s, emitting a tone of 1083 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 1158 Hz, a frequency increase of 75.024 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Worked example: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Physical setup: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 24.96 kg and radius 0.711 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 137.79 rad/s.

Relevant law: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Calculated result: The moment of inertia is 6.3089 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 59894 J.

Interpretation: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Conditions of validity: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Problem: 2.546 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 288.67 K to 264.94 K.

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Answer: The internal energy change is -753.34 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Spring oscillator

A mass of 16.565 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 474.47 N/m and displaced by 0.117 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 5.3519 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.85179 Hz, and turning-point energy is 3.2475 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 5.338 kg and 15.961 kg and initial signed speeds -5.705 and -3.326 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is -3.9222 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 11.32 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Problem: A rod with initial length 23.634 m has expansion coefficient 1.0014e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 196.16 K.

Solution method: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is 46.426 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.

## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 11.78 cm^2 and 12.88 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 1.273 m/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 684.35 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.63 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

The ideal stopping distance is 20.81 m. After the available distance its speed is 3.7003 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 0.51975 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 46.508 kg changes signed velocity from -16.552 to -8.636 m/s during 0.742 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is 368.16 N s and the average net force is 496.17 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.061 m^3 and material density 972.61 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1230.6 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 736.16 N and the weight is 581.82 N; their signed upward difference is 154.34 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 5.979 kg and 16.99 kg and initial signed speeds 19.361 and -4.435 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 1.7593 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 1252.2 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Worked example: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Physical setup: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 29.861 kg and radius 0.432 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 35.138 rad/s.

Relevant law: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Calculated result: The moment of inertia is 2.7864 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 1720.1 J.

Interpretation: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Conditions of validity: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 2.505 kg is released from rest at a height of 9.512 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 13.659 m/s and the kinetic energy is 233.67 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 18.247 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -2.217 m/s^2 for 16.328 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is -17.952 m/s, and the signed displacement is 2.4069 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 84.434 kg follows a circle of radius 3.145 m at constant speed 76.858 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 1878.3 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 1.5859e+05 N, and rotation frequency is 3.8895 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Worked example: Pressure at depth

Physical setup: A stationary liquid has density 1016.1 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 151.44 m below a surface at pressure 92.488 kPa.

Relevant law: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Calculated result: The pressure increase is 1509 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1601.5 kPa.

Interpretation: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Conditions of validity: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 1120.6 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.316 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Ideal gas equation of state

A vessel contains 10.503 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 327.66 K in volume 85.593 liters.

The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

The equilibrium pressure is 334.3 kPa.

At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Worked example: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Physical setup: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 361.62 W/(m K), thickness 0.52 m, area 0.129 m^2, and temperature difference 71.292 K.

Relevant law: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Calculated result: The conduction rate is 6395.6 W.

Interpretation: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Conditions of validity: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum

Problem: A simple pendulum has length 0.452 m and an initial angular displacement of 5.194 degrees.

Solution method: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Answer: The estimated oscillation period is 1.3489 s and its frequency is 0.74133 Hz.

Physical check: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Idealizations: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 4.701 cm^2 and 2.386 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 0.274 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 0.53985 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.00012881 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 175.9 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 800.78 K and cold reservoir at 430.38 K, absorbing 4165.3 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 46.255 percent, corresponding to at most 1926.7 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Standing wave on a stretched string

A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 2.914 m, tension 874.6 N, and linear mass density 0.057 kg/m.

Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

The speed of transverse waves is 123.87 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 21.254 Hz.

The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 50.269 m/s, emitting a tone of 697.86 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 817.7 Hz, a frequency increase of 119.84 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1658.3 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 8029.3 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.0458 km/s and the orbital period is 119.34 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Worked example: Periodic wave propagation

Physical setup: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 16923 Hz and has spatial wavelength 4.984 m.

Relevant law: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Calculated result: The period is 5.9091e-05 s and the propagation speed is 84345 m/s.

Interpretation: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Conditions of validity: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Reversible isothermal gas work

7.083 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 694.35 K, changing volume from 30.576 to 13.025 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is -34893 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Projectile trajectory above level ground

The nonzero return time is 3.587 s, the horizontal range is 192.25 m, and maximum height above launch is 15.772 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 7.4304 km/s and the orbital period is 101.75 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 52.338 kg block starts at 29.8 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.387. The surface extends for 20.922 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 117 m. After the available distance its speed is 27.004 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 3.7952 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 620.04 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.679 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Answer: The ideal intensity level is 46.049 dB.

Physical check: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Idealizations: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 2.56 m and an initial angular displacement of 5.751 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 3.2103 s and its frequency is 0.3115 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 32.753 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 5.096 m/s^2 for 16.135 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 114.98 m/s, and the signed displacement is 1191.8 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 688.66 K and cold reservoir at 304.24 K, absorbing 1405.4 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 55.822 percent, corresponding to at most 784.51 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Problem: 1.683 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 747.7 K to 663.92 K.

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Answer: The internal energy change is -1758.5 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 1125.9 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 111.43 m below a surface at pressure 90.456 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

The pressure increase is 1230.3 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1320.8 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 29.766 kg changes signed velocity from -18.281 to 2.913 m/s during 0.057 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is 630.86 N s and the average net force is 11068 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Quantitative physics problem: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Problem: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 292.88 W/(m K), thickness 0.502 m, area 1.068 m^2, and temperature difference 30.508 K.

Idealizations: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 360.64 N acts at a distance of 2.331 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 149.42 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 427.65 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 84.386 m/s and elevation angle 50.738 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 13.325 s, the horizontal range is 711.62 m, and maximum height above launch is 217.65 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 27.321 m/s, emitting a tone of 1023.9 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 18.8 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 434.36 N/m and displaced by 0.343 m.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 4.8067 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.76501 Hz, and turning-point energy is 25.551 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 2.354 kg is released from rest at a height of 45.806 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 29.973 m/s and the kinetic energy is 1057.4 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.029 m^3 and material density 1186.6 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1133 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 322.23 N and the weight is 337.46 N; their signed upward difference is -15.233 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Lever arm and rotational effect

A force of magnitude 185.03 N acts at a distance of 0.241 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 77.817 degrees to the lever.

The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

The calculated torque magnitude is 43.589 N m.

For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 7.009 cm^2 and 10.195 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 0.84 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 0.57749 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.00058876 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 10.147 kg has specific heat capacity 2022.8 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 327.2 to 440.51 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 2325.8 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.046 m^3 and material density 962.9 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1108.8 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 500.17 N and the weight is 434.37 N; their signed upward difference is 65.799 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 9.882 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 3.401 m/s^2 for 15.354 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 62.101 m/s, and the signed displacement is 552.61 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Worked example: Escape speed from a central mass

Physical setup: Consider a test object at altitude 995.87 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Relevant law: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Calculated result: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.403 km/s.

Interpretation: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Conditions of validity: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 15.781 kg is released from rest at a height of 40.575 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 28.21 m/s and the kinetic energy is 6279.3 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 51.495 m/s, emitting a tone of 1586.5 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 1866.8 Hz, a frequency increase of 280.26 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 39.457 m/s and elevation angle 34.697 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 4.5806 s, the horizontal range is 148.6 m, and maximum height above launch is 25.721 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 17370 Hz and has spatial wavelength 3.648 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 5.757e-05 s and the propagation speed is 63366 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 4.806 kg and 4.968 kg and initial signed speeds 11.204 and 6.011 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 8.5645 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 32.938 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Quantitative physics problem: Spring oscillator

Problem: A mass of 13.38 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 274.23 N/m and displaced by 0.369 m.

Solution method: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Answer: The angular frequency is 4.5272 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.72053 Hz, and turning-point energy is 18.67 J.

Physical check: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Idealizations: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 190.45 kg follows a circle of radius 19.116 m at constant speed 79.743 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 332.65 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 63354 N, and rotation frequency is 0.66392 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Worked example: Pressure at depth

Physical setup: A stationary liquid has density 829.35 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 22.22 m below a surface at pressure 105.3 kPa.

Relevant law: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Calculated result: The pressure increase is 180.72 kPa and the absolute pressure is 286.01 kPa.

Interpretation: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Conditions of validity: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

Problem: A vessel contains 11.164 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 595.05 K in volume 172.92 liters.

Solution method: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Answer: The equilibrium pressure is 319.42 kPa.

Physical check: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 7.965 m and an initial angular displacement of 1.734 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 5.6626 s and its frequency is 0.1766 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 31.455 m/s and the kinetic energy is 3903.7 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Problem: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 7.401 W/(m K), thickness 0.211 m, area 2.573 m^2, and temperature difference 10.337 K.

Solution method: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Answer: The conduction rate is 932.92 W.

Physical check: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Idealizations: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Reversible isothermal gas work

2.369 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 220.78 K, changing volume from 34.928 to 80.754 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 3644.7 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1089.9 K and cold reservoir at 248.3 K, absorbing 5463.8 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 77.217 percent, corresponding to at most 4219 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 18.366 kg and 2.756 kg and initial signed speeds 9.682 and 5.473 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is 9.1328 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 21.227 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 31.213 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 4.654 m/s^2 for 7.197 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 64.708 m/s, and the signed displacement is 345.17 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Physical setup: A simple pendulum has length 0.66 m and an initial angular displacement of 1.124 degrees.

Relevant law: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Calculated result: The estimated oscillation period is 1.63 s and its frequency is 0.61349 Hz.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Conditions of validity: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 145.68 kg block starts at 12.224 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.245. The surface extends for 7.678 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 31.096 m. After the available distance its speed is 10.608 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 2.4026 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 1091.2 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 44.555 m below a surface at pressure 109.66 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

The pressure increase is 476.77 kPa and the absolute pressure is 586.43 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 7514.8 Hz and has spatial wavelength 2.596 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 0.00013307 s and the propagation speed is 19508 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

A sample of mass 9.947 kg has specific heat capacity 1648.6 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 338.2 to 359.05 K.

For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

The required energy is 341.9 kJ.

The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 16.296 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 594.24 N/m and displaced by 0.496 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 6.0386 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.96108 Hz, and turning-point energy is 73.096 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Quantitative physics problem: Thermal conduction measurement

Problem: A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

Solution method: For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

Answer: The fitted slope is 3.4998 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 3.5413 W/K.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 16.524 W.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 373.12 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 6744.1 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.6879 km/s and the orbital period is 91.864 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Problem: 4.546 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 558.15 K to 866.65 K.

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Answer: The internal energy change is 17491 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Ideal gas equation of state

A vessel contains 2.49 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 329.2 K in volume 52.493 liters.

The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

The equilibrium pressure is 129.83 kPa.

At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Problem: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 9.6644e-08 W/m^2.

Solution method: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Answer: The ideal intensity level is 49.852 dB.

Physical check: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Idealizations: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Lever arm and rotational effect

A force of magnitude 170.02 N acts at a distance of 1.545 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 91.146 degrees to the lever.

The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

The calculated torque magnitude is 262.63 N m.

For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.019 m^3 and material density 515.61 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 951.21 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 177.24 N and the weight is 96.071 N; their signed upward difference is 81.164 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 34.278 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 11.156 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 35.683 m/s and elevation angle 28.767 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 3.5022 s, the horizontal range is 109.55 m, and maximum height above launch is 15.035 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Worked example: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Physical setup: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 40.898 kg and radius 1.872 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 96.961 rad/s.

Relevant law: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Calculated result: The moment of inertia is 71.661 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 3.3686e+05 J.

Interpretation: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Conditions of validity: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 62.311 kg changes signed velocity from -19.344 to 11.578 m/s during 1.41 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is 1926.8 N s and the average net force is 1366.5 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Standing wave on a stretched string

A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 2.028 m, tension 567.64 N, and linear mass density 0.018 kg/m.

Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Worked example: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Physical setup: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 325.58 W/(m K), thickness 0.437 m, area 3.032 m^2, and temperature difference 27.885 K.

Relevant law: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Calculated result: The conduction rate is 62990 W.

Interpretation: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Conditions of validity: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.031 m^3 and material density 384.88 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1356.5 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 412.37 N and the weight is 117.01 N; their signed upward difference is 295.36 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 31.65 m/s and elevation angle 41.48 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 4.2754 s, the horizontal range is 101.38 m, and maximum height above launch is 22.407 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 8.076 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -0.381 m/s^2 for 3.733 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 6.6537 m/s, and the signed displacement is 27.493 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 8.626 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 319.36 K, changing volume from 42.667 to 106.11 liters.

Answer: The work by the gas is 20868 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 6007.4 Hz and has spatial wavelength 1.167 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 0.00016646 s and the propagation speed is 7010.6 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Worked example: Uniform circular motion

## Quantitative physics problem: Spring oscillator

## Quantitative physics problem: Hooke-law force calibration

Problem: A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

Solution method: For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 412.1 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 411.57 N/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.33289 N.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1167.9 K and cold reservoir at 258.52 K, absorbing 2005.6 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 77.866 percent, corresponding to at most 1561.7 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 53.521 m/s, emitting a tone of 1790 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 2120.9 Hz, a frequency increase of 330.95 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 3.062 kg and 14.569 kg and initial signed speeds -3.539 and -6.872 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is -6.2932 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 14.054 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 18.89 kg is released from rest at a height of 110.3 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 46.511 m/s and the kinetic energy is 20432 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 31.912 kg block starts at 3.864 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.278. The surface extends for 16.268 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 2.7383 m. After the available distance its speed is 0 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 2.7262 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1541.9 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7912.9 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 7.0974 km/s and the orbital period is 116.75 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 231.58 kg follows a circle of radius 7.775 m at constant speed 69.232 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 616.47 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 1.4276e+05 N, and rotation frequency is 1.4172 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Worked example: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Physical setup: A sample of mass 8.36 kg has specific heat capacity 1519.4 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 296.68 to 371.53 K.

Relevant law: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Calculated result: The required energy is 950.78 kJ.

Interpretation: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Conditions of validity: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 39.879 kg and radius 1.445 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 136.71 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 41.634 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 3.8908e+05 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Linear thermal expansion

A rod with initial length 7.873 m has expansion coefficient 2.0895e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 28.846 K.

For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

The calculated signed change in length is 4.7453 mm.

For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Worked example: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Physical setup: A fully submerged body has volume 0.063 m^3 and material density 1282.4 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1059.5 kg/m^3.

Relevant law: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Calculated result: The upward buoyancy is 654.55 N and the weight is 792.31 N; their signed upward difference is -137.76 N.

Interpretation: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Conditions of validity: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Problem: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

Solution method: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 4.0281 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.147 s^2.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Ideal gas equation of state

A vessel contains 4.967 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 480.45 K in volume 80.461 liters.

The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

The equilibrium pressure is 246.6 kPa.

At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Worked example: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Physical setup: 4.861 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 598.97 K to 829.87 K.

Relevant law: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Calculated result: The internal energy change is 13998 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Interpretation: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Conditions of validity: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 1608.2 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 9.9955 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Spring oscillator

A mass of 6.935 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 515.47 N/m and displaced by 0.075 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 8.6214 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.3721 Hz, and turning-point energy is 1.4497 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 819.22 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 176.94 m below a surface at pressure 103.17 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

The pressure increase is 1421.5 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1524.7 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 8.621 N acts at a distance of 0.38 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 20.4 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 1.1419 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 6262.3 Hz and has spatial wavelength 1.241 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 0.00015968 s and the propagation speed is 7771.6 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 32.889 kg changes signed velocity from -12.767 to 19.937 m/s during 1.732 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 1075.6 N s and the average net force is 621.02 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Physical setup: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 288.54 W/(m K), thickness 0.083 m, area 1.619 m^2, and temperature difference 73.937 K.

Relevant law: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Calculated result: The conduction rate is 4.1614e+05 W.

Interpretation: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Conditions of validity: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 884 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7255 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.4123 km/s and the orbital period is 102.5 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 0.427 m and an initial angular displacement of 3.869 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 1.3111 s and its frequency is 0.76272 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Worked example: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Physical setup: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 1.1085e-10 W/m^2.

Relevant law: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Calculated result: The ideal intensity level is 20.447 dB.

Interpretation: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Conditions of validity: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 25.727 m/s and elevation angle 70.659 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 4.9507 s, the horizontal range is 42.183 m, and maximum height above launch is 30.045 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Problem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 5.605 cm^2 and 12.616 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.756 m/s.

Solution method: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Answer: The speed in the second section is 1.2244 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0015447 m^3/s.

Physical check: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Idealizations: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 10.736 kg is released from rest at a height of 78.724 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 39.294 m/s and the kinetic energy is 8288.4 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 28.731 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 6.822 m/s^2 for 2.065 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 42.818 m/s, and the signed displacement is 73.875 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Standing wave on a stretched string

A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 3.145 m, tension 384.08 N, and linear mass density 0.006 kg/m.

Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

The speed of transverse waves is 253.01 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 40.224 Hz.

The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.

## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 20.14 kg and 18.028 kg and initial signed speeds -9.148 and 14.421 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 1.9844 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 2642.2 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 8.69 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 312.68 K, changing volume from 8.802 to 17.032 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is 14913 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.
