## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.077 m^3 and material density 1188.9 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 792.94 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 598.76 N and the weight is 897.74 N; their signed upward difference is -298.99 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

A sample of mass 7.605 kg has specific heat capacity 1050.4 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 273.09 to 362.97 K.

For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

The required energy is 717.93 kJ.

The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 19.832 kg is released from rest at a height of 3.162 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 7.8751 m/s and the kinetic energy is 614.96 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 124.74 kg follows a circle of radius 14.384 m at constant speed 79.821 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 442.95 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 55252 N, and rotation frequency is 0.8832 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 16.219 kg block starts at 20.299 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.182. The surface extends for 14.641 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 115.43 m. After the available distance its speed is 18.968 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.7848 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 10.881 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 2.081 m/s^2 for 13.133 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 38.211 m/s, and the signed displacement is 322.36 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Problem: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

Solution method: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 4.0309 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.083808 s^2.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 65.378 kg changes signed velocity from -2.407 to -15.203 m/s during 1.73 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -836.58 N s and the average net force is -483.57 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 21.845 kg and 19.896 kg and initial signed speeds -4.424 and 2.056 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is -1.3353 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 218.61 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 19606 Hz and has spatial wavelength 2.581 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 5.1006e-05 s and the propagation speed is 50602 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 5.356 cm^2 and 12.634 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 4.904 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 2.079 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0026266 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 54.872 m/s and elevation angle 61.761 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 9.8589 s, the horizontal range is 255.96 m, and maximum height above launch is 119.15 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 2.075 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 217.7 K, changing volume from 20.374 to 36.877 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is 2228.4 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 38.235 m/s, emitting a tone of 1131.7 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 1273.7 Hz, a frequency increase of 141.98 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 664.58 K and cold reservoir at 388.68 K, absorbing 3086.1 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 41.514 percent, corresponding to at most 1281.2 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 7.636 m and an initial angular displacement of 3.258 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 5.5444 s and its frequency is 0.18036 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Worked example: Ideal gas equation of state

Physical setup: A vessel contains 1.792 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 247.78 K in volume 38.312 liters.

Relevant law: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Calculated result: The equilibrium pressure is 96.363 kPa.

Interpretation: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Conditions of validity: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 5.765 cm^2 and 7.138 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 3.099 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 2.5029 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0017866 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Linear thermal expansion

A rod with initial length 14.712 m has expansion coefficient 2.5715e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 78.339 K.

For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

The calculated signed change in length is 29.637 mm.

For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Worked example: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Physical setup: A fully submerged body has volume 0.062 m^3 and material density 1162.3 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 857.72 kg/m^3.

## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 22.617 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 5.468 m/s^2 for 5.83 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 54.495 m/s, and the signed displacement is 224.78 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Quantitative physics problem: Pressure at depth

## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 3.08 m/s, emitting a tone of 709.78 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 716.21 Hz, a frequency increase of 6.4313 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 25.456 kg block starts at 27.424 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.386. The surface extends for 11.077 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 99.34 m. After the available distance its speed is 25.85 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 3.7854 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

7.486 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 434.4 K to 829.67 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 5.896 kg is released from rest at a height of 63.489 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 6.587 kg and radius 0.685 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 41.401 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 1.5454 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 1324.4 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.0155 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.092777 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 845.61 K and cold reservoir at 344.88 K, absorbing 8040.4 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 59.216 percent, corresponding to at most 4761.2 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Reversible isothermal gas work

0.739 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 680.22 K, changing volume from 34.148 to 67.067 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 2821.1 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

A fully submerged body has volume 0.035 m^3 and material density 808.18 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1062.1 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 364.55 N and the weight is 277.39 N; their signed upward difference is 87.153 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Physical setup: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 49.282 kg and radius 0.522 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 16.511 rad/s.

Relevant law: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Calculated result: The moment of inertia is 6.7143 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 915.2 J.

Interpretation: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Conditions of validity: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 28.067 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 5.881 m/s^2 for 11.261 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 94.293 m/s, and the signed displacement is 688.95 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1264.5 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7635.5 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.2252 km/s and the orbital period is 110.67 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 56.464 kg changes signed velocity from -18.755 to 18.579 m/s during 1.15 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is 2108 N s and the average net force is 1833.1 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Problem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 2.581 m, tension 762.08 N, and linear mass density 0.052 kg/m.

Solution method: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Answer: The speed of transverse waves is 121.06 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 23.452 Hz.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 3.197 m and an initial angular displacement of 3.793 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 3.5875 s and its frequency is 0.27875 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 75.83 kg block starts at 27.1 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.296. The surface extends for 19.082 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 126.5 m. After the available distance its speed is 24.973 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 2.9028 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.0735 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.17013 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Ideal gas equation of state

Physical setup: A vessel contains 7.19 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 605.23 K in volume 164.13 liters.

Relevant law: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Calculated result: The equilibrium pressure is 220.44 kPa.

Interpretation: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Conditions of validity: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 8.789 kg and 8.566 kg and initial signed speeds -1.973 and 10.054 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is 3.9632 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 313.75 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 6.604 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 561.67 K, changing volume from 48.314 to 52.082 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is 2316.4 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A force of magnitude 503.99 N acts at a distance of 3.455 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 145.52 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 985.69 N m.

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 45.02 m/s, emitting a tone of 1328.1 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 1528.8 Hz, a frequency increase of 200.66 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

Problem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 10.168 cm^2 and 14.851 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.62 m/s.

Solution method: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Physical check: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Idealizations: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 27.646 m/s and elevation angle 72.595 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 5.3801 s, the horizontal range is 44.491 m, and maximum height above launch is 35.482 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 15.258 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 778.59 N/m and displaced by 0.43 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 7.1434 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.1369 Hz, and turning-point energy is 71.981 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 978.69 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 154.43 m below a surface at pressure 96.153 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

The pressure increase is 1482.2 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1578.4 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Worked example: Linear thermal expansion

Physical setup: A rod with initial length 12.074 m has expansion coefficient 6.728e-06 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 151.46 K.

Relevant law: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Calculated result: The calculated signed change in length is 12.303 mm.

Interpretation: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Conditions of validity: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 230.5 kg follows a circle of radius 22.738 m at constant speed 32.355 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 46.039 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 10612 N, and rotation frequency is 0.22647 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 48.009 W/(m K), thickness 0.593 m, area 1.222 m^2, and temperature difference 18.04 K.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 1784.7 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 15.656 kg is released from rest at a height of 14.38 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 16.794 m/s and the kinetic energy is 2207.8 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

Problem: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 6.5938e-10 W/m^2.

Solution method: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Answer: The ideal intensity level is 28.191 dB.

Physical check: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Idealizations: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 148.48 kg follows a circle of radius 10.988 m at constant speed 78.527 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 561.2 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 83326 N, and rotation frequency is 1.1374 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 742.41 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7113.4 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 7.4857 km/s and the orbital period is 99.512 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 52.539 m/s and elevation angle 54.854 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 8.7615 s, the horizontal range is 264.99 m, and maximum height above launch is 94.1 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 11.924 kg changes signed velocity from -16.653 to 4.977 m/s during 1.816 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 257.92 N s and the average net force is 142.02 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Escape speed from a central mass

Physical setup: Consider a test object at altitude 1451.8 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Relevant law: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Calculated result: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.095 km/s.

Interpretation: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Conditions of validity: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.023 m^3 and material density 225.37 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 951.61 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 214.64 N and the weight is 50.833 N; their signed upward difference is 163.81 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 9.219 kg and 0.88 kg and initial signed speeds -7.153 and 5.478 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is -6.0524 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 64.082 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 16.967 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 118.66 N/m and displaced by 0.015 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 2.6445 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.42089 Hz, and turning-point energy is 0.013349 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Pressure at depth

Problem: A stationary liquid has density 1288.7 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 118.93 m below a surface at pressure 104.64 kPa.

Solution method: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Answer: The pressure increase is 1503.1 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1607.7 kPa.

Physical check: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Idealizations: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

8.585 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 244.99 K to 670.29 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

The internal energy change is 45537 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Worked example: Ideal gas equation of state

Physical setup: A vessel contains 1.38 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 392.68 K in volume 196.16 liters.

Relevant law: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Calculated result: The equilibrium pressure is 22.969 kPa.

Interpretation: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Conditions of validity: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 91.57 kg block starts at 19.939 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.349. The surface extends for 7.559 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 58.081 m. After the available distance its speed is 18.596 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 3.4225 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 527.06 K and cold reservoir at 241.28 K, absorbing 3795.4 J per cycle.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 54.222 percent, corresponding to at most 2057.9 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum

Problem: A simple pendulum has length 3.751 m and an initial angular displacement of 5.972 degrees.

Solution method: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Answer: The estimated oscillation period is 3.8859 s and its frequency is 0.25734 Hz.

Physical check: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Idealizations: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 17.913 m/s, emitting a tone of 1126.4 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 1188.4 Hz, a frequency increase of 62.065 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 34.357 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 5.21 m/s^2 for 9.98 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 86.353 m/s, and the signed displacement is 602.34 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Worked example: Periodic wave propagation

Physical setup: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 3120.2 Hz and has spatial wavelength 3.922 m.

Relevant law: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Calculated result: The period is 0.0003205 s and the propagation speed is 12237 m/s.

Interpretation: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Conditions of validity: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Problem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 4.243 m, tension 264.77 N, and linear mass density 0.039 kg/m.

Solution method: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Answer: The speed of transverse waves is 82.395 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 9.7096 Hz.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 5.893 kg is released from rest at a height of 35.979 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 26.564 m/s and the kinetic energy is 2079.2 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Lever arm and rotational effect

## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 11.608 cm^2 and 13.639 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 4.602 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 3.9167 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.005342 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 30.547 kg and radius 1.153 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 169.62 rad/s.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

Problem: A force of magnitude 278.33 N acts at a distance of 2.139 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 65.382 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 541.23 N m.

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 4.935 cm^2 and 10.816 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 4.802 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 2.191 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0023698 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 4981 Hz and has spatial wavelength 0.997 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 0.00020076 s and the propagation speed is 4966.1 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Projectile trajectory above level ground

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 56.495 kg changes signed velocity from -1.263 to -0.779 m/s during 1.163 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is 27.344 N s and the average net force is 23.511 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 34.381 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -2.563 m/s^2 for 4.243 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 23.506 m/s, and the signed displacement is 122.81 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1138.5 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7509.5 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 7.2856 km/s and the orbital period is 107.94 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Spring oscillator

A mass of 1.18 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 721.7 N/m and displaced by 0.43 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 24.731 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 3.936 Hz, and turning-point energy is 66.721 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

1.463 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 230.06 K to 861.42 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

The internal energy change is 11520 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 7.474 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 561.26 K, changing volume from 21.524 to 23.935 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is 3702.7 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Problem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 3.351 m, tension 555.12 N, and linear mass density 0.019 kg/m.

Solution method: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Answer: The speed of transverse waves is 170.93 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 25.504 Hz.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 39.667 kg block starts at 7.215 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.236. The surface extends for 4.031 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 11.246 m. After the available distance its speed is 5.7791 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 2.3144 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 23.791 kg and radius 1.547 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 31.791 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 28.468 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 14386 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1303.7 K and cold reservoir at 449.69 K, absorbing 5857.9 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 65.507 percent, corresponding to at most 3837.4 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 23.127 kg and 20.142 kg and initial signed speeds 4.519 and 17.227 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 10.435 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 869.3 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.007 m^3 and material density 1538.3 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 785.93 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 53.952 N and the weight is 105.6 N; their signed upward difference is -51.651 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Quantitative physics problem: Hooke-law force calibration

Problem: A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

Solution method: For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 103.8 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 104.06 N/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.33775 N.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Linear thermal expansion

A rod with initial length 4.944 m has expansion coefficient 5.456e-06 K^-1. Its temperature changes by -15.437 K.

For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

The calculated signed change in length is -0.4164 mm.

For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Worked example: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Physical setup: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 1.2454e-06 W/m^2.

Relevant law: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Calculated result: The ideal intensity level is 60.953 dB.

Interpretation: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Conditions of validity: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Quantitative physics problem: Hooke-law force calibration

Problem: A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

Solution method: For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 429.91 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 436.03 N/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.42132 N.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Reversible isothermal gas work

2.816 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 393.6 K, changing volume from 36.052 to 73.474 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 6561.2 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1169.3 K and cold reservoir at 224.08 K, absorbing 3081.9 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 80.836 percent, corresponding to at most 2491.3 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Pressure at depth

Problem: A stationary liquid has density 1037.4 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 25.043 m below a surface at pressure 99.936 kPa.

Solution method: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Answer: The pressure increase is 254.77 kPa and the absolute pressure is 354.7 kPa.

Physical check: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Idealizations: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 30.705 W/(m K), thickness 0.225 m, area 2.623 m^2, and temperature difference 70.879 K.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 25371 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Worked example: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Physical setup: A fully submerged body has volume 0.081 m^3 and material density 1672 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1063.6 kg/m^3.

Relevant law: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Calculated result: The upward buoyancy is 844.84 N and the weight is 1328.2 N; their signed upward difference is -483.31 N.

Interpretation: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Conditions of validity: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Problem: 3.241 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 630 K to 669.53 K.

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Answer: The internal energy change is 1597.8 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.

## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 17.929 kg is released from rest at a height of 78.396 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 39.212 m/s and the kinetic energy is 13784 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1443.5 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7814.5 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 7.142 km/s and the orbital period is 114.58 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 1301.9 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.193 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Answer: The final signed velocity is 25.774 m/s, and the signed displacement is 99.339 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 9138.9 Hz and has spatial wavelength 3.143 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 0.00010942 s and the propagation speed is 28723 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 49.352 kg changes signed velocity from -17.292 to 9.861 m/s during 0.113 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is 1340.1 N s and the average net force is 11859 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 38.178 kg and radius 0.866 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 161.22 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 14.316 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 1.8604e+05 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 7.542 cm^2 and 4.686 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 4.056 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 6.528 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.003059 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 100.65 kg block starts at 29.597 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.628. The surface extends for 29.169 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 71.119 m. After the available distance its speed is 22.731 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 6.1586 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 3.212 kg is released from rest at a height of 32.17 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 25.119 m/s and the kinetic energy is 1013.3 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 48.664 m/s and elevation angle 63.555 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 8.8862 s, the horizontal range is 192.58 m, and maximum height above launch is 96.797 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Problem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 12.277 cm^2 and 12.462 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 0.579 m/s.

Solution method: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Answer: The speed in the second section is 0.5704 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.00071084 m^3/s.

Physical check: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Idealizations: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.132 m^3 and material density 1204.4 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1295 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 1676.3 N and the weight is 1559.1 N; their signed upward difference is 117.17 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 4.092 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 263.18 K, changing volume from 17.861 to 26.327 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is 3474 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 660.54 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.648 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

4.031 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 862.63 K to 251.34 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

The internal energy change is -30731 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Worked example: Linear thermal expansion

Physical setup: A rod with initial length 17.009 m has expansion coefficient 2.5624e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 123.55 K.

Relevant law: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Calculated result: The calculated signed change in length is 53.847 mm.

Interpretation: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Conditions of validity: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Answer: The common final velocity is -6.1166 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 66.975 J.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 9.628 m/s, emitting a tone of 780.78 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 803.33 Hz, a frequency increase of 22.549 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 18.828 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 4.248 m/s^2 for 5.056 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 40.306 m/s, and the signed displacement is 149.49 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Problem: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

Solution method: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 4.0147 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.36994 s^2.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 52.902 kg changes signed velocity from -11.198 to 19.72 m/s during 0.435 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 1635.6 N s and the average net force is 3760.1 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 133.45 kg block starts at 11.165 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.248. The surface extends for 28.138 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum

Physical check: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Idealizations: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 641.05 K and cold reservoir at 231.59 K, absorbing 5411.5 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 63.874 percent, corresponding to at most 3456.5 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

The speed of transverse waves is 159.25 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 30.731 Hz.

The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 15.798 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 0.608 m/s^2 for 14.924 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 24.872 m/s, and the signed displacement is 303.48 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.149 m^3 and material density 1699.6 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1048 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 1531.4 N and the weight is 2483.5 N; their signed upward difference is -952.1 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 0.918 kg and 22.607 kg and initial signed speeds 8.397 and 9.597 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 9.5502 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 0.63517 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 7641.4 Hz and has spatial wavelength 4.79 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 0.00013087 s and the propagation speed is 36602 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Worked example: Escape speed from a central mass

Physical setup: Consider a test object at altitude 1742.8 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Relevant law: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Calculated result: The minimum escape speed at that position is 9.9123 km/s.

Interpretation: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Conditions of validity: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 147.18 kg block starts at 11.042 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.428. The surface extends for 21.897 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 14.524 m. After the available distance its speed is 0 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 4.1972 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 728.77 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7099.8 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.4929 km/s and the orbital period is 99.226 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Problem: A rod with initial length 21.288 m has expansion coefficient 1.9498e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 104.95 K.

Solution method: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is 43.564 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.

## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 3.008 m and an initial angular displacement of 7.233 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 3.4798 s and its frequency is 0.28737 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 11.095 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 134.34 N/m and displaced by 0.424 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 3.4797 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.55382 Hz, and turning-point energy is 12.076 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 66.485 kg changes signed velocity from 10.15 to 4.972 m/s during 0.021 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -344.26 N s and the average net force is -16393 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 62.412 N acts at a distance of 3.782 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 129.07 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 183.26 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 2.319 kg has specific heat capacity 4247.9 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 312.79 to 415.5 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 1011.8 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 56.692 m/s and elevation angle 67.056 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 10.647 s, the horizontal range is 235.31 m, and maximum height above launch is 138.96 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.
