## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 0.299 kg and 5.579 kg and initial signed speeds 9.083 and 9.697 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 9.6658 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 0.053494 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 3.231 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 418.13 K, changing volume from 46.399 to 65.701 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is 3907.2 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Quantitative physics problem: Spring oscillator

Problem: A mass of 2.514 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 17.371 N/m and displaced by 0.087 m.

Solution method: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Answer: The angular frequency is 2.6286 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.41836 Hz, and turning-point energy is 0.065741 J.

Physical check: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Idealizations: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 7.797 cm^2 and 10.933 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 0.701 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 0.49993 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.00054657 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 27.559 kg changes signed velocity from 8.323 to -1.578 m/s during 1.979 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is -272.86 N s and the average net force is -137.88 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 10011 Hz and has spatial wavelength 0.496 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 9.989e-05 s and the propagation speed is 4965.4 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.035 m^3 and material density 984.38 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1046.6 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 359.21 N and the weight is 337.87 N; their signed upward difference is 21.341 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 952.69 K and cold reservoir at 310.3 K, absorbing 8065.4 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 67.429 percent, corresponding to at most 5438.5 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 10.965 kg and radius 0.202 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 103.53 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 0.22371 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 1198.9 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 5.0855e-05 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 77.063 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.089 m^3 and material density 304.15 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 730.37 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 637.46 N and the weight is 265.46 N; their signed upward difference is 372 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Standing wave on a stretched string

A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 4.018 m, tension 340.96 N, and linear mass density 0.051 kg/m.

Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

The speed of transverse waves is 81.765 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 10.175 Hz.

The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 2.979 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 245.9 K, changing volume from 16.764 to 43.603 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is 5822.1 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Problem: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 6.0448e-10 W/m^2.

Solution method: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Answer: The ideal intensity level is 27.814 dB.

Physical check: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Idealizations: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 65.197 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 11.129 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 5.483 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 4.13 m/s^2 for 14.886 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 66.962 m/s, and the signed displacement is 539.21 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 34.048 kg block starts at 23.592 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.631. The surface extends for 6.226 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 44.973 m. After the available distance its speed is 21.898 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 6.188 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Worked example: Thermal conduction measurement

Physical setup: A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

Relevant law: For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 2.4131 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 2.4034 W/K.

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 3.0752 W.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 0.419 kg is released from rest at a height of 116.51 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 47.804 m/s and the kinetic energy is 478.75 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

5.085 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 312.72 K to 592.58 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

The internal energy change is 17748 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 78.933 m/s and elevation angle 45.668 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 11.515 s, the horizontal range is 635.15 m, and maximum height above launch is 162.53 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 181.41 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 6552.4 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 7.7996 km/s and the orbital period is 87.975 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Problem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 7.664 cm^2 and 1.875 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 0.762 m/s.

Solution method: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Answer: The speed in the second section is 3.1146 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.000584 m^3/s.

Physical check: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 50.417 m/s, emitting a tone of 573.38 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 672.19 Hz, a frequency increase of 98.804 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 13.732 kg and 2.333 kg and initial signed speeds 15.787 and -3.132 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is 13.04 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 356.89 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 7.584 m and an initial angular displacement of 7.526 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 5.5255 s and its frequency is 0.18098 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Worked example: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Calculated result: The conduction rate is 1.5407e+05 W.

Interpretation: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Conditions of validity: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 2.056 kg changes signed velocity from 10.29 to 19.241 m/s during 0.886 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is 18.403 N s and the average net force is 20.771 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 19204 Hz and has spatial wavelength 2.651 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 5.2072e-05 s and the propagation speed is 50910 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 11.664 kg has specific heat capacity 2589.7 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 271.61 to 433.5 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Uniform circular motion

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 46.203 kg changes signed velocity from 9.255 to -8.99 m/s during 1.454 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is -842.97 N s and the average net force is -579.76 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 8.363 cm^2 and 9.968 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 1.576 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 1.3222 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.001318 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 247.52 N acts at a distance of 3.548 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 76.849 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 855.16 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 4.107 kg has specific heat capacity 484.85 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 307.44 to 423.49 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 231.08 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 24.182 kg changes signed velocity from -14.663 to -2.664 m/s during 0.232 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 290.16 N s and the average net force is 1250.7 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Periodic wave propagation

Physical setup: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 5128.3 Hz and has spatial wavelength 2.307 m.

Relevant law: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Calculated result: The period is 0.000195 s and the propagation speed is 11831 m/s.

Interpretation: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Conditions of validity: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 8.285 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 698.92 K, changing volume from 41.267 to 62.231 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is 19777 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 23.335 kg and 21.462 kg and initial signed speeds 0.298 and 10.968 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is 5.4099 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 636.4 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 23.361 kg and radius 0.573 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 150.72 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 3.835 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 43561 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.075 m^3 and material density 439.87 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 786.68 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 578.6 N and the weight is 323.52 N; their signed upward difference is 255.08 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 3.838 kg is released from rest at a height of 39.604 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 27.871 m/s and the kinetic energy is 1490.6 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Worked example: Buoyant force on an immersed object

## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Problem: 4.428 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 390.22 K to 894.32 K.

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Answer: The internal energy change is 27839 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.

## Worked example: Thermal conduction measurement

Physical setup: A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

Relevant law: For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 1.9103 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 1.9072 W/K.

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 11.316 W.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Hooke-law force calibration

A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

The fitted slope is 637.55 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 641.06 N/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 2.9232 N.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 22.123 m/s, emitting a tone of 974.92 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 1042.1 Hz, a frequency increase of 67.216 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Worked example: Pressure at depth

Physical setup: A stationary liquid has density 890.54 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 92.756 m below a surface at pressure 97.878 kPa.

Relevant law: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Calculated result: The pressure increase is 810.06 kPa and the absolute pressure is 907.94 kPa.

Interpretation: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Conditions of validity: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 22.932 kg block starts at 27.305 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.646. The surface extends for 17.813 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 58.844 m. After the available distance its speed is 22.801 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 6.3351 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Quantitative physics problem: Spring oscillator

Problem: A mass of 16.406 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 773.13 N/m and displaced by 0.295 m.

Solution method: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Answer: The angular frequency is 6.8647 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.0926 Hz, and turning-point energy is 33.641 J.

Physical check: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Idealizations: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Ideal gas equation of state

A vessel contains 8.31 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 704.82 K in volume 142.15 liters.

The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

The equilibrium pressure is 342.59 kPa.

At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 1742 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 9.9127 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1104.4 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7475.4 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.3022 km/s and the orbital period is 107.2 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 58.453 kg follows a circle of radius 23.387 m at constant speed 46.391 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 92.022 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 5379 N, and rotation frequency is 0.3157 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Standing wave on a stretched string

A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 3.851 m, tension 610.33 N, and linear mass density 0.005 kg/m.

Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

The speed of transverse waves is 349.38 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 45.362 Hz.

The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.

## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 60.464 m/s and elevation angle 23.3 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 4.8776 s, the horizontal range is 270.87 m, and maximum height above launch is 29.163 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 2.9574e-08 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 44.709 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 3.9753 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.61717 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

Interpretation: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Conditions of validity: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

Problem: A vessel contains 2.782 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 661.16 K in volume 71.602 liters.

Solution method: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Answer: The equilibrium pressure is 213.59 kPa.

Physical check: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

A sample of mass 2.193 kg has specific heat capacity 4469 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 300.64 to 395.45 K.

For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

The required energy is 929.18 kJ.

The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 5.4766 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0013861 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 842.38 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 0.992 m below a surface at pressure 101.93 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 19.684 kg is released from rest at a height of 112.83 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 47.042 m/s and the kinetic energy is 21780 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A force of magnitude 95.018 N acts at a distance of 0.568 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 10.249 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 9.6027 N m.

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 25.865 m/s, emitting a tone of 1269.3 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 1372.8 Hz, a frequency increase of 103.52 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Worked example: Periodic wave propagation

Physical setup: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 19043 Hz and has spatial wavelength 0.244 m.

Relevant law: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Calculated result: The period is 5.2512e-05 s and the propagation speed is 4646.5 m/s.

Interpretation: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Conditions of validity: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 976.07 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7347.1 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 7.3657 km/s and the orbital period is 104.46 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Linear thermal expansion

A rod with initial length 28.715 m has expansion coefficient 9.118e-06 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 176.13 K.

For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

The calculated signed change in length is 46.116 mm.

For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Worked example: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Physical setup: A fully submerged body has volume 0.062 m^3 and material density 615.52 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1056.1 kg/m^3.

Relevant law: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Calculated result: The upward buoyancy is 642.12 N and the weight is 374.24 N; their signed upward difference is 267.88 N.

Interpretation: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Conditions of validity: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 8.941 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 307.3 K, changing volume from 27.018 to 54.738 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is 16130 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Worked example: Hooke-law force calibration

Physical setup: A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

Relevant law: For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 644.52 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 650.22 N/m.

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.43221 N.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 29.271 kg changes signed velocity from 5.342 to 6.013 m/s during 1.676 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is 19.641 N s and the average net force is 11.719 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Impulse and momentum change

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 66.656 kg block starts at 25.427 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.371. The surface extends for 6.103 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 88.852 m. After the available distance its speed is 24.538 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 3.6383 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 30.313 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 6.269 m/s^2 for 13.223 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 113.21 m/s, and the signed displacement is 948.89 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 1.034 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -2.169 m/s^2 for 4.153 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is -7.9739 m/s, and the signed displacement is -14.411 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

The required energy is 2495.5 kJ.

## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 35.447 kg changes signed velocity from -12.234 to 5.42 m/s during 1.537 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is 625.78 N s and the average net force is 407.14 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 7.207 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 575.09 K, changing volume from 30.176 to 20.248 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is -13749 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 241.08 W/(m K), thickness 0.273 m, area 0.166 m^2, and temperature difference 55.735 K.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 8170.2 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Problem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 8.008 cm^2 and 8.227 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 4.353 m/s.

Solution method: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Answer: The speed in the second section is 4.2371 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0034859 m^3/s.

Physical check: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Idealizations: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.0255 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.11684 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 10369 Hz and has spatial wavelength 0.766 m.

The period is 9.6438e-05 s and the propagation speed is 7942.9 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 22.821 kg and 2.882 kg and initial signed speeds 7.761 and 6.465 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 7.6157 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 2.1489 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 23.749 kg block starts at 7.018 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.27. The surface extends for 5.298 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 9.3006 m. After the available distance its speed is 4.6039 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 2.6478 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 22.605 m/s, emitting a tone of 510.5 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 546.52 Hz, a frequency increase of 36.018 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

Calculated result: The equilibrium pressure is 359.7 kPa.

Interpretation: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Conditions of validity: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 82.511 m/s and elevation angle 41.971 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 11.254 s, the horizontal range is 690.35 m, and maximum height above launch is 155.24 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 2.414 kg changes signed velocity from 14.969 to -8.335 m/s during 0.269 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is -56.256 N s and the average net force is -209.13 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Physical setup: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 239.82 W/(m K), thickness 0.232 m, area 0.174 m^2, and temperature difference 52.395 K.

Relevant law: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Calculated result: The conduction rate is 9423.9 W.

Interpretation: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Conditions of validity: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 8.274 kg and radius 0.328 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 3.032 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 0.44508 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 2.0458 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 5.679 m and an initial angular displacement of 4.962 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 4.7814 s and its frequency is 0.20914 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1442.4 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7813.4 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 7.1425 km/s and the orbital period is 114.56 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 60.837 kg block starts at 27.415 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.63. The surface extends for 20.817 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 60.825 m. After the available distance its speed is 22.234 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 6.1782 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Standing wave on a stretched string

A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 3.377 m, tension 83.606 N, and linear mass density 0.034 kg/m.

Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

The speed of transverse waves is 49.588 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 7.3421 Hz.

The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.

## Quantitative physics problem: Pressure at depth

Problem: A stationary liquid has density 1154 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 131.97 m below a surface at pressure 91.678 kPa.

Solution method: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Answer: The pressure increase is 1493.5 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1585.2 kPa.

Physical check: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Idealizations: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Reversible isothermal gas work

6.159 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 496.65 K, changing volume from 32.59 to 86.755 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 24901 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Worked example: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Physical setup: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 1.2123e-05 W/m^2.

Relevant law: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Calculated result: The ideal intensity level is 70.836 dB.

Interpretation: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Conditions of validity: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Quantitative physics problem: Thermal conduction measurement

Problem: A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

Solution method: For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

Answer: The fitted slope is 3.0376 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 2.9983 W/K.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 16.235 W.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 16.055 m/s, emitting a tone of 1769.7 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 1856.6 Hz, a frequency increase of 86.904 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

8.743 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 769.51 K to 479.17 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

The internal energy change is -31659 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 541.88 K and cold reservoir at 392.24 K, absorbing 729.83 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 27.614 percent, corresponding to at most 201.53 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Problem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 9.74 cm^2 and 14.666 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.291 m/s.

Solution method: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Answer: The speed in the second section is 1.5215 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0022314 m^3/s.

Physical check: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Idealizations: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Escape speed from a central mass

## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Worked example: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Physical setup: A fully submerged body has volume 0.118 m^3 and material density 1640.1 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1058.6 kg/m^3.

Relevant law: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Calculated result: The upward buoyancy is 1224.9 N and the weight is 1897.9 N; their signed upward difference is -672.92 N.

Interpretation: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Conditions of validity: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 29.108 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -2.273 m/s^2 for 10.799 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 4.5619 m/s, and the signed displacement is 181.8 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Linear thermal expansion

A rod with initial length 14.852 m has expansion coefficient 2.4129e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 60.907 K.

The calculated signed change in length is 21.827 mm.

The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.36312 s^2.

## Worked example: Uniform circular motion

## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 18.371 kg and 20.485 kg and initial signed speeds 2.455 and 8.014 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 5.3857 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 149.65 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 56.579 kg follows a circle of radius 15.229 m at constant speed 59.445 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 232.04 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 13128 N, and rotation frequency is 0.62125 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 314.8 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 6685.8 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 7.7214 km/s and the orbital period is 90.675 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 51.612 m/s and elevation angle 24.683 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 4.3956 s, the horizontal range is 206.14 m, and maximum height above launch is 23.685 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 7.488 kg is released from rest at a height of 111.77 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 46.822 m/s and the kinetic energy is 8207.8 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 1489.5 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.071 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 4.656 cm^2 and 13.807 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 0.774 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 0.26101 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.00036037 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Worked example: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Physical setup: 2.542 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 469.3 K to 443.48 K.

Relevant law: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Calculated result: The internal energy change is -818.64 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Interpretation: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Conditions of validity: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Spring oscillator

Problem: A mass of 18.499 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 261.06 N/m and displaced by 0.228 m.

Solution method: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Answer: The angular frequency is 3.7566 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.59789 Hz, and turning-point energy is 6.7855 J.

Physical check: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Idealizations: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

A sample of mass 8.723 kg has specific heat capacity 4183.9 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 332.85 to 478.37 K.

For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

The required energy is 5311 kJ.

The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.

## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 42.868 m/s, emitting a tone of 1757.8 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 2008.9 Hz, a frequency increase of 251.07 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Worked example: Standing wave on a stretched string

## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum

Problem: A simple pendulum has length 0.244 m and an initial angular displacement of 7.797 degrees.

Solution method: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Answer: The estimated oscillation period is 0.99109 s and its frequency is 1.009 Hz.

Physical check: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Idealizations: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.045 m^3 and material density 1433.1 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1062.1 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 468.69 N and the weight is 632.42 N; their signed upward difference is -163.74 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 4.752 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 669.39 K, changing volume from 38.854 to 112.87 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is 28205 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Problem: A rod with initial length 10.26 m has expansion coefficient 7.714e-06 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 156.09 K.

Solution method: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is 12.354 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 1067.1 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 127.76 m below a surface at pressure 100.07 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

The pressure increase is 1337 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1437 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 46.923 kg changes signed velocity from 2.67 to -6.606 m/s during 0.913 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is -435.26 N s and the average net force is -476.73 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 29.699 kg block starts at 29.489 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.31. The surface extends for 18.055 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 143.02 m. After the available distance its speed is 27.565 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 3.0401 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 20.643 kg and 8.195 kg and initial signed speeds 15.548 and 10.179 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is 14.022 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 84.55 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 4.1889e-10 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 26.221 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 17.667 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -2.634 m/s^2 for 3.454 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 8.5692 m/s, and the signed displacement is 45.31 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Problem: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

Solution method: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 4.0421 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.24138 s^2.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

The fitted slope is 4.0191 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.054215 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 92.594 kg block starts at 15.349 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.231. The surface extends for 24.901 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 51.999 m. After the available distance its speed is 11.08 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 2.2653 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

3.349 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 491.47 K to 714.37 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 13.254 kg and 2.416 kg and initial signed speeds -2.605 and 11.051 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is -0.49952 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 190.54 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 868.89 K and cold reservoir at 413.23 K, absorbing 144.79 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 52.442 percent, corresponding to at most 75.929 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Worked example: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Physical setup: A sample of mass 7.996 kg has specific heat capacity 1960.4 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 330.63 to 464.84 K.

Relevant law: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Calculated result: The required energy is 2103.8 kJ.

Interpretation: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Conditions of validity: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 14.738 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -1.667 m/s^2 for 12.12 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is -5.466 m/s, and the signed displacement is 56.188 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Spring oscillator

A mass of 16.508 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 688.03 N/m and displaced by 0.102 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 6.4559 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.0275 Hz, and turning-point energy is 3.5791 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work
