## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 5.799 kg is released from rest at a height of 41.661 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 28.585 m/s and the kinetic energy is 2369.2 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 19.998 kg follows a circle of radius 5.143 m at constant speed 27.312 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 145.04 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 2900.5 N, and rotation frequency is 0.8452 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 34.044 kg and radius 0.145 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 64.121 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 0.35789 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 735.73 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.071 m^3 and material density 380.15 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1280.9 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 891.88 N and the weight is 264.69 N; their signed upward difference is 627.19 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 12.592 cm^2 and 9.673 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 1.147 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 1.4931 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0014443 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Ideal gas equation of state

## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1377.5 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7748.5 km.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 23.092 kg changes signed velocity from -19.328 to 3.337 m/s during 0.337 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 523.38 N s and the average net force is 1553.1 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

Two carts have masses 10.852 kg and 5.389 kg and initial signed speeds -7.908 and 8.101 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is -2.596 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 461.43 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Physical setup: A simple pendulum has length 4.925 m and an initial angular displacement of 6.031 degrees.

Relevant law: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Calculated result: The estimated oscillation period is 4.4527 s and its frequency is 0.22458 Hz.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Conditions of validity: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Problem: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 39.537 W/(m K), thickness 0.479 m, area 3.077 m^2, and temperature difference 34.913 K.

Solution method: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Answer: The conduction rate is 8867.1 W.

Physical check: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Idealizations: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 46.033 m/s, emitting a tone of 984.2 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 1136.8 Hz, a frequency increase of 152.56 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Worked example: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Relevant law: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Calculated result: The internal energy change is 36324 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Interpretation: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Conditions of validity: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1189.4 K and cold reservoir at 231.76 K, absorbing 552.76 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 80.514 percent, corresponding to at most 445.06 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Linear thermal expansion

A rod with initial length 14.599 m has expansion coefficient 2.3761e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 147.86 K.

For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

The calculated signed change in length is 51.292 mm.

For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.

## Lever arm and rotational effect

A force of magnitude 172.61 N acts at a distance of 1.922 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 74.879 degrees to the lever.

The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

The calculated torque magnitude is 320.27 N m.

For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 199.78 kg follows a circle of radius 5.363 m at constant speed 33.508 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Worked example: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Physical setup: A fully submerged body has volume 0.02 m^3 and material density 471.69 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1178.7 kg/m^3.

Relevant law: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Calculated result: The upward buoyancy is 231.19 N and the weight is 92.514 N; their signed upward difference is 138.68 N.

Interpretation: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Conditions of validity: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 1615.2 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 9.9911 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 5.225 kg is released from rest at a height of 64.73 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 35.631 m/s and the kinetic energy is 3316.7 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Thermal conduction measurement

A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

The fitted slope is 2.7157 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 2.6895 W/K.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 20.54 W.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Periodic wave propagation

Physical setup: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 10133 Hz and has spatial wavelength 2.311 m.

Relevant law: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Calculated result: The period is 9.8685e-05 s and the propagation speed is 23418 m/s.

Interpretation: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Conditions of validity: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1054.3 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7425.3 km.

The circular speed is 7.3268 km/s and the orbital period is 106.13 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

Conditions of validity: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 11.59 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -2.427 m/s^2 for 8.966 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is -10.17 m/s, and the signed displacement is 6.3637 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Spring oscillator

A mass of 13.279 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 387.32 N/m and displaced by 0.157 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 5.4007 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.85955 Hz, and turning-point energy is 4.7735 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Problem: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 0.00043749 W/m^2.

Solution method: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Answer: The ideal intensity level is 86.41 dB.

Physical check: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Idealizations: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 8208.3 Hz and has spatial wavelength 2.596 m.

The period is 0.00012183 s and the propagation speed is 21309 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 17.19 kg and 0.151 kg and initial signed speeds -7.158 and 10.17 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is -7.0071 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 22.472 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 47.785 kg changes signed velocity from 7.866 to 13.931 m/s during 0.202 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is 289.82 N s and the average net force is 1434.7 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 34.28 m/s, emitting a tone of 1458 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 1619.9 Hz, a frequency increase of 161.9 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 380.05 N acts at a distance of 3.729 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 61.432 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 1244.7 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1408 K and cold reservoir at 397.16 K, absorbing 283.3 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 71.793 percent, corresponding to at most 203.39 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

5.682 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 326.21 K to 768.47 K.

For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

The internal energy change is 31340 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 4.064 cm^2 and 7.804 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 0.609 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 0.31714 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0002475 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum

Problem: A simple pendulum has length 1.421 m and an initial angular displacement of 2.69 degrees.

Solution method: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Answer: The estimated oscillation period is 2.3918 s and its frequency is 0.4181 Hz.

Physical check: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Idealizations: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

A sample of mass 7.365 kg has specific heat capacity 489.42 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 296.13 to 358.49 K.

For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

The required energy is 224.77 kJ.

The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Hooke-law force calibration

Problem: A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

Solution method: For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 380.99 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 382.52 N/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.50346 N.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

## Reversible isothermal gas work

7.408 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 204.64 K, changing volume from 48.514 to 59.381 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 2547.7 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 11.408 kg is released from rest at a height of 8.952 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 13.251 m/s and the kinetic energy is 1001.5 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Worked example: Pressure at depth

Physical setup: A stationary liquid has density 1206.8 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 50.579 m below a surface at pressure 97.21 kPa.

Relevant law: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Calculated result: The pressure increase is 598.57 kPa and the absolute pressure is 695.78 kPa.

Interpretation: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Conditions of validity: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1895.5 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 8266.5 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 6.944 km/s and the orbital period is 124.66 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 143.1 kg follows a circle of radius 14.328 m at constant speed 66.286 m/s.

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.038 m^3 and material density 1379.2 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1149.5 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 428.36 N and the weight is 513.95 N; their signed upward difference is -85.589 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

Problem: A cart begins at 23.764 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 4.356 m/s^2 for 10.54 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 69.676 m/s, and the signed displacement is 492.43 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Ideal gas equation of state

A vessel contains 4.339 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 406.04 K in volume 27.836 liters.

The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

The equilibrium pressure is 526.24 kPa.

At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 554.49 K and cold reservoir at 291.76 K, absorbing 5308.1 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 47.382 percent, corresponding to at most 2515 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 4.731 kg has specific heat capacity 1036.5 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 336.08 to 353.93 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 87.538 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1450.1 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7821.1 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.139 km/s and the orbital period is 114.72 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Worked example: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Physical setup: 8.041 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 611.73 K to 411.53 K.

Relevant law: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Calculated result: The internal energy change is -20077 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Interpretation: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Conditions of validity: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum

Problem: A simple pendulum has length 5.265 m and an initial angular displacement of 3.714 degrees.

Solution method: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Answer: The estimated oscillation period is 4.6038 s and its frequency is 0.21721 Hz.

Physical check: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Idealizations: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 14.713 cm^2 and 9.386 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.977 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 4.6666 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0043801 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 67.9 kg block starts at 12.18 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.356. The surface extends for 21.744 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 21.247 m. After the available distance its speed is 0 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 3.4912 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 27.095 kg changes signed velocity from -18.677 to -14.675 m/s during 1.473 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is 108.43 N s and the average net force is 73.615 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Worked example: Uniform circular motion

Physical setup: A mass of 160.43 kg follows a circle of radius 16.226 m at constant speed 52.793 m/s.

Relevant law: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Calculated result: The centripetal acceleration is 171.77 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 27557 N, and rotation frequency is 0.51783 Hz.

Interpretation: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Conditions of validity: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Quantitative physics problem: Spring oscillator

Problem: A mass of 17.88 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 506.78 N/m and displaced by 0.469 m.

Solution method: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Answer: The angular frequency is 5.3239 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.84732 Hz, and turning-point energy is 55.736 J.

Physical check: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Idealizations: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Hooke-law force calibration

A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

The fitted slope is 299.41 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 301.7 N/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 1.2431 N.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Linear thermal expansion

Physical setup: A rod with initial length 4.849 m has expansion coefficient 1.4081e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 140.53 K.

Relevant law: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Calculated result: The calculated signed change in length is 9.5956 mm.

Interpretation: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Conditions of validity: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 2804.8 Hz and has spatial wavelength 1.866 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 0.00035654 s and the propagation speed is 5233.7 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Reversible isothermal gas work

6.447 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 390.77 K, changing volume from 42.883 to 102.88 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 18329 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Worked example: Standing wave on a stretched string

Physical setup: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 2.236 m, tension 652.23 N, and linear mass density 0.04 kg/m.

Relevant law: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Calculated result: The speed of transverse waves is 127.69 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 28.554 Hz.

Interpretation: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Conditions of validity: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.

## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 26.806 kg and radius 0.802 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 20.553 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 8.6209 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 1820.8 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Worked example: Escape speed from a central mass

Physical setup: Consider a test object at altitude 643.34 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Relevant law: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Calculated result: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.661 km/s.

Interpretation: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Conditions of validity: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 9.2936e-08 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 49.682 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 0.388 kg is released from rest at a height of 88.772 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 41.727 m/s and the kinetic energy is 337.78 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.085 m^3 and material density 1025.1 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1226.3 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 1022.2 N and the weight is 854.49 N; their signed upward difference is 167.74 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Relevant law: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Calculated result: The conduction rate is 915.77 W.

## Quantitative physics problem: Pressure at depth

Problem: A stationary liquid has density 1228 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 79.307 m below a surface at pressure 100.25 kPa.

Solution method: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Answer: The pressure increase is 955.04 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1055.3 kPa.

Physical check: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Idealizations: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 5.5905e-08 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 47.475 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Worked example: Linear thermal expansion

Physical setup: A rod with initial length 5.238 m has expansion coefficient 1.0053e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 140.41 K.

Relevant law: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Calculated result: The calculated signed change in length is 7.3939 mm.

Interpretation: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Conditions of validity: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1217.1 K and cold reservoir at 383.56 K, absorbing 1097 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 68.486 percent, corresponding to at most 751.33 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 3.302 m and an initial angular displacement of 5.085 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 3.6459 s and its frequency is 0.27428 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 237.99 N acts at a distance of 3.289 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 139.37 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 509.68 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Standing wave on a stretched string

A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 2.803 m, tension 155.15 N, and linear mass density 0.044 kg/m.

Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

The speed of transverse waves is 59.381 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 10.592 Hz.

The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 0.731 kg is released from rest at a height of 3.413 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 8.1817 m/s and the kinetic energy is 24.467 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 29.675 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 4.219 m/s^2 for 11.015 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 76.147 m/s, and the signed displacement is 582.82 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 36.69 m/s and elevation angle 72.369 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 7.1312 s, the horizontal range is 79.248 m, and maximum height above launch is 62.338 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 34.834 m/s, emitting a tone of 845.63 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 941.22 Hz, a frequency increase of 95.587 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 11.341 cm^2 and 3.745 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.737 m/s.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 8.2885 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.003104 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 3.053 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 336.33 K, changing volume from 8.188 to 13.535 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is 4290.9 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Quantitative physics problem: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Problem: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

Solution method: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 4.0835 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.16283 s^2.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 7.408 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 69.441 N/m and displaced by 0.1 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 3.0617 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.48728 Hz, and turning-point energy is 0.34721 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Worked example: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Physical setup: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 26.096 kg and radius 0.78 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 25.001 rad/s.

Relevant law: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Calculated result: The moment of inertia is 7.9384 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 2480.9 J.

Interpretation: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Conditions of validity: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Problem: 4.202 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 586.31 K to 639.24 K.

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Answer: The internal energy change is 2773.7 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 8.062 kg and radius 0.077 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 1.397 rad/s.

## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Problem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 12.292 cm^2 and 6.705 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 4.579 m/s.

## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

A sample of mass 6.31 kg has specific heat capacity 2738.5 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 284.49 to 497.18 K.

For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

The required energy is 3675.4 kJ.

The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Worked example: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Physical setup: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 329.37 W/(m K), thickness 0.168 m, area 3.596 m^2, and temperature difference 49.616 K.

Relevant law: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Calculated result: The conduction rate is 3.498e+05 W.

Interpretation: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Conditions of validity: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A force of magnitude 126.31 N acts at a distance of 3.738 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 167.6 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 101.42 N m.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 10.045 kg and 12.001 kg and initial signed speeds 8.693 and -1.139 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 3.3408 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 264.3 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Worked example: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Calculated result: The ideal intensity level is 59.049 dB.

Interpretation: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Conditions of validity: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 7.8 kg is released from rest at a height of 82.973 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 40.341 m/s and the kinetic energy is 6346.8 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

Relevant law: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.39925 s^2.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Reversible isothermal gas work

8.838 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 222.52 K, changing volume from 38.686 to 61.782 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

## Worked example: Uniform circular motion

Physical setup: A mass of 91.013 kg follows a circle of radius 0.735 m at constant speed 74.242 m/s.

Relevant law: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Calculated result: The centripetal acceleration is 7499.1 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 6.8252e+05 N, and rotation frequency is 16.076 Hz.

Interpretation: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Conditions of validity: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.062 m^3 and material density 224.66 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 766.46 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 466.02 N and the weight is 136.59 N; their signed upward difference is 329.42 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 17.405 kg block starts at 26.751 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.42. The surface extends for 6.463 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 38.476 m/s, emitting a tone of 200.12 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 225.41 Hz, a frequency increase of 25.285 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 11.781 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 375.34 N/m and displaced by 0.402 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 5.6444 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.89834 Hz, and turning-point energy is 30.328 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Impulse and momentum change

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1292.2 K and cold reservoir at 311.09 K, absorbing 7513.9 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Problem: 7.318 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 387.69 K to 517.94 K.

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Answer: The internal energy change is 11888 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Lever arm and rotational effect

A force of magnitude 134.21 N acts at a distance of 0.867 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 37.729 degrees to the lever.

The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

The calculated torque magnitude is 71.202 N m.

For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 7.237 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 358.39 K, changing volume from 44.483 to 64.233 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is 7923.4 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Quantitative physics problem: Thermal conduction measurement

Problem: A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

Solution method: For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

Answer: The fitted slope is 3.1527 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 3.1569 W/K.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 5.4641 W.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 20.09 kg and radius 1.435 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 170.82 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 20.685 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 3.0179e+05 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Worked example: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Physical setup: A sample of mass 9.891 kg has specific heat capacity 3340.6 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 329.17 to 435.93 K.

Relevant law: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Calculated result: The required energy is 3527.8 kJ.

Interpretation: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Conditions of validity: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 19.555 kg is released from rest at a height of 51.417 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 31.756 m/s and the kinetic energy is 9860.2 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 41.943 kg follows a circle of radius 21.68 m at constant speed 79.249 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 289.69 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 12150 N, and rotation frequency is 0.58177 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Worked example: Escape speed from a central mass

Physical setup: Consider a test object at altitude 398.08 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Relevant law: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Calculated result: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.852 km/s.

Interpretation: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Conditions of validity: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 63.956 kg changes signed velocity from 4.272 to -0.893 m/s during 0.519 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is -330.33 N s and the average net force is -636.48 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Worked example: Linear thermal expansion

Physical setup: A rod with initial length 27.408 m has expansion coefficient 2.5968e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 153.53 K.

Relevant law: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Calculated result: The calculated signed change in length is 109.27 mm.

Interpretation: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Conditions of validity: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.

## Ideal gas equation of state

A vessel contains 2.703 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 533.68 K in volume 121.21 liters.

The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

The equilibrium pressure is 98.953 kPa.

At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 834.5 K and cold reservoir at 226.39 K, absorbing 1616.5 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 72.871 percent, corresponding to at most 1178 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1539.5 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7910.5 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 7.0985 km/s and the orbital period is 116.7 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Spring oscillator

A mass of 0.604 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 430.94 N/m and displaced by 0.245 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 26.711 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 4.2512 Hz, and turning-point energy is 12.934 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 6.243 kg and 0.306 kg and initial signed speeds 17.69 and 15.705 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is 17.597 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 0.57469 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Quantitative physics problem: Pressure at depth

Problem: A stationary liquid has density 840.16 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 125.75 m below a surface at pressure 98.296 kPa.

Solution method: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Answer: The pressure increase is 1036.1 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1134.3 kPa.

Physical check: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Idealizations: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Worked example: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Physical setup: A fully submerged body has volume 0.022 m^3 and material density 685.34 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1195.6 kg/m^3.

Relevant law: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Calculated result: The upward buoyancy is 257.95 N and the weight is 147.86 N; their signed upward difference is 110.09 N.

Interpretation: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Conditions of validity: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 0.00076747 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 88.851 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Physical setup: A simple pendulum has length 2.477 m and an initial angular displacement of 3.664 degrees.

Relevant law: Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

Calculated result: The estimated oscillation period is 3.1578 s and its frequency is 0.31668 Hz.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Conditions of validity: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 393.45 W/(m K), thickness 0.317 m, area 1.931 m^2, and temperature difference 62.283 K.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 1.4927e+05 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Hooke-law force calibration

A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

The fitted slope is 31.326 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 31.132 N/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.29974 N.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 74.33 m/s and elevation angle 21.94 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 5.664 s, the horizontal range is 390.51 m, and maximum height above launch is 39.325 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 25.449 m/s, emitting a tone of 568.66 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 614.24 Hz, a frequency increase of 45.574 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 12.561 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 7.015 m/s^2 for 9.011 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 75.773 m/s, and the signed displacement is 397.99 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Problem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 1.757 m, tension 134.4 N, and linear mass density 0.028 kg/m.

Solution method: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Answer: The speed of transverse waves is 69.283 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 19.716 Hz.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.

## Worked example: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Physical setup: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 146.68 W/(m K), thickness 0.399 m, area 0.407 m^2, and temperature difference 24.747 K.

## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 18.101 kg and radius 1.656 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 175.23 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 24.82 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 3.8104e+05 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 51.92 kg changes signed velocity from -9.167 to 4.002 m/s during 1.577 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 683.73 N s and the average net force is 433.57 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Pressure at depth

Physical setup: A stationary liquid has density 800.26 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 89.016 m below a surface at pressure 105.47 kPa.

Relevant law: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Calculated result: The pressure increase is 698.59 kPa and the absolute pressure is 804.06 kPa.

Interpretation: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Conditions of validity: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 19.508 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 7.005 m/s^2 for 12.978 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 110.42 m/s, and the signed displacement is 843.1 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 6.255 m and an initial angular displacement of 3.769 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 5.018 s and its frequency is 0.19928 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Worked example: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Physical setup: 1.551 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 860.59 K to 774.12 K.

Relevant law: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Calculated result: The internal energy change is -1672.7 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Interpretation: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Conditions of validity: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Problem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 1.426 m, tension 66.983 N, and linear mass density 0.013 kg/m.

Solution method: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Answer: The speed of transverse waves is 71.781 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 25.169 Hz.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.058 m^3 and material density 1036.1 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 820.89 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 466.91 N and the weight is 589.33 N; their signed upward difference is -122.42 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sound intensity and decibel scale

## Linear thermal expansion

A rod with initial length 2.622 m has expansion coefficient 1.0777e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 117.79 K.

For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

The calculated signed change in length is 3.3283 mm.

For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Worked example: Uniform circular motion

Physical setup: A mass of 180.32 kg follows a circle of radius 13.396 m at constant speed 10.083 m/s.

Relevant law: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Calculated result: The centripetal acceleration is 7.5893 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 1368.5 N, and rotation frequency is 0.11979 Hz.

Interpretation: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Conditions of validity: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 601.48 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.693 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 428.73 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 3.627 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 185.09 N/m and displaced by 0.256 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 7.1436 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.1369 Hz, and turning-point energy is 6.065 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 102.38 kg block starts at 18.517 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.104. The surface extends for 10.617 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 168.1 m. After the available distance its speed is 17.923 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.0199 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 57.494 m/s and elevation angle 33.887 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 6.5376 s, the horizontal range is 312.03 m, and maximum height above launch is 52.393 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 14.387 kg and 1.831 kg and initial signed speeds 1.36 and 5.363 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 1.8119 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 13.014 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 867.67 K and cold reservoir at 309.42 K, absorbing 6678.2 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 64.339 percent, corresponding to at most 4296.7 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.
