Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A force of magnitude 357.82 N acts at a distance of 0.89 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 87.635 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 318.19 N m.

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 7.524 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 746.77 N/m and displaced by 0.397 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 9.9625 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.5856 Hz, and turning-point energy is 58.849 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Standing wave on a stretched string

## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1015.6 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7386.6 km.

The circular speed is 7.346 km/s and the orbital period is 105.3 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 21.579 kg block starts at 21.822 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.468. The surface extends for 17.015 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 51.879 m. After the available distance its speed is 17.889 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 4.5895 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Ideal gas equation of state

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 985.05 K and cold reservoir at 372.02 K, absorbing 8319.1 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 62.234 percent, corresponding to at most 5177.3 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 17.887 kg and radius 0.894 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 16.55 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 7.148 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 978.92 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Worked example: Linear thermal expansion

Physical setup: A rod with initial length 22.266 m has expansion coefficient 2.5598e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 181.71 K.

Relevant law: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Calculated result: The calculated signed change in length is 103.57 mm.

Interpretation: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Conditions of validity: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 6.888 kg has specific heat capacity 3786.2 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 312.87 to 490.35 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 4628.6 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 65.64 kg follows a circle of radius 0.777 m at constant speed 46.565 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 2790.6 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 1.8318e+05 N, and rotation frequency is 9.538 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 54.776 kg changes signed velocity from 1.123 to -14.472 m/s during 1.54 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is -854.23 N s and the average net force is -554.7 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Problem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 6.086 cm^2 and 1.098 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 0.41 m/s.

Solution method: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Answer: The speed in the second section is 2.2726 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.00024953 m^3/s.

Physical check: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Idealizations: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 15.074 kg and 6.123 kg and initial signed speeds -9.145 and 4.112 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is -5.3156 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 382.63 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.0199 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.28723 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

Calculated result: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.443 km/s.

Interpretation: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 6440.8 Hz and has spatial wavelength 3.845 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 0.00015526 s and the propagation speed is 24765 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 1154 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 92.341 m below a surface at pressure 106.41 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 9.567 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 5.548 m/s^2 for 15.458 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 95.328 m/s, and the signed displacement is 810.73 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

Problem: A vessel contains 0.963 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 278.48 K in volume 65.244 liters.

Solution method: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Answer: The equilibrium pressure is 34.176 kPa.

Physical check: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 61.074 kg block starts at 15.46 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.097. The surface extends for 28.504 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 125.63 m. After the available distance its speed is 13.593 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 0.95125 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 48.445 m/s, emitting a tone of 250.44 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 291.62 Hz, a frequency increase of 41.189 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Standing wave on a stretched string

A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 2.145 m, tension 695.72 N, and linear mass density 0.051 kg/m.

Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

The speed of transverse waves is 116.8 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 27.225 Hz.

The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Worked example: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Physical setup: A sample of mass 14.459 kg has specific heat capacity 4304.2 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 321.08 to 389.72 K.

Relevant law: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Calculated result: The required energy is 4272 kJ.

Interpretation: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Conditions of validity: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 286.19 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.943 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 4.377 m and an initial angular displacement of 4.129 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 4.1977 s and its frequency is 0.23823 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 28.863 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 4.783 m/s^2 for 3.963 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 47.818 m/s, and the signed displacement is 151.94 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 37.194 kg changes signed velocity from 3.37 to -5.911 m/s during 0.585 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is -345.2 N s and the average net force is -590.08 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Problem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 3.863 cm^2 and 8.297 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 4.268 m/s.

Solution method: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Answer: The speed in the second section is 1.9871 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0016487 m^3/s.

Physical check: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Idealizations: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Reversible isothermal gas work

2.986 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 386.29 K, changing volume from 37.346 to 80.145 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 7323.2 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 56.337 N acts at a distance of 2.772 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 32.297 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 83.441 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Linear thermal expansion

A rod with initial length 14.72 m has expansion coefficient 2.0352e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 61.817 K.

For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

The calculated signed change in length is 18.519 mm.

For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.

## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 17.869 kg is released from rest at a height of 114.16 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 47.318 m/s and the kinetic energy is 20004 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 4.1549e-10 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 26.186 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1515 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7886 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 7.1095 km/s and the orbital period is 116.16 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 216.32 kg follows a circle of radius 2.74 m at constant speed 34.406 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 432.03 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 93456 N, and rotation frequency is 1.9985 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 0.327 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 130.03 N/m and displaced by 0.078 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 19.941 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 3.1737 Hz, and turning-point energy is 0.39555 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 39.305 m/s and elevation angle 58.363 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 6.8247 s, the horizontal range is 140.7 m, and maximum height above launch is 57.095 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1214.3 K and cold reservoir at 375.47 K, absorbing 4061.6 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 69.079 percent, corresponding to at most 2805.7 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Worked example: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Physical setup: 3.722 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 339 K to 386.68 K.

Relevant law: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Calculated result: The internal energy change is 2213.1 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Interpretation: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Conditions of validity: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 22.817 kg and radius 1.316 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 87.36 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 19.758 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 75394 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.057 m^3 and material density 850.22 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 922.48 kg/m^3.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

Answer: The speed in the second section is 0.76336 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.001037 m^3/s.

Physical check: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Idealizations: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 14460 Hz and has spatial wavelength 2.922 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 6.9156e-05 s and the propagation speed is 42252 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 20.346 kg and 1.364 kg and initial signed speeds 5.893 and -4.974 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is 5.2102 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 75.478 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 49.733 m/s, emitting a tone of 1294 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 1513.5 Hz, a frequency increase of 219.44 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 906.45 K and cold reservoir at 434.79 K, absorbing 219.84 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 52.033 percent, corresponding to at most 114.39 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 46.57 kg block starts at 12.654 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.192. The surface extends for 3.107 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 42.521 m. After the available distance its speed is 12.183 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.8829 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.024 m^3 and material density 666.64 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1143.4 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 269.12 N and the weight is 156.9 N; their signed upward difference is 112.22 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Ideal gas equation of state

A vessel contains 0.24 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 273.02 K in volume 18.546 liters.

The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

The equilibrium pressure is 29.375 kPa.

At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

Physical setup: A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

Relevant law: The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 4.0491 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

Interpretation: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.11367 s^2.

Conditions of validity: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 207.01 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 6578 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.7844 km/s and the orbital period is 88.491 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 17.906 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 5.989 m/s^2 for 12.588 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 93.296 m/s, and the signed displacement is 699.9 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Worked example: Thermal conduction measurement

Calculated result: The fitted slope is 1.2488 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 1.2523 W/K.

## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 1211.4 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.254 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Problem: A sample of mass 11.696 kg has specific heat capacity 1029 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 288.03 to 377.85 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 1080.9 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.

## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 1036.5 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 119.27 m below a surface at pressure 106.25 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

The pressure increase is 1212.4 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1318.6 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 9.549 kg and radius 1.46 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 76.264 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 10.177 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 29597 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 10.476 kg is released from rest at a height of 58.845 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 33.973 m/s and the kinetic energy is 6045.4 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1477 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7848 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 7.1267 km/s and the orbital period is 115.32 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 6126 Hz and has spatial wavelength 1.178 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 0.00016324 s and the propagation speed is 7216.4 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Thermal conduction measurement

A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

The fitted slope is 5.8631 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 5.8999 W/K.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 31.43 W.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 11.346 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 2.236 m/s^2 for 6.193 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 25.194 m/s, and the signed displacement is 113.14 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.0189 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.099106 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

Physical setup: A sample of mass 7.023 kg has specific heat capacity 1849.8 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 281.55 to 484.93 K.

Relevant law: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Calculated result: The required energy is 2642.2 kJ.

Interpretation: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Conditions of validity: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Problem: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 8.3198e-06 W/m^2.

Solution method: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Answer: The ideal intensity level is 69.201 dB.

Physical check: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Idealizations: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Hooke-law force calibration

A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

The fitted slope is 396.86 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 397.36 N/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.50435 N.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Ideal gas equation of state

Physical setup: A vessel contains 2.038 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 298.61 K in volume 167.14 liters.

Relevant law: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Calculated result: The equilibrium pressure is 30.274 kPa.

Interpretation: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Conditions of validity: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 3.177 cm^2 and 4.658 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 4.165 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 2.8407 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0013232 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 46.898 m/s, emitting a tone of 306.89 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 355.49 Hz, a frequency increase of 48.606 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Projectile trajectory above level ground

An object is launched at speed 77.908 m/s and elevation angle 50.809 degrees from level ground.

Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

The nonzero return time is 12.315 s, the horizontal range is 606.25 m, and maximum height above launch is 185.89 m.

The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 23.324 kg follows a circle of radius 12.198 m at constant speed 73.964 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 448.49 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 10461 N, and rotation frequency is 0.96505 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 591.2 N acts at a distance of 0.828 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 81.551 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 484.2 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 43.448 kg and radius 1.691 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 178.28 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 62.119 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 9.8715e+05 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 14.565 kg is released from rest at a height of 94.094 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 42.959 m/s and the kinetic energy is 13440 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Problem: A rod with initial length 18.818 m has expansion coefficient 1.6996e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 4.529 K.

Solution method: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is 1.4485 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.

## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 8.1 kg and 1.746 kg and initial signed speeds -2.724 and 15.854 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is 0.57045 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 247.88 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 22.526 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 420.6 N/m and displaced by 0.053 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 4.3211 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 0.68772 Hz, and turning-point energy is 0.59073 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 101.34 kg block starts at 10.612 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.185. The surface extends for 15.123 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 31.036 m. After the available distance its speed is 7.5988 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.8142 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 557.7 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.727 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 622.4 K and cold reservoir at 335.14 K, absorbing 4572.9 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 46.153 percent, corresponding to at most 2110.5 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 300.98 W/(m K), thickness 0.57 m, area 2.999 m^2, and temperature difference 10.152 K.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 16077 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

Calculated result: The conduction rate is 2.743e+05 W.

Conditions of validity: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 1678.1 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 9.952 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 8.412 cm^2 and 8.888 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 2.829 m/s.

For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

The speed in the second section is 2.6775 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0023798 m^3/s.

With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Worked example: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Physical setup: 6.287 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 845.92 K to 780.03 K.

Relevant law: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Calculated result: The internal energy change is -5165.9 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Interpretation: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Conditions of validity: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 35.494 m/s, emitting a tone of 566.31 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 631.68 Hz, a frequency increase of 65.367 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 8.03 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 298.02 N/m and displaced by 0.366 m.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 5496.4 Hz and has spatial wavelength 1.728 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 0.00018194 s and the propagation speed is 9497.7 m/s.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

A sample of mass 10.826 kg has specific heat capacity 2672.4 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 273.96 to 412.62 K.

For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

The required energy is 4011.5 kJ.

The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Worked example: Uniform circular motion

Physical setup: A mass of 169.98 kg follows a circle of radius 7.718 m at constant speed 3.782 m/s.

Relevant law: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Calculated result: The centripetal acceleration is 1.8533 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 315.02 N, and rotation frequency is 0.07799 Hz.

Interpretation: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Conditions of validity: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Problem: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 962.88 K and cold reservoir at 337.85 K, absorbing 3473.8 J per cycle.

Solution method: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Answer: The Carnot efficiency is 64.912 percent, corresponding to at most 2254.9 J of work per cycle.

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 246.5 N acts at a distance of 3.53 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 158.87 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 313.75 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1444.6 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7815.6 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 7.1415 km/s and the orbital period is 114.61 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 11.825 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 2.377 m/s^2 for 2.317 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 17.333 m/s, and the signed displacement is 33.779 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Worked example: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Physical setup: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 1.1528e-07 W/m^2.

Relevant law: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Calculated result: The ideal intensity level is 50.618 dB.

Interpretation: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Conditions of validity: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 5.344 kg block starts at 30.184 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.593. The surface extends for 13.549 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 78.334 m. After the available distance its speed is 27.45 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 5.8153 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.047 m^3 and material density 1235.7 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 934.02 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 430.5 N and the weight is 569.53 N; their signed upward difference is -139.03 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Worked example: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Physical setup: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 12.904 kg and radius 1.974 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 76.284 rad/s.

Interpretation: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Conditions of validity: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 24.599 kg and 18.673 kg and initial signed speeds -6.655 and 9.468 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is 0.3025 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 1379.7 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.0138 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.59829 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 23.907 kg changes signed velocity from -11.673 to 3.324 m/s during 1.7 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is 358.53 N s and the average net force is 210.9 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 66.502 m/s and elevation angle 45.629 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 9.6949 s, the horizontal range is 450.86 m, and maximum height above launch is 115.22 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

## Quantitative physics problem: Escape speed from a central mass

Problem: Consider a test object at altitude 1717.7 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

Solution method: The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

Answer: The minimum escape speed at that position is 9.9276 km/s.

Physical check: Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

Idealizations: No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Reversible isothermal gas work

1.466 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 536.17 K, changing volume from 48.556 to 38.408 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is -1532.3 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

## Quantitative physics problem: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Problem: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 384.48 W/(m K), thickness 0.507 m, area 0.414 m^2, and temperature difference 83.508 K.

Solution method: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Answer: The conduction rate is 26217 W.

Physical check: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Idealizations: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 7850.3 Hz and has spatial wavelength 4.115 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical check: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Idealizations: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.096 m^3 and material density 1390.1 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1142.7 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 1075.8 N and the weight is 1308.7 N; their signed upward difference is -232.84 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 39.12 m/s, emitting a tone of 1533.2 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 1730.6 Hz, a frequency increase of 197.38 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Linear thermal expansion

A rod with initial length 28.638 m has expansion coefficient 2.2892e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 131.82 K.

The calculated signed change in length is 86.42 mm.

For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 5.15 kg block starts at 4.864 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.581. The surface extends for 9.137 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 2.0762 m. After the available distance its speed is 0 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 5.6977 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 10.431 kg is released from rest at a height of 47.025 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 30.37 m/s and the kinetic energy is 4810.3 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 20.045 kg and radius 0.752 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 163.76 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 5.6678 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 75997 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Linear thermal expansion

## Quantitative physics problem: Spring oscillator

Problem: A mass of 6.943 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 390.01 N/m and displaced by 0.392 m.

Solution method: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Answer: The angular frequency is 7.4949 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.1929 Hz, and turning-point energy is 29.965 J.

Physical check: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Idealizations: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 134.23 kg block starts at 18.477 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.359. The surface extends for 25.207 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 48.486 m. After the available distance its speed is 12.803 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 3.5206 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

## Hooke-law force calibration

A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

The fitted slope is 713.43 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 713.96 N/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.60724 N.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 569.27 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.718 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.

## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 8.36 m/s, emitting a tone of 1229.8 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 1260.5 Hz, a frequency increase of 30.723 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Projectile trajectory above level ground

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 5.119 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 447.41 K, changing volume from 18.319 to 24.419 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 8.934 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 0.178 m/s^2 for 11.632 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 11.004 m/s, and the signed displacement is 115.96 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 69.727 kg block starts at 13.403 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.385. The surface extends for 5.065 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 23.79 m. After the available distance its speed is 11.891 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 3.7756 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Physical setup: A body with mass 58.978 kg changes signed velocity from -0.042 to 2.838 m/s during 0.197 s.

Relevant law: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Calculated result: The signed impulse is 169.86 N s and the average net force is 862.22 N.

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Conditions of validity: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Problem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 4.262 cm^2 and 9.717 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 4.33 m/s.

Solution method: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Answer: The speed in the second section is 1.8992 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0018454 m^3/s.

Physical check: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Idealizations: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 18.605 kg is released from rest at a height of 56.134 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 33.181 m/s and the kinetic energy is 10242 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sound intensity and decibel scale

## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 1191.9 Hz and has spatial wavelength 4.955 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 0.00083901 s and the propagation speed is 5905.8 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 15.167 kg and 22.116 kg and initial signed speeds 10.954 and 13.189 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 12.28 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 22.471 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Conditions of validity: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Problem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 3.15 m, tension 737.06 N, and linear mass density 0.025 kg/m.

Solution method: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Answer: The speed of transverse waves is 171.7 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 27.255 Hz.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 10.392 m/s, emitting a tone of 873.05 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 900.33 Hz, a frequency increase of 27.278 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Worked example: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Relevant law: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Calculated result: The internal energy change is -909.64 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Interpretation: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Conditions of validity: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.

## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.006 m^3 and material density 955.15 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 824.83 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 48.533 N and the weight is 56.201 N; their signed upward difference is -7.6685 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 990.27 K and cold reservoir at 255.9 K, absorbing 1765.5 J per cycle.
