Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 74.159 percent, corresponding to at most 1309.3 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 169.15 kg follows a circle of radius 23.556 m at constant speed 2.561 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 0.27843 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 47.097 N, and rotation frequency is 0.017303 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Steady heat conduction through a slab

A planar layer has thermal conductivity 184.21 W/(m K), thickness 0.468 m, area 2.442 m^2, and temperature difference 80.698 K.

Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

The conduction rate is 77567 W.

Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 20.838 kg block starts at 21.369 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.39. The surface extends for 16.14 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 59.697 m. After the available distance its speed is 18.253 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 3.8246 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 2323.4 Hz and has spatial wavelength 2.719 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 0.0004304 s and the propagation speed is 6317.4 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 1440.7 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.102 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1674.8 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 8045.8 km.

Relevant law: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Calculated result: The circular speed is 7.0386 km/s and the orbital period is 119.71 minutes.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

Problem: A vessel contains 8.632 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 714.4 K in volume 98.562 liters.

Solution method: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Answer: The equilibrium pressure is 520.21 kPa.

Physical check: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 14.291 kg and 19.847 kg and initial signed speeds 14.809 and -1.683 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 5.221 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 1129.9 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 9.825 cm^2 and 7.065 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 3.053 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 4.2457 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0029996 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A force of magnitude 283.74 N acts at a distance of 1.05 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 44.779 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 209.85 N m.

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 40.165 kg and radius 1.214 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 120.04 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 29.598 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 2.1324e+05 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 36.769 kg changes signed velocity from 13.838 to -12.667 m/s during 1.959 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is -974.56 N s and the average net force is -497.48 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 1.428 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 352.62 K, changing volume from 23.655 to 55.424 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is 3564.7 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.

## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

## Worked example: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Interpretation: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

## Quantitative physics problem: Spring oscillator

Problem: A sample of mass 14.434 kg has specific heat capacity 2541.2 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 287.21 to 389.27 K.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 3743.6 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Sliding friction and stopping distance

A 119.87 kg block starts at 34.911 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.397. The surface extends for 17.147 m.

The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

The ideal stopping distance is 156.52 m. After the available distance its speed is 32.943 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 3.8932 m/s^2 while sliding.

Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 5.548 kg is released from rest at a height of 77.176 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 38.906 m/s and the kinetic energy is 4198.9 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.

## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1410 K and cold reservoir at 433.68 K, absorbing 7882.3 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 69.243 percent, corresponding to at most 5458 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Worked example: Pressure at depth

Physical setup: A stationary liquid has density 841.98 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 49.673 m below a surface at pressure 93.863 kPa.

Relevant law: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Calculated result: The pressure increase is 410.15 kPa and the absolute pressure is 504.01 kPa.

Interpretation: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Conditions of validity: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Problem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 12.79 cm^2 and 9.187 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 4.745 m/s.

Solution method: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Answer: The speed in the second section is 6.6059 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0060689 m^3/s.

Physical check: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Idealizations: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 0.719 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 253.05 K, changing volume from 38.258 to 93.847 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is 1357.4 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 18.396 kg and radius 0.411 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 13.934 rad/s.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.

## Worked example: Impulse and momentum change

Interpretation: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 14.872 kg and 22.202 kg and initial signed speeds 0.41 and 17.224 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 10.479 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 1258.9 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 1041.9 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 117.21 kg follows a circle of radius 20.389 m at constant speed 57.002 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 159.36 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 18679 N, and rotation frequency is 0.44495 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 33.721 m/s, emitting a tone of 1565 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 1735.7 Hz, a frequency increase of 170.64 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Motion with constant acceleration

A fully submerged body has volume 0.042 m^3 and material density 359.18 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1150.2 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 473.76 N and the weight is 147.94 N; their signed upward difference is 325.82 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.

## Continuity in a narrowing pipe

## Worked example: Small-angle pendulum

Calculated result: The estimated oscillation period is 4.4842 s and its frequency is 0.223 Hz.

Interpretation: To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

Conditions of validity: The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 824.79 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7195.8 km.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Problem: A homogeneous solid disk with mass 34.763 kg and radius 1.849 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 139.42 rad/s.

Solution method: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

Answer: The moment of inertia is 59.424 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 5.7752e+05 J.

Physical check: Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Idealizations: Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 1134.9 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 147.57 m below a surface at pressure 103.87 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

The pressure increase is 1642.5 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1746.3 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Worked example: Gravitational energy during a fall

Physical setup: An object of mass 5.958 kg is released from rest at a height of 80.67 m.

Relevant law: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Calculated result: At the lower level the speed is 39.777 m/s and the kinetic energy is 4713.4 J.

Interpretation: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Conditions of validity: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 25.616 kg changes signed velocity from -19.552 to 18.421 m/s during 0.537 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is 972.72 N s and the average net force is 1811.4 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.

## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Problem: 4.423 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 619.67 K to 431.1 K.

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Answer: The internal energy change is -10402 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Reversible isothermal gas work

6.118 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 535.26 K, changing volume from 23.055 to 51.943 liters.

The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

The work by the gas is 22116 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

## Quantitative physics problem: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Problem: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 381.25 W/(m K), thickness 0.202 m, area 3.561 m^2, and temperature difference 53.369 K.

Solution method: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Answer: The conduction rate is 3.5869e+05 W.

Physical check: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Idealizations: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Spring oscillator

## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 40.196 m/s, emitting a tone of 388.29 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 439.84 Hz, a frequency increase of 51.544 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.

## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 0.00040097 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 86.031 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Quantitative physics problem: Perfectly inelastic collision

Problem: Two carts have masses 18.497 kg and 15.774 kg and initial signed speeds 0.69 and 16.045 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Solution method: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Answer: The common final velocity is 7.7575 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 1003.7 J.

Physical check: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Idealizations: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Periodic wave propagation

A periodic disturbance oscillates at 11010 Hz and has spatial wavelength 2.08 m.

One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

The period is 9.0827e-05 s and the propagation speed is 22901 m/s.

Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

## Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

A homogeneous solid disk with mass 47.68 kg and radius 1.758 m rotates around its symmetry axis at 172.39 rad/s.

For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

The moment of inertia is 73.679 kg m^2 and rotational energy is 1.0948e+06 J.

Concentrating the same mass farther from the axis would increase rotational inertia.

Rotation occurs about the disk symmetry axis, with no translation of its center.


## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 38.833 m/s, emitting a tone of 975.85 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 1100.4 Hz, a frequency increase of 124.59 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 95.617 kg block starts at 32.367 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.27. The surface extends for 15.822 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 197.83 m. After the available distance its speed is 31.046 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 2.6478 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 7.4823e-10 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 28.74 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Worked example: Pressure at depth

Physical setup: A stationary liquid has density 896.28 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 162.72 m below a surface at pressure 95.211 kPa.

Relevant law: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Calculated result: The pressure increase is 1430.2 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1525.4 kPa.

Interpretation: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Conditions of validity: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Quantitative physics problem: Buoyant force on an immersed object

Problem: A fully submerged body has volume 0.026 m^3 and material density 559.43 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 1312.2 kg/m^3.

Solution method: Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

Answer: The upward buoyancy is 334.58 N and the weight is 142.64 N; their signed upward difference is 191.94 N.

Physical check: If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Idealizations: Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Linear thermal expansion

A rod with initial length 2.571 m has expansion coefficient 7.543e-06 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 167.87 K.

For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

The calculated signed change in length is 3.2555 mm.

For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 532.85 K and cold reservoir at 231.21 K, absorbing 2539.4 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 56.608 percent, corresponding to at most 1437.5 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 25.966 m/s and elevation angle 73.502 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 5.0776 s, the horizontal range is 37.441 m, and maximum height above launch is 31.604 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 69.899 kg changes signed velocity from -15.029 to 8.96 m/s during 1.702 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 1676.8 N s and the average net force is 985.2 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Kinetic energy of a rotating disk

Relevant law: For a uniform disk I = m R^2/2, and the rotational kinetic energy is K = I omega^2/2.

## Quantitative physics problem: Circular Earth orbit

Problem: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 2167.5 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 8538.5 km.

Solution method: Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

Answer: The circular speed is 6.8325 km/s and the orbital period is 130.87 minutes.

Physical check: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Idealizations: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 5.202 kg is released from rest at a height of 9.754 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 13.831 m/s and the kinetic energy is 497.59 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Worked example: Periodic wave propagation

Physical setup: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 853.84 Hz and has spatial wavelength 3.495 m.

Relevant law: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Calculated result: The period is 0.0011712 s and the propagation speed is 2984.2 m/s.

Interpretation: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Conditions of validity: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A force of magnitude 473.68 N acts at a distance of 1.654 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 91.12 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 783.31 N m.

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 3.31 m and an initial angular displacement of 2.766 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 3.6503 s and its frequency is 0.27395 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 13.587 kg follows a circle of radius 12.648 m at constant speed 67.64 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 361.73 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 4914.8 N, and rotation frequency is 0.85114 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Escape speed from a central mass

Consider a test object at altitude 1357.2 km above the surface of an approximately spherical Earth.

The escape threshold in the Newtonian two-body model follows from total specific energy v^2/2 - GM/r = 0.

The minimum escape speed at that position is 10.157 km/s.

Escape speed is larger than circular-orbit speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).

No drag, engine thrust after launch, or perturbations from other bodies are included.


## Worked example: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Physical setup: 3.69 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 282.58 K to 519.43 K.

Relevant law: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Calculated result: The internal energy change is 10900 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Interpretation: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Conditions of validity: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Problem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 4.299 m, tension 844.68 N, and linear mass density 0.009 kg/m.

Solution method: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Answer: The speed of transverse waves is 306.35 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 35.631 Hz.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.

## Worked example: Motion with constant acceleration

Physical setup: A cart begins at 7.6 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 7.453 m/s^2 for 15.636 s.

Relevant law: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Calculated result: The final signed velocity is 124.14 m/s, and the signed displacement is 1029.9 m.

Interpretation: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Conditions of validity: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

A sample of mass 7.055 kg has specific heat capacity 2748.9 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 294.46 to 473.88 K.

For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

The required energy is 3479.6 kJ.

The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Physical setup: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 8.608 cm^2 and 5.988 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 1.845 m/s.

Relevant law: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Calculated result: The speed in the second section is 2.6523 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0015882 m^3/s.

Interpretation: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Conditions of validity: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

## Spring oscillator

A mass of 3.425 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 776.87 N/m and displaced by 0.238 m.

The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

The angular frequency is 15.061 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 2.397 Hz, and turning-point energy is 22.002 J.

The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.

## Quantitative physics problem: Hooke-law force calibration

Solution method: For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

Answer: The fitted slope is 549.22 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 550.12 N/m.

Physical check: The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.54475 N.

Idealizations: These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 23.555 m/s, emitting a tone of 833.51 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

The listener detects approximately 894.98 Hz, a frequency increase of 61.461 Hz.

Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Worked example: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Physical setup: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 215.96 W/(m K), thickness 0.214 m, area 1.86 m^2, and temperature difference 64.36 K.

Relevant law: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Calculated result: The conduction rate is 1.208e+05 W.

Conditions of validity: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Quantitative physics problem: Spring oscillator

Problem: A mass of 10.702 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 755.18 N/m and displaced by 0.479 m.

Solution method: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Answer: The angular frequency is 8.4003 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.3369 Hz, and turning-point energy is 86.635 J.

Physical check: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Idealizations: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Hooke-law force calibration

A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

The fitted slope is 689.54 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 700.89 N/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 1.6086 N.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Periodic wave propagation

Physical setup: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 6953.4 Hz and has spatial wavelength 2.923 m.

Relevant law: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Calculated result: The period is 0.00014381 s and the propagation speed is 20325 m/s.

Interpretation: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Conditions of validity: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.


## Quantitative physics problem: Standing wave on a stretched string

Problem: A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 1.622 m, tension 795.29 N, and linear mass density 0.017 kg/m.

Solution method: Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

Answer: The speed of transverse waves is 216.29 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 66.674 Hz.

Physical check: The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Idealizations: Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Perfectly inelastic collision

Two carts have masses 5.928 kg and 2.686 kg and initial signed speeds 0.634 and 8.714 m/s. They stick together after impact.

With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

The common final velocity is 3.1535 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 60.34 J.

Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.


## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 59.066 N acts at a distance of 1.136 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 43.467 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 46.16 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 4.917 kg is released from rest at a height of 40.945 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 28.338 m/s and the kinetic energy is 1974.3 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Uniform circular motion

A mass of 196.64 kg follows a circle of radius 2.036 m at constant speed 14.35 m/s.

For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

The centripetal acceleration is 101.14 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 19889 N, and rotation frequency is 1.1217 Hz.

The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.


## Worked example: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Calculated result: The ideal intensity level is 27.393 dB.

Interpretation: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Conditions of validity: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Quantitative physics problem: Impulse and momentum change

Problem: A body with mass 13.594 kg changes signed velocity from -17.89 to -3.482 m/s during 1.407 s.

Solution method: The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

Answer: The signed impulse is 195.86 N s and the average net force is 139.21 N.

Physical check: The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Idealizations: Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Pressure at depth

A stationary liquid has density 1204.1 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 80.518 m below a surface at pressure 98.23 kPa.

Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

The pressure increase is 950.79 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1049 kPa.

Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.

## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

## Worked example: Circular Earth orbit

Physical setup: A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 1922.3 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 8293.3 km.

Interpretation: Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Conditions of validity: Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 1.349 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 327.04 K, changing volume from 25.026 to 21.647 liters.

## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 11.025 kg block starts at 11.627 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.511. The surface extends for 25.184 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 13.489 m. After the available distance its speed is 0 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 5.0112 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

Solution method: For constant heat capacity without a phase change, the absorbed energy is Q = m c (T_final - T_initial).

Answer: The required energy is 2975.3 kJ.

Physical check: The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Idealizations: Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 65.599 kg changes signed velocity from -7.502 to 13.787 m/s during 0.568 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 1396.5 N s and the average net force is 2458.7 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Perfectly inelastic collision

Physical setup: Two carts have masses 20.179 kg and 24.624 kg and initial signed speeds 9.582 and 8.5 m/s. They stick together after impact.

Relevant law: With negligible external impulse, linear momentum obeys (m1+m2) v_after = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

Calculated result: The common final velocity is 8.9873 m/s and the kinetic-energy decrease is 6.492 J.

Interpretation: Momentum remains conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic event.

Conditions of validity: The collision is isolated, one-dimensional, and completely inelastic.

## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 721.17 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 7092.2 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 7.4969 km/s and the orbital period is 99.067 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Physical setup: A mass of 6.875 kg is attached to a linear spring of stiffness 350.08 N/m and displaced by 0.076 m.

Relevant law: The equation m x_double_dot + k x = 0 gives angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). At the turning point, the stored spring energy is k A^2/2.

Calculated result: The angular frequency is 7.1358 rad/s, the ordinary frequency is 1.1357 Hz, and turning-point energy is 1.011 J.

Interpretation: The frequency is independent of amplitude in the ideal linear model, while the stored energy grows quadratically with displacement.

Conditions of validity: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 13.683 kg is released from rest at a height of 85.757 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 41.012 m/s and the kinetic energy is 11507 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Linear thermal expansion

A rod with initial length 24.55 m has expansion coefficient 1.0385e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 185.83 K.

For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

The calculated signed change in length is 47.378 mm.

For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Worked example: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Physical setup: 1.446 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 315.69 K to 731.24 K.

Relevant law: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Calculated result: The internal energy change is 7493.9 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Interpretation: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Conditions of validity: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Problem: An object is launched at speed 16.528 m/s and elevation angle 19.158 degrees from level ground.

Solution method: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Answer: The nonzero return time is 1.1062 s, the horizontal range is 17.271 m, and maximum height above launch is 1.5 m.

Physical check: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Idealizations: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Spring oscillator

## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 30.521 N acts at a distance of 1.254 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 161.44 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 12.181 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Quantitative physics problem: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Problem: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 13.788 m/s, emitting a tone of 1622.8 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Solution method: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Answer: The listener detects approximately 1690.8 Hz, a frequency increase of 67.968 Hz.

Physical check: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Idealizations: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Hooke-law force calibration

A simulated Hooke-law force calibration estimates spring stiffness from force and elongation observations.

For a zero-intercept least-squares model F = k*x, the fitted coefficient is sum(x_i*F_i)/sum(x_i^2).

The fitted slope is 224.83 N/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 224.68 N/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.74603 N.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Physical setup: 4.096 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 261.79 K, changing volume from 10.077 to 11.044 liters.

Relevant law: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Calculated result: The work by the gas is 817.25 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Interpretation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Quantitative physics problem: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Problem: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 382.1 W/(m K), thickness 0.095 m, area 0.513 m^2, and temperature difference 45.302 K.

Solution method: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Answer: The conduction rate is 93473 W.

Physical check: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Idealizations: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Ideal gas equation of state

A vessel contains 8.345 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 443.36 K in volume 165.2 liters.

The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

The equilibrium pressure is 186.21 kPa.

At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.

## Small-angle pendulum squared-period fit

A simulated small-angle pendulum experiment compares squared period with pendulum length.

The small-angle prediction is T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)*L; the fitted coefficient can be found from sum(L_i*T_i^2)/sum(L_i^2).

The fitted slope is 4.0297 s^2/m, compared with a reference coefficient of 4.0257 s^2/m.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.023582 s^2.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.


## Worked example: Sound intensity and decibel scale

Physical setup: A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 8.9488e-10 W/m^2.

Relevant law: The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

Calculated result: The ideal intensity level is 29.518 dB.

Interpretation: A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

Conditions of validity: The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.


## Quantitative physics problem: Pressure at depth

Problem: A stationary liquid has density 1200 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 150.62 m below a surface at pressure 95.731 kPa.

Solution method: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Answer: The pressure increase is 1772.6 kPa and the absolute pressure is 1868.3 kPa.

Physical check: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Idealizations: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Reversible heat engine upper bound

A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 567.88 K and cold reservoir at 318.5 K, absorbing 5730.1 J per cycle.

A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

The Carnot efficiency is 43.913 percent, corresponding to at most 2516.3 J of work per cycle.

No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.

## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 17.445 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 0.702 m/s^2 for 11.633 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 25.611 m/s, and the signed displacement is 250.44 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.

## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 20.014 kg follows a circle of radius 7.441 m at constant speed 46.333 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 288.5 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 5774.1 N, and rotation frequency is 0.99101 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.

## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 5.401 m and an initial angular displacement of 4.481 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 4.6629 s and its frequency is 0.21446 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.

## Quantitative physics problem: Periodic wave propagation

Problem: A periodic disturbance oscillates at 8950.7 Hz and has spatial wavelength 0.093 m.

Solution method: One full cycle travels one wavelength during period T = 1/f, so the phase speed is v = f lambda.

Answer: The period is 0.00011172 s and the propagation speed is 832.41 m/s.

Physical check: Frequency is set by temporal repetition, whereas wavelength describes the spatial pattern.

Idealizations: A monochromatic wave in a uniform nondispersive medium is assumed.

## Standing wave on a stretched string

A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 1.42 m, tension 620.07 N, and linear mass density 0.013 kg/m.

Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

The speed of transverse waves is 218.4 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 76.901 Hz.

The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.

## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 125.31 kg block starts at 12.013 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.161. The surface extends for 28.349 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 45.701 m. After the available distance its speed is 7.4023 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.5789 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Quantitative physics problem: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

Problem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional areas are 14.659 cm^2 and 4.465 cm^2. At the first section the speed is 1.051 m/s.

Solution method: For steady incompressible flow, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and the volume flow rate is Q = A1 v1.

Answer: The speed in the second section is 3.4505 m/s and the volume-flow rate is 0.0015407 m^3/s.

Physical check: With steady incompressible flow, average speed is greater in the smaller cross section and lower in the larger one.

Idealizations: The pipe remains filled, there are no leaks, and the fluid is incompressible.

Idealizations: The spring is massless and linear; damping and external driving are ignored.


## Sensible heat and specific heat capacity

A sample of mass 9.568 kg has specific heat capacity 3936.5 J/(kg K). Its temperature rises from 326.84 to 395.36 K.

The required energy is 2580.6 kJ.

The same temperature increment requires greater energy for larger mass or specific heat.

Heat losses and the temperature dependence of c are neglected.

## Gravitational energy during a fall

An object of mass 19.058 kg is released from rest at a height of 25.284 m.

Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

At the lower level the speed is 22.269 m/s and the kinetic energy is 4725.5 J.

Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 25.655 m/s and elevation angle 31.139 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 2.7056 s, the horizontal range is 59.412 m, and maximum height above launch is 8.9737 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 7.904 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 404.14 K, changing volume from 5.851 to 4.4702 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is -7149.4 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 20.231 kg changes signed velocity from -0.624 to 17.222 m/s during 0.285 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 361.04 N s and the average net force is 1266.8 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 696.26 K and cold reservoir at 307.67 K, absorbing 8803.7 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 55.812 percent, corresponding to at most 4913.5 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Linear thermal expansion

Problem: A rod with initial length 21.114 m has expansion coefficient 1.5242e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by 152.77 K.

Solution method: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Answer: The calculated signed change in length is 49.166 mm.

Physical check: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Idealizations: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Standing wave on a stretched string

A stretched string fixed at both ends has length 3.621 m, tension 273.21 N, and linear mass density 0.042 kg/m.

Wave speed is v = sqrt(F_tension/mu), and the fundamental frequency for fixed ends is f1 = v/(2L).

The speed of transverse waves is 80.654 m/s and the fundamental frequency is 11.137 Hz.

The lowest standing wave has a node at each end and a wavelength equal to twice the string length.

Bending stiffness and air loading are ignored, and tension is uniform.


## Worked example: Spring oscillator

Idealizations: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.


## Small-angle pendulum

The estimated oscillation period is 1.1751 s and its frequency is 0.85101 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

## Worked example: Continuity in a narrowing pipe

## Worked example: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Physical setup: A 26.017 kg block starts at 18.359 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.541. The surface extends for 28.35 m.

Relevant law: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Calculated result: The ideal stopping distance is 31.765 m. After the available distance its speed is 6.0197 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 5.3054 m/s^2 while sliding.

Interpretation: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Conditions of validity: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.

## Worked example: Classical Doppler shift of moving sound

Physical setup: A sound source approaches a stationary listener at 17.607 m/s, emitting a tone of 1647.8 Hz. Sound travels at 343 m/s in the medium.

Relevant law: For a moving source and stationary observer, the nonrelativistic Doppler relation is f_observed = f_source c_sound/(c_sound-v_source).

Calculated result: The listener detects approximately 1736.9 Hz, a frequency increase of 89.16 Hz.

Interpretation: Approaching wavefronts are compressed in the rest frame of the medium.

Conditions of validity: The source moves at less than the sound speed; wind and acceleration are ignored.


## Quantitative physics problem: Lever arm and rotational effect

Problem: A force of magnitude 510.34 N acts at a distance of 1.58 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 121.95 degrees to the lever.

Solution method: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Answer: The calculated torque magnitude is 684.17 N m.

Physical check: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Idealizations: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.

## Thermal conduction measurement

A simulated steady-state heat-conduction experiment compares heat-transfer rate with temperature difference.

For an ideal constant-conductance slab, P = G*DeltaT and G is the fitted slope through the origin.

The fitted slope is 0.7225 W/K, compared with a reference coefficient of 0.72529 W/K.

The RMS residual for this simulated series is 0.96059 W.

These statistics describe a synthetic dataset, not a physical measurement. A constrained zero-intercept fit does not establish that the intercept is truly zero.

## Quantitative physics problem: Motion with constant acceleration

Problem: A cart begins at 19.988 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of -1.437 m/s^2 for 2.837 s.

Solution method: Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

Answer: The final signed velocity is 15.911 m/s, and the signed displacement is 50.923 m.

Physical check: The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Idealizations: Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Buoyant force on an immersed object

A fully submerged body has volume 0.021 m^3 and material density 338.46 kg/m^3. The surrounding fluid density is 717.17 kg/m^3.

Archimedes principle gives F_b = rho_fluid V_disp g. The object weight is m g = rho_body V g.

The upward buoyancy is 147.69 N and the weight is 69.702 N; their signed upward difference is 77.991 N.

If buoyancy exceeds weight, the net vertical force is upward unless other forces intervene; a negative difference indicates a downward net force.

Both densities are uniform, and the entire body is submerged.


## Worked example: Lever arm and rotational effect

Physical setup: A force of magnitude 162.25 N acts at a distance of 1.803 m from a fixed rotation axis, at an angle of 118.41 degrees to the lever.

Relevant law: The torque magnitude is tau = r F sin(theta), with theta measured between the radial lever and the force vector.

Calculated result: The calculated torque magnitude is 257.29 N m.

Interpretation: For fixed force and lever length, a perpendicular force gives the largest torque.

Conditions of validity: The lever is rigid and the pivot is fixed; this is a static torque evaluation.


## Quantitative physics problem: Reversible isothermal gas work

Problem: 0.581 mol of ideal gas expands or compresses reversibly at 364.72 K, changing volume from 31.317 to 25.899 liters.

Solution method: The reversible work done by the gas is W_by = integral(P dV) = nRT ln(V_final/V_initial).

Answer: The work by the gas is -334.66 J, with a positive sign denoting expansion work.

Physical check: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, so isothermal Delta U is zero.

Idealizations: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Motion with constant acceleration

A cart begins at 9.965 m/s and experiences a constant signed acceleration of 7.484 m/s^2 for 11.991 s.

Integrating acceleration gives v(t) = v0 + at; integrating velocity gives Delta x = v0 t + (a t^2)/2.

The final signed velocity is 99.706 m/s, and the signed displacement is 657.53 m.

The sign of velocity specifies motion relative to the chosen positive axis; signed displacement and total distance can differ.

Constant acceleration and one-dimensional motion are assumed; rolling and aerodynamic losses are not independently modeled.


## Worked example: Reversible isothermal gas work

Conditions of validity: This is a quasistatic ideal-gas process at uniform fixed temperature.


## Quantitative physics problem: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas

Problem: 9.538 mol of a monatomic ideal gas changes temperature from 673.1 K to 983.06 K.

Solution method: For a classical monatomic ideal gas with only translational quadratic degrees of freedom, U = 3 n R T/2.

Answer: The internal energy change is 36871 J; the sign reflects the signed temperature change.

Physical check: The result is independent of the thermodynamic path between the states.

Idealizations: Vibrational and electronic excitations, interactions, and quantum degeneracy are neglected.


## Sound intensity and decibel scale

A sound wave has time-averaged intensity 2.3193e-05 W/m^2.

The sound-intensity level relative to I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels.

The ideal intensity level is 73.653 dB.

A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, rather than multiplying the decibel number by ten.

The reference intensity is the conventional air-acoustics value; this is not a frequency-weighted sound-pressure rating.

## Quantitative physics problem: Ideal gas equation of state

Problem: A vessel contains 11.153 mol of an ideal gas at temperature 579.54 K in volume 77.263 liters.

Solution method: The ideal-gas relation P V = n R T gives pressure P = n R T/V, using SI volume in cubic meters.

Answer: The equilibrium pressure is 695.57 kPa.

Physical check: At fixed particle number and container volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Idealizations: Intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes are neglected.


## Small-angle pendulum

A simple pendulum has length 5.713 m and an initial angular displacement of 3.939 degrees.

Approximating sin(theta) by theta leads to theta_double_dot + (g/L) theta = 0, with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

The estimated oscillation period is 4.7957 s and its frequency is 0.20852 Hz.

To leading order in angle, the period depends on length and gravitational acceleration but not on the bob mass.

The initial angle is small; air resistance and pivot friction are neglected.


## Worked example: Pressure at depth

Physical setup: A stationary liquid has density 1224.9 kg/m^3; the point of interest lies 2.036 m below a surface at pressure 96.037 kPa.

Relevant law: Hydrostatic balance yields p(depth) = p_surface + rho g h for an incompressible uniform-density liquid.

Calculated result: The pressure increase is 24.457 kPa and the absolute pressure is 120.49 kPa.

Interpretation: Pressure increases linearly with depth within the incompressible approximation.

Conditions of validity: Gravity is uniform, the liquid is static, and density does not change with depth.


## Quantitative physics problem: Sliding friction and stopping distance

Problem: A 73.576 kg block starts at 32.414 m/s on a horizontal surface, with kinetic friction coefficient 0.127. The surface extends for 19.161 m.

Solution method: The horizontal kinetic friction force is mu m g, so the magnitude of deceleration is mu g. Energy balance gives v^2 = v0^2 - 2 mu g d until the block stops.

Answer: The ideal stopping distance is 421.8 m. After the available distance its speed is 31.669 m/s, with deceleration magnitude 1.2454 m/s^2 while sliding.

Physical check: Friction removes mechanical energy as heat; once the block stops, the sliding formula should not be extrapolated to imaginary speeds.

Idealizations: The coefficient is uniform, and there are no other horizontal forces.


## Circular Earth orbit

A satellite follows an ideal circular orbit 2092.4 km above Earth, with center-to-satellite radius 8463.4 km.

Balancing GMm/r^2 with mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r), and T = 2 pi r/v.

The circular speed is 6.8627 km/s and the orbital period is 129.15 minutes.

Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbit radius but not on the satellite mass.

Earth is approximated as a spherically symmetric gravitating body; atmospheric drag and oblateness are neglected.


## Worked example: Linear thermal expansion

Physical setup: A rod with initial length 29.721 m has expansion coefficient 2.4306e-05 K^-1. Its temperature changes by -6.436 K.

Relevant law: For a sufficiently small fractional expansion, Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T.

Calculated result: The calculated signed change in length is -4.6494 mm.

Interpretation: For a positive expansion coefficient, heating lengthens an unconstrained rod and cooling shortens it.

Conditions of validity: The rod is unconstrained and the coefficient is approximately constant.


## Quantitative physics problem: Gravitational energy during a fall

Problem: An object of mass 11.748 kg is released from rest at a height of 63.647 m.

Solution method: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy mgh equal to the gained kinetic energy mv^2/2 gives v = sqrt(2gh).

Answer: At the lower level the speed is 35.332 m/s and the kinetic energy is 7332.7 J.

Physical check: Mass cancels from the speed prediction, but heavier objects at the same height have more kinetic energy.

Idealizations: Uniform g and negligible air drag are assumed, with height measured from the final level.


## Impulse and momentum change

A body with mass 32.166 kg changes signed velocity from -15.45 to 19.682 m/s during 0.703 s.

The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Delta p = m(v_final-v_initial), and average net force F_avg = J/Delta t.

The signed impulse is 1130.1 N s and the average net force is 1607.5 N.

The signs track direction; the average force need not equal the instantaneous force at any given moment.

Motion is one-dimensional and mass is constant throughout the interaction.


## Worked example: Projectile trajectory above level ground

Physical setup: An object is launched at speed 54.125 m/s and elevation angle 68.124 degrees from level ground.

Relevant law: Split the initial velocity into v_x = v cos(theta) and v_y = v sin(theta). Vertical displacement obeys y(t) = v_y t - gt^2/2.

Calculated result: The nonzero return time is 10.244 s, the horizontal range is 206.58 m, and maximum height above launch is 128.63 m.

Interpretation: The horizontal velocity remains constant in this idealized problem, while gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

Conditions of validity: Launch and impact heights match; air resistance, lift, and Earth rotation are neglected.


## Quantitative physics problem: Steady heat conduction through a slab

Problem: A planar layer has thermal conductivity 362.83 W/(m K), thickness 0.34 m, area 0.853 m^2, and temperature difference 29.039 K.

Solution method: Fourier law for a uniform one-dimensional steady profile gives heat-transfer power P = k A Delta T/L.

Answer: The conduction rate is 26434 W.

Physical check: Doubling the thickness halves the conduction rate when all other properties stay constant.

Idealizations: There is no internal heat generation or changing temperature field within the layer.

## Worked example: Reversible heat engine upper bound

Physical setup: A heat engine operates between an ideal hot reservoir at 1474.5 K and cold reservoir at 234.73 K, absorbing 8200.6 J per cycle.

Relevant law: A reversible Carnot cycle has maximum efficiency eta_C = 1 - T_c/T_h, and W_max = eta_C Q_h.

Calculated result: The Carnot efficiency is 84.08 percent, corresponding to at most 6895.1 J of work per cycle.

Interpretation: No engine operating cyclically between these two reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency.

Conditions of validity: Reservoir temperatures are fixed and heat exchange in the benchmark is reversible.


## Quantitative physics problem: Uniform circular motion

Problem: A mass of 203.41 kg follows a circle of radius 16.508 m at constant speed 1.281 m/s.

Solution method: For constant-speed circular motion, a_c = v^2/r and the inward net force is F_c = m v^2/r; the rotation frequency is v/(2 pi r).

Answer: The centripetal acceleration is 0.099404 m/s^2, the force magnitude is 20.22 N, and rotation frequency is 0.01235 Hz.

Physical check: The force is radial even though velocity is tangent to the path; radial acceleration does not change speed by itself.

Idealizations: The required force is supplied by an unspecified constraint and the orbit is circular.
